SNS package restore); backend Docker image rebuilt + booted against compose Postgres/Redis — **"Application started", health green, DI graph resolved with zero errors** (so `OtpService`/`SnsSmsProvider` construct and the SNS SDK loads in-container). No schema change (AM0 already added `otp_codes`). End-to-end OTP flow is exercised once an endpoint consumes `IOtpService` (AM9) and via the CI test suite. **Security review owed before merge** (auth/PII). **Not committed.**

## D-079 · AM2 — trusted-device enrollment + challenge-response crypto core (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented, Docker-verified end-to-end with real EC P-256 keys.** The cryptographic heart of the platform (ADR-A3/A9/AM12).

**`IChallengeService`/`ChallengeService`** issues single-use signed-nonce challenges (32-byte CSPRNG base64url nonce + 2-digit anti-fatigue match number, TTL from `AUTH_CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS`, default 120s) and verifies device signatures over the nonce, consuming the challenge atomically (replay-safe: single-use + TTL). **`DeviceSignatures.VerifyEs256`** verifies ECDSA-P256/SHA-256 against the stored base64 SPKI public key, accepting both DER and IEEE-P1363 signature encodings (native Keystore/Enclave vs. WebAuthn), never throwing. **`ITrustedDeviceService`/`TrustedDeviceService`** does two-step proof-of-possession enrollment (register public key → device PendingVerification → device signs enrollment challenge → Trusted), plus list/revoke; every lifecycle transition (ADR-AM12 FSM) writes a `security_event` + `audit_log` row. Endpoints `POST /v1/auth/devices/enroll`, `/enroll/verify`, `GET /v1/auth/devices`, `POST /v1/auth/devices/{id}/revoke` (all authenticated). List query maps the enum state **in memory**, never `enum.ToString()` in the SQL projection (D-061 lesson).

Additive: these are new endpoints on new tables; the flag-gated login cutover that *uses* trusted devices to sign in (no OTP) lands in AM4/AM9. Endpoints are not yet feature-flag-gated (auth-required, new tables only) — production rollout gating happens at the login-cutover layer.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/{IChallengeService.cs,ITrustedDeviceService.cs}`, `Infrastructure/Auth/{DeviceSignatures.cs,ChallengeService.cs,TrustedDeviceService.cs}` (new), `Api/Endpoints/TrustedDeviceEndpoints.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, `Api/Program.cs`.

**Verification:** `dotnet build` 0/0; backend Docker image rebuilt + booted; then a **real end-to-end drive** (openssl-generated P-256 keypair + curl): dev-login → enroll with the SPKI public key → sign the returned nonce (`openssl dgst -sha256 -sign`) → `/enroll/verify` returned `{"ok":true,"state":"Trusted"}`; a signature over the wrong message returned **`400 invalid_signature`**; `GET /v1/auth/devices` showed the trusted device (`state:"Trusted"`, `lastSeenAt` set) and the failed one (`PendingVerification`). UUID-v7 ids confirmed time-ordered. **Security review owed before merge** (auth/PII). **Not committed.**

## D-080 · AM4 — trusted-device push-approval login (passwordless, OTP-free) (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented, driven end-to-end against the live stack.** The headline flow (ADR-A3/A9/AM17).

`ILoginApprovalService`/`LoginApprovalService` + endpoints `POST /v1/auth/login/{start,status,approve,reject}` and `GET /v1/auth/login/pending`. Web calls `/start` with an identifier (no session); the server resolves the user, confirms a Trusted device exists, issues a Login challenge, and **pushes it to the user's FCM devices**; the app fetches the nonce via `/pending`, signs it (biometric on real devices), and calls `/approve`; the waiting web client polls `/status` and receives a **device-bound session** (`auth_sessions` row + refresh token carrying `SessionId`). `/start` and `/status` are anonymous and rate-limited under the existing `otp` policy.

**Three security properties, each verified (not assumed):** (1) **anti-enumeration** — an unknown identifier, a moderated account, or a user with no trusted device all get a *decoy* challenge, so responses are byte-shape-identical and never reveal account existence; (2) **poll-token binding** — `/start` returns a CSPRNG poll token whose SHA-256 is stored in the challenge `ContextJson`, and `/status` returns nothing without it, so knowing a challenge id is not enough to collect someone's tokens; (3) **single-issue** — tokens are minted on the *first* successful poll after approval and the challenge flips to `Consumed` in the same transaction, so a replayed poll returns `consumed` and cannot re-mint. Every approve/reject writes a `security_event` + `audit_log` row.

**Deliberate scope note:** the waiting screen uses polling; the SignalR push of status (ADR-AM17) lands with the web client (AM9) — polling is the required fallback anyway, and the anonymous pre-session hub connection is a client-side design concern. Storing the poll-token hash in `ContextJson` avoids a second migration; if it needs indexing later it becomes a column.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/ILoginApprovalService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/LoginApprovalService.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/DeviceLoginEndpoints.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, `Api/Program.cs`.

**Verification:** `dotnet build` 0/0; then a full curl+openssl drive against the running stack — start → `pending` → **wrong poll token still `pending`** → device signs nonce → `approve` ok → poll → `approved` + tokens → **`GET /v1/me` with the new token returned the right user** → replayed poll → `consumed` → unknown identifier returned an identical decoy → FCM push confirmed in logs. **No OTP involved in the login.**

**⚠ Infra gotcha found (cost a false 404):** `docker compose up -d --force-recreate` **re-creates the container from the stale image** on this setup — the rebuilt image is ignored, so new endpoints silently 404 while older ones work. Confirmed by the container's `Kurx.Api.dll` timestamp lagging the build and by the app's own `/swagger/v1/swagger.json` route list. **Correct verify loop: `docker rm -f kurx-backend` then `docker compose up -d --no-deps backend`.** Querying the running app's OpenAPI doc is the fastest way to prove which routes are actually deployed. **Security review owed before merge** (auth/PII). **Not committed.**

## D-081 · AM5 — device-bound sessions, sender-constrained (PoP) refresh, family-scoped revocation, "your devices" (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented; full suite green (286/286).** Turns the AM0 session substrate into real behavior (ADR-A8/AM11).

**A refresh token is no longer a bare bearer secret.** A session minted by device-approval login (D-080) pins the approving device's public-key **thumbprint** (SHA-256 over the SPKI) onto its refresh token. Rotating that token now requires `deviceId` + `signature` on `POST /v1/auth/refresh`, where the device signs the *raw refresh token* with the private key that never leaves its Keystore/Secure Enclave. **A stolen refresh string alone is inert.** The constraint survives rotation — the new token carries the same thumbprint — so it cannot silently decay back into a bearer token. Signing the token itself (rather than a fresh server nonce) needs no extra round-trip and no new table; single-use rotation already makes a captured signature worthless the moment it is spent.

**A failed proof refuses but never revokes.** Deliberate: revoking on a bad signature would hand anyone holding the stolen string a way to *destroy* the victim's session. Wrong proof ⇒ `401 proof_required`, session untouched, `security_event` written.

**Reuse revokes the family, not the account (supersedes D-009/D-014 for device-bound tokens only).** Reuse of a spent token still means theft, but the blast radius is now the `FamilyId` of the offending session — signing out your phone should not sign out your laptop. **Legacy OTP-login tokens carry no session and keep the original kill-every-session behavior**, so D-009/D-014 remains literally true for every token that existed before AM5; this is additive, not a weakening. `CLAUDE.md` §10's "JWT reuse-revokes-all" invariant is hereby scoped to legacy bearer tokens.

**"Your devices" is now real.** `GET /v1/auth/sessions` lists live sessions joined to their device (name/platform); `POST /v1/auth/sessions/{id}/revoke` is remote sign-out, killing the session's refresh chain. Device revocation was **incomplete before this**: it blocked re-enrollment but left existing sessions refreshing until expiry — `RevokeAsync` now revokes the device's sessions and their refresh tokens in the same operation, which is what "lost my phone" has to mean. Both surfaces are user-scoped and return **404, not 403**, for another user's id (D-018).

**Design note:** sessions were added to `ITrustedDeviceService` rather than a new service — two methods over the same aggregate did not justify a parallel interface and DI registration.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IAuthService.cs`, `Application/Abstractions/ITrustedDeviceService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/AuthService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/TrustedDeviceService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/LoginApprovalService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/DeviceSignatures.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/AuthEndpoints.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/TrustedDeviceEndpoints.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/TrustedDeviceAuthTests.cs`.

**Verification:** `dotnet build` 0 warnings / 0 errors; **full suite 286/286 green** in the container runner (244 before this work → 286 after; 42 new tests covering AM1–AM5). No migration needed — `refresh_tokens.SessionId`/`PoPKeyThumbprint` and `auth_sessions` all shipped nullable/inert in AM0. **Security review still owed before merge** (auth/PII, `CLAUDE.md` §10).

## D-082 · AM0–AM5 get an automated test suite; local Windows `dotnet test` is not a valid verifier (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Closes the largest gap in the auth workstream: AM0–AM4 shipped on **manual curl+openssl drives only**, with zero automated coverage.

**42 integration tests** (`TrustedDeviceAuthTests`) against real Postgres via `WebApplicationFactory<Program>`, no mocked persistence (`CLAUDE.md` §9): OTP issue/verify/replay, attempt cap, resend cooldown, per-destination rate limit, TTL expiry, purpose isolation, E.164 + email rejection, security-event audit; device enrollment (valid signature, wrong-key signature, malformed signature bytes, expired challenge, single-use challenge, cross-user 404, revocation cascading to credentials); the full push-approval login plus its three security properties (**anti-enumeration**, **poll-token binding**, **single-issue/replay**) and reject/expiry/untrusted-device/cross-user branches; and the AM5 surfaces above. Error and authz branches are covered, not just happy paths. **OTP tests drive `IOtpService` through a DI scope** because AM1 has no HTTP surface yet (legacy login is untouched); delivery is asserted via the existing capturing WhatsApp sender, and clock-dependent windows are crossed by shifting row timestamps rather than sleeping.

**The environment finding matters more than the tests.** Windows **AppControl (0x800711C7)** blocks freshly-built test assemblies — but *intermittently*, because an older already-allowed DLL may still be on disk. That path silently runs **stale assemblies** and produces confident-looking nonsense: this session chased a `42P01: relation "otp_codes" does not exist` failure for a migration that was, in fact, correctly applied to both databases. **A local Windows `dotnet test` result is not evidence — pass or fail.** The authoritative local runner is a container sharing the Postgres network namespace, built from an isolated copy of the source (mounting the tree read-write makes the Linux build collide with Windows file locks and pollutes `bin/obj`):

```bash
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker run --rm --network container:kurx-postgres \
  -v "D:/event/Kurx/backend:/src:ro" mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 bash -c \
  "mkdir /work && cd /src && tar cf - --exclude=bin --exclude=obj . \
   | (cd /work && tar xf -) && cd /work && dotnet test Kurx.sln"
```

**A second false signal worth recording:** mid-session, full-suite runs produced wildly inconsistent totals (276 → 410 → 334 → 286) with mass failures in untouched classes. The cause was **not** a test defect and not a DB race — the *other* concurrently-running session was editing and then committing the shared tree between runs, so each container copy compiled a different codebase. Two consecutive runs after the tree settled were clean. When a suite's **total test count** changes between runs, suspect the tree, not the tests.

## D-083 · AM7 — account recovery codes, redeemable only as a second factor (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented; full suite green (300/300); driven live.**

A device-bound auth platform creates a new failure mode: **lose the phone, lose the account**. Recovery codes are the escape hatch. Ten 64-bit CSPRNG codes, SHA-256 at rest (**no pepper** — unlike a 6-digit OTP these are not brute-forceable, so the pepper would protect nothing), single-use, and generating a new sheet **deletes the unused old one** so a printout the user believes they replaced cannot still open the account. Redemption normalizes away dashes/case, so retyping never fails on formatting.

**Redemption is two-factor on purpose.** A leaked code sheet must not be a login: `POST /v1/auth/recovery/redeem` requires the code **and** an OTP delivered to the account's registered phone. Every failure mode — unknown identifier, wrong OTP, wrong code, already-used code — returns the same opaque `invalid_recovery`, so the endpoint never reveals which half was wrong or whether the account exists. `/recovery/start` always returns `ok` for the same reason.

**A successful recovery is treated as a possible compromise, not a convenience.** It revokes every session, revokes every refresh token, and moves every Trusted device to **Suspended** — recovery implies the old devices may be lost or in someone else's hands, so they must re-enroll before they can approve anything again. The recovered session is deliberately a **plain bearer session with no PoP constraint**: the user has no trusted device left to bind it to, and the client's next step is enrolling one (AM2).

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IRecoveryCodeService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/RecoveryCodeService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/AuthIdentifiers.cs` (new — see below), `Api/Endpoints/RecoveryEndpoints.cs`, DI + `Program.cs`.

**Identifier resolution was extracted, not copied.** `AuthIdentifiers.ResolveUserAsync` is now shared by device-approval login (D-080) and recovery. If those two disagreed about what an identifier matches, one surface would leak the existence of accounts the other denies — so this is a correctness constraint, not tidiness.

## D-084 · AM6 — step-up authentication, enforced on a real action (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented; full suite green; driven live.**

A valid session is enough to browse; a genuinely sensitive action additionally demands a **fresh device signature**, so a stolen access token alone cannot do damage. `POST /v1/auth/step-up/{start,verify}` + `GET /status`, grant window 5 minutes (`AUTH_STEPUP_TTL_SECONDS`).

**No new table.** An `auth_challenges` row with purpose `StepUp` that reached `Approved` inside the window **is** the grant. Reusing the challenge record keeps a single audit trail for "who proved what, with which device, when", instead of a second parallel one that could drift out of agreement with the first. A `Login` challenge can **not** be redeemed as a step-up (purpose is checked), and a step-up is scoped to its own user (another user's challenge is a 404, D-018).

**It is enforced, not merely available.** Minting recovery codes (D-083) mints new account-access credentials, so `POST /v1/auth/recovery-codes` now requires a satisfied step-up. **Users with no trusted device are exempt** — they have no way to step up, and demanding it would lock them out of the very feature that protects them from lockout. Choosing an endpoint inside this workstream to enforce on was deliberate: it proves the mechanism end-to-end without editing the concurrent platform workstream's files.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IStepUpService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/StepUpService.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/StepUpEndpoints.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/RecoveryEndpoints.cs`, DI + `Program.cs`.

## D-085 · AM8 — transactional outbox dispatcher + auth risk engine (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented; full suite green.**

**Outbox (ADR-AM16).** `login.approved`, `device.revoked` and `recovery.redeemed` now write an `outbox_messages` row **in the same transaction as the state change**, drained every minute by `OutboxDispatchJob` (Hangfire). This matters because the "a device just signed in" alert is exactly the alert a victim needs when it wasn't them — losing it to a push-provider outage is a security failure, not a cosmetic one. At-least-once with `IdempotencyKey` for downstream dedup; retries stay `Pending` and only a message that exhausts 5 attempts is parked `Failed` for an operator.

**Risk engine (ADR-AM22) — layered on `IFraudService`, not beside it.** Blacklists and aggregate subject scoring already exist there, so `IRiskEngine` adds only the auth-specific signals from the `security_events` feed (repeated invalid signatures, recent refresh reuse, repeated PoP failures, a very recent recovery) and turns the combination into a decision. Wired into `LoginApprovalService.StartAsync`: **a denial returns the same decoy as an unknown identifier**, so an attacker who has already tripped alarms cannot tell they have been singled out.

**A design flaw the tests caught, and the fix.** `RiskAction` originally had three values — `Allow` / `RequireStepUp` / `Deny` — but **nothing consumed `RequireStepUp`**, so a 75-score login was scored, logged as elevated, and then silently allowed anyway. The enum promised an enforcement tier that did not exist. It is now **two-valued**: a device-approval login already *is* strong authentication (a fresh signature from a trusted device), so there is no weaker-then-stronger ladder to climb at that point. Thresholds are tuned so **no single signal locks a legitimate user out** — a replayed refresh chain (50) or repeated bad signatures (25) alone still allow; any two independent signals together deny (≥70). The weights are an explicit first cut carrying a `ponytail:` marker, so tuning later is a number change, not an architecture change.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IRiskEngine.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Auth/RiskEngine.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Jobs/OutboxDispatchJob.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Auth/LoginApprovalService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/TrustedDeviceService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/RecoveryCodeService.cs`, DI + `Program.cs`.

**Sequencing note (deviation from the requested order, stated not hidden):** AM3 (WebAuthn/passkeys) was requested before AM6–AM8 but was taken **last** of the backend modules — it is the only one needing a new third-party dependency (`fido2-net-lib`) *and* a browser client (AM9) before it can be exercised end-to-end, whereas AM6–AM8 were fully testable against the existing substrate. AM3, AM9, AM10 and the AM23 security review remain open.

**Verification (D-083/084/085):** `dotnet build` 0 warnings / 0 errors; **full suite 300/300 green** in the container runner (286 → 300, 14 new tests); routes confirmed deployed via `swagger.json`; live curl+openssl drive of the whole chain — enroll device → recovery-codes refused with `step_up_required` → `step-up/start` → device signs → `status.satisfied=true` → recovery codes issued. **Security review still owed before merge** (auth/PII, `CLAUDE.md` §10).

## D-086 · AM3 — WebAuthn / passkeys as the second credential rail (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented; full suite green (310/310) including the cryptographic happy path; routes verified live.** `fido2-net-lib` 4.0.0 (`Fido2` + `Fido2.AspNet`).

**A passkey enrolls as an ordinary `TrustedDevice`.** That is the whole design decision: rather than a parallel passkey aggregate, the WebAuthn rail reuses `trusted_devices` + `device_credentials` (`CredentialType = WebAuthn`), so everything already built on that aggregate — "your devices" and remote sign-out (D-081), revocation, step-up (D-084), the risk gate (D-085), recovery suspension (D-083) — works on passkeys with **no new code**. The rails differ only in signature format. `POST /v1/auth/passkeys/{register/options,register,login/options,login}` + `GET /v1/auth/passkeys`.

**Unlike the device-key rail, enrollment is one round trip.** A verified attestation *is* the proof of possession, so a passkey reaches `Trusted` immediately — the AM2 two-step (register key, then sign a challenge) exists precisely because a raw device key carries no attestation.

**Three storage/design calls, each deliberate:**
- **`PublicKeySpki` holds a COSE key for WebAuthn rows**, not SPKI. The column is the aggregate's generic public-key material and the rails are distinguished by `CredentialType`; a parallel column would have meant a migration for zero behavioral gain. Documented at the class, because the name now under-describes the contents.
- **Ceremony state lives in `auth_challenges.ContextJson`**, not server session state — the flow stays stateless across instances and lands in the same audit trail as every other challenge, with the same single-use + TTL semantics.
- **A passkey session is device-bound but NOT sender-constrained.** A WebAuthn authenticator signs WebAuthn assertions, not arbitrary payloads, so it cannot produce the raw-refresh-token signature D-081 requires. Issuing a token that *looked* PoP-constrained and silently wasn't would be worse than the gap, so the limitation is explicit in code, pinned by a test, and stated here.

**Anti-enumeration holds on this rail too:** an unknown identifier, a moderated account, or a user with no passkey all receive well-formed assertion options with an empty `allowCredentials` and **no persisted challenge** — same shape, nothing that can satisfy it. Confirmed live.

**Testing needed an authenticator, so one was written.** A real passkey requires browser + platform authenticator hardware, which would have left the security-critical path with zero automated coverage. `Kurx.Tests/SoftwareAuthenticator.cs` implements just enough of CTAP/WebAuthn to be accepted by the library — ES256 key pair, `none` attestation, correctly framed `authenticatorData` (rpIdHash ‖ flags ‖ big-endian counter ‖ attested credential data) and COSE key — using the BCL's `System.Formats.Cbor`, so **no test-only package was added**. This buys real coverage: full register→sign-in, **counter advance**, **cloned-authenticator rejection** (rewound counter), wrong-key rejection, single-use + owner-scoped ceremonies, malformed attestation, revoked-passkey refusal.

**Still needs a browser drive.** The software authenticator proves the server's verification logic; it cannot prove that a real Chrome/Safari platform authenticator interoperates with these exact options (RP ID/origin config in particular is environment-specific and is what makes passkeys phishing-resistant). That drive belongs to AM9, and until it happens AM3 is "server-verified, not yet browser-verified".

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IPasskeyService.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Auth/PasskeyService.cs` (new), `Api/Endpoints/PasskeyEndpoints.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Kurx.Infrastructure.csproj`, DI (`AddFido2`) + `Program.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/SoftwareAuthenticator.cs` (new), `Kurx.Tests/KurxApiFactory.cs` (pins `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID`/`WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS` for the test RP).

**New config:** `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID` (default `localhost`), `WEBAUTHN_RP_NAME` (default `Kurx`), `WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS` (falls back to `ALLOWED_ORIGINS`). These are deliberately explicit rather than derived from the request — deriving the RP ID from the incoming Host header would hand an attacker the phishing resistance for free.

**Verification:** `dotnet build` 0 warnings / 0 errors; **full suite 310/310 green** (300 → 310); routes confirmed in the deployed container's `swagger.json`; live curl showed a well-formed registration ceremony and an empty-`allowCredentials` decoy for an unknown identifier. **Security review still owed before merge.**

## D-087 · AM9 (backend half) — realtime login status over an anonymous hub; E.164 backfill deliberately NOT done (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED for the realtime slice (implemented, 313/313 green, verified live). The E.164 storage backfill is DEFERRED pending an explicit go-ahead — reasoning below.**

**Closes D-080's stated gap.** AM4 shipped the waiting sign-in screen on polling and recorded that the SignalR push (ADR-AM17) would land with the client work. `LoginHub` at `/hubs/login` now pushes `login_status` to group `login:{challengeId}` the moment a device approves or rejects.

**This is the one anonymous hub, and that is the whole design problem.** Every other hub is `[Authorize]`, but a browser waiting to be told its login succeeded *has no session yet* — that is the entire point of the screen. Authorization therefore comes from the **poll token**: `Watch(challengeId, pollToken)` verifies the token against the challenge before joining the group, so knowing a challenge id is not enough to subscribe, exactly as it is not enough to collect tokens. The binding rule was extracted into one `PollTokenMatches` helper used by **both** `/status` and the hub — if those two ever disagreed about who may watch a login, one transport would leak what the other denies. Verified live: `/hubs/login/negotiate` returns **200** while `/hubs/notifications` and `/hubs/sales` return **401**.

**The hub carries the status signal, never the tokens.** The client still calls `/v1/auth/login/status` to collect its session. This keeps D-080's "minted exactly once" guarantee on a single code path instead of duplicating token issuance across two transports — a realtime push is a UX accelerator, and **polling remains the required fallback**, so a broadcast failure is caught and logged rather than failing the approval.

**Files:** `Api/Hubs/LoginHub.cs` (new), `Api/Realtime/SignalRBroadcaster.cs`, `Application/Abstractions/IRealtimeBroadcaster.cs`, `Application/Abstractions/ILoginApprovalService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/LoginApprovalService.cs`, `Api/Program.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/TrustedDeviceAuthTests.cs`.

### Why the E.164 backfill was not done in this session
AM9 also called for a libphonenumber-backed E.164 canonicalization + backfill. **Deliberately deferred, not forgotten**, for two reasons worth stating plainly:

1. **It changes user identity semantics on a live auth path.** `users.Phone` currently stores bare digits (`919000000001`, per `AuthService.NormalizePhone`). Canonicalizing storage to `+919000000001` touches the legacy OTP login, `AuthIdentifiers` resolution, phone-change, and the `/v1/me` contract — the login path that **300+ existing tests** depend on. `CLAUDE.md` §3.6 requires flagging a destructive/identity-level data change before making it, and this qualifies.
2. **Adding libphonenumber *without* the backfill would be speculative.** The digits-only matching already normalizes `+91 98765 43210`, `09876543210` and `919876543210` to the same account, so a parser buys nothing until storage actually changes. Adding a dependency for a use case that does not yet exist is the thing to avoid, not a step toward it.

**Recommended shape when it is greenlit:** add a nullable `users.PhoneE164` column, backfill it from `Phone` with libphonenumber (region `IN` for the 10-digit legacy rows), have new auth surfaces read/write only the new column while legacy paths keep using `Phone`, then cut over and drop the old column once nothing reads it. Additive, reversible, no big-bang rewrite.

**Also still open in AM9:** the Flutter and Next.js clients themselves, and the **browser drive of passkeys** that D-086 flagged as the missing half of AM3's verification.

**Verification:** `dotnet build` 0 warnings / 0 errors; **full suite 313/313 green** (310 → 313) including three real `HubConnection` tests — approved-status push, rejected-status push, and refusal to subscribe with a wrong poll token; live negotiate check confirmed the anonymous/authorized hub contrast above.

## D-088 · Challenge purpose binding is enforced centrally, not per caller (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Found by the D-081→D-087 consistency review, fixed, test added.**

**The finding.** D-084 claims "a Login challenge must never be redeemable as a step-up", and D-080 relies on a login challenge being login-only. But `IChallengeService.VerifySignatureAsync` never took or checked a purpose — the invariant was re-implemented ad-hoc in each caller, and **`TrustedDeviceService.CompleteEnrollmentAsync` had no check at all**. A pending *Login* challenge could therefore be spent completing a device enrollment.

**Severity: low, but it was a real hole in a claimed invariant.** It is not privilege-escalating — you already need a valid session for the account *and* the private key of the device being enrolled, and you could just request a proper enrollment challenge instead. The concrete harm is that enrolling a device could silently consume the user's pending login challenge (a self-inflicted DoS), and that a stated security property was not actually enforced.

**The fix is at the root, not the symptom.** `expectedPurpose` is now a **required parameter** of `VerifySignatureAsync`, checked inside `ChallengeService` where all three ceremonies converge — so no future call site can forget it, which is exactly how this one was missed. Callers pass `Login` / `StepUp` / `DeviceEnroll`. A purpose mismatch reports `challenge_not_found` rather than a distinct error, so probing a challenge id cannot reveal which ceremony it belongs to.

**Rest of the consistency review: no other divergence found.** Passkey sessions correctly carry no PoP thumbprint and so skip D-081's proof requirement while still honouring session revocation; recovery (D-083) suspends passkeys as well as device keys because both are `TrustedDevice` rows; the passkey rail writes the same `login.approved` outbox message and idempotency-key shape as the device-key rail; `CanWatchAsync` (D-087) and `StatusAsync` share one binding helper.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IChallengeService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/ChallengeService.cs`, `LoginApprovalService.cs`, `StepUpService.cs`, `TrustedDeviceService.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/TrustedDeviceAuthTests.cs`.

## D-089 · Global phone identity — staged, additive, reversible E.164 migration (Phase 1 complete) (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Phases 1–4 implemented and verified against the populated dev database. Phases 5–6 pending client migration.** Backed by `libphonenumber-csharp` 9.0.19.

**The problem being fixed.** `AuthService.NormalizePhone` treated any 10-digit input as Indian and prefixed `91`. That single line made the platform structurally India-only and, worse, would silently route an OTP for a foreign national-format number to whichever Indian number shared those digits. **There is now no default region anywhere in the request path**: a caller supplies E.164 (unambiguous alone) or names a region explicitly; a national-format number with no region is a **failed parse, not a guess**.

**Schema (additive, never in-place).** Three nullable columns on `users` — `PhoneE164` (canonical identifier, unique when set via a filtered index), `CountryCode` (ISO-3166 alpha-2, captured rather than inferred because E.164 cannot always recover region unambiguously), `PhoneNational` (display only, never a lookup key). **The legacy `Phone` column and its unique index are untouched.** A null in the new columns means "not yet migrated", never "no phone" — which is what makes the fallback safe.

**Phase status:**
- **1 — Add columns.** Migration `20260718100000_AddPhoneE164`, hand-authored + hand-synced snapshot (the EF design-time host is AppControl-blocked here). ✅
- **2 — Backfill.** `PhoneE164BackfillJob`: idempotent (only null rows), batched, **validates every conversion**, **never writes a row it cannot convert**, logs each failure with its user id, and refuses to resolve a canonicalization **collision** between two legacy rows — that is a data problem for a human, not something to settle by whichever row was hit first. Triggered by `POST /v1/admin/phone-backfill` (`KurxAdmin`), never automatically on boot: a deploy should not silently rewrite identity columns with nobody watching the failure count. ✅
- **3 — Dual-read.** `AuthIdentifiers.ResolveUserAsync` matches `PhoneE164` **or** legacy `Phone` in one query, so a half-backfilled table authenticates everyone. Every pre-session path (device login, passkey login, recovery) routes through this one method. ✅
- **4 — Dual-write.** Registration and phone-change write both representations through a single `ApplyCanonicalPhone` helper, so they cannot drift apart while both exist. ✅
- **5 — Switch APIs to PhoneE164.** Pending: requires the AM9 clients to send region/E.164. Legacy compatibility stays until then.
- **6 — Drop legacy `Phone`.** Only after 5 is complete and no reader remains.

**Verification on real data, not just tests.** The migration was applied to the **populated** dev database (12 users) and the backfill run through the admin endpoint: `scanned=12, converted=6, failed=6, skipped=0`. **The 6 failures are correct behaviour** — they are the fictional `+1555…` numbers created by earlier curl drives, and libphonenumber rightly rejects the reserved 555 range. All six real-format numbers converted with `CountryCode=IN`. Each failure was logged with its user id and **left byte-identical**. Afterwards, both a backfilled row **and** an unconverted row still authenticated successfully — the zero-downtime property demonstrated rather than asserted. Non-admin access to the backfill endpoint returned **403**.

**Rollback procedure, per phase:**
| Phase | To roll back | Data loss |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (columns) | `Down()` drops the index + three columns | **None** — everything is re-derivable from `Phone` |
| 2 (backfill) | `UPDATE users SET "PhoneE164"=NULL, "CountryCode"=NULL, "PhoneNational"=NULL` | None; re-run the job to redo |
| 3 (dual-read) | Revert `AuthIdentifiers` to the legacy-only match | None; legacy column was never stopped being written |
| 4 (dual-write) | Remove the `ApplyCanonicalPhone` calls | None; canonical columns simply go stale |
| 5 (API switch) | Revert the API layer to legacy resolution | None **provided phase 6 has not run** |
| 6 (drop legacy) | **Point of no return** — restore from backup | Irreversible; do not run until 5 has been stable in production |

**Naming note:** the helper class is `PhoneCanonicalizer`, not `PhoneNumbers` — libphonenumber's own root namespace is `PhoneNumbers`, and the collision resolved silently-but-wrongly outside `Kurx.Infrastructure.Auth`. Renamed rather than papered over with qualification.

**Files:** `Domain/Entities/Users.cs`, `Infrastructure/Migrations/20260718100000_AddPhoneE164.cs` (new), `KurxDbContextModelSnapshot.cs`, `Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/PhoneCanonicalizer.cs` (renamed from `PhoneNumbers.cs`), `Infrastructure/Auth/AuthService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/AuthIdentifiers.cs`, `Infrastructure/Jobs/PhoneE164BackfillJob.cs` (new), `Api/Endpoints/PhoneMigrationEndpoints.cs` (new), DI + `Program.cs`, `.env.example`.

**Verification:** `dotnet build` 0 warnings / 0 errors; **full suite 325/325 green** (313 → 325, 12 new tests covering dual-write, dual-read of an un-backfilled row, multi-format resolution, backfill conversion + refusal + idempotency, and non-India parsing for US/GB/JP).

## D-090 · AM9 Phase 2 — Next.js auth client shipped; Flutter deliberately NOT written blind (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED for the web client (built, typechecked, deployed, rendered against the live backend). Flutter is NOT delivered — reasoning below, and it is a capability limit, not an oversight.**

**Web client delivered.** `lib/webauthn.ts` (browser WebAuthn glue), `lib/auth-api.ts` (typed client for AM3–AM9), `components/auth/login-waiting.tsx`, `passkey-sign-in.tsx`, `security-manager.tsx`, `recovery-panel.tsx`, routes `/settings/security` and `/recover`, plus passkey + recovery entry points wired into the existing login panel so nothing shipped as dead code.

**Design points worth recording:**
- **base64url conversion lives in exactly one module.** The server speaks fido2-net-lib JSON (base64url everywhere), the browser speaks ArrayBuffers. Getting that subtly wrong is the classic passkey failure mode — it surfaces as an opaque server-side "invalid signature" rather than a useful client error — so all conversion is centralised in `webauthn.ts` and done by hand rather than via `PublicKeyCredential.parseCreationOptionsFromJSON`, which is not yet available across the target browsers.
- **SignalR is an accelerator; polling always runs.** `LoginWaiting` starts the poll loop unconditionally and treats the hub as best-effort, so a blocked socket (corporate proxy, offline) degrades to slower rather than broken — matching the backend contract in D-087 that tokens are only ever minted on the HTTP path.
- **The match number is displayed prominently**, because it is the anti-push-fatigue defence (ADR-A9) and is worthless tucked into small print.
- **The UI cannot leak account existence.** `/passkeys/login/options` and `/recovery/start` deliberately succeed for unknown identifiers, so both components show one generic failure message and never branch on "account not found" — the anti-enumeration property is preserved end-to-end rather than undone at the last mile.
- **WebAuthn `DOMException`s are translated.** The raw messages ("The operation either timed out or was not allowed") cover both user-cancelled and wrong-domain, so `passkeyErrorMessage` disambiguates on `err.name` into something a person can act on.
- **A 403 from recovery-code generation is rendered as the step-up prompt it actually is** (D-084), not as a generic permissions error.

**Verification:** `tsc --noEmit` clean; `next build` succeeded with `/settings/security` and `/recover` compiled; both deployed in the `kurx-web` container against the live backend. `/recover` renders **200** with its real content; `/settings/security` correctly **307**s when unauthenticated and renders **200** with live server data (Passkeys / Trusted devices / Where you're signed in / Recovery codes) once authenticated. The login page now offers passkey sign-in and an account-recovery link.

### Why Flutter was not written
There is **no Flutter SDK on this machine** (`flutter`/`dart` are absent), so nothing written for `mobile/` could be compiled, analysed, or run — not even a type check. Producing the nine requested screens under those conditions would mean adding roughly two thousand lines of Dart whose correctness is pure assertion, into the *most* security-critical surface of the platform (device-key generation, biometric gating, secure-storage of private keys). `CLAUDE.md` §11 requires a change to be exercised live before it is called done, and §4 forbids ending at "should work". Writing it blind would also make the eventual real verification harder, because a reviewer could no longer tell reviewed code from generated guesswork.

**Recommendation:** install the Flutter SDK (or point me at a machine with one) and the mobile client becomes ordinary verifiable work. If the code is wanted regardless, say so explicitly and it will be delivered clearly marked **UNVERIFIED — DOES NOT COMPILE HERE**, which is the only honest way to hand it over.

**Also still open in AM9:** the E.164 phases 5–6 cut-over (D-089) waits on the remaining legacy rows being backfilled. The clients no longer submit a `+91`-prefixed form: web, admin and Flutter all collect through the shared country-picker phone field and send E.164.

## D-091 · AM9 Phase 2b — Flutter auth client; mobile app made to compile for the first time (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Analyzer clean, 12 new tests passing, full mobile suite 64/65.**

**Correction to D-090, stated plainly.** D-090 claimed the Flutter SDK was unavailable and used that to justify not writing the mobile client. **That was wrong.** Flutter 3.44.6 / Dart 3.12.2 is installed at `~/flutter`; it is simply not on `PATH`, so a bare `which flutter` returned nothing and the conclusion was drawn from a single negative check. The lesson is the same one D-082 recorded about `dotnet test`: **on this machine a "tool not found" result is not evidence the tool is absent** — check the well-known install locations before concluding. D-090's Flutter section is superseded by this entry; its Next.js content stands.

**Two environment quirks worth recording**, both costing a failed run before diagnosis: Flutter's native-assets build step breaks on an SDK path containing a space (`C:\Users\CHAITANYA REDDY\flutter` → `'C:\Users\CHAITANYA' is not recognized`), so the SDK was copied to `C:\flutter` for test runs; and `flutter analyze` alone does not surface that, because it never invokes the native-assets step.

> **Superseded by D-105 (2026-07-18) for current paths.** The copy at `C:\flutter` is now the *only* Flutter SDK, the spaced one at `C:\Users\CHAITANYA REDDY\flutter` is deleted, and the Android SDK has moved to `C:\Android\Sdk`. Do not treat any path named above as a live location — see D-105 for the standard. The diagnosis recorded here stands.

### Pre-existing defect found: the mobile app has never compiled
`mobile/lib/core/storage/` — `token_store.dart` and `event_cache.dart` — **was never committed** (`git ls-tree HEAD` returns nothing; no history at all). `main.dart`, `session_controller.dart`, `auth_interceptor.dart`, the events repository, the theme controller and the profile/bookmarks providers all import it. So the D-019 mobile app was **broken from a clean checkout**, with 10 distinct compile errors, and nobody knew because no analyzer or test run could ever have passed.

Both files were reconstructed from their call sites rather than guessed:
- **`TokenStore`** — `flutter_secure_storage` only (Keychain / Android EncryptedSharedPreferences). A refresh token is a bearer credential for the entire account, so it must not sit in Hive or SharedPreferences. iOS accessibility is `first_unlock_this_device` so tokens never ride an iCloud backup onto a different handset; Android forces the `encryptedSharedPreferences` implementation. `hasSession()` keys off the *refresh* token, because an expired access token is not "logged out" — the interceptor can still rotate it.
- **`EventCache` + `cacheBoxProvider`** — the non-secret Hive cache, deliberately separate from token storage. `cacheBoxProvider` throws unless overridden in `main()`, which is exactly the contract the existing `ThemeModeController` already coded against ("falls back to system when no box is available, e.g. in unit tests").

Result: **0 analyzer errors** (down from 10), 71 → 46 issues, all remaining being pre-existing lint infos.

### Delivered
`core/security/device_key_service.dart`, `features/auth/data/models/trusted_device_dtos.dart`, `.../datasources/trusted_device_remote_data_source.dart` (every AM2–AM7 endpoint), `.../repositories/trusted_device_repository.dart`, `presentation/pages/approve_login_page.dart`, `test/features/auth/trusted_device_test.dart`.

**Design decisions:**
- **Device keys are a `MethodChannel`, not Dart crypto.** The entire value of the rail is that the private key cannot leave the device — that is what makes a stolen refresh token inert (D-081). A Dart-generated key lives in the app heap and is recoverable from a rooted handset or a backup, so the interface is defined against AndroidKeyStore (`EC`/`secp256r1`, `setUserAuthenticationRequired`, StrongBox where present) and the iOS Secure Enclave (`biometryCurrentSet | privateKeyUsage`, so re-enrolling a fingerprint invalidates the key). **The native halves are not yet written** — see below.
- **Biometrics gate `sign`, which is what makes approval a user-present assertion** rather than a call any background malware could make. `DeviceKeyException.requiresReenrollment` distinguishes "biometrics changed, key destroyed" (a normal lifecycle event) from a real failure.
- **Reject never signs.** Declining a suspicious sign-in must not require biometrics, or a user who cannot authenticate is left unable to say no. Pinned by a test.
- **Revoking *this* device deletes the local key**, so a later enrollment cannot silently reuse a key the server already marked revoked.
- **The match number is rendered prominently and never auto-confirmed** (ADR-A9); the approval card also shows request IP/UA, since that is what lets a user notice a sign-in that isn't theirs. Approve and reject get equal visual weight so the safe action is never the harder one.

**Verification:** `flutter analyze` — **0 errors** across the new code; `flutter test` — **12/12** new tests pass, covering DTO parsing (including that a `Suspended` device does not read as trusted, per D-083), the enrollment ceremony (exact nonce signed, signature and device id posted to `/verify`), key reuse, approve/reject, revocation key-deletion, and three widget tests on the approval screen (match number shown, empty state, cancelled biometric prompt not surfaced as an error). Full mobile suite **64 passed / 1 failed**; the single failure is `guest_browse_test.dart` "the bottom nav shell switches branches", a **pre-existing** UI/test mismatch expecting a `NavigationBar` that the shell does not render — unrelated to auth, and it had simply never run before because the app did not compile.

### Explicitly UNVERIFIED / remaining for the mobile client
- **Native `DeviceKeyPlugin` (Kotlin + Swift) is not written.** Without it `PlatformDeviceKeyService` throws `unavailable` on a real device. All Dart-side ceremony logic is tested against a fake; the keystore/Secure Enclave integration itself is **pending device validation** and cannot be exercised in this environment.
- **Not yet built:** passkey registration/login on mobile (needs platform WebAuthn APIs), device-management and recovery/step-up screens (repository methods exist and are tested; the screens are not), SignalR login-waiting on mobile, FCM handling for the approval push, offline queueing.
- No emulator/device run was performed — **widget tests are host-VM only**. Nothing here is claimed as runtime-verified on Android or iOS.

## D-092 · Native device-key plugins — Android verified on-device, iOS written but UNCOMPILED (2026-07-18)
**Status: PARTIALLY ACCEPTED. Android: compiled and runtime-verified on a real emulator. iOS: written, never compiled — see the evidence table.**

Closes the largest gap D-091 left open: `PlatformDeviceKeyService` had no native half, so it threw `unavailable` on any real device.

### Android — `DeviceKeyPlugin.kt`
EC P-256 (`secp256r1`) generated **inside AndroidKeyStore**; the app only ever holds an opaque handle, never private key bytes. That is the property the whole rail depends on (D-081: a stolen refresh token is inert without a signature from this key).

- **StrongBox attempted, TEE fallback.** StrongBox is absent from most handsets and every emulator; a hard requirement would lock out the majority of users for no gain, since TEE-backed is already non-exportable. Firmware that advertises StrongBox and then rejects the spec is handled by regenerating without it.
- **`setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` with `BIOMETRIC_STRONG or DEVICE_CREDENTIAL`.** Biometric-only would strand users whose sensor fails or who have none enrolled. Validity window is **0 seconds** — every signature needs a fresh prompt, no grace period.
- **`setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)`** — enrolling a new biometric destroys the key, because the set of people who can unlock the phone changed. Surfaced to Dart as `key_invalidated` → "re-enroll this device", a normal lifecycle event rather than an error.
- **One authentication binds to one signature.** The `Signature` is handed to `BiometricPrompt` inside a `CryptoObject`, so the keystore releases the key for *that* operation only. Authenticating and signing separately would leave a window in which any code could sign.
- **`MainActivity` now extends `FlutterFragmentActivity`.** `BiometricPrompt` needs a `FragmentActivity`; plain `FlutterActivity` compiles fine and then throws at the first prompt — a failure that would only ever appear on a real device.
- **`securityInfo` reads the posture back off the key** (`KeyInfo.securityLevel` / `isInsideSecureHardware`, `isUserAuthenticationRequired`) rather than assuming what was requested. This is what the integration test asserts on, and what lets the app tell a user the truth about their device instead of claiming protection it may not have.

### iOS — `DeviceKeyPlugin.swift` · ⚠️ UNVERIFIED
Secure Enclave (`kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave`), access control `.privateKeyUsage + .biometryCurrentSet`, accessibility `WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`. Deliberately **no passcode fallback** (unlike Android): every Enclave-capable device has biometrics, so a thief who knows the passcode still cannot sign. `SecKeyCopyExternalRepresentation` returns a bare X9.63 point, **not** SPKI, so the DER header is prepended — sending the raw point is the single most likely integration bug on this platform and produces an opaque server-side parse failure.

**It has never been compiled.** No macOS or Xcode exists on this host. It is a reviewed design, not working code. The simulator has no Secure Enclave either, so even a future simulator run would not validate it — `isSecureEnclaveAvailable()` returns false under `targetEnvironment(simulator)` specifically so a simulator run cannot masquerade as hardware validation.

### Evidence
| Claim | Status | How |
|---|---|---|
| Kotlin plugin compiles | **VERIFIED** | `flutter build apk --debug` → `app-debug.apk` built |
| Channel registered / reachable from Dart | **VERIFIED on device** | `securityInfo` returned real values over the MethodChannel |
| Device posture reported accurately | **VERIFIED on device** | `{strongBoxSupported: false, biometricStatus: 11, apiLevel: 37, hasKey: false}` — emulator, API 37, no StrongBox, nothing enrolled |
| Fail-closed with no credential enrolled | **VERIFIED on device** | `createKey()` threw a setup error and left **no key behind**, rather than creating one that could never be used |
| Signing with no key → `not_enrolled` | **VERIFIED on device** | typed exception, no crash |
| Dart-side ceremony logic | **VERIFIED (host VM)** | 12/12 tests — exact nonce signed, reject never signs, revoke deletes local key |
| Key **generation** into secure hardware (`insideSecureHardware`, `userAuthenticationRequired`) | **PENDING** | needs a credential enrolled; see below |
| iOS anything | **UNVERIFIED** | no macOS/Xcode on this host |

**Why the positive key path is still pending, honestly.** It requires an enrolled PIN/biometric. Enrolling one (`adb shell locksettings set-pin`) put the emulator behind a lock screen with credential-encrypted storage locked (`ceDataInode=0`), after which no activity could launch (`Activity class ... does not exist`) and the test host could not start the app — scripted unlock attempts did not clear it. The PIN was cleared, the emulator rebooted, and the suite re-confirmed green in its no-credential state. **The test is written to assert the full path and will do so unattended on any device with a credential enrolled** — it branches on `biometricStatus`, so it is one CI device away from covering this, not a rewrite.

**Not fabricated:** at no point is the hardware-backed key generation claimed as verified. What ran, ran.

## D-093 · Mobile auth Phase 1 — offline/retry policy, realtime login status, recovery + step-up screens (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED for what is listed as delivered. Passkeys and FCM are NOT done — see the gap table.**

### The offline decision: there is deliberately no approval queue
The obvious design — queue an approval offline, flush it when connectivity returns — was **rejected on security grounds**, not skipped for effort:

- **Useless.** A login challenge lives ~120s (`AUTH_CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS`). Anything queued long enough to need a queue has already expired server-side; flushing it just produces a confusing `challenge_consumed` minutes later.
- **Unsafe.** Approving a sign-in asserts "that is me, right now, at that location". Replaying that intent later, against context the user can no longer see, is exactly the confused-deputy case number-matching (ADR-A9) exists to prevent.

So an approval that cannot reach the server **fails fast and visibly**; the user re-approves from a fresh push. What *is* retried is short-lived transient faults where the user's intent is still current.

**`AuthRetry`** encodes the distinction that actually matters — **what must never be retried**:
- **No 4xx is ever retried.** The server made a decision; repeating re-asks a settled question, and `challenge_consumed` will never become un-consumed. **429 is excluded on purpose** — the server is asking for *less* traffic.
- **Timeouts are retried only for idempotent actions.** A timeout is ambiguous: the request may already have been applied. So `approveLogin` (single-use challenge) and `redeemRecovery` (single-use code) are **not** retried on timeout, while `rejectLogin`, `revokeSession` and `startRecovery` are.
- **Connection errors are always retryable** — the request never reached the server, so it cannot double-apply.
- **Bad certificates are never retried past.**
- Exponential backoff **with jitter**, because a backend restart drops every device at once and identical backoff would bring them all back in the same instant. Total budget 20s, deliberately **under** the challenge TTL so a retry can never outlive the thing it retries.

### Also delivered
- **`LoginStatusStream`** (`signalr_netcore`) — the mobile *waiting* client for when a user signs in on their phone and approves from another device. Carries **status only, never tokens**, so D-080's mint-exactly-once guarantee stays on the HTTP path; a failed connection returns `false` and is never surfaced, because polling is the required fallback.
- **`RecoveryPage`** — two-step identify → redeem. Shows **one generic failure** for every outcome, mirroring the server's single opaque `invalid_recovery`; branching further would undo the anti-enumeration property at the last mile.
- **`StepUpPage`** — pops `true` only when the server recorded the step-up; cancelling returns a definite `false` rather than an ambiguous null, so a caller cannot accidentally treat "cancelled" as "authorised".
- **`SecurityPage`** (from D-092) covers trusted devices, sessions and recovery codes.
- Repository gained `startRecovery`/`redeemRecovery` and now owns token persistence after recovery — the screens call the repository, never the data source directly, so no business logic is duplicated in the UI.

| Device-key ceremonies (sign/approve/reject/revoke) | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | 12 tests (D-091) |
| All mobile code compiles | **VERIFIED** | `flutter analyze lib` → **0 errors** |
| Full mobile suite | **VERIFIED** | **75 passed / 1 failed** (was 64/1). The failure is the pre-existing `guest_browse_test` nav-shell mismatch, unrelated to auth |
| Recovery / step-up / security screens render + behave | **UNVERIFIED** | written and analyzing clean; **no widget tests yet**, no device run |
| SignalR login status against a live hub | **UNVERIFIED** | compiles; never connected to the running backend |
| Android hardware key generation | **PENDING HARDWARE VALIDATION** | unchanged from D-092 — needs a device with a credential enrolled |
| iOS anything | **UNVERIFIED** | no macOS/Xcode |

## D-094 · Mobile login waiting screen + connection-aware offline behaviour — and a retry layer that was dead code (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. 90 mobile tests passing (was 75); analyzer 0 errors.**

### The bug this phase found: `AuthRetry` never ran
D-093 shipped a retry/offline policy that classified **`DioException`**. But the data layer's `guard()` converts every transport failure into **`ApiError`** *before* it escapes the datasource — by design (D-064), so no raw Dio error reaches feature code. Therefore:

- `_isRetryable` hit `error is! DioException` → **false for everything** → nothing was ever retried.
- `isOffline` → **always false** → offline was never detected, so the UI could never have said "waiting for network".

The whole layer was inert in production. **D-093's tests passed because they threw raw `DioException`s directly at `AuthRetry`, bypassing the data layer** — the textbook case of a test that validates the test's own fiction rather than the system. It surfaced only when a test drove the real datasource end to end.

**Fixed** by classifying `ApiError`, which is the app's single error model. The distinction is now sharper than before, because `ApiError` separates the two ambiguity classes explicitly:
- `network_error` (status 0) — the request never left; a repeat cannot double-apply, so **always retryable**.
- `timeout` (status 0) — ambiguous, it may already have been applied server-side, so **retryable only for idempotent actions**.
- `rate_limited` / any 4xx — **never**. The server made a decision; `challenge_consumed` will never become un-consumed, and 429 is a request for *less* traffic.
- `response_parse_failed` — **never**. That is a contract bug, not weather; retrying re-runs the bug.
- 5xx — retryable.

`isOffline` is now `network_error` only: a timeout means we *did* reach the network, so telling the user "you're offline" would send them to debug the wrong thing.

### Connection-aware waiting screen (Phase 2 as specified)
`LoginWaitController` + `LoginWaitingPage` implement the six required states — `waitingForApproval`, `waitingForNetwork`, `expired`, `connectionRestored`, `approved`, `rejected` (plus `starting`/`failed`).

- **"No answer yet" and "no network" are distinct states with distinct wording**, because the user's remedy differs completely (walk to your phone vs. fix your wifi). A single spinner conflates them and leaves the user nothing to do.
- **Reachability is inferred from actual request failures, not radio state.** A phone can be associated to wifi with no route to the internet; reporting that as "online" is a lie the user then has to debug. No `connectivity_plus` dependency was added for this reason.
- **Automatic recovery on expiry starts a brand-new challenge** and discards the dead one's id *and* poll token. Nothing stale is ever replayed — consistent with the approved no-queue decision. `restartCount` is surfaced so a user who has waited through a cycle is told why the number changed rather than seeing it silently swap.
- **A rejection never auto-restarts.** Declining is a deliberate human decision; silently re-asking would be push-fatigue by design. It offers an explicit "Try again" instead.
- **Polling stops the moment a session is minted** (asserted).

### Evidence
| Claim | Status | How |
|---|---|---|
| Retry/offline classification against the **real** error model | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | 11 tests, now using `ApiError` — 4xx/429/parse-failures never retried, timeout only when idempotent, offline vs timeout distinguished |
| Waiting-screen state machine (offline → restored, expiry → new challenge, rejection terminal, approval stops polling) | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | 8 controller tests driving the real datasource through a scripted adapter |
| Waiting-screen rendering + accessibility | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | 7 widget tests incl. `Match number` exposed as a semantics label (`container: true, excludeSemantics: true`, so a screen reader says "Match number 73", not a bare "73") |
| All mobile code compiles | **VERIFIED** | `flutter analyze lib test` → **0 errors** |
| Full mobile suite | **VERIFIED** | **90 passed / 1 failed** (was 75/1) — failure is the pre-existing `guest_browse_test` nav-shell mismatch, unrelated |
| SignalR against a live hub | **UNVERIFIED** | `LoginStatusStream` compiles; never connected to the running backend |
| Recovery / step-up / security screens | **UNVERIFIED** | render-clean, still no widget tests |
| Android hardware key generation | **PENDING HARDWARE VALIDATION** | unchanged (D-092) |
| iOS anything | **UNVERIFIED** | no macOS/Xcode |

### Testing note worth keeping
Two harness details cost a cycle each and are recorded so they are not rediscovered: an **autoDispose** provider read without a listener is torn down immediately (cancelling its timers, so no poll ever fires — use `container.listen`), and `find.bySemanticsLabel` needs `tester.ensureSemantics()` or the semantics tree is never built.

## D-095 · Widget tests for the auth screens + the hardware validation guide (2026-07-18)
**Status: ACCEPTED. 110 mobile tests passing (was 90); analyzer 0 errors.**

### A UX bug the tests caught before it shipped
`SecurityPage._generateRecoveryCodes` ended in a bare `catch (_)` that reported **every** non-`DeviceKeyException` failure as *"Confirm it's you on this device first"*. So a user who was simply **offline** was told to perform a step-up — which they also could not do without a network. The advice was not merely unhelpful, it was impossible to act on.

Fixed by classifying properly: **only a 403 is the step-up gate**; any other `ApiError` shows its own `userMessage` (so offline reads as *"Can't reach Kurx…"*), and anything else is a generic failure. Both branches are pinned by tests, including an explicit regression test named for the offline case.

### 20 widget tests across the three screens
- **RecoveryPage (5)** — send disabled until an identifier is entered; advancing demands **both** factors; the redeem failure shows **one opaque message** and asserts the absence of anything more specific (`no account`, `expired`), because the UI must not undo the server's anti-enumeration at the last mile; the "signs out every session" warning is present; a failed start does not advance the step.
- **StepUpPage (6)** — reason rendered; success records the step-up; **a cancelled biometric prompt shows no error** (cancelling is a choice); `key_invalidated` produces *"Set this device up again"* rather than a generic failure; offline reads as offline; and **cancelling pops `false`, never null**, so a caller cannot mistake "cancelled" for "authorised".
- **SecurityPage (9)** — loading, empty states, listing with a *this device* label, revoke-confirmation (asserting that **cancelling the dialog revokes nothing**), the `isThisDevice` flag that drives local key deletion, session sign-out, codes shown once with the keep-them warning, 403-as-step-up, and the offline regression above.

**Test-harness note:** a fake that resolves instantly can never show a loading state, so the fake repository grew an injectable `listDelay` — the in-flight state is now genuinely observed rather than assumed.

### Hardware validation guide — `docs/mobile/HARDWARE_VALIDATION.md`
Production acceptance procedure: 15 cases across a 9-device matrix (Pixel/StrongBox, Samsung/Knox, mid-range TEE-only, emulator, PIN-only Android; Face ID / Touch ID / iPad / simulator on iOS). Each case carries prerequisites, steps, expected results, a failure-mode table with explicit **release blocker** calls, logs to capture, and acceptance criteria.

Grounded in this implementation rather than generic: it asserts on the plugin's actual `securityInfo` fields and its real error codes (`user_canceled` / `not_enrolled` / `key_invalidated` / `unavailable`), and records the measured emulator baseline (`strongBoxSupported: false, biometricStatus: 11, apiLevel: 37`).

**The section that matters most is §7 — what the emulator and simulator can never prove.** An emulated TEE can report `insideSecureHardware: true`, so a green emulator run must never be read as hardware acceptance; **TC-01/03/04/07 are hardware-only and have no valid emulator result at all.** TC-03 (biometric enrollment change must invalidate the key) is flagged as the single most important case: if it fails, anyone who adds their own fingerprint to a stolen unlocked phone inherits the victim's trusted device.

## D-096 · Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android — login-approval push (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Build integration verified with the real project config; runtime FCM registration PENDING (see evidence).** Firebase project `kurx-a14d1`, Android app `in.kurx.kurx_mobile`.

### Two blocking findings, resolved before any code
1. **Package mismatch.** The first `google-services.json` supplied was registered for `com.kurx.kurxproduction`, while the app builds as `in.kurx.kurx_mobile`. The Google Services Gradle plugin matches on package name and **hard-fails** the build — this is not workaroundable in code. Rather than silently change `applicationId` (which is app *identity*: it breaks existing installs, invalidates Play/signing association, and desynchronises the Kotlin package path), a second Android app was registered in Firebase for the real package. Verified programmatically: `google-services.json package_name == gradle applicationId`.
2. **A live credential arrived in chat.** `google-services.json` is now **gitignored**, with `google-services.json.example` committed as a documented template. Android Firebase keys ship inside the APK and are restricted by package + SHA-1, so this is not a high-severity secret — but a real project credential should not enter git history, where rotating it later means creating a new Firebase app.

### Design: a push is a hint, never an instruction
The login-approval push carries **no nonce, no token, nothing signable** — only `type`, `challenge_id`, `match_number`. On receipt the app does exactly one thing: **invalidate `pendingLoginsProvider`**, forcing a re-fetch of `/v1/auth/login/pending`. The nonce the device signs always comes from that server response.

So a forged, replayed, or tampered push can at worst make the app refresh a list. It can never cause an approval, pre-authorise one, or change the match number the user is shown (the approval screen renders it from the pending-challenge DTO, not the payload). A test asserts this by construction — `PushMessage` has exactly three fields, so there is nowhere for attacker-supplied signable material to land.

**Push is also strictly optional.** `Firebase.initializeApp()` is wrapped in try/catch in `main()`, and `PushService.start()` returns `false` rather than throwing on denied permission, missing Play Services, or absent config. All of those degrade to the existing polling path (D-094) — approvals keep working, just less instantly. A China-market handset with no Play Services is a fully functional Kurx install.

**No new backend work.** Token upload reuses the existing `POST /v1/devices/register` — the same `devices` table `LoginApprovalService.PushToDevicesAsync` already reads. Deliberately *not* conflated with `trusted_devices`: a push destination and a cryptographic trust anchor are different concepts, and merging them would let an FCM token rotation look like a device-trust event. `onTokenRefresh` re-registers, because a stale token is a silent delivery failure.

**Deliberately not added:** `firebase-analytics` and the Firebase BoM. FlutterFire plugins pin their own native versions, so the BoM is redundant here, and analytics is an unrequested data-collection surface with consent implications (D-101 defaults). Only `firebase_core` + `firebase_messaging` are included.

### Evidence
| Claim | Status | How |
|---|---|---|
| Gradle plugin wiring correct | **VERIFIED** | `flutter build apk --debug` succeeded — first with a placeholder, then with the real config |
| **Real project config is baked into the APK** | **VERIFIED** | plugin-generated `build/app/generated/res/processDebugGoogleServices/values/values.xml` contains `google_app_id 1:799279844747:android:7a4ec03d0803d912c9f38e`, `project_id kurx-a14d1`; `build/app/gmpAppId/debug.txt` matches |
| Package name matches applicationId | **VERIFIED** | asserted programmatically against both files |
| Real config stays out of git | **VERIFIED** | `git check-ignore` confirms |
| Payload parsing + security properties | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | 6 tests: login-approval parsed; other event types not treated as approvals; empty/unknown/malformed payloads degrade instead of throwing; nothing signable can enter the model |
| All mobile code compiles | **VERIFIED** | `flutter analyze lib test integration_test` → **0 errors** |
| Full host suite | **VERIFIED** | **116 passed / 1 failed** (was 110/1) — the failure is the pre-existing `guest_browse_test` nav-shell mismatch |
| **FCM token acquisition + upload at runtime** | **PENDING** | see below |
| Actual push delivery end-to-end | **PENDING PHYSICAL DEVICE** | needs a real handset with Play Services, plus a server-side send |
| iOS push (APNs) | **UNVERIFIED / NOT STARTED** | no `GoogleService-Info.plist`, no APNs key, no macOS |

**Why runtime is still PENDING, precisely.** `integration_test/push_test.dart` is written and analyses clean; it initialises Firebase, obtains a token, asserts it is uploaded exactly once, and — on a device without Play Services — asserts the *degradation* path instead. It could not be executed: the Pixel_7 AVD's package-manager service repeatedly died (`cmd: Can't find service: package`, plus a `StorageManager.allocateBytes` exception on install) **despite ~8 GB free on `/data`**, across a reboot, a cache trim and an uninstall. The APK builds every time, so this is an emulator fault, not a code fault. **The test will run unattended on any working device** — it is one healthy emulator or one USB handset away, not a rewrite.

**Added to the hardware validation guide** as a push-latency case once a device is available; TC-15's FCM prerequisite is now satisfied at build level.

## D-097 · Native Android passkeys via Credential Manager (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Kotlin + Dart compile; 126 mobile tests passing; runtime PENDING HARDWARE VALIDATION.** Completes the mobile half of AM3 (D-086).

### The design: the plugin is a JSON shuttle, deliberately
Credential Manager speaks the **W3C WebAuthn JSON serialization** — the same shape fido2-net-lib already produces and consumes server-side. So `PasskeyPlugin.kt` does **no** parsing, no base64url handling, and no credential bookkeeping: the server's options JSON goes straight to the platform, and the platform's `registrationResponseJson` / `authenticationResponseJson` comes straight back.

That is the whole point. Decoding fields client-side would re-implement the WebAuthn schema in a second place and give the encoding somewhere to drift — historically the most common way these integrations fail, and always with an opaque server-side "invalid signature" rather than a useful client error. A test pins this by sending an unknown extension field through and asserting it arrives **byte-identical**.

`PasskeyCeremonyDto.optionsJson` is likewise kept as a raw `Map` rather than modelled, for the same reason.

### No parallel identity system
A passkey enrols as an ordinary `TrustedDevice` server-side (D-086), so **revocation (D-081), step-up (D-084), risk (D-085) and recovery-suspension (D-083) apply to it with zero passkey-specific code**. The management UI proves it: "Remove" on a passkey calls the *same* `revokeDevice` path as any other device. `passkeysProvider` exists only so the UI can show them under their own heading.

### Error codes carry meaning, not just failure
Native codes cross the boundary unchanged so callers can branch on a stable vocabulary:
- `user_canceled`, `already_registered` (the server's `excludeCredentials` did its job), `no_credential` → **benign**; explain and offer an alternative, never show an error.
- `no_provider`, `unavailable` → **needs fallback**; this device cannot do passkeys, so route the user to the device-key rail rather than dead-ending them. `unavailable` is also what iOS returns today, since no plugin exists there — the app degrades instead of throwing `MissingPluginException`.
- `dom_error` → almost always a Digital Asset Links mismatch, which the user cannot fix; the message asks them to report it rather than blaming them.

### ⚠ Deployment prerequisite that will block runtime validation
Android verifies an app may use a relying party's ID via **Digital Asset Links**. Before any passkey ceremony can succeed on a device:

1. `https://<WEBAUTHN_RP_ID>/.well-known/assetlinks.json` must be served, listing
   `in.kurx.kurx_mobile` and the app's **SHA-256 signing-certificate fingerprint** with relation
   `delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds`. **Debug and release builds have different
   fingerprints — both must be listed** or passkeys work in one and not the other.
2. **`WEBAUTHN_RP_ID` cannot remain `localhost`.** Asset Links is fetched over HTTPS from a real
   registrable domain, so passkeys are untestable against a local backend on a physical device.
   Runtime validation needs a staging domain with the correct `WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS`.

Neither is code, and neither can be verified from this machine. They are prerequisites for the single Android validation pass.

### Evidence
| Claim | Status | How |
|---|---|---|
| Credential Manager API usage is correct | **VERIFIED** | Kotlin compiles — types, exception hierarchy, suspend/coroutine usage and `CreatePublicKeyCredentialDomException`/`InvalidStateError` all resolve. `flutter build apk --debug` succeeded; `PasskeyPlugin*.class` present in `build/app/tmp/kotlin-classes/debug/`, `credentials-1.3.0.aar` on the compile classpath |
| Dart service is a faithful JSON shuttle | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | 10 tests: options pass through unreshaped (incl. an unknown extension field), response returned as-is, correct platform method per ceremony |
| Native error codes survive the boundary | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | benign vs fault vs needs-fallback classification; malformed and non-object responses rejected rather than silently accepted |
| Unimplemented platform degrades | **VERIFIED BY TESTS** | absent plugin → `unavailable` + `needsFallback`, and `isAvailable()` returns false rather than throwing |
| All mobile code compiles | **VERIFIED** | `flutter analyze lib test integration_test` → **0 errors** |
| Full host suite | **VERIFIED** | **126 passed / 1 failed** (was 116/1); failure is the pre-existing `guest_browse_test` nav-shell mismatch |
