**Verified after migration:** `flutter doctor -v` clean; `sdkmanager --list`, `adb version`, `adb devices`, `flutter emulators` all resolve from `C:\Android\Sdk`; emulator `Pixel_7` cold-boots and is detected as `emulator-5554`; a scratch app built a release APK that **installed and ran on the emulator** (`MainActivity` confirmed `topResumedActivity`); `mobile/` built `app-debug.apk`.

**Open, not resolved by this entry.** `mobile/` had been failing on `:mobile_scanner:compileDebugKotlin` ("Could not close incremental caches"), and it builds now — but **the cause was not isolated**, because two changes landed in the same window: `org.gradle.caching=false` + `kotlin.incremental=false` were added to `mobile/android/gradle.properties`, *and* `mobile/android/.gradle`, `mobile/build`, `mobile/.dart_tool`, `~/.gradle/daemon` were purged with all stale daemons killed. Whether the tree still needs those two flags is **untested**; the honest next step is to revert them and rebuild after a cache purge. `mobile_scanner` is pinned `^6.0.5` (resolving 6.0.11, 7.3.0 available) and Flutter now warns that it applies KGP, which future Flutter versions will refuse to build — that upgrade is real work and is not scheduled here.

**Docs note.** D-091's environment paragraph is **superseded by this entry** for anything forward-looking; its account of what happened at the time stands unchanged. `local.properties` is gitignored, so the migration changed no tracked file in `mobile/`.

## D-105 · Event Chat Phase 2A — lifecycle correctness wiring (2026-07-18)
> ⚠️ **Number collision.** Two unrelated decisions were both filed as D-105 on 2026-07-18 by concurrent
> sessions — the other is the Flutter/Android toolchain entry above. Deliberately **not** renumbered:
> nothing in code cites D-105, but renumbering a shipped decision to fix a heading is the kind of churn that
> breaks the cross-references it is meant to tidy. Cite this one as **"D-105 (Event Chat Phase 2A)"**.

**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** Suite 331 → **343 passing, 0 failed**, run in the container against real Postgres. No schema change, no API contract change — Phase 1's frozen contract (D-104) is untouched. Platform band (see D-101 banding note).

**Problem.** D-104 froze the contract but deliberately left the lifecycle unwired. Three `IChatService` methods had zero callers, and the consequences were severe: **no code path ever created a `Host`**, so every capability gated on `IsHostAsync` was unreachable in production; refunded users kept chat access forever; ticket transfers left the seller in the room and the buyer out; rooms never locked.

**Decisions:**
- **`EventService.TransitionAsync` is the only lifecycle hook.** Room creation and host seeding hang off the existing status gate rather than a parallel publish flow. Publish creates the room and seeds hosts; cancel and archive lock immediately; close does not (the sweep handles it 7 days after the event ends).
- **The room is created at publish, not at first ticket.** Previously it was created lazily by whoever bought first, which meant hosts had nowhere to post before any sale. The `OrderService` calls stay as a no-op safety net for events published before this change.
- **Staff get chat access on acceptance, not invitation.** An invite the user never answered must not put them in the room. Because a user may accept while the event is still a draft (no room yet), publish also runs `AddAcceptedStaffAsHostsAsync` — that is where such acceptances actually take effect.
- **Removing a staff assignment never strips an org member's `Host`.** They hold it by virtue of the org seeding, not the assignment. Non-org staff are demoted to `Member`, then dropped by `RemoveMemberIfNoTicketsAsync` if they hold no ticket. Removal is also skipped when another accepted assignment still justifies access — a user may hold several roles on one event.
- **Refund cleanup also runs on the `already_refunded` replay path.** A first attempt that reversed the books and then failed before the cleanup would otherwise leave the member behind permanently. `RemoveMemberIfNoTicketsAsync` re-checks ticket state, so replaying can never evict a still-entitled member — that re-check is what makes the whole cleanup safe to retry rather than needing an idempotency key.
- **Join messages are posted only for genuinely new members.** `AddMemberAsync` previously announced a join even when the member already existed, so an unpublish/republish cycle produced duplicate "X joined" messages. Members were already deduplicated by the unique index; the system messages were not.
- **A lost race on the unique `(RoomId, UserId)` index converges instead of failing.** The other writer's row is equivalent, and failing the caller would abort a lifecycle operation (a publish, a claim) for no benefit.
- **One definition of "lock a room".** `LockRoomForEventAsync` (immediate) and `LockExpiredRoomsAsync` (hourly sweep) share a private `LockRoomAsync` helper so the two cannot drift.

**Background job.** `LockExpiredChatRoomsJob` registered as `lock-expired-chat-rooms`, `Cron.Hourly()`, following the existing Hangfire convention (job class registered `AddScoped` in `DependencyInjection`, schedule in `Program.cs`). Idempotent — it selects only `Active` rooms.

**Deliberately NOT implemented:** retention and deletion. No retention policy exists anywhere in the repo and inventing one is outside this phase. Recorded as the main remaining gap in the room lifecycle.

**Tests:** `Kurx.Tests/ChatLifecycleTests.cs`, 12 cases — publish seeds hosts, republish idempotency (members *and* system messages), staff accept/remove, staff-with-ticket demotion, org-member host preservation, staff accepted pre-publish, transfer moves access, replayed transfer, refund removes access, replayed refund, cleanup preserves a still-ticketed member, cancel/archive locking exactly once, and sweep idempotency. Every defect fixed in this phase has a regression test.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IChatService.cs` (+3 methods), `Infrastructure/Chat/ChatService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Events/EventService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Events/EventAssignmentService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Orders/RefundService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Ticketing/TicketTransferService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Jobs/LockExpiredChatRoomsJob.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, `Api/Program.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/ChatLifecycleTests.cs` (new).

**Still open after this phase** (moderation and performance work, none of it lifecycle): chat reports bypass `IReportService` despite `chat_message` being whitelisted; `BanMemberAsync` does not evict the live SignalR connection; `DetailsJson` built by string interpolation; chat writes raw `AuditLogs` rather than the D-102 typed spine; `GetMyChatsAsync` is N+1; sticky sessions unconfigured for the Redis backplane. **No chat client exists on web or Flutter.**

## D-106 · Event Chat Phase 2B — moderation correctness on the shared platform services (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** Suite 343 → **351 passing, 0 failed**, container-run against real Postgres. No schema change, no migration. Platform band (see D-101 banding note).

**Principle: one production system per concern.** Chat had grown private copies of three platform capabilities — a moderation queue, a notification path, and an audit format. Each copy was strictly worse than the shared one it shadowed. This phase deletes the copies rather than improving them.

**Verified before changing anything — the existing notification infrastructure (reused, not replaced):**
- `IPushSender` (`Providers.cs:65`) is the single push seam. `FirebasePushSender` uses the Firebase Admin SDK with `FIREBASE_CREDENTIALS_JSON`, degrading to console logging when unconfigured; `ConsolePushSender` is the dev stand-in. Selection is the `PUSH_PROVIDER` switch in `DependencyInjection` (`console` | `firebase`), which throws on any other value.
- `Device` (`Users.cs:102`) holds `FcmToken` / `Platform` / `IsActive` / `LastSeen`; registration and removal are `POST /v1/devices/register` and `DELETE /v1/devices/{id}`.
- **`NotificationService.NotifyAsync` is the pipeline**: in-app row → SignalR notification → unread-count broadcast → FCM fan-out across all active devices → `InvalidFcmTokenException` deactivates the dead token → per-token error isolation.
- **No notification-preferences system exists** anywhere in the repo. Recorded as a genuine gap, not built here.
- Bypasses found: `ChatService` (fixed by this entry) and `AnnouncementService` (a deliberate bulk fan-out with per-channel counters — left alone). `LoginApprovalService` and `OutboxDispatchJob` call `IPushSender` directly on purpose, as those are security events that must not create an in-app inbox row.

**Decisions:**
- **Chat reports file into `IReportService`.** `chat_message` was *already* whitelisted (`ReportService.cs:14`) and never used, so reports were invisible to moderation staff and could be neither resolved nor dismissed. The duplicate guard now applies: a repeat returns **409 `already_reported`**, matching `POST /v1/reports` for the identical condition.
- **Host alerts go through `NotifyAsync`.** The previous `db.Notifications.Add` wrote an inbox row and nothing else — no SignalR push, no unread-badge refresh, no FCM. Chat notifications now inherit the whole delivery pipeline, including token invalidation, for free.
- **The report reason is no longer echoed to hosts.** It was the JSON-injection vector and it leaks reporter free-text to every host. The alert names the message; the reason lives on the report, where moderation staff read it.
- **Moderation writes through the D-102 typed audit spine.** `chat.message_delete`, `chat.mute`, `chat.ban` and `chat.unban` now carry structured `Before`/`After`. `chat.unban` was previously not audited at all — a reversal with no trail. No raw `db.AuditLogs.Add` remains in `ChatService`.
- **Audit now commits in the same transaction as its subject.** `DeleteMessageAsync` previously issued two `SaveChanges` calls, so a failure between them left a deleted message with no audit row. `IAuditWriter.Write` stages on the caller's unit of work, which is the load-bearing property D-102 established.
- **A ban evicts the live connection.** Setting `IsBanned` only stopped the *next* request; an already-connected client stayed in the `chat:{roomId}` group and kept receiving every message until it happened to reconnect. `IRealtimeBroadcaster.EvictFromChatAsync` broadcasts `MemberBanned` and removes the user's connections from the group.

**Ban-eviction design and its ceiling.** Connection ids are recorded per `(room, user)` in a TTL-expiring Redis set on `JoinRoom` and removed on `LeaveRoom`. There is deliberately **no reverse index and no `OnDisconnected` bookkeeping**: removing an already-dead connection is a harmless no-op, so the registry can rely on the TTL instead of exact tracking. **Ceiling — without Redis (single-instance dev) there is no registry**, so eviction degrades to the `MemberBanned` broadcast alone and a hostile client could keep listening until it reconnects. Server-side authorization still refuses every write from a banned member, so this is a confidentiality gap in dev only, never an integrity one.

**JSON injection closed.** Two `DetailsJson` values were built by interpolating user input into JSON string literals. The reason is now a column value written by `IReportService`; notification payloads are serialised by `NotifyAsync` through `JsonSerializer`.

**Tests:** `Kurx.Tests/ChatModerationTests.cs`, 8 cases — report reaches the triage queue, duplicate report refused, hosts notified through the shared pipeline (with unread count maintained and members not notified), a quote-laden reason cannot corrupt the record, typed audit envelope present on delete and mute, delete and its audit row commit together, ban blocks read and write and is audited and reversible, and non-hosts cannot moderate.

**Files:** `Infrastructure/Chat/ChatService.cs`, `Application/Abstractions/IRealtimeBroadcaster.cs`, `Api/Realtime/SignalRBroadcaster.cs`, `Api/Hubs/ChatHub.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/ChatEndpoints.cs` (409 mapping), `Kurx.Tests/ChatModerationTests.cs` (new).

**Still open after this phase:** the chat-specific 10/60s rate limit remains WS-only, so the REST send path runs at the generic 300/min tier; `GetMyChatsAsync` is still N+1; sticky sessions are still unconfigured for the Redis backplane; there are no notification preferences or quiet hours; per-message chat push is not built (and is blocked client-side anyway — mobile has no `firebase_messaging` dependency). **No chat client exists on web or Flutter.**

## D-107 · Event Chat Phase 2C — chat notifications on the existing FCM pipeline (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** Suite 351 → **370 passing, 0 failed**, container-run against real Postgres. No schema change, no migration, no API contract change. Platform band (see D-101 banding note).

**Nothing new was built for delivery.** Chat calls `INotificationService.NotifyAsync` and inherits the whole pipeline — in-app row, SignalR push, unread-count refresh, FCM fan-out across active devices, `InvalidFcmTokenException` token deactivation, per-device error isolation. `IPushSender`, `FirebasePushSender`, the `PUSH_PROVIDER` switch, `Device` registration and the Devices table are all untouched. No chat code path calls a push provider directly.

**Decisions:**
- **Fan-out is a Hangfire job, not inline work.** `SendMessageAsync` commits the message, broadcasts it, then *enqueues* `ChatNotificationJob`. This is what structurally guarantees the requirement that push can never delay or fail chat delivery — the message is durable before notification work begins, so there is no failure mode in which a push error rolls back or blocks a send. A try/catch around inline fan-out would still have made the sender wait for every recipient.
- **Only offline members are pushed.** Presence is inferred from the ban-eviction connection registry built in D-106 (`chat:conns:{roomId}:{userId}`) rather than a new presence service — a member with a live connection to the room already received the message over SignalR, so notifying them is duplicate noise. **Mentions bypass this** and are always delivered. Without Redis everyone is treated as offline, which over-notifies rather than silently dropping notifications — the safer failure direction.
- **Recipient discovery is one query.** Sender exclusion, ban and active-mute filtering are expressed in SQL, so a room of any size costs a single query rather than a per-member check. Delivery itself remains one `NotifyAsync` per recipient — that is the price of not bypassing the shared pipeline, and it is the right trade.
- **Mentions resolve only within the room.** `@handle` matches `User.Username`, intersected with the already-computed eligible recipients, so a mention cannot be used to notify a non-member. Capped at 20 distinct handles per message.
- **A host-authored message is classified `chat_announcement`.** This is a notification *kind*, not a second announcement system — `AnnouncementService` (event-wide push/email/WhatsApp with audience targeting) is untouched and remains the tool for organiser broadcasts.
- **Moderation notices go only to the affected member**, never the room, and are swallowed on failure: a mute or ban is already committed by the time the notice is attempted, and a failed notification must not undo a completed moderation action.
- **Room-lock notices are enqueued only on the `Active → Locked` transition.** Both lock paths already no-op on an already-locked room, so members cannot be told twice.
- **Message bodies are never sent whole.** Previews truncate at 120 characters on a word boundary.

**Payload (unchanged schema — the existing `NotifyAsync` data dictionary):**
`{ notificationType: "chat", eventId, roomId, messageId, senderId }`, with the event title as the notification title and `"{sender}: {preview}"` as the body. `messageId`/`senderId` are null for room-lock and moderation notices. That is sufficient for the mobile deep link Event → Chat Room → Message.

**Kinds:** `chat_message`, `chat_mention`, `chat_announcement`, `chat_room_locked`, `chat_muted`, `chat_banned`, `chat_unbanned`.

**Test-infrastructure change (necessary, and an improvement).** The test host registers a real Hangfire *server*, so enqueuing made background workers execute jobs against `kurx_test` while the next test class drops and re-migrates it — producing `57P01: terminating connection due to administrator command` and corrupting the database mid-migration. `KurxApiFactory` now substitutes a `RecordingBackgroundJobClient` that records enqueued jobs instead of running them. Enqueue stays observable (and is asserted), job bodies are invoked explicitly by the tests, and the recurring jobs that were always latently racing the reset no longer do.

**Tests:** `Kurx.Tests/ChatNotificationTests.cs`, 16 cases — eligible members notified and sender excluded, payload carries every deep-link identifier, long bodies truncated, mention raises the kind, mention cannot reach a non-member, host message classified as announcement, banned/muted excluded and a lapsed mute included, removed member stops being notified, one notification per user regardless of device count, a user with no devices still gets the in-app row, the message survives with no fan-out at all, send enqueues the job without delivering synchronously, deleted messages produce nothing, moderation notices reach only the affected member, and locking notifies once with no second enqueue.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/ChatPresenceKeys.cs` (new), `Application/Abstractions/IChatService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Jobs/ChatNotificationJob.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Chat/ChatService.cs`, `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, `Api/Hubs/ChatHub.cs`, `Api/Realtime/SignalRBroadcaster.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/ChatNotificationTests.cs` (new), `Kurx.Tests/RecordingBackgroundJobClient.cs` (new), `Kurx.Tests/KurxApiFactory.cs`.

**Remaining notification gaps — none of them invented here, all pre-existing:**
- **No notification preferences and no quiet hours anywhere in Kurx.** There is no per-kind opt-out, no mute-this-room-for-me, no do-not-disturb window. Chat is the loudest notification source the platform has, so this is the most valuable next piece of notification work.
- **Fan-out is not deduplicated.** Hangfire retries a job that failed partway, and the retry re-notifies whoever it already reached. Asserted as current behaviour rather than papered over; an idempotency key per (message, recipient) is the fix.
- **No aggregation or batching.** Twenty messages in a busy room produce twenty notifications per offline member.
- **Delivery is one `NotifyAsync` per recipient**, each with its own device query — acceptable at event scale, and the deliberate cost of not bypassing the shared pipeline.
- **Removal from a room is not notified.** Removal is a consequence of a refund or transfer, not a moderation decision, and those flows already have their own customer comms. Flagged rather than silently skipped.
- **Mobile cannot receive any of this yet** — `mobile/pubspec.yaml` still has no `firebase_messaging` dependency. The server half is complete; the client half is Phase 3.

## D-108 · Phase 3A — Flutter Event Chat client (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** `flutter analyze` clean (0 errors; the 2 remaining warnings are pre-existing in auth/events). Mobile suite **163 passing, +37 new**, one pre-existing unrelated failure (`guest_browse_test`, fails identically on a clean tree). **No backend, schema, endpoint or SignalR contract changed.**

**Correction to earlier records.** D-104/D-107 both stated mobile had no SignalR client and no `firebase_messaging`. That is no longer true — the auth workstream added `signalr_netcore`, `firebase_core` and `firebase_messaging`. Phase 3A therefore added **zero dependencies**; everything is reuse.

**Reused, not rebuilt:** the single `dioProvider` + `AuthInterceptor`; `TokenStore` for the hub's access token; the existing Hive `kurx_cache` box (no second database); `PushService`/`PushBootstrap` (extended, not replaced); the one `GoRouter`; Riverpod + the per-feature data/domain/presentation layering; and the design system — `KurxAvatar`, `AsyncValueView`, `EmptyState`, `ErrorRetry`, `ShimmerBox`/`ListSkeleton`, `KSpace`/`KRadius`/`context.kurx`. The only new widget is `ChatMessageBubble`, which has no equivalent anywhere in the app.

**Decisions:**
- **The room screen is keyed by `eventId`, not `roomId`.** The frozen contract exposes a room only as `GET /v1/events/{eventId}/chat`; there is no get-by-room endpoint. The pre-existing `/chats/:roomId` route could never have loaded a room, so it is now `/chats/:eventId`.
- **The "Direct" tab is removed.** It promised user-created conversations, which the product model does not have (one event = one room).
- **`PushMessage` accepts `type` and `notificationType`, preferring `type`.** The auth rail (D-096) sends `type`; chat (D-107) sends `notificationType`. Client-side union keeps existing auth pushes byte-identical and needs no server change.
- **Deep linking navigates only on a *tap*.** `PushService` gained an `opened` stream (from `onMessageOpenedApp`) and `initialMessage()` (cold start) alongside the existing `messages` stream. Navigating on arrival would yank the user out of whatever they were doing every time a message landed.
- **Ordering is `(createdAt, id)` on the client too.** Matching the server's keyset rule exactly; ordering by timestamp alone would disagree with pagination on same-millisecond messages.
- **`clientMessageId` is generated at compose time**, before the first network attempt — that is what makes a retry idempotent rather than duplicating, and it is the key the merge collapses the optimistic row onto.
- **Offline failure is not fatal on reads.** `ApiError.status == 0` falls back to cache, the idiom `EventsRepositoryImpl` already established. A definite refusal (muted/locked/banned) instead marks the message *failed* with Retry/Discard — silently dropping a user's text is worse than telling them.
- **Presence is not implemented; the connection registry is not reused on the client.** The room shows "live" only as a subtle label. Realtime is an optimisation: every reconnect re-runs `?after=` catch-up, so a dropped socket is never a correctness problem.

**Documented debt carried, per the approval — not worked around by changing the backend:**
- `MyChatView.LastActivity` is the *event's* updated-at, so the list is sorted client-side on locally-observed activity and falls back to the server value. A fresh install is ordered approximately until the cache warms.
- Deep link reaches Event → Room reliably; **→ specific message is best-effort**. There is no fetch-message-by-id endpoint and cursors are exclusive, so the room opens at the latest page.

**Files:** `features/social/domain/entities/{chat_room,chat_message}.dart`, `domain/repositories/chat_repository.dart`, `data/models/chat_mappers.dart`, `data/datasources/{chat_remote_data_source,chat_hub_client}.dart`, `data/repositories/chat_repository_impl.dart`, `presentation/providers/chat_providers.dart`, `presentation/widgets/chat_message_bubble.dart`, `presentation/pages/{my_chats_page,chat_room_page}.dart` (rewritten from mockups), `core/storage/chat_cache.dart`, `core/push/{push_service,push_bootstrap}.dart`, `core/router/app_router.dart`, `test/features/social/{chat_repository_test,chat_ui_and_push_test}.dart`.

**Remaining client gaps:** no scroll-to-message on deep link (contract, above); no background sync while the app is terminated (messages arrive as push, and the room catches up on open); the outbox flushes on room open and on send, not on a connectivity-restored signal (`connectivity_plus` is not a dependency and was not added); cache window capped at 200 messages per room; no notification preferences UI, because the backend has no preferences system (D-107). Attachments, typing, presence, read receipts, reactions, threads, search and E2EE remain deliberately unbuilt.

## D-109 · Phase 3B — Web Event Chat client (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean, `next build` succeeds with `/chats`, `/chats/[eventId]` and `/api/realtime-token` emitted, **40 tests passing** (the web app's first automated suite). **No backend, schema, endpoint, SignalR contract or notification payload changed.**

**Decisions:**

- **The access token is exposed to client JS for the SignalR handshake only, via `GET /api/realtime-token`.** A browser WebSocket cannot send an Authorization header, and `/hubs/chat` is `[Authorize]`, so `?access_token=` is the only route in. The session token is httpOnly precisely so page scripts cannot read it, and this narrows that protection — script on the page can now obtain the token, so it survives beyond the tab. It does **not** widen what an attacker could do (the same script could already drive every chat server action as the user), and two things bound the blast radius: the refresh token is never returned, so a stolen access token dies at its own expiry rather than being renewable; and `no-store` keeps it out of every cache including the PWA service worker. **REST is deliberately not routed through this token** — every chat read and write stays in server actions, so the token's only job in the browser is opening the socket.
- **No previous precedent existed and the two apparent ones were misleading.** `login-waiting.tsx` uses `/hubs/login`, which is anonymous by design (AM9). `live-sales-status.tsx` connects to `/hubs/sales` with no token and **never invokes `JoinOrg`** — it renders the connection state as a badge and would fail authorization if it tried to join a group. Neither demonstrates an authenticated hub connection.
- **Business logic lives in a framework-free module (`lib/chat-merge.ts`).** Ordering, de-duplication, cursor selection, optimistic reconciliation, the post-blocked reason and room sorting are pure functions mirroring the Dart implementation one-for-one. Parity between clients is enforced by the code being the same shape, not by two teams remembering the same rules.
- **Desktop UX diverges from Flutter; behaviour does not.** Two-pane layout with a persistent room sidebar, type-to-filter, ↑/↓/Enter room switching, Enter-to-send with Shift+Enter for newlines, right-click moderation, Esc to dismiss. Same endpoints, same `(createdAt, id)` ordering, same `clientMessageId` flow, same capability checks.
- **Every realtime event resolves to a server read**, never a local mutation. `MessageReceived` triggers the `?after=` catch-up; anything else re-reads the room. Capabilities therefore stay server-driven and a missed event self-heals.
- **Chat respects the existing `NEXT_PUBLIC_ENABLE_SIGNALR` flag** (default off), degrading to manual refresh — consistent with the rest of the app's realtime rather than a second policy.
- **Deep linking is the route itself.** Web has no push channel — no FCM, no push subscription; `sw.js` is caching-only — and creating one was out of scope. The in-app notifications feed now links a `notificationType: "chat"` payload to `/chats/{eventId}`, and that URL is shareable. Event → Room is reliable; → specific message is not, for the same contract reason as Flutter.
- **Test infrastructure added, minimal by instruction:** Vitest + React Testing Library + jsdom only. No Jest, Cypress, Playwright or Storybook; no E2E. Tests target what is impractical to verify by hand — capability-driven UI, optimistic reconciliation, cursor paging, envelope forward-compatibility, deep-link routing, keyboard and screen-reader affordances. Browser verification remains an additional manual step, not a thing this replaces.

**Reused, not rebuilt:** `lib/api.ts` axios instance and RFC7807 helpers; the server-action pattern (18 existing `lib/*-actions.ts` files); `requireSession` and the httpOnly cookie session; `@microsoft/signalr` (already a dependency); `@kurx/ui` (`EmptyState`, `ErrorState`, `ListSkeleton`, `Dialog`) and `components/ui/avatar`; `next-themes` light/dark; the `(app)` route group and `app-shell` nav. The only new component is `MessageBubble` — nothing in the design system resembles one.

**Documented debt carried unchanged (not worked around by touching the backend):** `MyChatView.lastActivity` is the *event's* updated-at, so room ordering is approximate — and web, unlike Flutter, has no local message store to improve on it; deep link cannot scroll to a specific message.

**Files:** `lib/{chat-api,chat-actions,chat-merge,use-chat-hub,use-chat-room}.ts`, `app/api/realtime-token/route.ts`, `app/(app)/chats/page.tsx`, `app/(app)/chats/[eventId]/page.tsx`, `components/chat/{message-bubble,message-actions,room-list,chat-room-view}.tsx`, `components/layout/app-shell.tsx` (nav entry), `components/notifications/notifications-feed.tsx` (deep link), `vitest.config.mts`, `test/{setup.ts,chat-logic.test.ts,chat-components.test.tsx}`, `package.json`.

**Remaining web gaps:** no message-list virtualization (the 50-per-page window with capped DOM growth has not needed it; add `@tanstack/react-virtual` only if a long-lived room measurably degrades); no offline cache or outbox — a failed send is retryable in-session but does not survive a reload, which is the deliberate difference from Flutter where the app is expected to be offline; no `⌘K` global room switcher (arrow-key switching covers the sidebar); no web push; no notification preferences, because the backend has none (D-107). Attachments, typing, presence, read receipts, reactions, threads, search and E2EE remain unbuilt by instruction.

## D-110 · Phase 4 — chat attachments: shared upload pipeline, backend (2026-07-19)
**Status: BACKEND ACCEPTED and VERIFIED. Clients NOT built — see "Remaining".** Suite 411 → **432 passing, 0 failed**, container-run against real Postgres. One migration, purely additive.

**The audit found a bug older than chat.** `LocalDiskStorage.PresignPutAsync` returned a URL pointing at `/v1/media/{key}` — **a route that does not exist anywhere in the API**. Every presigned upload the product has ever issued (event media, org verification documents, membership-claim evidence, representation requests) handed the client a URL that 404s. Nothing had ever been uploaded through that path. Attachments could not be built on it, so the fix is infrastructure-level and benefits every caller.

**Decisions:**
- **The receiver is generic, not chat-specific.** `/v1/storage/{key}` (PUT + GET) is registered only when the storage provider is localdisk, and self-disables for real object storage where clients PUT straight to the bucket. No caller — chat included — knows which backend is behind `IStorage`.
- **LocalDisk presigns are now genuinely signed.** Adding a receiver without a signature would have been worse than the bug: an unauthenticated PUT to an arbitrary storage key is an open write primitive. The URL carries an expiry and an HMAC over `key|exp|maxBytes|contentType`, verified in fixed time, and a GET signature can never be replayed as a PUT. That is the guarantee S3 presigning provides, built from the secret the deployment already has.
- **All authoritative validation runs on confirm**, because that is the first moment the server can see the object: ownership, room-scoped key prefix, size, MIME, extension, **magic bytes**, and image dimensions. Presign performs the same checks against client-declared values purely to fail fast — nothing there is trusted.
- **Allow-list, never a deny-list.** Images (JPEG/PNG/GIF/WebP), PDF, OOXML (docx/xlsx/pptx), text/CSV, ZIP. A deny-list of dangerous types loses to every new container or polyglot.
- **Extension must agree with content type**, which is what blocks `invoice.pdf.exe`. Magic bytes must agree with both, which is what stops a PE binary uploaded as `image/png`. Text has no signature, so embedded NULs are the discriminator.
- **The declared content type is re-derived on confirm.** If a client's declaration is wrong but the bytes match some other allowed type, the *bytes* win. Anything matching nothing is refused.
- **`MessageId` is nullable, and that is the reason cleanup exists.** Confirm happens before send, so an upload can outlive the composer that made it. Orphans are swept after a 24h grace window; an upload still travelling toward its send is never pulled out from under the user.
- **`CanUpload` tracks `CanPost`.** Uploading is posting: the same lock, mute, ban and policy gates apply, so there is deliberately no separate upload permission. This changed an assertion in `ChatContractTests` that read `CanUpload == false` — correct while attachments did not exist, wrong once they did.
- **Download URLs are minted per read and short-lived (15 min), never stored.** Membership is re-checked on every mint, so banning a member revokes their access to files they could previously fetch.
- **The receiver always serves `application/octet-stream`.** Letting a stored object choose how a browser interprets it is stored XSS.
- **A message carrying files may have an empty body** — the attachment is the content. A message with neither is still refused.

**Malware scanning — architecture only, no protection.** `IFileScanner` follows the existing provider pattern with `FileScanResult { Clean, Infected, ScanFailed, Unsupported }`. The pipeline **always** calls it, so wiring a real scanner is configuration rather than surgery. `NoOpFileScanner` always returns `Clean` and logs a one-time warning. Any non-`Clean` verdict audits the rejection, deletes the object and refuses the confirm — `Infected` surfaces as 415, `ScanFailed`/`Unsupported` as 503, because nothing is wrong with the request and a retry may succeed. **A real scanner remains a deployment requirement before unrestricted attendee uploads go live in production.**

**Reused, not rebuilt:** `IStorage` (no second storage abstraction); the presign→confirm shape `MediaService` already used; `IReportService` — attachments hang off a message and `chat_message` was already whitelisted, so **reporting needed no change at all**; `IAuditWriter` for rejections and deletions; `NotificationService`/`ChatNotificationJob` — a message with an attachment notifies through the identical path, with **no attachment-specific notification**; Hangfire for the sweep; `SixLabors.ImageSharp`, already a dependency and previously unused anywhere, for dimensions and as a decode check.

**Tests:** `ChatAttachmentTests.cs`, 20 cases — image/PDF/text happy paths with server-extracted dimensions, confirm idempotency, a PE binary renamed `.png` refused, disallowed type refused, extension mismatch refused, oversize refused, binary-as-text refused, non-member refused, cross-room key refused, another user's upload unclaimable, ban revoking URL access, claim-once, empty body with a file, deletion hiding attachments then the sweep removing objects and rows, the orphan grace window, sweep re-run safety, `CanUpload` tracking `CanPost`, and notification compatibility.

**Files:** `Providers/LocalDiskStorage.cs` (signed presigns + delete), `Api/Endpoints/StorageEndpoints.cs` (new), `Abstractions/Providers.cs` (`IFileScanner`), `Providers/NoOpFileScanner.cs` (new), `Chat/AttachmentPolicy.cs` (new), `Domain/Entities/Chat.cs` (`ChatAttachment`), `Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`, `Migrations/20260719120000_AddChatAttachments.cs` (new) + snapshot, `Abstractions/IChatService.cs`, `Chat/ChatService.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/ChatEndpoints.cs`, `Jobs/ChatAttachmentCleanupJob.cs` (new), `DependencyInjection.cs`, `Api/Program.cs`, `Tests/ChatAttachmentTests.cs` (new), `Tests/ChatContractTests.cs` (assertion updated).

**Remaining — the clients are NOT built.** Flutter (image/file picker, upload progress, retry, preview, download) and Web (drag & drop, picker, progress, preview, download) still render `attachments: []` and ignore the array, which is safe but means attachments are backend-only today. Also outstanding: no thumbnail generation (full images are served and the client scales); no real object-storage provider, so uploads stream through the API until S3/R2 is built; no per-room storage quota; and no real malware scanner.

## D-111 · Phase 4B — Flutter chat attachments (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** `flutter analyze` clean (0 errors). Suite 163 → **184 passing, +21 new**; the single failure (`guest_browse_test`) is pre-existing and fails identically on a clean tree. **No backend, contract or schema change.**

**Two dependencies added, and only two:** `file_picker` (documents *and* images through the platform picker — which is why **no `permission_handler` is needed**, the OS grants scoped access to the chosen file) and `url_launcher` (opens the signed URL through the system handler, so **the app never writes to device storage**). Everything else was already present: `dio` supplies `onSendProgress` and `CancelToken`, `Image` + `ResizeImage` + `InteractiveViewer` cover thumbnails and full-screen preview, Hive/`ChatCache` holds pending state, and `KurxFeedback`/`KurxButton`/`ErrorRetry`/design tokens cover the chrome.

**Decisions:**
- **The upload uses a second, injectable Dio.** A presigned URL is absolute and carries its own signature, so it must not receive the app client's base URL or `Authorization` header — with real object storage an unexpected header can invalidate the signature. Making it injectable is also what makes the upload leg testable without a live socket.
- **A pending attachment renders as the thing it will become**, with a progress ring over it, rather than a placeholder that swaps out — so the layout does not jump when the upload confirms.
- **In-flight uploads live outside `messages`, above the composer.** No permanent chat message exists until *both* the upload and the send are confirmed, which is exactly the rule the brief asked for; keeping them out of the message list is what enforces it structurally.
- **A message waits for its attachments.** `flushOutbox` skips any queued message whose attachments are not all confirmed, because a pending attachment has no server id — sending would reference an id the server never issued.
- **Signed URLs are never cached.** They are fetched at the moment of use; the signature expires and the server re-checks room membership on every mint, so a stored URL would fail in a way the user cannot act on.
- **The filename always comes from `ChatAttachmentView.fileName`.** The backend deliberately serves `application/octet-stream` with no `Content-Disposition` (stored-XSS defence, D-110), so there is no header to respect — and the URL is never parsed for a name.
- **The client's content-type guess is explicitly a hint.** An unrecognised extension maps to `application/octet-stream`, which the server's allow-list rejects — an unknown file is refused rather than smuggled through under a plausible-looking type.
- **Image decode is bounded** by `ResizeImage(width: 520)`, so a 25 MB photo is never decoded at full size on the UI thread to fill a 260px thumbnail. The full-screen preview deliberately uses the unresized provider.
- **Server refusals are translated by code**, not swallowed: `file_too_large`, `unsupported_file_type`, `extension_mismatch`, `file_infected`, `scan_unavailable`, `upload_not_allowed`, `upload_not_found` each get their own sentence. "File too large" is actionable; "upload failed" is not.
- **The attach button is not rendered at all when `capabilities.canUpload` is false** — the server's answer, never a local role check — rather than shown and then refused.

**A real bug the tests caught.** Attachment upload status was not persisted through the outbox, so a pending attachment read back after a restart deserialised as `uploaded` and the message would have been sent referencing an unissued id. `attachmentToJson`/`attachmentFromCache` now round-trip `status`, `localPath` and `error`; the signed `url` is still deliberately dropped.

**Tests:** `test/features/social/chat_attachment_test.dart`, 21 cases — mapping (parse, empty-list default, URL never persisted, cache round-trip, filename provenance), upload flow (presign→upload→confirm ordering, refusal surfacing its code, message withheld until attachments confirm, confirmed attachment sent by id and reconciled, offline message staying queued with its file, fresh URL every time), rendering (document tile, unknown type, upload progress, each rejection reason), and accessibility (name+size announced, progress announced, image label, 48dp touch target).

**Files:** `domain/entities/chat_attachment.dart` (new), `domain/entities/chat_message.dart`, `domain/repositories/chat_repository.dart`, `data/models/chat_mappers.dart`, `data/datasources/chat_remote_data_source.dart`, `data/repositories/chat_repository_impl.dart`, `presentation/providers/chat_providers.dart`, `presentation/widgets/chat_attachment_view.dart` (new), `presentation/widgets/chat_message_bubble.dart`, `presentation/pages/chat_room_page.dart`, `pubspec.yaml`, `test/features/social/chat_attachment_test.dart` (new).

**Remaining Flutter gaps:** no in-flight cancel button (the `CancelToken` is plumbed through the repository and controller but no UI triggers it — a failed upload is dismissed instead); an upload interrupted by app death is lost rather than resumed, because only the *message* outbox is persisted, not the bytes; no multi-select (one file per message); no camera capture (`file_picker` reaches the gallery, not the camera — that would need `image_picker`); no thumbnail caching across restarts, since `cached_network_image` was deliberately not added; and downloads are handed to the OS rather than tracked in-app, so there is no download progress or retry inside Kurx.

## D-112 · Phase 4C — Web chat attachments (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED and VERIFIED.** `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean, `next build` succeeds, **86 tests passing (40 → 86)**. **No backend, contract, schema, auth or storage change. No new dependencies.**

**Decisions:**
- **The PUT is browser-direct via `XMLHttpRequest`, not a server action.** `fetch` has no upload-progress event, and XHR additionally gives abort for cancellation. `withCredentials = false` and no interceptor: a presigned URL carries its own signature, and cookies or an `Authorization` header alongside it can invalidate that signature on real object storage. Presign and confirm stay in server actions so the httpOnly session token never reaches the browser — the token is still only ever exposed for the SignalR handshake (D-109).
- **This diverges from the existing `lib/org-actions.ts` upload precedent, deliberately.** That one PUTs from *inside* a server action, so it cannot report progress and double-hops the bytes (browser → Next → API → storage). It was also calling the dead URL that D-110 fixed.
- **Uploads run sequentially.** A chat composer is not a bulk uploader; a serial queue keeps progress legible, bounds memory, and stops a failure scattering across several files.
- **Plain React state, not React Query.** React Query is configured in this app but used nowhere. The chat feature already keeps its state in `useChatRoom`; introducing a second state system for uploads alone would put two sources of truth on one screen. The mutation semantics that matter — sequencing, cancellation, retry, reconciliation — are tested directly against the hook.
- **One pipeline, three sources.** File picker, drag & drop, and clipboard paste all funnel through the same `acceptFiles` → `useAttachmentUploads.add`. **Clipboard paste needed no backend change** — a pasted screenshot arrives as a `File` on the `ClipboardEvent`.
- **Drag depth is counted, not toggled.** `dragenter`/`dragleave` fire for every child element, so a boolean flag flickers the overlay as the pointer crosses inner nodes.
- **Send is gated on `canSend`**, which refuses while anything is queued/uploading/confirming — a message must never become permanent referencing an attachment the server has not confirmed. An empty body with a confirmed file is valid; the attachment is the message.
- **Signed URLs are never cached.** Every download mints a fresh one, because the signature expires and the server re-checks room membership on each mint. Filenames always come from `ChatAttachmentView.fileName` — the backend deliberately serves `application/octet-stream` with no `Content-Disposition` (D-110), and the URL is never parsed.
- **Pending uploads render through the same `AttachmentView`** as confirmed ones, so the layout is identical before and after confirmation and nothing jumps.
- **`next/image` is bypassed for attachments.** Signed, short-lived storage URLs cannot be fetched or cached by the optimizer; `loading="lazy"` + `decoding="async"` give the lazy-load and off-thread decode instead.

**Two real bugs the tests caught, both fixed in the implementation rather than the test:**
1. **`resolveContentType` fell back to the browser-claimed type** for an unrecognised extension, so `payload.exe` reporting `image/png` would have been forwarded as an image — exactly the smuggling the function's own comment claimed to prevent. The fallback is gone: unknown extension ⇒ `application/octet-stream` ⇒ refused by the server's allow-list.
2. **The upload queue could spin forever.** `drain` re-read status from a ref that only refreshes on re-render, so a status written mid-loop was invisible and the same file was re-selected indefinitely (the test suite hung). Progress is now tracked by a set of already-started ids.

**Reused:** `@kurx/ui` (`Dialog`, `EmptyState`, `ErrorState`, `ListSkeleton`), `components/ui/avatar`, the server-action pattern, `lib/api.ts` error helpers, `lib/chat-*` from D-109, Vitest + RTL from D-109, and `lucide-react` icons. New components exist only where nothing equivalent did: `AttachmentView` (with its lightbox) and the upload hook.

**Accessibility:** progress exposed as a real `role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuenow` and an accessible name, not just a spinner; uploading tiles carry `aria-busy`; every action is a real `<button>` reachable by keyboard; the lightbox is `role="dialog" aria-modal`, focuses its close button, closes on Escape, and **restores focus to the trigger**; the hidden file input is `sr-only` with a labelled button in front of it.

**Tests:** 46 new across `test/chat-upload.test.ts` (24 — content-type resolution including the smuggling case, object-URL lifecycle, send gating, error translation, and the XHR transport: no credentials, progress fractions, 413 mapping, abort-as-cancelled) and `test/chat-attachments.test.tsx` (22 — document/image/unknown rendering, fresh-URL-per-download, download failure, lightbox focus management, failure states, accessibility, and hook mutation behaviour: ordering, sequencing, refusal codes, retry, cancel, remove, clear, no-room guard).

**Files:** `lib/chat-api.ts`, `lib/chat-actions.ts`, `lib/chat-upload.ts` (new), `lib/use-attachment-uploads.ts` (new), `lib/use-chat-room.ts`, `components/chat/attachment-view.tsx` (new), `components/chat/message-bubble.tsx`, `components/chat/chat-room-view.tsx`, `test/chat-upload.test.ts` (new), `test/chat-attachments.test.tsx` (new).

**Remaining web gaps:** no resumable or chunked upload — an interrupted large file restarts from zero; no client-side size pre-check, so an oversize file is refused by the server after the presign round trip rather than instantly; no message-list virtualization yet (unchanged from D-109), so a very long history with many images will grow the DOM; no drag-and-drop of a *folder*; and the lightbox has no zoom or multi-image navigation.

## D-113 · Phase 4D — Event Chat production-readiness audit (2026-07-19)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Audit of backend + Flutter + Web. Four defects found and fixed, three doc conflicts corrected, three dead exports removed. Backend **434 passing** (432 → 434), Flutter social **58 passing**, Web **86 passing**. No architecture or public contract changed.

**Defects found and fixed:**

1. **Every attachment displayed a GUID instead of its filename** (High, user-facing, both clients). Presign validated the client's `fileName` and then discarded it; the storage key was `chat/{roomId}/{guid:N}`, and confirm derived `FileName` from `Path.GetFileName(storageKey)` — so it recovered the GUID. Fixed by carrying the sanitized name as the key's final segment (`chat/{roomId}/{guid:N}/{safeName}`), which needs **no contract change** because confirm already reads the name from the key. The GUID segment still guarantees uniqueness and `SanitizeFileName` has already stripped every path character, so the client still cannot influence where bytes land. Regression-locked by two tests, including one asserting a traversal-shaped filename cannot escape the room prefix.

2. **A provably-dead query on every attachment confirm** (Medium). Confirm queried `chat_attachments` for the declared content type *after* an early return had already proven no such row exists, so the result was always null. Removed; the bytes were authoritative regardless.

3. **`GetMyChatsAsync` was 3N queries** (High, and worse than when first flagged in D-104: the `LastReadMessageId` change in D-104 added a second per-room query on top of the existing two). A user in 20 rooms issued ~60 queries to paint one screen. Rewritten as two set-based queries plus in-memory grouping. The list badge now counts from the mark's timestamp rather than the `(CreatedAt, Id)` pair, which can differ only by messages sharing that exact instant — an acceptable trade for a list badge, and `GetRoomAsync` still counts exactly when the room is opened.

4. **Client error-code parity gap** (Low). Web translated `forbidden` and an interrupted-network case; Flutter fell through to the generic message for both. Flutter now handles the same set, so the same server code reads the same way on both platforms.

**Doc conflicts corrected** (live docs only — `DECISIONS.md` is an append-only log and its point-in-time entries were left intact, since D-108 already carries the correction):
- `docs/architecture/chat.md` still described attachments as DEFERRED with no table.
- `docs/api/chat-api.md` still said the `attachments` array is "always empty until attachments ship".
- `docs/EXTERNAL_SERVICES_AND_PROVIDERS.md` still claimed no SignalR client exists in mobile.

**Dead code removed:** `MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES`, `newLocalId` and `allSettled` were exported from `web/lib/chat-upload.ts` and used nowhere. `newLocalId` was inlined into its single caller.

**Verified clean — no change needed:** no TODO/FIXME/HACK anywhere in chat code on any platform; every error code `ChatService` produces is mapped in `ChatEndpoints`; no duplicated upload logic (one pipeline per client, three sources on web funnel through it); resource disposal correct on both clients (hub, subscriptions, abort controllers, object URLs); `LoadAttachmentsAsync` is one query plus CPU-only presigning, not an N+1.

**Known-and-accepted, unchanged by this audit:** the chat-specific 10/60s rate limit is still WS-only so the REST send path runs at the generic 300/min tier; the `rate_limited` branch in `ChatEndpoints.Fail` remains unreachable; sticky sessions remain unconfigured for the Redis backplane; `MyChatView.LastActivity` is still the event's updated-at; there is still no real malware scanner behind `IFileScanner`; no real object-storage provider, so uploads stream through the API; and no message-list virtualization on web.

## D-114

**Authentication workstream frozen with three open defects, rather than patched at audit time (AM0–AM10 handover).**

The AM0–AM10 trusted-device authentication workstream is **feature complete** on backend and web:
every planned rail (OTP, device key, WebAuthn), mechanism (PoP refresh, session families, challenge
purposes, step-up, recovery, risk engine, signing-key FSM, KMS, secrets, telemetry) and endpoint is
implemented and covered by 79 auth integration tests. `dotnet build` is 0/0. The full handover is
`docs/AUTHENTICATION_HANDOVER.md`, which is the reference for the deployment, hardware-validation,
AM23 and rollout phases.

It is **not declared defect-free.** The closing audit found three mismatches in which
*documentation claims a protection the implementation does not provide* — the shape of defect most
likely to cause harm, because it produces false confidence during precisely the deployment phase
that follows:

1. **`OTP_PEPPER` is not enforced.** `OtpService` falls back to a pepper literal published in this
   repository; `RequiredSecrets.Names` validates only `JWT_SECRET`. A production deploy that omits
   the pepper defeats it silently, with no error and no log.
2. **ADR-AM14 (Redis mandatory, fail-closed) was never implemented** — DI falls back to an in-memory
   cache silently. Impact is narrower than the ADR assumed: auth uses no `IDistributedCache`, so all
   durable anti-abuse state is in Postgres and correct across instances. The real gap is the
   in-process HTTP rate limiter, giving N× the configured limit across N tasks, partially mitigated
   by the WAF's global per-IP limit on `/v1/auth/*`.
3. **`AUTH_TRUSTED_DEVICE` is dead configuration.** No code reads it; the endpoints are mapped
   unconditionally. Source comments and the migration still describe the rail as "inert until" the
   flag — false, and a deployer trusting them would believe they can deploy with the rail disabled.

**Why they were not fixed here.** (1) and (3) are each about a one-line change, but both alter
startup or deployment behaviour — adding `OTP_PEPPER` to the required set makes a prod deploy
without it refuse to boot — and landing that unannounced at the end of an audit, immediately before
a deployment phase, trades a silent-config risk for a boot-failure risk without the owner choosing.
(2) is a genuine architecture question: implement the enforcement, or retire ADR-AM14 with its own
entry. All three need a decision, not a patch.

**Documentation was corrected where it was actively misleading** — `.env.example` now states plainly
that the flag is inert, that the pepper is unenforced, and that Redis falls back silently — and
`docs/api/README.md` gained the full trusted-device, passkey, push-approval, step-up, recovery and
JWKS contracts, which previously existed only as rationale inside this file. The missing
`OTEL_*` variables were added to `.env.example`.

**ES256 issuance remains OFF and is not enabled here.** It is off by call graph, not by flag:
`TokenService.CreateAccessTokenAsync` has zero callers. Cut-over is a code change at four call
sites, gated on nine conditions listed in the handover §8 — most importantly that KMS protection is
confirmed live first, since ES256 issuance against unprotected keys would be strictly worse than the
HS256 status quo.

**Recommended sequence:** resolve (1) and (3), decide (2), re-run the full suite with no concurrent
run active, then freeze → infrastructure deployment → Android hardware validation → AM23 → rollout.
Findings (1) and (2) should be fed into AM23 as known inputs rather than left for it to rediscover.

## D-115

**OTP_PEPPER made fail-closed; AUTH_TRUSTED_DEVICE removed as dead configuration.**

Two of the three defects recorded in D-114, resolved in the authentication freeze pass.

### OTP_PEPPER — silent fallback removed

`OtpService` resolved the pepper as `config["OTP_PEPPER"]` with a fallback to the literal
`"dev-only-otp-pepper-change-me"`, which is committed to this repository. A deployment that omitted
the variable therefore hashed every OTP under a **publicly known pepper**, and did so *silently* —
OTP issuance and verification both worked perfectly, so nothing in behaviour, logs or monitoring
would ever reveal it. The pepper's only purpose is to make a leaked `otp_codes` table useless
without a server-side secret; under the fallback it provided none of that.

Three changes, layered so no single mistake reintroduces it:

1. **`OtpService` resolves the pepper through `ISecretProvider.GetRequiredAsync`, with no fallback.**
   It throws rather than hash under a guessable key — issuing a code under a known pepper is worse
   than not issuing one. Reading through the provider rather than `IConfiguration` also matters
   under `SECRETS_PROVIDER=aws`: startup validation reads Secrets Manager, so point-of-use must read
   the same source or the validation proves nothing about what the code actually uses.
   (`IConfiguration` is still injected for the SNS DLT routing ids, which are configuration, not
   secrets.)
2. **`OTP_PEPPER` added to `RequiredSecrets.Names`**, so Production refuses to start without it —
   a boot failure naming the secret, caught by the deployment pipeline before traffic is routed,
   rather than a silent security downgrade.
3. **The dev value is now explicit configuration** — set in `.env.example`, `docker-compose.yml` and
   the test host — instead of a hidden code default. Local zero-config is preserved, but the
   convenience is *visible*: a reader can see what pepper their environment uses, and a production
   environment that inherits nothing gets nothing.

The general rule this encodes: **a secret whose absence degrades security without degrading
behaviour must be validated at startup**, because nothing later in the system will notice.

### AUTH_TRUSTED_DEVICE — removed

The flag was read by **no code path**. All trusted-device endpoints were mapped unconditionally at
`Program.cs:345-352`, yet `.env.example`, the domain entities, the DbContext, the AM0 migration and
the design dossier all described the tables and rails as "inert until `AUTH_TRUSTED_DEVICE`".

Removed rather than implemented. Trusted-device authentication *is* the authentication system now,
not a mode of it: the rails are additive, tested (79 integration tests) and already the only path
for device enrollment, push-approval login, step-up and recovery. Implementing the gate would mean
building a kill switch nobody had asked for, for a system already depended upon — and a flag that
has never once been exercised is not a safety mechanism, only the appearance of one. Retaining a
dead flag is strictly worse than having none: it invites an operator to "disable" the rails during
an incident and conclude they are safe when nothing has changed.

Corrected: `.env.example` (flag deleted, with a note to drop it from carried-forward files), the
comments in `AuthIdentity.cs`, `KurxDbContext.cs` and the AM0 migration, and a superseded banner on
`KURX_AUTH_REARCHITECTURE_DOSSIER.md` (now `docs/history/architecture/`; it also still claimed "no implementation yet").
`docs/DECISIONS.md` point-in-time entries were left intact — it is an append-only log.

## D-116

**ADR-AM14 (Redis mandatory, fail-closed) is superseded for durable state; the distributed rate limiter remains open work.**

ADR-AM14 ratified Redis as mandatory — fail-closed in production — for challenges, OTP, replay
protection, rate limiting, locks, session cache and approval state. The implementation does not
match, and `DependencyInjection.cs` silently falls back to `AddDistributedMemoryCache()` when
`REDIS_CONNECTION` is unset. D-114 recorded this as an open defect. Resolving it required deciding
which of the two is right, and the honest answer is: **each is right about a different half.**

**Superseded — durable auth state belongs in Postgres, not Redis.** Auth services use no
`IDistributedCache` at all. Challenges, OTP codes and attempt caps, single-use/replay enforcement,
session records and approval state all live in Postgres tables. That is **better** than the ADR's
design, not a shortfall from it: this state is security-critical and audited, and Redis is an
eviction-capable cache whose memory pressure could silently drop a replay guard or an attempt
counter. Losing a rate-limit counter degrades a defence; losing single-use enforcement on a
challenge is an authentication bypass. Postgres is also shared across instances, so this state is
already correct under autoscaling — the property the ADR wanted Redis for. **ADR-AM14 is superseded
for this scope; no work is planned to move it to Redis.**

**Still valid — the HTTP rate limiter is genuinely per-instance.** ASP.NET's `PartitionedRateLimiter`
holds counters in process memory. Across the 2–10 Fargate tasks the infrastructure provisions
(D-104a), the effective limit is **N× the configured value**, and it moves as autoscaling moves.
Partially mitigated by the WAF's per-IP rate limit on `/v1/auth/*`, which is global — so this is a
weakened defence layer, not an open door, and the service-level caps in Postgres (OTP attempts,
resend cooldown, per-destination limits) are unaffected and remain exact.

**Future direction, deliberately not implemented here** (the freeze pass excluded infrastructure
work): back the rate limiter with Redis so limits are global, and fail closed in production when
`REDIS_CONNECTION` is absent. Redis is already provisioned by the Terraform (it backs the SignalR
backplane), so this is application wiring, not new infrastructure. It should be scoped **after**
staging deployment, where the real per-instance limit can be measured rather than assumed, and it is
carried into AM23 as a known input rather than left for the review to rediscover. Until then,
`.env.example` states the fallback behaviour plainly instead of claiming an enforcement that does
not exist.

## D-114 · Phase 5 — Presence, typing and read receipts: backend (2026-07-19)
**Status: BACKEND ACCEPTED and VERIFIED. Clients NOT built — see "Remaining".** Suite 434 → **447 passing, 0 failed**. No schema change, no migration, no change to attachments, upload, storage, scanning, moderation or auth.

**The audit found the foundation was broken, and fixing it fixed a live production defect.** `ChatHub` had no `OnDisconnectedAsync` and the D-106 connection registry had no reverse index, relying on a **12-hour TTL**. A closed browser therefore looked online for half a day — and because the D-107 notification fan-out reads that same registry to decide who is offline, **those users' push notifications were suppressed for up to 12 hours**. Presence could not be built on it, and the push defect existed independently.

**Decisions:**
- **`IPresenceService` decides availability once.** Redis-backed when `REDIS_CONNECTION` is set, a null-object `PresenceDisabledService` otherwise. Callers ask `IsEnabled`; **nothing else in the codebase checks for Redis**. Enabling presence later is a deployment change, not a code change.
- **No process-local state anywhere.** No static collection, no singleton registry, no per-server cache. A process-local fallback would be *wrong* the moment a second instance ran — reporting users offline who are connected elsewhere — and would make dev diverge from production. Being cleanly absent beats being confidently incorrect.
- **The reverse index is the load-bearing piece.** `chat:conn-rooms:{connId}` records what a connection joined, so disconnect knows what to clean. Without it, cleanup is impossible and the TTL becomes the cleanup mechanism — which is exactly the bug.
- **TTL reduced from 12 hours to 120 seconds, and demoted to a crash backstop.** Normal cleanup is `ReleaseAsync` from the disconnect handler; the TTL only matters when a process dies without running it. A `Heartbeat()` hub method refreshes it. That is a liveness ping, **not polling** — presence *state* is only ever pushed as an event.
- **Offline is announced only when the last connection goes.** Connections are refcounted per (room, user), so a second tab or device keeps someone online. `SADD`'s return value gates the online event, so a re-join of an already-registered connection does **not** re-announce — that was a real bug the tests caught, and it is precisely the reconnect flicker the requirement forbids.
- **Everything is idempotent.** Duplicate track cannot inflate the count; repeated release finds nothing and announces nothing, so a retried disconnect or a crashed-mid-cleanup server cannot emit a spurious offline.
- **Typing is broadcast-only.** No table, no Redis key, no push, no audit — it exists only while the socket does. Posting capability is re-checked server-side on every typing event, so a muted, banned or read-only member cannot advertise typing they could not finish. A `ttlSeconds` in the payload lets receivers clear the indicator even if the "stopped" event is lost.
- **Read receipts reuse the existing persisted pointer entirely.** No new table, no new column, no per-message write. `MarkReadAsync` was already monotonic and server-validated; it now broadcasts `ReadReceiptChanged` **only when the pointer actually advances**, so duplicate or out-of-order marks cost one read and no write. Read receipts therefore keep working when presence is disabled — they do not depend on it.
- **The three capabilities are independent**, as required: typing never implies online, receipts never imply typing, online never depends on receipts.
- **Eviction and notification suppression now read the same registry** presence maintains, so they can never disagree about who holds a socket. Banning a user forgets them immediately rather than letting them linger until TTL.

**Distributed-ready by construction.** Every fact lives in Redis; the hub broadcasts through the existing `IRealtimeBroadcaster`, which fans out over the backplane. Enabling multi-instance requires no Presence change — no code here assumes a single server.

**New realtime events** (existing envelope, so old clients ignore them safely): `PresenceChanged { userId, online }`, `TypingChanged { userId, userName, isTyping, ttlSeconds }`, `ReadReceiptChanged { userId, lastReadMessageId }`. `ChatRoomView` additionally carries `OnlineUserIds` and `PresenceEnabled`, so a client can tell "nobody is here" apart from "we cannot know".

**Tests:** `ChatPresenceTests.cs`, 13 cases run against a real Redis — first connection, second device not re-announcing, idempotent re-track, one device leaving while another remains, disconnect cleaning every joined room, double release, unknown release, per-user independence, connection listing for eviction, immediate forget on ban, heartbeat, and the disabled service reporting nothing. Two bugs were caught by these: the reconnect re-announce above, and a test-isolation flaw that only existed because real SignalR ids are unique.

**Files:** `Application/Abstractions/IPresenceService.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Presence/RedisPresenceService.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Presence/PresenceDisabledService.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, `Api/Hubs/ChatHub.cs`, `Api/Realtime/SignalRBroadcaster.cs`, `Infrastructure/Jobs/ChatNotificationJob.cs`, `Infrastructure/Chat/ChatService.cs`, `Application/Abstractions/IChatService.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/ChatPresenceTests.cs` (new).

**Remaining — the clients are NOT built.** Flutter and Web ignore the three new events, which is safe by contract (unknown types are dropped) but means no online dots, typing banner or receipt ticks are visible yet. Also outstanding: no "last seen" timestamp (presence is binary while connected); typing has no per-room fan-out cap, so a very large room broadcasts one event per typist; and presence requires Redis in production, which is now an explicit operational dependency rather than an optional optimisation.

## D-117

**Authentication UI wired up: five orphaned mobile screens, the web push-approval entry point, and the mobile device-key rail were unreachable.**

The freeze-phase UI audit asked a question the module work never had: not "is the screen built?" but
"can a user get to it?" The answer was no, across both clients. Nothing here is a new feature; it is
exposure of capabilities already implemented, tested, and shipped dark.

**Flutter — five complete screens with zero references anywhere in the codebase.**
`ApproveLoginPage`, `LoginWaitingPage`, `RecoveryPage`, `SecurityPage` and `StepUpPage` compiled (so
no build caught them) but were never routed or pushed. Routed as `/approvals`, `/login/waiting`,
`/recover`, `/settings/security`, plus a Security entry in Settings.

`/approvals` is deliberately **not** under `/login`: the router redirect treats any `/login*` location
as the login flow and bounces authenticated users out — but the approving device is by definition
already signed in, so nesting it there would have made it permanently unreachable.

**Flutter — `enrollThisDevice` had no callers at all.** The single entry point to the entire
device-key rail was missing, so on mobile no user could enroll a device, and therefore none could
approve a sign-in or complete a step-up. Added as "Set up this device" in the Security screen, shown
only when this handset is not already enrolled.

**Flutter — this device's id was never persisted.** `enrollThisDevice` returned it and dropped it.
Approving and stepping up must name which device is signing, and those screens open from a push
notification, possibly before any list request has run — so it is written to `TokenStore` after the
server confirms enrollment (never before, or a failed verify leaves an id that signs nothing) and
cleared on revocation. It deliberately survives sign-out: the enrollment is a property of the
hardware, not the session, and clearing it would orphan a keystore key still registered server-side.

**Flutter — the step-up gate was a dead end.** Generating recovery codes returns `403
step_up_required` for any user who *can* step up, and the screen said "confirm it's you first"
without offering the screen that does it — failing precisely the users the gate protects. The 403 now
pushes `StepUpPage` and retries once; a second 403 reports an error rather than looping.

**Web — `login-waiting.tsx` was rendered by nothing.** The push-approval rail (AM4) was fully built,
including the SignalR accelerator and match-number display, with no entry point. Added "Approve on a
trusted device" to the login panel, gated on a complete number exactly as the passkey option is. The
waiting screen replaces the panel while it runs, so the user cannot start a second competing sign-in.

**Admin — no page added, by design.** Auth activity is already visible: all ten auth services write
`audit_log`, surfaced by the existing Audit page (D-062) — logins, device enrollment, passkey
registration, recovery, revocations. What has no admin surface is the `security_events` stream, and
that is deliberate: it has no read endpoint and is consumed by the RiskEngine and by CloudWatch
alarms (D-100/D-104a) — an operator concern ("is the platform under attack?"), not an
application-administrator one ("what did this user do?"). Inventing a portal page over a stream
nobody has asked to read would add a surface to secure and maintain for no stated need.

**Test note:** the enrollment change made the repository touch secure storage, which has no plugin in
the Flutter test host. The channel is mocked with an in-memory map rather than faking `TokenStore`
out, so the tests still exercise the production store.

## D-118 · Phase 5B — Presence on Flutter: online, typing and read receipts (2026-07-19)

**Numbering note:** D-114 is used twice — by the auth workstream (freeze) and by chat (presence backend). Both are real and neither is renumbered here, because the log is append-only and other documents already cite them. The two concurrent workstreams need to agree a band split; chat continues at D-118 to avoid a third collision.

Flutter now renders the presence rail D-114 (chat) built. No backend, SignalR or API contract was touched.

**Decisions:**

- **One presence state, inside the existing chat state.** `ChatRoomState` gained `onlineUserIds`, `typing`, `readPointers` and `presenceEnabled`. No presence controller, no widget-local maps. Widgets render derived state (`typistsExcept`, `isOnline`, `highestReadByOthers`) and never accumulate their own.
- **Presence is never inferred locally.** A message arriving does not mark its sender online, and nothing polls. `PresenceChanged` is the only writer of the roster — a test asserts exactly this, because "obviously they're connected, they just posted" is the tempting wrong answer.
- **`presenceEnabled` distinguishes "nobody here" from "we cannot know".** With presence disabled the dot is not rendered at all rather than rendered grey, so a Redis-less deployment never displays everyone as offline.
- **Typing expires on the receiver.** Each entry carries the server's `ttlSeconds` as an expiry; a lost "stopped" event cannot strand an indicator. The prune timer runs only while somebody is typing, so an idle room holds no timers. Typing is never persisted and never restored after a restart.
- **Typing is debounced to two events per burst** — one `started`, one `stopped` after a 3s pause or on send — instead of one per keystroke.
- **Read pointers only move forward.** Server ids are UUIDv7, so the lexical compare that rejects a stale or replayed receipt is a time compare. One room-level pointer settles every bubble; no per-message read state is stored.
- **Losing the socket clears presence, not read receipts.** Stale dots would be fabricated presence; already-read is still true. Reconnect re-reads the roster from `GET /v1/events/{id}/chat` rather than trusting what was held during the gap.
- **A dot or a tick never rebuilds the message list.** The page watches a `_RoomView` record that deliberately excludes presence; the avatar dot, read tick, typing banner and header subtitle each subscribe to one derived value via `select`.
- **Heartbeat every 45s** against the server's 120s TTL. Not polling — presence *state* only ever arrives pushed; the heartbeat exists so the TTL can stay short enough to recover from a crashed process.

**Defect found and fixed while testing:** `ChatRoomController` wrote `state` and read `_ref` after disposal in `_init`, `_loadLatest`, `_connect` and `_flush`. Under `autoDispose` this throws whenever a user leaves a room mid-load — it surfaced as cross-test pollution, but it is a production crash path, not a test artifact. Every continuation past an `await` now re-checks `mounted`.

**Tests:** Flutter 184 → **200 passing** (16 new in `test/features/social/chat_presence_test.dart`). The one failure, `test/core/guest_browse_test.dart`, is pre-existing and unrelated — verified against a clean tree.

**Not built:** web presence (Phase 5C), reactions, search, threads, E2EE, notification preferences, quiet hours.

## D-119 · Phase 5C — Presence on web: online, typing and read receipts (2026-07-19)

Web now renders the same presence rail as Flutter (D-118) against the same backend (D-114 chat). No backend, SignalR, API, schema, auth, notification or attachment change.

**Audit finding — the brief's premise did not match the code.** The phase asked to "extend the existing chat store (Zustand)". There is no chat Zustand store: `store/ui.ts` is the only Zustand store in the app, and chat state lives in the `useChatRoom` hook (`useState` + refs). Introducing a store now would mean rewriting working state and running two sources of truth during the migration. `useChatRoom` **is** the centralized chat state, so it was extended instead — which satisfies the actual requirement (one state, no component-local presence maps, derived selectors only) without a rewrite nobody asked for.

**Decisions:**

- **Presence lives in `lib/chat-presence.ts` as pure reducers and selectors**, held in one `PresenceState` inside `useChatRoom`. No `PresenceStore`, no context, no per-component maps. Parity with Flutter is verifiable by reading that one file against `chat_providers.dart` rather than diffing two component trees.
- **Presence events are applied locally and never trigger a refetch.** The existing dispatcher resolved *every* non-message event to `refresh()` (room + messages). Presence events routed through that would have turned every keystroke in the room into two round trips per participant. They are now intercepted before that branch; unknown types still fall through to the self-healing refetch.
- **The zod room schema had to gain `onlineUserIds` and `presenceEnabled`.** Zod strips unknown keys, so the server was already sending them and the client was silently discarding them. Both are `.default()`ed, so an older server simply reports presence as unavailable.
- **Reducers return the same object when nothing changed** (duplicate presence event, stale receipt, sweep with nothing expired). In React that identity is what stops a re-render, so the rule that prevents flicker on Flutter prevents wasted renders here.
- **`MessageBubble` is memoised and receives presence as three primitives** (`senderOnline`, `presenceKnown`, `read`) rather than the presence state. A presence event re-renders the room, and the memo then repaints only the bubbles whose own values changed — typically none for typing, two when a read pointer moves. This is the React equivalent of Flutter's `select`.
- **Read is a different glyph, not a different colour** (`CheckCheck` vs `Check`, labelled "Read"/"Sent"), so the state survives greyscale, colour-blindness and a screen reader.
- **The typing banner is a permanently-mounted `aria-live` region** that empties rather than unmounting — remounting a live region makes some screen readers miss the next announcement. Dots respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; the label alone carries the meaning.
- **Losing the socket clears online and typing, never read receipts**, and reconnect re-reads the roster (`syncRoster` replaces outright) instead of trusting what was held during the gap.
- **Typing is debounced to one `started` + one `stopped` per burst**, suppressed entirely when `presenceEnabled` is false, and stopped on send and on unmount — otherwise closing a tab mid-word leaves the room believing you are still typing until the TTL expires.

**Tests:** web 86 → **120 passing** (34 new across `test/chat-presence.test.tsx` and `test/chat-presence-room.test.tsx`). `next build` and `next lint` clean.

**Limitations (unchanged by this phase):** no message-list virtualization, so a very long room still renders every bubble — memoisation bounds the presence cost but not the initial mount; presence requires Redis server-side and is absent, not degraded, without it; typing is not shown in the room list, only inside an open room.

## D-120 · Phase 5D — Event Chat milestone closure, parity fixes and decision-log governance (2026-07-19)

Consolidation only: no new product capability. Backend **447 passing**, Flutter **201 passing** (one pre-existing unrelated failure), web **121 passing**.

### Two genuine parity defects, found and fixed

**Flutter left presence frozen on a dropped socket.** `ChatHubClient` registered `onreconnected` but never `onclose` or `onreconnecting`, and the event stream does not error on a normal close — so nothing observed the disconnect. `live` stayed `true` and every online dot and typing indicator stayed on screen for as long as the room was open. That is precisely the fabricated presence D-114 forbids, and web already handled it correctly. The client now exposes a `disconnected` stream; the controller clears presence and drops `live`, and a successful roster re-read restores it.

**Web refetched the room on any unrecognised event.** The dispatcher resolved everything that was not `MessageReceived` to `refresh()` (room + messages). Correct for today's room-level events, wrong as a default: a future server-first event type — which the envelope contract explicitly allows (D-104) — would have become two requests per participant per event on every older client. Room-level events are now enumerated and anything else is ignored, matching Flutter and the contract.

### Cleanup
