## D-213 · Fixed a `DefaultTabController` length regression introduced by D-212 (2026-07-31)

**Context.** An independent verification pass counted the actual `Tab` widgets D-212 added to
`event_manage_detail_page.dart` and found `DefaultTabController(length: 13, ...)` while the
`TabBar` declared 14 `Tab` widgets and `TabBarView` declared 14 children (7 original tabs + 7
added: Team, Attendees, Check-in, Invitations, Announcements, Analytics, Certificates — one more
than the "6" the fix was mentally counted as while writing it). `docs/DECISIONS.md`'s own D-212
entry repeated the same wrong number ("7 → 13"), confirming a single consistent counting mistake,
not a transcription slip between code and doc.

**Impact.** `TabBar`/`TabBarView` assert their tab/child count against `TabController.length`; a
mismatch throws in debug/profile builds — every organizer's Event Manage screen would have failed
to open, for every event, not just the newly-added tabs. `org_detail_page.dart`'s equivalent
change (4 → 6 tabs) was independently re-counted and confirmed correct — this was isolated to the
one file.

**Fix.** `length: 13` → `length: 14`, verified against two independent automated counts (`grep -o
"Tab(text:" | wc -l` and a count of the `TabBarView` children's labeling comments) rather than a
third manual recount, precisely to avoid repeating the same counting mistake a third time.
`docs/DECISIONS.md`'s D-212 entry corrected to match.

**Why this wasn't caught earlier.** Zero widget-test coverage exists for `EventManageDetailPage` —
confirmed by grepping `mobile/test/` for the class name. `flutter analyze` cannot catch this class
of bug: a hardcoded integer is syntactically valid regardless of whether it matches a sibling
list's length, so static analysis has no signal to flag. `flutter test`'s passing suite was
consequently not evidence this specific page worked, only that no *covered* code path regressed —
a distinction worth stating plainly rather than letting "tests pass" imply more than it does. No
new test was added for this specific invariant in this fix, matching the verification-only scope
of the pass that found it; recorded here as a real, disclosed gap (an assertion on
`tabController.length == tabWidgets.length` would catch this class of bug if it recurs) rather
than silently closed.

**Files.** `mobile/lib/features/organizer/presentation/pages/event_manage_detail_page.dart`,
`docs/DECISIONS.md` (D-212's tab count corrected).

## D-214 · Mobile checkout was unreachable — `TicketTypeTile.onBook` was never wired, and its dead-code stub sat alongside it (2026-07-31)

**Context.** A full-codebase read-through (backend, admin, web, mobile, and every `.claude`/`docs`
markdown file) found that `event_detail_page.dart` constructed `TicketTypeTile(ticket: t)` with no
`onBook` callback — the tile's own `tappable = onBook != null && !ticket.soldOut` guard was
consequently always `false`, so no ticket type on any event's detail page was ever tappable. A
real, working `checkout_page.dart` already existed (calls the real `POST
/v1/events/{eventId}/orders`, settles free tickets inline, and deliberately stops before creating
an order for a priced ticket while the payment gateway is mock) with a registered `go_router` route
(`/events/:slug/checkout/:eventId/:ticketTypeId`) that nothing in the app ever pushed to.

**Fixed.** Wired the callback: `onBook: () => context.push('/events/${page.detail.slug}/checkout/
${page.detail.id}/${t.id}')`. Free tickets now check out end-to-end from a tap on the event detail
page; a priced ticket type reaches the same screen and stops there with an explanation — exactly
the behavior `checkout_page.dart` was already built to provide (D-070's mock-gateway stop, not a
new restriction). Also deleted `book_register_page.dart` — the superseded stub `checkout_page.dart`
had replaced (hardcoded ₹500 placeholder price, a `// TODO: navigate to checkout/order-summary
(SECURITY STOP — D-061)` snackbar-only button) — and its route (`/events/:slug/book/:ticketTypeId`)
and now-unused import in `app_router.dart`. It had the identical reachability problem and, unlike
`checkout_page.dart`, nothing behind it actually worked. Dropped a stale doc comment on
`TicketType` claiming "purchasing has no backend yet (D-019)" — it does, and the client can now
reach it.

**Cross-reference.** `D-212`'s Files section also lists this same deletion — its repository-wide
dead-code sweep found the identical orphaned file independently, in parallel with this fix, and
its prose doesn't mention `onBook`/`checkout`. This entry is the one that documents *why* the
screen was dead (the missing callback wiring) and the corresponding checkout fix; D-212 did not
touch `event_detail_page.dart`.

**Test.** `mobile/test/features/events/event_detail_page_test.dart` gained a widget test that taps
a ticket tile against a real `GoRouter` (mirroring `transfer_claim_page_test.dart`'s pattern — a
bare `Navigator` wouldn't exercise `context.push`) and asserts it lands on the checkout route with
the correct event and ticket-type ids — the regression this exact bug would reintroduce if the
callback were ever dropped again.

**Files.** `mobile/lib/features/events/presentation/pages/event_detail_page.dart`,
`mobile/lib/features/events/domain/entities/ticket_type.dart` (stale comment removed), deleted
`mobile/lib/features/events/presentation/pages/book_register_page.dart`,
`mobile/lib/core/router/app_router.dart` (dead route + import removed),
`mobile/test/features/events/event_detail_page_test.dart` (new test).

**Verification.** `flutter analyze` on the touched files: 0 issues (full-repo baseline unaffected).
`flutter test test/features/events/event_detail_page_test.dart`: 2/2 passing (the pre-existing
render test plus the new tap-to-checkout test).

**Consequences.** Free-ticket checkout is reachable end-to-end on mobile for the first time. This
narrows the `docs/roadmap/README.md` "client parity" gap: its payment-checkout line described the
D-070 gateway stop, without distinguishing that *reachability* — not just payment — was broken.
Paid checkout remains deliberately stopped pending a real payment gateway, unchanged by this fix.

## D-215 · Login OTP storage moved off unsalted SHA-256 onto the HMAC-peppered `IOtpService` substrate, with the login contract deliberately unchanged (2026-08-01)

**Context.** Two OTP systems have coexisted since AM1. The hardened platform (`OtpService`,
ADR-A4, D-115) stores codes in `otp_codes` as `HMACSHA256(OTP_PEPPER)` with a `PepperVersion`
column for rotation, and is used by password reset, account recovery and email verification. The
legacy path (`AuthService.RequestOtpAsync`/`VerifyOtpAsync`) stored codes in `otp_requests` as
`TokenService.Sha256(code)` — a **plain, unsalted, un-peppered** digest. `OtpService`'s own header
recorded the intent to converge ("nothing cuts over until the client migration, AM9"), but the
cut-over never happened, and the legacy path is what `POST /v1/auth/otp/request|verify` calls —
i.e. the primary and only login for web (`web/lib/api.ts`), admin (`admin/lib/api.ts`) and mobile
(`auth_remote_data_source.dart`).

**Problem.** An OTP is a six-digit code, so its entire keyspace is 10⁶. An unsalted SHA-256 over
that space is fully precomputable in about a second on commodity hardware, which makes
`otp_requests.CodeHash` **functionally plaintext** to anyone who can read the table — a database
dump, a backup, a read replica, or SQL injection. The consequence is account takeover for every
user with a login in flight. This is precisely the failure mode `OTP_PEPPER` was introduced to
prevent (D-115), and it was already recorded as finding **C5** ("`otp_requests` is unsalted") in
`docs/history/architecture/KURX_AUTH_REARCHITECTURE_DOSSIER.md` — but that document is archived, so
the finding had fallen out of every live tracking file, including `docs/roadmap/README.md`, which
declares itself the canonical build-status authority. Worth naming plainly: refresh tokens are
hashed with the same unsalted `Sha256` helper and that is fine, because they are 48 random bytes.
Unsalted hashing protects a high-entropy secret and does nothing for a six-digit one; the OTP was
the single credential in the system where the construction was actually broken.

**Decision.** `AuthService` now delegates the OTP code lifecycle — minting, peppered hashing,
storage, TTL, attempt cap and single-use consumption — to `IOtpService`, under
`OtpPurpose.PhoneVerification`. `otp_requests` is no longer written or read by the login path.
`AuthService` retains everything that constitutes the endpoint's *contract*: phone normalization
(`NormalizePhone`), the per-IP hourly shield, user provisioning, the ban/suspend check, the audit
row, token issuance, and the concurrent-first-login merge (D-037).

**Rationale — why the policy did not come with the substrate.** `IOtpService` bundles two
separable things: a security substrate (CSPRNG, peppered storage, TTL, attempt cap) and a stricter
*policy* (E.164 validation via libphonenumber, a 30-second resend cooldown). Only the substrate was
defective. Adopting the policy wholesale was attempted first and produced two distinct regressions,
both caught by the integration suite before merge:

1. `PhoneCanonicalizer.TryToE164` runs libphonenumber's `IsValidNumber`, whereas the legacy
   `NormalizePhone` never validated at all. Routing login through it made **any number
   libphonenumber considers invalid unable to log in** — 43 tests failed, and the real-world
   equivalent is locking out users whose numbers fall outside libphonenumber's allocated ranges.
2. The 30-second resend cooldown refused a legitimate second request seconds after the first,
   breaking flows that request a code twice for one phone (including "log in again as the same
   user") — a user-visible UX change, not a security fix.

`IOtpService.IssueAsync`/`VerifyAsync` therefore gained two explicitly-named opt-outs,
`destinationIsCanonical` and `enforceResendCooldown`, **both defaulting to the strict behavior** so
password reset, recovery and email verification are untouched. The legacy login bridge is the only
caller that sets them, and each carries an inline comment naming the contract it preserves.

**Security improvements.** Login codes are now `HMACSHA256(OTP_PEPPER)` rather than bare SHA-256,
so a leaked `otp_codes` table yields nothing without the server-side pepper, which is resolved
through `ISecretProvider` (so `SECRETS_PROVIDER=aws` works) and has no fallback — issuance throws
rather than silently hashing under a guessable value (D-115). Codes gain a `PepperVersion` column,
making pepper rotation possible without invalidating live codes. Every issue and verify now also
writes a `security_events` row (`otp.issued` / `otp.verified`), which the legacy path never did, so
login OTP activity becomes visible to the audit spine for the first time.

**Compatibility.** The HTTP contract is byte-for-byte unchanged: same routes, same request bodies,
same success shape, same error codes (`invalid_phone`, `rate_limited`, `otp_not_found`,
`too_many_attempts`, `invalid_code`), same status codes. **Accepted phone formats are identical** —
bare 10-digit, `91`-prefixed, and every other form `NormalizePhone` accepted still works. **Rate
limits are unchanged** — three per destination per ten minutes (`MaxPerDestinationPer10Min`
numerically matches the retired `MaxPerPhonePer10Min`), plus the same per-IP hourly cap, now counted
over `otp_codes`. No client on any platform required a change. `AuthEndpoints` additionally maps
`resend_cooldown` to 429 alongside `rate_limited`, which is inert for login (the cooldown is off
there) and correct if it is ever enabled.

**Migration.** None required, and none performed. Codes are single-use with a five-minute TTL, so
the two tables never need reconciling: any code minted before deploy simply expires unused, and the
worst case for a user mid-login is re-requesting a code. `otp_requests` is left in place with its
data intact rather than dropped — an empty, unreferenced table is harmless, and dropping it is a
destructive schema change that belongs in its own decision. Both login and the D-037 authenticated
phone change use `OtpPurpose.PhoneVerification`, deliberately the *same* purpose, because D-037 has
them share one request endpoint; a different purpose would mean a code issued at
`/v1/auth/otp/request` could not verify at `/v1/me/phone/verify`.

**Consequences.** One OTP system now backs every flow in the platform. `otp_requests` is dead
storage pending a separate drop decision. The `destinationIsCanonical` escape hatch is a real,
disclosed compromise: the login path keeps a phone contract wider than E.164, so the D-089
canonicalization program still has a caller to migrate, and that migration remains the right place
to tighten validation — as a deliberate product decision with its own entry, not as a side effect of
a hashing fix. Adding a resend cooldown to login is likewise still open and probably desirable
(every other OTP flow has one); it is not done here because it changes user-visible behavior.

**Verification.** Full backend suite in a container against real Postgres: **882 passed, 0 failed,
883 total** (up from 880 — see D-216 for the three added). The two intermediate failure sets
described under *Rationale* are the evidence that the policy/substrate split is load-bearing rather
than theoretical.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Auth/AuthService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Auth/OtpService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IOtpService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/AuthEndpoints.cs`.

## D-216 · `TICKET_HMAC_SECRET` is mandatory in Production and resolved through `ISecretProvider` (2026-08-01)

**Context.** `TICKET_HMAC_SECRET` signs the gate-entry ticket code
(`TokenService.SignTicketCode`) and is verified at the gate by `GateEntryService`, with further
call sites in `OrderService`, `TicketTransferService`, `SeatBlockService` and `WalkInService`.
Despite that, `JwtOptions.FromSecret` read it as `config["TICKET_HMAC_SECRET"] ?? secret` — an
unvalidated read with a **silent fallback to the JWT signing key** — and it appeared in neither
`RequiredSecrets.Names` nor any `RequireStrongProductionSecret` call. The guard had in fact been
half-written: `SecretValidation.KnownDevValues` already listed the committed placeholder
`dev-only-ticket-hmac-change-me`, waiting for a caller that never arrived. Two documents actively
asserted the opposite of the code — `.env.example` ("Not yet read by any code path (ticket QR
issuance is unbuilt)") and `docs/security/secret-management.md` ("nothing reads it, so it isn't
validated") — which is what would tell an operator it was safe to skip.

**Decision.** Production now refuses to start unless `TICKET_HMAC_SECRET` is set, at least 32
characters, and not the committed placeholder. It is resolved in `Program.cs` through
`ISecretProvider` alongside `JWT_SECRET` and passed into `JwtOptions.FromSecret` as an explicit
parameter. Outside Production the fallback to the JWT secret is retained so a contributor who set
only `JWT_SECRET` still gets a zero-config local run.

**Security rationale.** Ticket signing and session signing are distinct security domains. Under the
old fallback a single key served both, so compromising either compromised both, and rotating one
silently rotated the other — invalidating every outstanding ticket the moment `JWT_SECRET` was
rotated. Worse, an unvalidated secret meant a production deployment could run on the placeholder
that is published in this repository, in `.env.example`, in `appsettings.Development.json` and in
`docker-compose.yml`. The realistic severity is Medium rather than Critical, and the reason is worth
recording so it is not overstated later: `GateEntryService` looks the ticket up in the database
*before* comparing the HMAC, so a wholly fabricated code still fails on `invalid_code`. The HMAC is
defence-in-depth against a tampered or derived code, and a published key defeats that layer without
by itself opening the gate.

**Reading through `ISecretProvider` rather than `IConfiguration`** matters for the same reason it
does for `JWT_SECRET` (D-101a): with `SECRETS_PROVIDER=aws` the value lives in Secrets Manager and
is absent from `IConfiguration`, so a configuration read would have validated a secret the
application does not actually use — proving nothing while appearing to prove something.

**Operational implications and deployment requirements.** Every Production deployment must now
provision `TICKET_HMAC_SECRET` as a distinct, strong value (`openssl rand -base64 48`), in whichever
store `SECRETS_PROVIDER` selects. This is a **breaking deployment requirement** for any Production
environment that previously relied on the implicit fallback. It is safe to introduce now precisely
because no Production environment exists yet (`cd.yml` has no provisioned host), which is the
cheapest moment such a requirement can ever be added.

**Failure modes.** Unset in Production → `InvalidOperationException` at startup naming the variable
and explaining that reusing the session key would make a leak of either compromise both. Set but
under 32 characters → the existing length message. Set to the committed placeholder → the existing
placeholder message. All three abort before the host serves traffic, so a deployment pipeline
catches them rather than a user discovering it at a gate. Unset outside Production → falls back to
`JWT_SECRET`, unchanged.

**Alternatives rejected.** Adding the name to `RequiredSecrets.Names` alone was rejected as
insufficient: that checks presence only, so the placeholder — the likelier mistake — would still
pass. Keeping the fallback and merely warning was rejected because a warning in a startup log is
not a control. Generating a random key per boot was rejected outright: it would invalidate every
previously issued ticket on every restart and deploy.

**Backward compatibility.** No schema change, no API change, no client change. Existing signatures
remain valid as long as the same key is supplied, which is exactly what setting the variable to the
value already in use achieves. Development and test behavior is unchanged.

**Verification.** Three new tests in `SecretValidationTests` cover the new rule (missing rejected in
Production, placeholder rejected in Production, fallback retained outside Production), and the
existing acceptance test now additionally asserts `Secret != TicketHmacSecret` so the key-reuse bug
has a standing regression test. These are the three tests that took the suite from 880 to 883.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/SecretValidationTests.cs`, `.env.example`,
`docs/security/secret-management.md`.

## D-217 · Production refuses to start without Redis — ADR-AM14's fail-closed check, finally implemented (2026-08-01)

**Context.** ADR-AM14 specified a fail-closed check on `REDIS_CONNECTION`; it was never
implemented, and `.env.example` said so in its own comment. `AddKurxInfrastructure` simply fell back
to `AddDistributedMemoryCache()` whenever the variable was absent, in every environment.

**Previous behavior.** A Production deployment with `REDIS_CONNECTION` unset started cleanly and
reported healthy while being silently incorrect on three axes at once: the SignalR backplane lost
cross-instance fan-out, so a chat message or scan event reached only the clients on the emitting
instance; `IPresenceService` resolved to `PresenceDisabledService`, so presence, typing indicators
and read receipts were absent rather than degraded; and both the `ChatHub` sliding-window limiter
and the distributed cache became per-process, so *N* instances served *N* times the configured
limit. The health endpoint only probes Redis when the variable is set, so its absence removed the
very check that would have surfaced it. All three failures look identical to a working system from
the outside, which is what makes silent fallback the wrong default here.

**New behavior.** `AddKurxInfrastructure` throws at startup when `isProduction` is true and
`REDIS_CONNECTION` is empty, with a message naming the three subsystems that would be wrong and
telling the operator to set the variable, or to point it at a local Redis if a single instance is
genuinely intended. The check sits at the one place that already decides the cache implementation,
so there is no second source of truth about whether Redis is available.

**Development and local behavior — unchanged.** Outside Production the in-memory fallback is
retained exactly as before: `docker compose up` and a bare `dotnet run` both still work with no
Redis, presence stays cleanly disabled rather than faked with process-local state, and the chat
rate limiter keeps its always-allow single-instance path. Contributors see no difference.

**Reliability considerations and tradeoffs.** The cost is a new hard dependency for Production:
Redis being unreachable at boot is now a failed deploy rather than a degraded one. That is the
intended trade — a deploy that fails loudly is recoverable in minutes, whereas silent per-instance
rate limiting and half-delivered realtime traffic are the kind of fault discovered days later
through user reports. Note the check covers *configuration*, not liveness: it fires when the
variable is absent, not when Redis later goes down, and runtime Redis loss remains the existing
health-check and SignalR concern rather than something this decision changes.

**Operational impact.** `REDIS_CONNECTION` becomes a required Production variable, joining
`JWT_SECRET`, `OTP_PEPPER` (D-115), the Postgres connection string, and now `TICKET_HMAC_SECRET`
(D-216). Documented in `docs/deployment/README.md` and `.env.example`.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`.

## D-218 · `FixtureView.Participants` returns a dedicated output DTO carrying a server-resolved `SubjectName` (2026-08-01)

**Context.** `FixtureView.Participants` was typed `IReadOnlyList<FixtureSubjectInput>` — the record
used for the *request* body of fixture creation. Its sibling views had already been fixed:
`StageParticipantView` and `ResultView` both carry a server-resolved `SubjectName`, added on
2026-07-25 for exactly this reason. `FixtureView` was left alone deliberately and the reasoning was
recorded in `docs/roadmap/README.md`: adding a name to `FixtureSubjectInput` would force API
*callers* to supply one, because the same record served both directions.

**Previous contract.** A fixture's participants came back as `subjectType` + `subjectId` + `seed`,
with no display name. Any bracket, draw sheet or fixture list could therefore only render raw
GUIDs, or issue a second round of lookups per participant to resolve them. This is why admin
fixture *creation* was deferred rather than built — the roadmap explicitly declined to build UI on
a degraded contract.

**Decision.** Added `FixtureSubjectView(SubjectType, SubjectId, SubjectName, Seed)` as a distinct
output record and re-typed `FixtureView.Participants` to it. Names resolve through the existing
`ResolveSubjectNamesAsync`/`SubjectName` helpers already used by `StageParticipantView` and
`ResultView`, so person and team subjects resolve identically across all three views with no new
resolution logic. `ListFixturesAsync` resolves once for every fixture's participants in a single
grouped call rather than per fixture, so the read stays free of an N+1.

**API evolution rationale.** Splitting the request and response records is the correct shape here
and generalizes: an input contract states what a caller must supply, an output contract states what
the server knows. Fusing them forces one side to carry fields the other should not, which is what
produced the original dilemma. Retaining `FixtureSubjectInput` unchanged for request bodies means no
caller has to send a name it does not have.

**Compatibility and client impact.** This is an **additive, breaking-only-by-widening** response
change: `subjectType`, `subjectId` and `seed` keep their names, types and meanings, and `subjectName`
is new alongside them. Any existing consumer that reads the three original fields is unaffected;
tolerant JSON deserialization ignores the addition. No client currently consumes these routes — the
admin competitions screens do not render fixtures — so real-world client impact is nil today, and the
contract is correct before the first consumer is written rather than after. Request bodies for
fixture creation are entirely unchanged.

**Consequences.** Fixture UI is now buildable without per-participant lookups, and the roadmap item
that deferred admin fixture creation on contract grounds is unblocked. The three competition views
(`StageParticipantView`, `ResultView`, `FixtureView`) now expose display names consistently, closing
the last of that family of gaps. Recorded in the same pass, and tracked in `docs/roadmap/README.md`
rather than as its own decision because it introduces no architecture: the 15 value-returning
competition routes also gained `.Produces<T>()` annotations, so those five view types now appear in
the generated OpenAPI schema. The remaining ~400 endpoints still cannot be annotated — they return
anonymous objects, which have no nameable type — and closing that needs a dedicated response-DTO
extraction pass, not a mechanical edit.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/ICompetitionService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/CompetitionService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/CompetitionEndpoints.cs`.

## D-219 · Profile write surface — the four visibility flags, per-connection ally visibility, profile-image upload, and the editable fields on `/v1/me` (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 0 of Professional Identity V2
(`docs/architecture/PROFESSIONAL_IDENTITY_V2_REVIEW.md`). Pure defect closure — no new concept, no
schema change, no redesign. Everything here existed on the **read** side already and had no writer.

**Context.** A profile audit found that `ProfilePublic`, `ShowAttended`, `ShowCertificates`,
`ShowAllies` (`Users.cs:54-57`) and `AllyConnection.Visibility` were enforced on every public read
path but settable by **nothing** — no endpoint, no admin tool; the tests set them through `DbContext`
directly, which is the tell. `ShowAttended` defaults to `false`, so one of the three event lanes
D-201 specified was dark for 100% of users, permanently, and `/events?type=attended` was a 403
nobody could clear. `AvatarKey`/`CoverKey` were accepted by `PATCH /v1/me/profile` and returned
publicly with no endpoint to upload the image they name.

**Decision — the flags get one partial-PATCH endpoint, not four.** `PATCH /v1/me/privacy` takes
`{profilePublic?, showAttended?, showCertificates?, showAllies?}`, every field nullable, absent
meaning "leave unchanged" — the same convention `UpdateProfileBody` already uses. Kept off
`PATCH /v1/me/profile` deliberately: privacy is a different resource with a different failure
consequence, and folding it in would make a rejected profile save (e.g. `username_taken`) silently
discard a privacy change made in the same submit. The response body and the new `privacy` block on
`GET /v1/me` share **one serializer** (`AuthEndpoints.PrivacyJson`) so the read and write shapes can
never drift. Phase 1's per-section visibility map lands as one more optional property on the same
body and one more key in the same block, so a client written against this today keeps working.

**Decision — `GET /v1/me` now returns the editable display fields**
(`headline`, `bio`, `education_json`, `skills`, `links_json`, `avatar_key`, `cover_key`). This is the
**root-cause fix for a silent data-loss bug**, not a convenience: because those fields were absent
from `/v1/me`, the web settings page prefilled its edit form from `getPublicProfile(username)` — a
call that returns nothing for an unclaimed username, a non-public profile, or any transient error —
and the form always submits every field, so a failed prefill rendered blanks and overwrote real
headline/bio/skills on save (the backend treats an empty string as a value, not as absent). Fixing
the prefill source removes the failure mode; guarding the write against blanks would only have
hidden it, and would have made deliberately clearing a field impossible.

**Decision — per-connection ally visibility is a shared flag either party may set.** `PATCH
/v1/allies/{id}/visibility` with `{visibility: "public"|"hidden"}`. The genuinely ambiguous part is
that `AllyConnection` is **one row per unordered pair**, so `Visibility` is shared: if either party
hides it, it disappears from *both* public profiles. Chosen over adding per-party columns because it
is consistent with the invariant D-201 already established — either party's `ProfilePublic = false`
hides the pair, so the more private choice already wins — and because Phase 0 is explicitly a
no-schema-change phase. A non-party gets **404, never 403** (hidden-resource convention, D-018):
confirming the row exists would leak that two specific people are connected. Deliberately allowed in
every status rather than gated to `Accepted`: visibility is a display preference, not a state
transition, so there is no `invalid_state` branch to write or test, and a non-`Accepted` row is
already absent from the public list.

**Decision — profile images reuse the existing presign pattern, with a stricter boundary.**
`POST /v1/me/profile-image/presign` calls `IMediaService.PresignProfileImageAsync(userId, slot, …)`,
modelled on `PresignRepresentationDocAsync` (user-scoped, no org, no role check — you may always
replace your own picture). Two differences from the document presigns, both deliberate: the `slot`
is a closed set (`avatar`/`cover`) because it becomes part of the storage key, so an unchecked value
would let a caller write outside its own `users/{userId}/{slot}/` prefix; and the content type is an
**allowlist of real image types**, because unlike an evidence PDF this key is rendered directly in an
`img` tag on a public page. Size ceiling is 5 MB, not the 25 MB document ceiling. One method with a
`slot` parameter rather than two methods, matching how `AttachAsync` already takes a `kind`. The key
is persisted through the existing `PATCH /v1/me/profile` — no second write path.

**Also fixed.** `IAllyService.GetMutualDetailAsync`'s XML doc still said "not gated on being allies"
after D-211 changed it to require an `Accepted` connection — a doc contradicting the code it
documents, on a privacy boundary. Corrected. `links_json` was accepted, stored, returned, and
present in both clients' schemas while being rendered and editable in neither; both clients now do
both. Flutter had **no profile editing at all** beyond the username claim, and
`ProfileController.update({bio})` wrote a `bio` into a local Hive box that no screen ever read and
nothing ever sent — deleted rather than migrated, now that `/v1/me` serves the field.

**Why not more.** No section-visibility jsonb, no provenance envelope, no new profile sections —
those are Phases 1–3 and each needs the architecture review's foundations first. Phase 0 deliberately
ships zero schema change so it can land independently of that approval.

**Files.** Backend: `Kurx.Api/Endpoints/{AuthEndpoints,AllyEndpoints,MediaEndpoints}.cs`,
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{IAllyService,IMediaService}.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/AllyService.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/MediaService.cs`,
new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileWriteSurfaceTests.cs`. Web: `lib/api.ts`, `lib/profile-actions.ts`,
`app/(app)/settings/page.tsx`, `app/u/[username]/page.tsx`,
`components/profile/{profile-form,privacy-form,profile-links}.tsx`. Mobile: new
`features/profile/presentation/pages/{edit_profile_page,profile_privacy_page}.dart`,
`features/profile/presentation/providers/profile_providers.dart` (rewritten),
`features/auth/domain/entities/current_user.dart`,
`features/auth/domain/repositories/auth_repository.dart`,
`features/auth/data/models/current_user_dto.dart`,
`features/auth/data/datasources/auth_remote_data_source.dart`,
`features/auth/data/repositories/auth_repository_impl.dart`,
`features/profile/presentation/pages/profile_page.dart`,
`features/public_profile/presentation/pages/public_profile_page.dart`, `core/router/app_router.dart`,
`test/features/auth/current_user_dto_test.dart`, `test/features/auth/registration_flow_test.dart`.

**Verification.** Backend: `dotnet build -c Debug -warnaserror` 0 warnings / 0 errors; full suite in
the container runner against real Postgres — **899 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped / 900 total**
(883 total before this change; +17 new `ProfileWriteSurfaceTests` covering privacy round-trip and
partiality, the `ShowAttended` unlock end-to-end, `ProfilePublic=false` returning 404, ally
visibility hide/reverse/either-party/non-party-404/invalid-value, presign key scoping for both slots,
slot and content-type rejection, auth on every new endpoint, and the presign→PATCH→`/v1/me` round
trip; the 883 baseline already includes a concurrent workstream's additions). Web: `tsc --noEmit`
clean, full `next build` green. Mobile: `flutter analyze` **0 issues**, `flutter test` **250 passed /
0 failed** (248 before; +2 `CurrentUserDto` cases covering the new fields and the missing-`privacy`
-block default). One test-only bug found and fixed while writing these: an assertion compared
`links_json` byte-for-byte, but the column is `jsonb`, so Postgres reparses and reserializes it —
the test now compares the parsed value rather than Postgres's whitespace.

**Consequences.** Every user can now make their profile private, publish their attended events, hide
an individual connection, upload a picture, and edit their profile from Flutter — none of which was
possible before. Admin is untouched (no administrative need; D-201's finding still holds). The four
boolean columns stay the source of truth until Phase 1 migrates them into `section_visibility`, where
they will be dual-written for one release before being dropped.

## D-220 · `EducationJson` is retained as self-declared data — superseding D-041's promise to migrate it into `membership_claims` (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Resolves a long-standing inconsistency between the decision log and the code.

**Context.** D-041 (M1) stated that `users.EducationJson` "is migrated into evidence-backed
`membership_claims` and the column dropped in M6 (D-044), not now — dropping it before M6 exists to
receive the data would lose it." Two things are wrong with that sentence today: the D-number is
wrong (D-044 is *Organization verification lifecycle*, M5; M6 is D-045), and **M6 shipped without
the migration**. The column is still live, still written by `PATCH /v1/me/profile`, and still
rendered as the public profile's `college` block. A reader following the decision log would conclude
the field is deprecated and about to disappear. It is not.

**Decision — keep the column, permanently, as self-declared display data.** The migration D-041
promised cannot be performed without either fabricating evidence or losing data, which is why it
never happened: a `MembershipClaim` requires an **existing organization row**, a `ClaimedRole` drawn
from a closed enum, evidence documents in `verification_documents`, and reviewer approval (D-045). A
free-text education string supplies none of these. Auto-converting it would mean creating unreviewed
claims — breaking D-045's "reviewed only from the claim and its documents" invariant, which is the
whole basis of "bio is never proof" — or silently dropping every user's education on migration day.

**Instead:** the field stays exactly what D-041 already made it — authority-zero, consumed by nothing
that gates access, displayed as an explicitly **unverified** affiliation. Phase 1's provenance
envelope will mark it `source: self_declared` with no `evidence` array, which is a stronger and more
honest signal than the current caption. A user who wants a *verified* affiliation files a real
membership claim — the evidence-backed path D-045 already built. The two coexist by design: one is a
display string, the other is proof.

**Why not just drop it.** It is populated, rendered on both clients, and losing it would delete real
user-entered data to satisfy a sentence in a decision record. The sentence is what was wrong.

**Files.** `docs/DECISIONS.md` (this entry; D-041's bullet annotated as superseded),
`docs/architecture/PROFESSIONAL_IDENTITY_V2_REVIEW.md` §23.2.

## D-221 · Profile visibility becomes one central resolver with four tiers, and trust exposes positive signals only (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 1 of Professional Identity V2. One new nullable column; no data migration.

**Context.** After D-219 gave the four visibility booleans a writer, the same authorization question
was still being answered in **nine separate places** — six in `PublicProfileService`, three in
`AllyService` — each re-deriving the rule from raw booleans. That is the shape a leak eventually
grows out of: the tenth site is the one that forgets. The product also needed more than on/off per
section.

**Decision — one resolver, and it is the only boundary.** `IProfileVisibilityResolver` resolves every
section for one (owner, viewer) pair and returns a `SectionAccess`. All nine checks now call it.
**[Corrected 2026-08-02: only the six checks inside `PublicProfileService` were migrated.
`AllyService` still gates on the legacy `ProfilePublic`/`ShowAllies` columns directly. It is correct
today because the section writer dual-writes those booleans, but "all nine" was not true as written.
Migrating it is a prerequisite for dropping the columns — tracked in D-230.]**
`SectionAccess` has a **private constructor and one factory**, so a read path cannot fabricate one;
every gated method takes it as a required parameter, which makes "forgot to check" a compile error
rather than a silent leak. `CanSee` **fails closed** — a section missing from the map is not visible,
and a test asserts every `ProfileSection` member has a decision, so adding a section without deciding
its visibility fails the build.

*Deviation from the architecture review, recorded deliberately:* the review proposed a
`SectionView<T>` wrapper threaded through every DTO. That would have changed the shape of every
response object and broken the frozen-root contract the same document guarantees — a worse outcome
than the risk it addressed. The required-parameter + private-constructor design gives the same
guarantee (you cannot read a section without a resolver-produced token) without touching a single
wire shape.

**Decision — four tiers, resolved lazily.** `Public` / `Connections` (an accepted `AllyConnection`) /
`EventParticipants` (≥1 shared public event) / `OnlyMe`. The two relationship checks run **at most
once each per request**, and only if some section actually uses that tier — a profile whose sections
are all Public issues zero extra queries, which is what keeps this off the hot path. The owner always
sees everything, so "only me" means "only me", not "nobody".

**Decision — storage is one jsonb column with a three-step fallback.** `users.SectionVisibilityJson`,
matching the existing `LinksJson`/`EducationJson` convention rather than a table that would add a join
to every profile read. Resolution order is **stored override → legacy boolean → documented default**.
That chain is what makes this reversible: a user who never touches the new settings resolves exactly
as they did before, and a malformed value falls back rather than throwing the profile away. Writes
**dual-write** the four booleans, and a tier the boolean cannot express (Connections/EventParticipants)
maps to `false` — a rollback then over-hides rather than over-shares, which is the safe direction.

**Decision — public endpoints become optionally authenticated.** The Connections and EventParticipants
tiers are meaningless without knowing who is asking, so the public profile handlers now read the
bearer token when present. They remain anonymous-allowed: an absent or unparseable token simply reads
as anonymous, and no existing caller changes.

**Decision — trust exposes positive signals only, and the exclusions are structural.**
`VerificationBadges` grows from 5 to 8: **Email Verified** (`EmailVerifiedAt`, present since D-182 and
never surfaced), **Speaker Verified** (an organizer linked a `Speaker` row to the account, D-208 — an
act by someone who ran an event, which is what makes it evidence), and **Community Verified**
(`IsOrgVerifiedRep` — a verified membership of an org that is itself Verified, computed by
`ITrustService` and never exposed). Phone is stated as true by construction rather than stored as a
redundant column: an account only exists because an OTP login succeeded.

**Never public, and a test enforces it:** risk score, fraud signals, report counts, moderation flags,
suspension/ban state, trusted-device details, and the KYC component breakdown. Two reasons, not one:
they are moderation internals (`VerificationBadges`' own contract already said the Trust Center never
leaks them), *and* a public risk number tells a bad actor exactly when they have been flagged. The
absence of a badge is the only negative information, and it is deliberately indistinguishable from a
privacy choice.

**Decision — provenance ships as a parallel `_meta` object.** Every root field is classified
`verified` / `self_declared` / `derived`, so a client never has to guess whether a value is proof or a
claim, and one shared renderer per category replaces per-section styling judgement. It is a constant
map because a field's category is a property of the field, not of the user. Additive by construction:
the flat keys are untouched, so a client that ignores `_meta` behaves exactly as before.

**Files.** Backend: `Kurx.Domain/{Enums/Enums.cs, Entities/Users.cs}`,
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{IProfileVisibilityResolver.cs (new), IPublicProfileService.cs}`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{ProfileVisibilityResolver.cs (new), PublicProfileService.cs}`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`,
`Kurx.Api/Endpoints/{PublicProfileEndpoints.cs, AuthEndpoints.cs}`, migration
`AddProfileSectionVisibility`, new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileVisibilityTests.cs`. Web: `lib/api.ts`,
`lib/profile-actions.ts`, `components/profile/privacy-form.tsx`, `app/(app)/settings/page.tsx`.
Mobile: `features/auth/domain/entities/current_user.dart`,
`features/auth/data/models/current_user_dto.dart`,
`features/auth/data/datasources/auth_remote_data_source.dart`,
`features/auth/{domain/repositories/auth_repository,data/repositories/auth_repository_impl}.dart`,
`features/profile/presentation/{providers/profile_providers,pages/profile_privacy_page}.dart`.

## D-222 · Four verified data sources that already existed are wired into the profile (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 2 of Professional Identity V2. **Zero schema change, zero backfill.**

**Context.** A full audit of the backend against the profile found four complete, tested, HTTP-exposed
data sources with a real person FK that had **never reached the profile at all**. This was the single
largest gap between what Kurx knows about a person and what it shows.

**Decision — competition results become a first-class profile section and a third achievement source.**
`StageResult` carries a real judged `Rank`, a `FinalScore`, a published state and an append-only
correction trail; the profile had been inferring "wins" from `Certificate.Kind` alone. New
`/competitions` sub-resource. **Only `Published` results surface** — a `Provisional` result is not yet
a fact about the person and a `Disputed` one is explicitly contested, so surfacing either would be
exactly the overclaim this system exists to prevent. Team results (`SubjectType = Team`) are **not**
attributed to individuals: the team roster, not the result row, decides who shares the credit, and
inventing that attribution is a product decision nobody has made.

Adding it to Achievements took **one new method** (`AchievementsFromCompetitionResultsAsync`) returning
the existing `AchievementCard` shape, concatenated into the existing merge — no DTO, endpoint or
consumer changed. This is D-203's source-agnostic design paying off exactly as designed.

**Decision — assignments surface with their completion, which participation cannot show.**
`EventAssignment` carries the 14-role operational vocabulary and, crucially, `CompletedAt`. The
existing participation lane flattens those 14 roles onto a handful of slugs and records only that a
role was held, never that the duty was carried out. New `/assignments` sub-resource; a `Custom` role
renders the organizer's own label rather than the literal word "Custom". `ShowOnProfile` composes with
the section tier as **AND** — a section set to public never overrides a row the user chose to hide.

**Decision — speaker sessions come from the organizer-made link.** `Speaker.UserId` (D-208) →
`EventSessionSpeaker` → `EventSession` gives real talks with titles and times. That the *organizer*
made the link is what makes it verified rather than self-claimed. Only `Session` items count — a
`Break` is scheduling furniture, not a talk anyone gave.

**Decision — event media is deliberately NOT exposed as a person's media.** `EventMedia` belongs to an
*event*, with no owner column and no person FK. Presenting an event's gallery as someone's portfolio
would invent a relationship the data does not contain — the same reasoning that excluded Projects.
Recorded here as a considered exclusion rather than an oversight; person-attributed media needs a real
owner column, which is a new-domain decision.

**Also:** three new timeline lanes (`competition_result`, `speaker_session`, `assignment_completed`),
each gated by the section that owns its evidence.

**Files.** `Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IPublicProfileService.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/PublicProfileService.cs`, `Kurx.Api/Endpoints/PublicProfileEndpoints.cs`,
new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileVerifiedSourcesTests.cs`.

## D-223 · Professional Journey — a first-attainment ladder, not a second timeline (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 3 flagship. Owns no tables; every tier is a query over existing rows.

**Context.** The product direction asked for a signature feature that shows a career path built from
verified activity. The risk was building a second Timeline with different formatting.

**Decision — it answers a different question, so it is a different shape.** The Timeline answers
"what has this person done" (every milestone). The Journey answers "**how have they grown**" — the
first time each professional tier was provably reached, with the occurrence count since and a pointer
to the earliest instance. Same source rows, no duplicated aggregation.

**Decision — chronological ordering, never a canonical ladder.** Someone can organize an event before
ever volunteering at one. Rendering a fixed Participant→Volunteer→…→Mentor sequence would assert a
progression the data does not support, and would make an unusual-but-real career read as incomplete.
Tier weight affects visual emphasis only; order is strictly by first attainment. A test seeds the
"wrong" order (organized two years before volunteering) and asserts it is preserved.

**Decision — no suggested next step.** "You are two events from Organizer" would turn an identity
record into a progress bar — the fictional level/tier concept D-212 deleted rather than patched.

**Decision — eleven tiers, each with a real backing row.** attendee (`Ticket.CheckedIn`), participant,
volunteer, team_lead (`TeamRole.Captain`), competition_winner (`StageResult.Rank = 1`, Published),
speaker, judge, mentor, organizer, host, verified_member (`Membership.VerifiedAt`). Where two sources
feed one tier — a volunteer role recorded both as a participation and as an assignment — the earliest
attainment wins and the occurrences sum. Occurrences dedupe by event, matching the rule every other
count on this profile uses (D-201).

Assignment roles with no corresponding tier (Media Team, Photographer, …) are real service but not a
distinct professional rung; they are counted by the assignments section and deliberately **not**
invented into a tier.

**Decision — privacy is applied once, at the end, by dropping whole nodes.** Every tier declares the
section that gates it, and a node whose section this viewer cannot see is removed entirely rather than
summarised or counted. Without that, the Journey would be a side channel around the resolver — a
"you have 3 competition wins" node would leak precisely what a hidden Achievements section conceals.

**Decision — an empty journey is the correct output.** A user with one checked-in ticket has a
one-node journey; a user with nothing has none. No aspirational placeholders.

**Files.** `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/JourneyEngine.cs` (new),
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IPublicProfileService.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/PublicProfileService.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`,

## D-224 · The profile fact-set — one materialisation of a person's verified facts, projected by pure engines (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 3B of Professional Identity V2. **No schema change, no API change, no
user-visible change** — a refactor whose entire purpose is to make the phases after it small.
Full design: `docs/architecture/PROFESSIONAL_IDENTITY_V2_PHASE3_5_DESIGN.md` §6.

**Context.** Every profile section loads its own rows. At four sections that is correct and cheap. The
Phase 3–5 design adds six more (skills, metrics, experience, heatmap, connections, resume), and two
things break at that size: a profile request fans out past thirty queries, and the Resume — which by
definition needs every section at once — has no sane way to assemble itself. The problem is not any
one query; it is that the same rows are re-fetched per section because nothing owns "this person's
facts".

**Decision — one `ProfileFactSet`, loaded once per request, projected by pure engines.** The loader
materialises events, participations, assignments, attendance, sessions, published results, memberships
and teams into one immutable record. Every engine becomes
`ProfileFactSet × SectionAccess → output` with no database access of its own. `JourneyEngine` is
converted first and becomes a `static` class — it opens no connection and issues no query.

**Decision — the fact-set is DATA WITH NO BEHAVIOUR.** No method that makes a product decision may be
added to it. Dedup, ranking, tier mapping and wording all stay in the engines. This is the stated R3
mitigation from the design doc: the obvious failure mode of a shared aggregate is that it accretes
logic until it is a god object that every feature must be read to understand. The record has no
methods at all, which makes the rule easy to enforce in review.

**Decision — the fact-set is VIEWER-INDEPENDENT, and this is the load-bearing property.** It holds the
person's facts, not "the facts this viewer may see". Privacy is applied at emission by each engine
through `SectionAccess`, exactly as the Journey already does. Two consequences, both deliberate: one
load serves every viewer (so the memo can be keyed by subject alone), and — more importantly — the
resolver remains the *single* privacy boundary. Filtering at load would split the privacy decision
across a loader and an engine, which is precisely the nine-scattered-checks situation D-221 was
created to end. A test asserts `LoadAsync` takes no viewer parameter, so the property cannot be
quietly lost.

**Decision — the private-event invariant moves into the loader.** Events are loaded once, filtered to
non-private, and every other fact is filtered to events that survived. A fact whose event is private
cannot enter the fact-set at all. Previously the `Visibility != Private` clause was repeated in every
query touching an event — roughly a dozen sites, each of which could have been the one that forgot.
It now exists once. A consequence worth stating: engines may index `facts.Events[fact.EventId]`
without a guard, because the loader guarantees the reference resolves; a test enforces that contract.

**Decision — scoped and memoised per user, not distributed-cached.** Registered `Scoped` with an
internal per-user memo, so one request projecting several sections pays for one load. The memo is
keyed by user id rather than being a single field because `ConnectionEngine` will load two people in
one request — a single-field cache would hand back the wrong person's facts, so the test suite pins
this. Cross-request reuse is deliberately left to the existing 10-minute summary cache: serialising a
full fact-set into the distributed cache trades a large, repeated serialisation cost for a benefit the
per-request sharing already delivers, and the hot path (the profile root) is already cached.

**Decision — load supersets, filter in engines.** The loader takes all published results, not just
first places; all `ShowOnProfile` memberships, not just verified ones. Same tables, same joins, no
extra queries — and it means an engine added in 3C does not have to change the loader to ask a
slightly different question. Only rows that are *never* a fact are excluded at load: private events,
non-public participations, unpublished competition results.

**Query cost.** Eight queries for a full load, versus the seven the Journey alone used to issue —
and that count is fixed regardless of how many sections a request projects, rather than growing per
section. **[Corrected 2026-08-02: D-229 added the badge load and three trust-fact loads, taking the
total to 15. The load is still flat with respect to section count, which is the property that
matters, but the figure "8" is no longer accurate and the loader's own comment now states 15.]**

**Why a refactor with no user-visible change ships first.** It de-risks everything after it: the shape
is proven against a feature that already works and has tests, rather than being designed speculatively
alongside six new ones. The existing `ProfileVerifiedSourcesTests` passing unchanged is the regression
proof that moving the engine onto the fact-set altered no output.

**What this does NOT do.** No caching change, no privacy change, no endpoint change, no DTO change,
no client change. Tags are deliberately absent from the fact-set: they arrive with the Skills work,
which is blocked on tag-vocabulary curation (Phase 5A of the design doc).

**Files.** `Kurx.Application/Abstractions/ProfileFactSet.cs` (new — records + `IProfileFactSetLoader`),
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/ProfileFactSetLoader.cs` (new),
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/JourneyEngine.cs` (converted to a static pure function),
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/PublicProfileService.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`,
new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileFactSetTests.cs`.

**Verification.** `dotnet build -c Debug -warnaserror` 0 warnings / 0 errors. Full suite in the
container runner against real Postgres — **932 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped / 933 total** (927 before;
+6 `ProfileFactSetTests`: per-scope memoisation, memo keyed by user, a new scope reloads, the
private-event invariant, every event-referencing fact resolving against `Events`, and the
loader-takes-no-viewer contract). **The regression proof is that `ProfileVerifiedSourcesTests` and
`ProfileVisibilityTests` passed unchanged** — the Journey's output is identical before and after the
engine moved onto the fact-set, which is exactly what a refactor phase must demonstrate. No client
build was needed: no API, DTO or wire shape changed.

## D-225 · Identity, Experience and Metrics engines — and the headline merged into identity labels (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 3C. Three pure functions over the D-224 fact-set. **No schema change.**

**Decision — the headline is not its own engine; it is the short form of the identity labels.** The
Phase 3–5 design found that a separate "headline engine" would re-derive exactly what
`BuildIdentityLabels` already produced — "Verified Organizer", "Public Speaker", "Hackathon Winner" —
in the same priority order. Two derivations of one thing can disagree, and eventually would. They are
now one `IdentityEngine` with two outputs (`labels[]`, `headline`), and the old
`BuildIdentityLabels`/`ParticipantIdentityLabels` pair is deleted rather than left as a second path.
A test asserts every headline token comes from the label pool, so the short form can never claim
something the long form does not.

**Decision — no manual headline override.** A self-written headline is precisely the self-declared
claim this system exists to replace, and `bio` already exists for anything a user wants to say in
their own words. A user may *pin* which of their **earned** labels leads; an unrecognised pin is
ignored rather than rendered, so a stale pin degrades to default ordering instead of displaying
something untrue. The headline is capped at 3 tokens / 60 characters, and an overflowing token is
**dropped rather than truncated** — a half-word label reads as a bug, and the remaining tokens are
still true on their own.

**Decision — `derived_headline` is a new root key, not a replacement for `headline`.** The existing
`headline` field is the user's own self-declared line and stays exactly as it is; `_meta` marks one
`derived` and the other `self_declared`. Collapsing them would destroy the distinction the whole
provenance model exists to express, and would have been a breaking change besides.

**Decision — Experience is a band, never a score.** A single number invites comparison the data
cannot support: twelve hackathons and twelve conferences are not interchangeable and no weighting
makes them so. The band (Building / Emerging / Active / Established / Distinguished) **always renders
with the counts that produced it**, so a reader can disagree with the summary and still see the
facts. Below the first threshold it reads "Building", not "Level 0" — the D-212 precedent.
Thresholds are deliberately coarse and reconstructible from the counts shown beside them, with a
leadership floor (running five events outweighs attending twenty).

**Decision — employment and education are permanently excluded from Experience.** Employment has no
entity, no evidence and no event linkage; including it would make Kurx a CV host. Education is
self-declared (D-220) and must never contribute to a derived value, or a typed string would inflate
it.

**Decision — Event DNA is a metric, not a subsystem.** It is one distribution over the curated
`EventKind` registry, computed by `MetricsEngine` and rendered as a chart. The name survives in the
UI because it is good product language; it is no longer an architectural concept.

**Decision — metrics gate before counting, and null means hidden.** Every count is computed from the
**viewer-visible** fact subset: a hidden section shrinks the number rather than being counted and then
relabelled, because a total computed over hidden rows is an oracle for what they contain. Nullable
members mean *hidden for this viewer*, never zero — clients render "—", so a privacy choice is never
read as a statement about the person. A test flips `showAttended` and asserts the metric moves
between a real count and `null`.

**Deliberately absent, each for a reason:** profile views (vanity, surveillance-adjacent); points and
leaderboard rank (engagement, not accomplishment — D-212 already deleted the fictional tier concept);
ally count as a headline stat (network size is not achievement); any percentile or
rank-against-others (turns identity into a ladder). A test asserts none of these strings appear in
the payload.

**No-show rate: approved but not built, and deliberately not faked.** The design approved it as an
owner-only metric. It needs tickets a person held for past events they did *not* check into, and the
fact-set carries only checked-in attendance. A placeholder was written during implementation and
**removed before commit** — emitting a fabricated `0` would be exactly the invented number this
system exists to prevent. Deferred until the fact-set carries issued-but-unused tickets, which is a
one-method addition when an owner-facing surface needs it.

**New:** `ProfileSection.Metrics` (defaults Public), `/metrics` and `/experience` sub-resources,
`derived_headline` on the frozen root. `ProfileCertificateFact` added to the fact-set — the first
proof that D-224's "one method per new fact family" extensibility works as claimed.

**Files.** `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{IdentityEngine,ExperienceEngine,MetricsEngine}.cs` (new),
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{PublicProfileService,ProfileFactSetLoader,ProfileVisibilityResolver}.cs`,
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{IPublicProfileService,ProfileFactSet}.cs`,
`Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`, `Kurx.Api/Endpoints/PublicProfileEndpoints.cs`,
new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileDerivationTests.cs`.

## D-226 · Professional relationships — why two people know each other, derived not scored (2026-08-01)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 3D. **No new tables, no second connection system.**

**Context.** Kurx had a *connection* (yes/no) but not a *relationship*. `AllyConnection` records that
two people consented; nothing explained what they actually did together.

**Decision — the connection is verified, the relationship is derived.** `AllyService` continues to own
the consented row (existence, state machine, privacy). `ConnectionEngine` only explains it, by
intersecting two fact-sets. That split is what keeps this from becoming a parallel system, and it maps
cleanly onto the provenance model: connection existence is `verified`, relationship type is `derived`
with the shared context as evidence.

**Decision — relationships are directional.** "A judged B" is not the same statement as "B judged A".
Every relationship is produced from one subject's perspective and the inverse is a separate type
(`judged` / `judged_by`, `mentored` / `mentored_by`, `spoke_at_their_event` / `hosted_their_talk`,
`led_their_team` / `team_led_by`). A symmetric model would quietly assert things that are false.

**Decision — no connection-strength score.** A number invites a leaderboard of friendships and is not
defensible from this data. The output is ranked *reasons* in plain language with the count of shared
contexts and one named example — the same choice `GetSuggestionsAsync` already makes. Labels are
verbs and facts ("Judged their entry"), never adjectives ("Strong connection").

**Decision — co-attendance is not collaboration.** Two people at the same event as attendees produce
no relationship. The `worked_together` catch-all requires each side to have held a role other than
`attendee`; otherwise the profile would claim a working relationship from co-presence in a room.

**Decision — a shared *verified* org is reported as a community, separately from a shared org.** "We
are both verified members of X" is a materially stronger statement than "we are both in X", and
collapsing them would flatten the distinction the verification exists to make.

**Shared achievements** — both recognised at the same event — is the most interesting shared context
Kurx can show, and costs one intersection over facts already loaded.

**Decision — depth stays 1.** No second-degree traversal, no graph feature. That is a product decision
about becoming a social network, not a technical extension, and it is not one this system needs.

**Performance.** The engine is pure: two fact-sets in, relationships out, zero queries. Both loads are
memoised for the request — which is exactly why D-224 keyed the memo by **user** rather than storing a
single fact-set per request. Surfaced first on `GET /v1/me/allies/mutual/{id}`, which already carries
D-211's accepted-connection gate; the addition is additive and that gate is unchanged.

**Files.** `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/ConnectionEngine.cs` (new),
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/AllyService.cs`, `Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IAllyService.cs`,
`Kurx.Api/Endpoints/AllyEndpoints.cs`.

## D-227 · Client rendering for the derivation engines — provenance made visible, and "hidden" made distinct from "zero" (2026-08-02)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 4B (client half). **No backend change, no schema change, no new endpoint** —
this closes the cross-platform gap left by D-225/D-226, whose engines shipped with no client rendering
them.

**Context.** D-225 and D-226 added metrics, experience, a derived headline and professional
relationships to the API. Nothing displayed them, so a phase that was "done" on the backend was
invisible to every user — the exact divergence the cross-platform gate exists to prevent.

**Decision — `null` renders as an em dash, never as zero.** The metrics contract distinguishes
*hidden from this viewer* (`null`) from *genuinely none* (`0`). Rendering a hidden section as "0"
would convert the owner's privacy choice into a factual claim about them — "organized 0 events" is a
statement the data does not make. Both clients implement `formatCount(null) => "—"`, and the Flutter
DTO test pins `events_attended: null` surviving as `null` rather than defaulting to `0`, which is the
mistake a `@Default(0)` on a nullable field would silently introduce.

**Decision — the derived headline leads, the self-declared one follows, and both are labelled.** The
hero renders `derived_headline` in primary type with a "Derived" badge, and the user's own `headline`
beneath it in muted type with a "Self-declared" badge. Showing only one would lose the distinction the
provenance model exists to express; showing them unlabelled would let a claim borrow the authority of
proof.

**Decision — a new shared `ProvenanceBadge` primitive, driven by `_meta` rather than by field name.**
The badge takes the server's provenance string, so a client physically cannot mislabel a field by
misremembering which section it belongs to. An unrecognised category renders **nothing** — a wrong
badge is worse than no badge.

**Decision — Event DNA is drawn as proportional bars, not a sparkline.** The Phase 3–5 design
suggested reusing the existing `sparkline` primitive. That was wrong on inspection: a sparkline reads
as a *time series*, and Event DNA is a *categorical distribution* — using one would imply a trend
across event kinds that the data does not describe. Bars need no new dependency on either platform
(`LinearProgressIndicator` on Flutter, a styled span on web). Recorded as a deliberate correction to
the design rather than a silent deviation.

**Decision — relationships lead the "Shared history" sheet, above the raw shared events/orgs.** "How
you know each other" is the question a reader opened the sheet to answer; the shared events and orgs
below are the evidence for it. `label` is written from the viewer's perspective server-side and is
rendered **verbatim** — re-wording it on the client would risk inverting a directional relationship
("Judged their entry" vs "Judged by them").

**Decision — each section is its own independent fetch on both platforms.** Web fetches metrics and
experience with `.catch(() => null)`; Flutter gives each its own Riverpod provider and reads
`valueOrNull`. A 403 is the *normal* outcome for a section this viewer may not see, not an error — so
a restricted section renders nothing and never takes the rest of the profile down with it.

**Not included, and still outstanding:** the contributions heatmap (its backend does not exist yet)
and the Resume (Phase 4A). Neither is faked or stubbed on the client.

**Files.** Web: `lib/api.ts`, `components/profile/{provenance-badge,metrics-panel}.tsx` (new),
`components/profile/mutual-detail-sheet.tsx`, `app/u/[username]/page.tsx`. Mobile:
`features/public_profile/presentation/widgets/metrics_panel.dart` (new),
`features/public_profile/data/models/public_profile_dto.dart`,
`features/public_profile/data/datasources/public_profile_remote_data_source.dart`,
`features/public_profile/presentation/providers/public_profile_providers.dart`,
`features/public_profile/presentation/pages/public_profile_page.dart`,
`test/features/public_profile/public_profile_dto_test.dart`.

**Verification.** Backend untouched, so its suite stands unchanged at **942 passed / 0 failed / 1
skipped / 943 total**. Web: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `eslint` 0 errors / 0 warnings, full `next build`
green. Mobile: `flutter analyze` **0 issues**, `flutter test` **255 passed / 0 failed** (250 before;

relationships, a pre-D-226 backend omitting `relationships`, and the derived headline plus new trust
signals defaulting safely when absent).

## D-228 · The Professional Resume and the contributions heatmap — the two surfaces that aggregate everything (2026-08-02)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Phase 4A + the remainder of 4B. **No schema change.** Both are projections of
the D-224 fact-set; between them they close Professional Identity V2's planned scope.

**Context.** These were held back deliberately: both aggregate across *every* section, so both are
the surfaces where a privacy mistake does the most damage. Neither could be built honestly before the
fact-set (D-224) and the section resolver (D-221) existed.

### The Resume

**Decision — it is a projection, not a template engine.** `ResumeEngine` introduces no model: the
header's headline comes from `IdentityEngine`, the spine from `JourneyEngine`, the counts from
`ExperienceEngine`, the rest straight off the fact-set. **If a fact is not on the profile it is not on
the resume**, which is what stops the two from becoming two different claims about one person. This
is also the first surface that needs every section at once — the case D-224 was designed for, and it
is one load and one render rather than a per-section fan-out.

**Decision — composed for the requesting viewer, through the resolver.** A section hidden from that
viewer is absent from *their* copy. Without this the PDF would be a trivial bypass of the entire
privacy model: download the file and read what the page refuses to show. A test asserts a hidden
profile returns 404 for a stranger while the owner still downloads their own, and that hiding a
section measurably shrinks a stranger's document while leaving the owner's intact.

**Decision — one template, no custom sections, never stored.** A template picker is personalisation
with no trust value and multiplies the surface to maintain. A free-text custom section is a
self-declared claim inside a document whose entire worth is that it is not self-declared. And a saved
copy is stale the moment the next event completes, creating a "which version is real" problem on a
document people forward — so it is always regenerated and the footer carries the generation date,
which makes a stale printout self-evident.

**Decision — the self-declared introduction is last and labelled.** The bio appears at the foot of
the document under an explicit "Written by this person — not verified by Kurx." A résumé that mixed
the two would let a claim borrow the authority of the proof above it.

**Decision — verification is the profile URL plus the existing certificate codes.** Footer reads
"Every entry is verifiable at …"; each certificate prints its `VerifyCode`. No new verification
entity, no signing infrastructure — the document points at the live source rather than trying to be
self-authenticating.

**Decision — rate-limited, and the caller controls nothing about composition.** A new `resume` policy
(10/min per IP) because this is the most expensive public operation on the platform: a full fact-set
load plus a QuestPDF render, on an anonymous-allowed endpoint. There is deliberately no template or
section parameter, so there is no injection surface into the document.

### The contributions heatmap

**Decision — gate, then bucket. Never bucket, then gate.** This is the subtlest privacy trap in the
whole system and the reason the heatmap was designed before it was built. If a day's contributions
were counted first and the hidden ones suppressed afterwards, the day's *intensity* would still
reflect them, and a viewer could read the presence of hidden activity straight off the grid. Each
contributing fact is filtered by its own section **before** it reaches a bucket. The test asserts a
day whose only activity is hidden **disappears entirely** — not "reduced", because a remaining bucket
of any intensity would leak that something happened.

**Decision — contributions are events, not engagement.** Inputs are check-ins, participations,
completed assignments, sessions, certificates, published results and membership verifications. **Not**
logins, page views or points: those measure engagement with Kurx rather than contribution to events,
and a heatmap that lit up for browsing would be the vanity surface D-225 spent effort excluding.

**Decision — only days with activity cross the wire.** A year of explicit zeroes is 365 rows of
nothing; the client fills gaps when laying out the grid. Server sends a 0–4 intensity band per day so
the client never re-decides the scale.

**Decision — 52 weeks on web, 26 on Flutter.** A full year of columns does not fit a phone at a
legible cell size, and shrinking cells to fit makes the grid unreadable rather than merely smaller.
Both scroll horizontally inside their own viewport so the page never does. Colour is not the only
encoding — every cell carries its date and count.

**Files.** Backend: `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{ResumeEngine,ContributionsEngine}.cs` (new),
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{PublicProfileService,ProfileVisibilityResolver}.cs`,
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IPublicProfileService.cs`, `Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`,
`Kurx.Api/Endpoints/PublicProfileEndpoints.cs`, `Kurx.Api/Program.cs` (rate-limit policy),
new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileResumeTests.cs`. Web: `lib/api.ts`,
`components/profile/contributions-heatmap.tsx` (new), `app/u/[username]/page.tsx`. Mobile:
`features/public_profile/presentation/widgets/contributions_heatmap.dart` (new),
`features/public_profile/data/{models/public_profile_dto,datasources/public_profile_remote_data_source}.dart`,
`features/public_profile/presentation/{providers/public_profile_providers,pages/public_profile_page}.dart`.

**Verification.** Backend: `dotnet build -c Debug -warnaserror` 0 warnings / 0 errors; full suite in
the container runner against real Postgres — **950 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped / 951 total** (943
before; +8 `ProfileResumeTests`: the resume renders a real PDF (`%PDF-` magic bytes, non-trivial
size), a zero-activity user still gets a valid document, a hidden profile has no downloadable resume
while its owner does, hiding a section shrinks a stranger's copy but not the owner's, contributions
bucket by day with the right intensity band, **a day whose only activity is hidden disappears
entirely**, out-of-window activity is excluded, and contributions 404 for a hidden profile). Web:
`tsc --noEmit` clean, `eslint` 0 errors / 0 warnings, full `next build` green. Mobile:
`flutter analyze` **0 issues**, `flutter test` **255 passed / 0 failed**.

Note on runtime: the suite took 13m29s versus the usual ~6m, consistent with D-198's finding that
QuestPDF's cold font resolution costs ~26.7s on first render. That is a known one-off warm-up, not a
regression introduced here.

## D-229 · Production-audit remediation — one canonical pipeline, viewer parity, and privacy-safe caching (2026-08-02)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Closes every Critical and High finding from
`docs/architecture/PROFESSIONAL_IDENTITY_V2_PRODUCTION_AUDIT.md`. **No schema change.** The audit was
run against my own implementation; these are fixes to my own defects, and the framing below is
deliberately blunt about that because the lesson matters more than the code.

**The lesson.** All three Criticals shipped with a **green 950-test suite**. The suite proved the
backend contract in isolation and proved nothing about whether two surfaces agreed with each other,
whether the web client exercised the feature at all, or whether an intermediary could re-serve a
private response. Every regression test added here targets that class of gap.

### C2 + H1 + H4 — fixed together, because they were one problem

**Root cause.** D-224 introduced the fact-set as the canonical pipeline but added it *alongside* the
cached summary, the separate org query and the direct achievement queries rather than replacing them.
Two live read paths meant two definitions, and "events organized" ended up with **three**: the root
summary (past events, all memberships, includes `CreatedBy`), the metrics engine (no time filter,
gated memberships) and the experience engine (no time filter, `ShowOnProfile` memberships). One
profile page could display three different numbers for one concept — on a product whose entire claim
is that its numbers are trustworthy.

**Decision — "organized" becomes a property of the fact, not a query each caller writes.**
`ProfileEventFact.IsOrganizedByUser` is computed once in the loader. A consumer cannot re-derive it
differently because there is nothing left to re-derive. `ProfileCounts` then owns every countable
definition and **returns sets of event ids rather than integers**, so a caller needing the events
themselves gets the same set instead of writing a second query.

**Decision — delete the parallel path entirely.** `CachedProfile`, `GetSummaryAsync`,
`GetOrgViewsAsync`, `BuildDnaAsync` and the three `AchievementsFrom*` query methods are **gone**,
replaced by `AchievementEngine` and `OrganizationsEngine` projecting the fact-set. The root profile,
`/metrics`, `/experience`, the timeline and the resume now share one derivation. Patching the three
counts to agree would have delayed the next divergence rather than preventing it.

**H1 falls out structurally:** the loader only admits `ShowOnProfile` memberships, so a hidden
membership can no longer contribute to a count anywhere — it is not that every consumer remembers to
filter, it is that the fact never claims the user organized it.

**Withdrawn during implementation:** a distributed cache of the whole fact-set, added to replace the
summary cache being deleted. Round-tripping the record through System.Text.Json broke the timeline in
a way the type system did not catch, and a fragile cache on the profile's hot path is worse than
none. Removed before merge and documented in the loader. The performance case was weak anyway — the
root profile now does *less* work than the audited state, because the parallel queries are gone.

### C1 — viewer parity between web and Flutter

**Root cause.** D-221 made the profile endpoints viewer-aware. Flutter attaches `Bearer` through an
interceptor; the web axios instance has none and passes auth explicitly per call — and **none of the
twelve `getPublicProfile*` functions passed a token.** Every signed-in web viewer was silently
reduced to the anonymous view, so the Connections and EventParticipants tiers did nothing on web
while working correctly on Flutter. No test caught it because no test exercises the web client.

**Decision — every profile reader takes an optional viewer token, and the page resolves the session
first.** `currentSession()` now runs *before* the fan-out rather than inside it, because fetching
before you know who is asking is the bug. A backend regression test asserts the contract both clients
must satisfy: an accepted ally gets 200 on a `connections`-tier section where anonymous gets 403.

### C3 — viewer-aware responses must never be shared-cacheable

**Root cause.** These routes were genuinely public and cacheable until D-221 made them
viewer-dependent. Nothing in that change flagged that their caching semantics had changed.

**Decision — an endpoint filter on the whole route group**, not per-route: `Cache-Control: private,
no-store, no-cache, max-age=0` plus `Vary: Authorization`. Applying it to the group means a route
