added later inherits it, which is the opposite of the failure mode that produced the finding. A
`[Theory]` asserts the headers on eight routes including the resume PDF, whose body may contain
sections hidden from the public.

### H2 — hidden is null, never zero

`ProfileStats`, `ProfileMetrics` and `VerificationBadges.VerifiedCertificates` are now nullable
end-to-end, and both clients render an em dash. Previously a hidden section produced `0`, which turns
the owner's privacy choice into a factual claim — "organized 0 events" is a statement the data does
not make and the owner did not authorise. The web and Flutter stat rows also refuse to *sum* two
counts when either is hidden, since a partial total presented as a whole is the same lie in
aggregate form.

### H3 — every section is user-configurable

`ProfileSection` had ten members; both privacy screens offered eight, so `metrics` and
`contributions` published with no control at all. Both clients now list all ten, and two tests hold
the line: one sets every enum member through the API, another asserts `/v1/me`'s privacy payload
exposes every section key. The old exhaustiveness test checked only the *resolver*, which is why it
gave false confidence — a section can have a perfect resolver entry and still be ungovernable.

**A pleasing outcome:** completing the web list made `tsc` fail on the `Record<ProfileSectionKey, …>`
copy map, so the type system now enforces that a new section ships with user-facing copy.

### H5 — documentation matched to implementation

`IHeadlineGenerator` was described in D-225 and the Phase 3–5 design as "the only interface in the
derivation layer". **It never existed.** The seam was speculative, so the documents are corrected
rather than the interface built — introducing an interface with one implementation to make a
sentence true would be the wrong repair. Every stale reference across both architecture documents now
says what the code actually does: a static function, with an interface to be introduced only when a
second implementation exists.

### A real bug the fixes surfaced

`ProfileCounts.AchievementKinds` was first declared as `IReadOnlySet<CertificateKind>`. EF Core
translates `HashSet.Contains` to SQL but **throws on the interface**, so the timeline started
returning 500 at runtime with no compile-time signal. Declared as the concrete `HashSet` — a rare
case where the less abstract type is the correct one, and noted as such in the code.

**Files.** Backend: new `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{ProfileCounts,AchievementEngine,OrganizationsEngine}.cs`;
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/{PublicProfileService,ProfileFactSetLoader,MetricsEngine,ExperienceEngine}.cs`;
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{ProfileFactSet,IPublicProfileService}.cs`;
`Kurx.Api/Endpoints/PublicProfileEndpoints.cs`; new `Kurx.Tests/ProfileAuditRegressionTests.cs`.
Web: `lib/api.ts`, `app/u/[username]/page.tsx`, `components/profile/{privacy-form,metrics-panel}.tsx`.
Mobile: `features/public_profile/data/models/public_profile_dto.dart`,
`features/public_profile/presentation/{widgets/metrics_panel,pages/public_profile_page}.dart`,
`features/profile/presentation/pages/profile_privacy_page.dart`.
Docs: `PROFESSIONAL_IDENTITY_V2_{REVIEW,PHASE3_5_DESIGN,PRODUCTION_AUDIT}.md`, `docs/api/README.md`.

**Verification.** Backend: `dotnet build -c Debug -warnaserror` 0 warnings / 0 errors; full suite in
the container runner against real Postgres — **968 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped / 969 total** (951
before; +18, of which 10 are `ProfileAuditRegressionTests` covering metric agreement across three
surfaces, hidden memberships contributing nowhere, every hidden count being null, cache headers on
eight routes, authenticated-vs-anonymous tier access, and section governance). Web: `tsc --noEmit`
clean, `eslint` 0 errors / 0 warnings, `next build` green. Mobile: `flutter analyze` **0 issues**,
`flutter test` **255 passed / 0 failed**.

## D-230 · Allies multi-party policy — the more private choice wins, moderation reaches display, and decline is a cooldown (2026-08-02)

**Context.** A red-team audit of the shipped Allies system reproduced four defects with failing tests.
None was caught by the 969-test suite, and the reason is structural: the suite exercises each party's
actions **in isolation**, while all four defects live in the interaction between two users with
opposing intentions, or between a user and moderation. The state machine, the pair canonicalization
and the concurrency contract were all sound — the gap was policy layered on top of them.

**BUG-A — a party could silently un-hide a connection the other party hid.** `IAllyService` documents
"Either party may set it and the flag is shared: **the more private choice wins**". The implementation
was `row.Visibility = parsed` — last-writer-wins. Alice hides a sensitive affiliation, Bob publishes
it, and Alice's choice is reverted with no notification and no way to win. The existing three
visibility tests covered A-hides, B-hides, and A-hides-then-A-unhides; the one case that
distinguishes the two behaviours — **A hides, then B publishes** — was untested, and test #2's own
doc comment recited the rule it never exercised.

*Options compared before changing schema.* (1) *Shared column, "hidden is sticky"* — rejected: with
both parties hidden, one un-hiding reveals the pair, so it fails the contract exactly where it
matters. (2) *Reject `public` unless the caller is the one who hid it* — rejected: same both-hide
flaw, and it needs a column anyway to know who hid it. (3) **Chosen: per-party flags.**
`HiddenByLow`/`HiddenByHigh` booleans; the pair is public only when neither is set. This is the
smallest shape that is actually correct, because it is the only one that survives both parties
hiding. `Visibility` is retained as a **derived stored mirror** (Hidden when either flag is set) so
every existing read and filter (`Visibility == Public`) works untouched — the blast radius is one
method plus a migration, not every query.

*Migration.* Additive, two booleans defaulting false, plus a backfill setting **both** flags on rows
already `Hidden`. Without the backfill the defect survives its own fix for existing data: the flags
would default false and the next toggle by either party would recompute the mirror to Public and
reveal a connection someone had deliberately hidden. We cannot know which party hid a legacy row, so
both are set — the conservative direction for a privacy flag, at the cost of each party un-hiding
once. The predicate matches the enum **name** (`'Hidden'`), since Status/Visibility are mapped `text`
on this table; an integer comparison would have silently matched nothing.

**BUG-B — moderation did not reach display surfaces.** `AuthService` blocks a banned or suspended
account from logging in and revokes its sessions, but no public-facing service filtered
`BannedAt`/`SuspendedAt` — a repository-wide grep found moderation predicates **only** in auth and
admin paths. A banned account's name, username and avatar therefore kept appearing on every ally's
public profile and in public user search. Fixed at the chokepoints rather than per-endpoint:
`PublicProfileService.LoadAsync` (which every gated profile section routes through, so profile,
timeline, metrics, experience, contributions, journey, certificates, allies and the resume are all
covered by one gate), public user search, the ally-card projection, and suggestions. Gating the
loader — not the individual endpoints — is deliberately the shape that prevents the original miss
from recurring when a section is added later.

**BUG-C — unlimited request-notification spam via decline → re-request.** Decline is reversible and
re-request reactivates the same row, notifying the target each time; `MaxPendingOutgoing` does not
apply because a declined row is not pending. With no block feature to fall back on, a target's only
recourse was to keep declining forever. *Options compared.* A per-pair lifetime cap was rejected —
it permanently forecloses a legitimate reconnect years later and needs a counter column. Abuse
detection was rejected as disproportionate and overlapping a future moderation feature. **Chosen: a
30-day cooldown after a decline, applied only to the same requester being declined again.** It bounds
notifications to one per pair per month, delays rather than forecloses a genuine reconnect, needs
**no schema change** (it reuses `Status` + `RespondedAt`), and is orthogonal to a future block, which
would be separate and permanent. The decliner may ask immediately — that is a change of mind, not
spam, and is never blocked. Surfaced as `declined_recently` → **429**, alongside the sibling throttle.

**BUG-D — suggestions leaked a non-public profile's real name.** `GetSuggestionsAsync` nulled
`Username` and `AvatarKey` for `ProfilePublic == false` users but still returned `Name`, plus a reason
string naming a shared organization or event count. That is both a privacy contradiction and a UX
defect: with no username the client cannot link anywhere, so it rendered an unnavigable card.
Non-public profiles are now excluded from suggestions outright, which resolves both.

**Consequences.** Two pre-existing tests re-requested immediately after a decline and now correctly
hit the cooldown; both were updated to age `RespondedAt` past the window rather than weakening the
policy, preserving their original intent (row reactivation, and the pending cap). A new
`AllyPolicyConflictTests` class encodes the multi-party contracts the suite structurally lacked:
opposing visibility writes including concurrent ones, both-hide/one-unhide, repeated toggling,
profile-privacy interaction, ban/suspend/restore across ally list + profile + search, cooldown
expiry, decliner-initiated reconnect, and concurrent retries during cooldown.

**Verification.** 17 new tests; all 56 ally/profile tests green; full backend suite green.

**Files.** `Kurx.Domain/Entities/Allies.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/AllyService.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/PublicProfileService.cs`, `Kurx.Api/Endpoints/AllyEndpoints.cs`,
`Migrations/20260802061719_AddPerPartyAllyVisibility.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/AllyPolicyConflictTests.cs`,
`Kurx.Tests/AllyConnectionTests.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/AllyConcurrencyProbeTests.cs`.

## D-231 · Privacy writes become one atomic jsonb merge — and the row lock that "fixed" it first is recorded as forbidden (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `ProfileVisibilityResolver.UpdateSettingsAsync` implemented a `PATCH /v1/me/privacy` as
read-modify-write against the `SectionVisibilityJson` column: read the effective ten-section map,
merge the requested sections into it, write **the whole map** back. Two concurrent calls both read the
pre-existing map, each merged only its own section, and the slower write won — silently discarding the
other change.

This is not a synthetic-load defect. The Flutter privacy screen saves **per toggle, immediately** (a
deliberate choice — a privacy control that sits unsaved is its own failure), so a user flipping two
switches in quick succession fires two overlapping requests. They watch a toggle move and the setting
silently reverts. On a privacy control that is the worst class of failure available: the user believes
something is hidden when it is public.

**The first fix was wrong, and is recorded here so nobody re-derives it.** A `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` row
lock is the textbook answer and it made the system strictly worse. Measured on the full suite:

| | Duration | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `FOR UPDATE` row lock | **5 h 42 m** | 987 passed, **2 failed** |
| Reverted (defect present) | 9 m 54 s | 987 passed, 3 skipped |
| Atomic jsonb merge (chosen) | see Verification | — |

Postgres applies **no default lock timeout**. One transaction that takes the row lock and does not
commit blocks every later writer indefinitely, so the two failures logged at 8m41s and every
subsequent privacy write queued behind them for five and a half hours. In production that converts a
lost update into a hang on the privacy endpoint — a worse outcome than the bug. Reverted rather than
tuned: a `lock_timeout` would have turned the hang into an error, which is still a regression traded
for a fix, and the tuning would have to hold under every future call pattern.

**Chosen: one statement, no explicit lock.** `UPDATE … SET "SectionVisibilityJson" =
COALESCE(current, jsonb_build_object()) || patch` — Postgres takes and releases the row-level write
lock *inside* the statement, so no lock is ever held across an `await` and no dying request can strand
one. The `||` operator on `jsonb` is a shallow right-wins merge, which is exactly patch semantics, and
it reads the current value within the same statement, so a concurrent write cannot be clobbered from a
stale snapshot.

Two consequences worth stating, because both are behaviour changes and not merely mechanism:

*The patch now carries only the sections being changed.* Sending the full merged map is what made the
writes destructive in the first place — every request rewrote all ten sections from a snapshot taken
before the other request landed. Stored settings become sparse, which the existing fallback chain
(stored override → legacy boolean → documented default) already handles unchanged.

*The legacy D-221 boolean dual-write is recomputed in the same statement, and only for sections the
patch mentions* (`ELSE <current>` for the rest) — an absent key means "unchanged", not "reset to
default". This drops one accidental behaviour of the old code: because it rewrote everything, it
incidentally self-healed a boolean that had drifted from the stored map. That healing only ever fired
on an unrelated write, and drift is only possible because `AllyService` still reads the booleans
directly (six sites: `AllyService.cs:247,249,264,423,454,463`) instead of calling the resolver. The
real remedy is migrating those call sites, which is **still open and has no decision number** — not an
unrelated write papering over it. Reads through the resolver are unaffected either way, since the
stored map takes precedence over the boolean.

*The response is re-read after the update rather than assembled from the request's own merge.* If a
concurrent write landed in between, the caller sees the true current state instead of a private
fiction of its own change.

**Verification.** `ProfileConcurrencyTests` — 4 tests. The two that prove this fix (two sections
hidden simultaneously; eight sections hidden from eight parallel callers) **failed against the
read-modify-write implementation and pass against the atomic statement**, which is the only ordering
that makes them evidence. They were briefly `[Fact(Skip)]` while the defect was open rather than
deleted, so a known bug could not decay into an unknown one.

**Files.** `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/ProfileVisibilityResolver.cs`,
`Kurx.Tests/ProfileConcurrencyTests.cs`.

## D-232 · The public allies route becomes viewer-aware — and the counterparty gate deliberately stays on the boolean (2026-08-02)

> **Partly superseded by D-233 (same day).** The route fix stands. The decision to leave the
> counterparty gate on `ProfilePublic` was reversed once the N+1 objection behind it was removed by a
> batched primitive: that gate, and 14 others, now resolve through the resolver. The enumeration of
> the 15 sites below is the survey that motivated D-233 and is kept for that record.

**Context.** `GET /v1/public/users/{username}/allies` was the only route in the public-profile group
whose handler did not take `ClaimsPrincipal` and did not pass `ViewerId(p)`. Every sibling route had
been made viewer-aware by D-221 and re-checked by D-229/C1; this one was missed, and the miss was
invisible because the route still returned a valid `200 []`.

`AllyService.GetAlliesForProfileAsync` therefore gated on the legacy columns:

```csharp
if (user is null || !user.ProfilePublic) return Fail("not_found");
if (!user.ShowAllies) return Success(Array.Empty<AllyProfileCard>());
```

Because D-221 dual-writes a non-Public tier to `false`, setting the `network` section to
**Connections** or **EventParticipants** wrote `ShowAllies = false` and this route returned an empty
list **to everyone — the owner and their accepted allies included**. Setting `profile` to Connections
wrote `ProfilePublic = false` and returned `not_found` on the same terms. Two of the four tiers were
dead on this surface, and a user could not see their own allies list.

This is D-229/C1 — "the Connections and EventParticipants tiers are non-functional" — surviving on the
one site that fix did not reach. It over-hides rather than leaks, so it was never a disclosure bug;
it was a feature that silently did not work. Both clients already sent the token (Flutter's dio
interceptor, web's `viewerHeaders`), which is exactly why the backend ignoring it went unnoticed.

**Owner gate: resolved, like everything else.** The handler now takes `ClaimsPrincipal`, and the
service resolves the owner's `Profile` and `Network` sections against the viewer —
`Profile` invisible ⇒ 404 (D-018, indistinguishable from a missing user), `Network` invisible ⇒ empty
200 (a hidden section, not an error). The moderation gate (D-230/BUG-B) is repeated here explicitly
because this route does not pass through `PublicProfileService.LoadAsync` and so does not inherit that
chokepoint.

**Counterparty gate: stays on `ProfilePublic`, deliberately.** Showing Y on X's page exposes Y's
identity, so Y's own choice must gate it independently of X's `network` tier. Resolving that properly
is one resolver call per card — N+1 on a paginated list of up to 100. The boolean is kept for the
batch filter instead. It is the conservative direction: a counterparty whose `profile` tier is
Connections is omitted even from a viewer who *is* one of their connections. That over-hides and never
leaks, which is the acceptable failure for this gate.

*Cost, stated plainly — and it is larger than this route.* A repo-wide sweep done while writing this
entry found `ProfilePublic` read as a display gate at **15 sites across 8 services**, not the one or
two a reading of the profile code suggests:

| Service | Reads | What the gate decides |
|---|---|---|
| `AllyService` | 4 | ally-card counterparties, suggestion cards, notification deep-link target |
| `EventReviewService` | 4 | whether a review shows its author's identity |
| `GamificationService` | 2 | whether a leaderboard row links to a profile |
| `PublicProfileService` | 1 | user search results |
| `AttendeeService`, `EventAssignmentService`, `SpeakerService`, `OrderService` | 1 each | attendee / assignee / speaker / org-member cards |

Every one is the same question — "may this *other* person's username and avatar be shown here" — and
every one answers it with the pre-D-221 boolean. The consequence is uniform and consistent with the
counterparty decision above: a user whose `profile` tier is Connections or EventParticipants is
rendered as an unlinked, un-named card **everywhere in the product**, including to viewers who are
entitled to see them. It over-hides, never leaks, so nothing here is a disclosure defect — but the two
middle tiers are only partially functional outside the profile surface, and **the boolean columns
cannot be dropped until all 15 are migrated** (D-221's planned follow-up).

The unblocking piece is one batched primitive — resolve many users' section tiers in a single query,
the way `GetStatusBatchAsync` did for ally status — not 15 per-row resolves. Recorded here as the
prerequisite rather than left as an unexplained column dependency.

**Verification.** Two tests in `ProfileVisibilityTests`: `network` set to Connections is visible to an
accepted ally and to the owner and empty to a stranger/anonymous — asserting the **array length**, not
merely a 200, because the defect returned 200 with an empty body; and `profile` set to Connections
returns 404 on this route to a stranger while an ally and the owner get 200.

**Files.** `Kurx.Api/Endpoints/PublicProfileEndpoints.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/AllyService.cs`,
`Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IAllyService.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/PublicProfileService.cs`
(stale doc comment), `Kurx.Tests/ProfileVisibilityTests.cs`, `docs/api/README.md`.

## D-233 · One batched visibility primitive replaces 15 scattered `ProfilePublic` reads (2026-08-02)

**Context.** D-232 closed the last profile-surface gate but recorded a larger finding: `ProfilePublic`
was read directly as a "may this other person be shown here" gate at **15 sites across 8 services** —
allies (4), event reviews (4), leaderboards (2), user search, attendees, assignments, speakers and
group members. Each answered the question independently, none went through the resolver, and
collectively they were the reason D-221's boolean columns could not be dropped. Any tier other than
Public rendered a person as an unlinked, unnamed card *product-wide*, including to viewers who were
entitled to see them.

**The constraint that shaped the design.** The obvious fix — call `ResolveAsync` per row — is an N+1 on
surfaces that are read constantly and can carry 100 rows (a leaderboard page, an attendee list). The
resolver's two relationship checks each cost a query, so a 50-row leaderboard could have issued 150.
That is not a trade worth making to tidy up a boolean.

**Chosen: one batched primitive.**

```csharp
Task<IReadOnlySet<Guid>> VisibleProfileIdsAsync(
    IReadOnlyCollection<Guid> userIds, Guid? viewerId, CancellationToken ct = default);
```

**Cost is independent of the batch size.** One query loads the users. The connection check becomes a
single `AllyConnections` query over the whole id set; the shared-event check fetches the *viewer's*
event ids once and intersects server-side. Both run **only if some user in the batch actually uses the
tier that needs them**, so the overwhelmingly common batch — everyone Public — costs exactly one query.
Moderation (D-230/BUG-B) moved *inside* the primitive: "may this person be shown" has one answer, and
eight services separately remembering to exclude banned accounts is how that bug happened the first
time.

**Where the viewer is real, and where it is deliberately anonymous.** This is the part most likely to
be misread later, so it is stated explicitly. Three sites now resolve against a genuine viewer and
gained behaviour they should always have had: ally cards (against the profile's reader), ally
suggestions (against the caller), and the ally notification deep-link (against the *recipient* — so an
"accepted" notification now links to a Connections-tier profile the recipient has just become entitled
to see, where the boolean sent them to `/allies`).

The remaining sites pass `null`. Not an oversight: an attendee list, a leaderboard, a speaker card and
a review byline carry no caller identity down to the projection, and threading one through would mean
changing eight public service signatures and their endpoints — a cross-surface refactor well outside
Professional Identity V2. Anonymous resolves to "Public only", which is **exactly** what
`ProfilePublic` meant, so behaviour is preserved bit-for-bit. Making those surfaces viewer-aware is a
real improvement and a separate piece of work.

**The one read that stays.** `PublicProfileService.SearchUsersAsync` keeps `u.ProfilePublic` in its
SQL `WHERE`, because the filter precedes `Skip`/`Take` and post-filtering a page in memory returns
short pages. It is also deliberately *not* viewer-aware: global discoverability is a product rule —
only fully-public profiles are searchable — not a per-viewer entitlement. It is safe because
`UpdateSettingsAsync` dual-writes the column, so it is equivalent to "Profile tier is Public".

**Therefore the boolean columns still cannot be dropped**, and the remaining prerequisite is now
exactly one thing rather than fifteen: backfill `SectionVisibilityJson` for every existing row so the
tier can be filtered in SQL without a boolean fallback. Stated here so the next person does not
rediscover the search predicate the hard way.

**Also fixed in passing.** `GetEventLeaderboardAsync` issued one user query per entry; it now batches,
because the migration touched that loop anyway and leaving a known N+1 in place while adding a
paragraph about avoiding N+1 would be absurd.

**Verification.** `ProfileVisibilityBatchTests` — the full tier matrix resolved inside one batch,
anonymous sees Public only, the owner always sees themselves, banned/suspended never visible (even to
themselves), unknown ids absent rather than throwing, the batched shared-event intersection agreeing
with the single-resolve path, plus one per-surface test for leaderboards, review bylines and speaker
cards asserting that a hidden profile contributes no username while its display name survives.

**Files.** `Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IProfileVisibilityResolver.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/ProfileVisibilityResolver.cs`, `Users/AllyService.cs`,
`Users/PublicProfileService.cs`, `Social/EventReviewService.cs`, `Gamification/GamificationService.cs`,
`Events/AttendeeService.cs`, `Events/EventAssignmentService.cs`, `Events/SpeakerService.cs`,
`Orders/OrderService.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/ProfileVisibilityBatchTests.cs`.

## D-234 · Every profile metric counts completed activity only (2026-08-02)

**Context.** The fact-set loads every non-private event a person touches, future ones included, and the
metric engines counted them. Registering for a conference next month raised "events participated";
accepting a speaker slot raised "speaker sessions"; an upcoming hackathon appeared in Event DNA and its
city in Cities. A profile could advertise experience its owner had not yet had — on a product whose
entire claim is that its numbers are verifiable, that is the worst available failure.

**Why it survived so long.** The event *listings* in `GetEventsAsync` have always filtered
`EndsAt < now` — both branches. So the counts and the lists described different sets, and a tab could
read "Events (8)" above five rows. Nobody compared the two, because each looked right on its own.

**The rule.** A profile is a record of what someone has done, so **nothing counts until its event has
ended**. `OrganizedEventIds` already worked this way (D-229); the rule is now applied uniformly and
expressed as one shared predicate, `HasEnded`, rather than repeated per count.

| Count | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `OrganizedEventIds` | completed | unchanged |
| `ParticipatedEventIds` | **all** | completed |
| `AssignedEventIds` | **all** | completed |
| `LeadershipEventIds` | **all** | completed |
| `DistinctEventIds` | mixed | completed (incl. the speaking lane) |
| `SpeakerSessionCount` | **all** (read raw off `facts.Sessions.Count`) | completed |
| `EventDna`, `Cities` | **all** | completed |
| `AttendedEventIds` | — | unchanged; a check-in can only be recorded *at* the event |
| `CompetitionsWon`, `CompetitionEventIds` | — | unchanged; a published result exists only after judging |

The last two rows are exceptions in appearance only — both are completed by construction, and each now
says so where it is defined, so the next reader does not "fix" them.

**An event absent from the fact set is treated as not ended** — the conservative direction, since the
alternative is counting something we cannot date as completed experience.

**Scheduled activity is deliberately not surfaced.** Adding an "upcoming" metric would be a new
feature. The honest minimum is that no existing number overstates.

**Verification.** `ProfileMetricTimeTests` seeds one person with exactly one finished and one future
event in every lane and asserts each metric reports 1, not 2 — including that Cities and Event DNA
carry only the past event's city and kind. A separate test asserts the events count now equals the
length of the listing it labels, which is the inconsistency that made the defect reachable.

**Files.** `Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/ProfileCounts.cs`, `Users/MetricsEngine.cs`,
`Users/ExperienceEngine.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/ProfileMetricTimeTests.cs`.

## D-235 · A privacy refusal and an outage must not render the same way (2026-08-02)

**Context.** Both clients conflated "you may not see this" with "we could not load this", in opposite
directions — which is why neither looked wrong in isolation.

*Web* swallowed everything: each of the eleven section fetches on the profile page ended in
`.catch(() => [])`. A 403, a 500, a dropped connection, a timeout and a schema mismatch all rendered
identically to a genuinely empty section. **A backend outage made someone's profile look like the
profile of a person who had done nothing** — and the tab counts, derived from a failed metrics fetch,
would have printed zeros.

*Flutter* did the reverse: `AsyncValueView` routed every error to `ErrorRetry`, so a section the owner
had deliberately hidden rendered as "Something went wrong · Retry", inviting the viewer to hammer an
endpoint that would keep refusing while implying the app was broken.

**The rule.** A 403 is a *successful* answer to "may I see this" and renders as absence, with no error
and no retry. Everything else — 5xx, timeout, DNS, parse failure — renders as an explicit "couldn't be
loaded" notice, because none of those are evidence about the person.

**Web** gains `SectionResult<T>` (`ok` | `hidden` | `unavailable`) and a `section()` helper that
classifies by status; the page renders `SectionUnavailable` for failed panels. Critically, a count
whose fetch failed is now `null` rather than a number — a count we could not fetch is not a count of
zero, and asserting one would be a lie told by an outage.

**Flutter** gains an optional `hidden` widget on `AsyncValueView` (403 renders it; everything else
keeps the retry view, so screens that pass nothing are unaffected) and a `SectionPanel` for the
panel-style sections that read `.valueOrNull` and therefore could not tell hidden from broken.

404 on a *section* is treated as hidden rather than as a failure: the page has already resolved the
profile at the root, so a section 404 means the profile itself is hidden or gone (D-018).

**Verification.** Seven Flutter widget tests covering 403 to hidden, 500 to retry, offline (status 0)
to retry, and `response_parse_failed` to unavailable-not-privacy, on both `AsyncValueView` and
`SectionPanel`.

**Files.** `web/lib/api.ts`, `web/components/profile/section-unavailable.tsx`,
`web/app/u/[username]/page.tsx`, `mobile/lib/common/widgets/async_value_view.dart`,
`mobile/lib/features/public_profile/presentation/widgets/section_unavailable.dart`,
`mobile/lib/features/public_profile/presentation/pages/public_profile_page.dart`,
`mobile/test/features/public_profile/section_error_states_test.dart`.

## D-240 · Shared money counters are mutated in SQL, never read-modify-write (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `OrganizationWallet` is a projected cache of the append-only ledger (D-103), and three
paths mutated it by loading the row, adjusting the property and letting `SaveChangesAsync` flush it:
`OrderService.ConfirmPaymentAsync` (capture), `RefundService.RefundOrderAsync` (refund) and
`CollectedToAvailableLedgerJob` (daily maturation). EF compiles that to
`SET "CollectedPaise" = <literal>`, and Postgres READ COMMITTED does not prevent a lost update there —
the second writer blocks on the row lock, then overwrites with a value it computed before the first
one landed.

**Measured, not theorised.** Six concurrent captures for one org produced six correct ledger rows
summing to 60000 paise and a wallet crediting **10000** — five payments missing from the org's
balance. Six concurrent refunds of different orders netted the ledger to 0 and left **50000 paise**
of phantom, still-withdrawable funds, i.e. money already returned to customers that the org could
withdraw again. In both cases the ledger stayed correct and only the cache drifted, so nothing
surfaced as an error.

**Decision.** Any counter that more than one request can touch is mutated with a single SQL statement
whose new value is computed by the database (`.SetProperty(w => w.X, w => w.X + n)`), and any
precondition on it lives in the `WHERE` so it is evaluated under the row lock. This is the contract
`InventoryService.TryConsumeManyAsync` already used for seat capacity — the wallet simply never
adopted it, while `WalletService.InitiateWithdrawalAsync` had independently reached for
`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`. One idiom now, not three.

Consequences: the entity must NOT also be loaded into the change tracker, or `SaveChangesAsync` emits
a second, stale `UPDATE` that undoes the increment. `LastLedgerEntryId` is a real FK, so it is stamped
only after the `SaveChanges` that inserts the ledger row. A missing wallet still throws rather than
silently affecting 0 rows — banking a payment whose funds land nowhere is worse than failing the
webhook. `CollectedToAvailableLedgerJob` additionally claims each entry's `Collected → Available`
transition conditionally, which makes maturation idempotent under Hangfire re-dispatch.

**Verification.** `WalletConcurrencyTests` — six concurrent captures and six concurrent refunds of
different orders in one org, both asserting `wallet == SUM(ledger)`. Both reproduce the old failure
and pass on the fix. Full suite 1007 tests, 0 failures.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Orders/OrderService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Orders/RefundService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Jobs/CollectedToAvailableLedgerJob.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/WalletConcurrencyTests.cs`, `.claude/memory/database-conventions.md`.

## D-241 · Refresh rotation is claimed atomically; the race loser is refused, not treated as theft (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `AuthService.RefreshAsync` tested `stored.RevokedAt is not null`, then later assigned
`stored.RevokedAt` as a tracked change flushed by `IssueTokensAsync`. Between the read and the write,
a second request carrying the same token passed the same read. Verified: two parallel
`POST /v1/auth/refresh` calls with one token **both returned 200**, each minting its own chain. A
stolen refresh token could therefore be forked into a parallel live session, and because neither
caller observed `RevokedAt`, reuse detection never fired — the guarantee D-009/D-014 exist to provide.

**Decision.** Rotation is claimed with a conditional
`UPDATE … WHERE "Id" = @id AND "RevokedAt" IS NULL`, the same claim idiom
`ConfirmPaymentAsync` uses for `Pending → Paid`. Exactly one caller sees one affected row.

**The loser is refused (401) but its session family is NOT revoked.** Two refreshes arriving together
is ordinary client behaviour — parallel prefetches, a burst of 401s — not evidence of theft, and
revoking the family would sign a legitimate user out of every device for it. Genuine reuse (the same
token presented after rotation has settled) still trips full family revocation through the
pre-existing `RevokedAt` branch, so the D-009/D-014 response is unchanged for the case it was written
for. The session is also validated *before* the claim, so a token whose session is already gone is
refused without being consumed.

**Client consequence, shipped with it.** Because rotation is now strictly single-use, a client that
fires concurrent refreshes off one cookie will have losers. Mobile was already safe
(`auth_interceptor.dart` single-flights via `_inFlightRefresh ??=`). Web and admin were not: Next.js
middleware runs per request including every `<Link>` prefetch, and both answered a failed refresh by
clearing the auth cookies — signing the user out mid-navigation (admin additionally redirects to
`/login`). Both now de-duplicate by presented token, retaining the result briefly after it settles
because a racing request captured the OLD cookie and can arrive after the winner finished. Keyed by
token and never a single shared promise, which would hand one user's tokens to another. The map is
per-process; web and admin are single-instance in `docker-compose`, and scaling either out needs a
shared store.

**Verification.** `AuthRotationConcurrencyTests` — parallel rotation mints exactly one chain and the
winner's chain stays rotatable; losing the race leaves the family intact. `AuthTests
.Refresh_rotates_and_reuse_revokes_all_sessions` continues to pin the revoke-everything response for
real sequential reuse. `tsc --noEmit` clean on web and admin.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Auth/AuthService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/AuthRotationConcurrencyTests.cs`, `web/middleware.ts`, `admin/middleware.ts`.

## D-242 · Count-based limits are serialised with advisory locks, not hoped for (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `PerUserLimit` and a group's target size are *counts*, so no unique index can enforce
them. Both were read before the order transaction opened and acted on after: two simultaneous orders
from one buyer each saw "one slot left" and each took it, and two simultaneous `POST /v1/groups/join`
calls could push a group past its `OrderItem.Qty`.

**Decision.** Evaluate both inside the transaction, behind a transaction-scoped Postgres advisory
lock — the guard `SeatBlockService` already used for its reassign limit. `PerUserLimit` locks on
(ticket type, buyer), so unrelated buyers never contend; the group check locks on the group id. The
pre-transaction check stays as a friendly early-out that spares the paid path a wasted gateway-order
call, exactly like the sold-out pre-check above it.

Lock ordering is fixed — group, then buyer — and `AddMemberToGroupAsync` is the only path taking
both, while `CreateOrderAsync` takes the buyer lock alone, so the pair cannot deadlock. Guest buyers
have no user id, so their key derives from a SHA-256 of the normalised phone; a key collision only
makes two unrelated buyers serialise occasionally, never a correctness issue.

**Verification.** `OrderLimitConcurrencyTests` — two simultaneous orders against `PerUserLimit = 1`
issue exactly one ticket; two simultaneous joins into a 2-seat group leave exactly two members.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Orders/OrderService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/OrderLimitConcurrencyTests.cs`, `docs/api/README.md`.

## D-243 · Recurring jobs are single-run and cadence-tuned; per-message jobs are not (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `AddHangfireServer()` runs on every API replica and no job carried
`[DisableConcurrentExecution]` or `[AutomaticRetry]`. A recurring job whose invisibility timeout
lapses is re-dispatched while the first run is still executing — which for `OutboxDispatchJob` means
duplicate at-least-once deliveries, and for the ledger sweep meant applying a wallet delta twice.

**Decision.** Every *recurring* job gets `[DisableConcurrentExecution]` plus a retry count matched to
its cadence: frequent jobs (minutely to hourly) use `Attempts = 0`, because the next tick is soon and
replaying a failed sweep buys nothing; daily jobs use `Attempts = 3`, because a lost run costs 24
hours. Lock wait is 10s for frequent jobs and 60s for daily ones — long enough to ride out an overlap,
short enough that a stuck run does not queue up behind itself.

**Two deliberate exclusions.** `ChatNotificationJob` is enqueued *per message*, so a class-level lock
would serialise every chat notification on the platform behind one worker — the attribute is right for
sweeps and wrong for fan-out. `PhoneE164BackfillJob` is not a Hangfire job at all: it is resolved
directly by an admin endpoint, so the attributes would be inert.

Idempotency is still the real guarantee — the lock reduces the window, it does not close it. The
ledger sweep's conditional state claim (D-240) is what makes a duplicate run harmless.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Jobs/*.cs`.

## D-244 · Required secrets are strength-checked, not just presence-checked (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `RequiredSecrets.ValidateAsync` confirmed each secret was non-empty. `JWT_SECRET` and
`TICKET_HMAC_SECRET` were separately strength-checked in `JwtOptions.FromSecret`, but `OTP_PEPPER` had
only the presence check — so `dev-only-otp-pepper-change-me`, committed in `.env.example`,
`docker-compose.yml` and the test factory, booted a Production host completely clean.

That is the worst secret to leave unguarded: its failure mode is silent (D-115). OTP hashes computed
under a guessable pepper verify correctly and look identical to properly peppered ones, so nothing
downstream ever surfaces the mistake.

**Decision.** Every name in `RequiredSecrets.Names` is run through
`SecretValidation.RequireStrongProductionSecret` in Production, and the OTP placeholder joins the
known-dev-values list. The check runs **outside** the per-secret `try`, deliberately: that block
converts any exception into "secret unavailable", which would have reported a present-but-unusable
secret as missing and hidden the real reason.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Secrets/RequiredSecrets.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Configuration/SecretValidation.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/SecretValidationTests.cs`.

## D-245 · Own-list endpoints are bounded, and hand-written client schemas are the weak link (2026-08-03)

**Context.** `GET /v1/orders` and `GET /v1/groups` returned every row a user had ever accumulated, with
no cap. Each also built its views in a loop — two queries per order, four per group — so cost scaled
with history on both axes at once. The loops are gone (batched to three and five queries); this entry
is about the bound.

**Decision.** Both take optional `page` / `pageSize`, capped at `OrderPaging.MaxPageSize` (200), which
is *also* the default. That is deliberately not a UI page size. Both shipped clients call these routes
with no query string, so a conventional default of 20–50 would have silently hidden a buyer's older
tickets — a data-loss bug dressed as a feature. 200 is far above any realistic personal order count, so
it closes the unbounded tail without truncating a real user. The response stays a bare JSON array; no
consumer has to change. A caller that genuinely wants pages passes them.

**The bug this uncovered.** `web/lib/api.ts` declared `myTicketSchema` with a **required `order_id`**
that `ToOrderJson` has never emitted, so `z.array(...).parse()` threw on every non-empty response, and
the page's `.catch(() => [])` rendered "No tickets yet." **Every buyer with tickets saw an empty My
Tickets page, and nothing was logged.** The schema also declared `event_title`, `event_slug` and
`ticket_type`, which the server did not send — so even a passing parse showed a raw event GUID as the
title.

Both halves are fixed: the schema now mirrors `ToOrderJson`, and the list endpoint denormalises
`event_title` / `event_slug` / `ticket_type` (batched, no extra round trip per row) because the client
was right about what a ticket card needs — the server simply never provided it.

This is the concrete cost of having no generated contract: 435 endpoint mappings carry 15 `.Produces<T>()`
declarations, responses are hand-written anonymous objects, and the clients hand-maintain their models.
Nothing mechanical could have caught this, and nothing did. Mobile's `OrderDto` happened to match; web's
did not, and only web broke.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IOrderService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Orders/OrderService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/OrderEndpoints.cs`,
`web/lib/api.ts`, `web/app/(app)/tickets/page.tsx`, `docs/api/README.md`.

## D-246 · Response-schema coverage is a ratchet, because a lying contract beats no contract only in theory (2026-08-03)

**Context.** D-259 gave the platform a committed contract (`docs/api/openapi.json`) and a CI drift gate.
The gate is only as useful as what the spec actually describes, and it described **18 of 426 operations'
response bodies**. The rest advertise "200, no content schema", which is why nothing mechanical caught
`web/lib/api.ts` requiring an `order_id` the server never sent (D-245).

**Why it cannot simply be finished.** ~190 endpoints answer with a hand-written anonymous object
(`Results.Ok(ToOrderJson(...))`). Swashbuckle cannot infer a schema from an anonymous type, and the keys
are frequently *not* the snake_case of the view type — `ToOrderJson` emits `ticket_type` where
`OrderView.TicketTypeName` would give `ticket_type_name`, and several mappers transform values
(`status.ToLowerInvariant()`). Bolting `.Produces<SomeView>()` onto those would publish a schema that
disagrees with the bytes on the wire. **A contract that lies is worse than one that is silent**: silence
makes a client author read the handler, a wrong schema makes them trust it. Generated clients would be
confidently broken. Those endpoints need a named response DTO each — a real refactor, not an annotation.

**Decision.** Coverage rises endpoint by endpoint as each gains a truthful response type, and
`OpenApiCoverageTests` ratchets it so it can only go up. This pass added the 26 endpoints that return an
`Application.Abstractions` record directly out of `Results.Ok` — for those `.Produces<T>()` is exactly
true, because `SnakeCaseResponseConverter` (runtime) and `SnakeCaseResponseSchemaFilter` (spec) already
agree on the naming. **18 → 44.**

**Not every response type is covered by the convention.** The converter keys on the
`Kurx.Application.Abstractions` namespace, so a response record declared elsewhere still serializes
camelCase — `DevCapabilityPreview` (in `Kurx.Infrastructure.Dev`) is one, and its endpoint genuinely
returns `canRepresentOrg`. Dev-only, so harmless today, but the namespace rule has that hole and a future
response type declared outside Abstractions will silently escape the platform convention.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/*.cs` (26 endpoints across 8 files),
`backend/Kurx.Tests/OpenApiCoverageTests.cs`, `docs/api/openapi.json`.

## D-250 · Convergence backfills leave the boot path; reference seeders stay (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `Program.cs` ran, inline and synchronously on every boot: migrations, six reference-data
seeders, then eight per-row convergence passes. The convergence passes are the problem. Each is an
anti-join over a user-data table followed by a serial per-row loop — `IEventRegistrationService.BackfillAsync`
scans the whole `orders` table twice and then projects order-by-order, each projection opening its own
scope, transaction and per-person advisory lock. Boot time therefore scaled with data volume, and a
rolling deploy had every replica running those same scans over those same rows simultaneously.

**The split.** The two groups are not the same kind of work and do not belong in the same place.

*Reference seeders stay at boot, fail-closed.* `SystemTemplateSeeder`, `EventTaxonomySeeder`,
`KindRegistrySeeder`, `CapabilityRegistrySeeder`, `ParticipantRoleSeeder`, `DesignTemplateSeeder` write a
fixed, bounded set of platform rows that the API cannot serve a single request without. They are guarded
by an "already populated" check, cost nothing on a warm database, and do not grow with tenant data.
Deferring them would mean serving traffic against a database with no taxonomy.

*Convergence passes move to `DataBackfillJob`.* Every one of them is driven exclusively by a user-data
table (`Events`, `EventAssignments`, `TicketTypes`, `Orders`, `Groups`, `EventSearchDocuments`) and is
idempotent — it selects only rows still missing their projection. Running them hourly converges the data
exactly as boot-time execution did, off the critical path. The job carries
`[DisableConcurrentExecution]`, so Hangfire's Postgres lock keeps concurrent replicas off each other
rather than having them duplicate the scan. The ordering constraints are preserved inside the job: kinds
before capabilities (the Kind×Capability defaults key on the kind slug), pools before the registration
chain (admissions link to a pool).

**Deploy-time convergence is preserved.** `jobs.Trigger("data-backfill")` enqueues one run at startup.
It *enqueues* — the host finishes starting while a worker does the scan — so a deploy still converges
promptly without blocking readiness.

**Boot stays fail-closed** on secret validation, `MigrateAsync` and connectivity. That guarantee is
untouched; only work that was never a precondition for serving traffic moved.

**Known follow-up.** The reference seeders are still the sole source of taxonomy/registry rows for the
integration suite: `KurxApiFactory.EnsureTemplate` builds the template database with `Database.Migrate()`
only — schema, no data — so the boot-path seeding is what populates every freshly-cloned `kurx_test`.
Moving the seeders too would require the factory to seed explicitly after reset (better still: seed the
template once, which would also make the suite faster). That change belongs in `Kurx.Tests` and is not
made here.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Jobs/DataBackfillJob.cs`.

## D-251 · 429 is not exempt from the one error model (2026-08-02)

**Context.** CLAUDE.md §2 mandates a single error shape: RFC7807 `ProblemDetails` carrying `error` and
`correlationId`. The rate limiter's `OnRejected` hand-wrote its JSON with `WriteAsJsonAsync`, producing an
anonymous object with neither field — so 429 was the only response on the platform a client could not
handle with the shared error parser, and the only one an incident could not be traced through.

**Root cause, not the symptom.** Adding the two fields to that literal would have fixed this instance and
left the next hand-written writer free to drift again. `correlationId` is not something a call site should
know how to produce: it is stamped by `CustomizeProblemDetails`, which only runs for responses written
through `IProblemDetailsService`. The fix is therefore to route rejections through that service — the same
path `GlobalExceptionHandler` already uses — so the contract is applied by construction.

**Shape.** `Title` and `error` are both `rate_limited`, matching the endpoint convention where the error
code is the title. `Retry-After` is still set from the lease metadata before writing.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`.

## D-252 · No elevated admin tier in the global throttle (2026-08-02)

**Context.** The global limiter partitioned authenticated callers with
`ctx.User.HasClaim("kurx_admin", "true") ? 3000 : 300`. That branch was unreachable. The limiter runs
between `UseAuthentication` and `UseAuthorization`, and `kurx_admin` is emitted by
`PlatformRoleClaimsTransformation`, which runs during authorization — so the claim is never present when
this delegate executes, and every authenticated caller has always taken the 300 path.

**The decision is to delete it, not to make it work.** Making it real means resolving platform roles from
the database *before* the throttle: an unthrottled query per request gated on nothing, handing an attacker
a cheap amplifier through the exact component that exists to prevent one. Admin-console throughput, when it
is actually measured to be a problem, gets dedicated per-endpoint limits behind authorization where the
role is known.

An unreachable branch that silently does nothing is worse than its absence, because it reads as a working
feature.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`.

## D-253 · Redis connects lazily, once, and tolerates being down (2026-08-02)

**Context.** Three lines held two independent faults.

`ConnectionMultiplexer.Connect(redisConn)` was called during service *registration*, so it ran on the boot
thread before the host existed. A Redis that was briefly unavailable therefore took the entire API down,
and the exception escaped where nothing could retry it — the API became strictly less available than the
cache it depends on, which inverts the point of a cache.

Separately, `AddStackExchangeRedis(connectionString)` constructs its own multiplexer. The process held two
full connection pools to the same server: one for the SignalR backplane, one for everything resolving
`IConnectionMultiplexer`.

**Resolution.** `AbortOnConnectFail = false` turns "down at boot" into a degraded dependency that
reconnects in the background. A `Lazy<IConnectionMultiplexer>` defers the connect to first use and is
thread-safe by default. SignalR is handed that same instance through `RedisOptions.ConnectionFactory`, so
there is exactly one multiplexer.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`.

## D-254 · The signing-key resolver must not do I/O (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `IssuerSigningKeyResolver` is a synchronous contract — `JwtBearerOptions` exposes no async
variant — so the ES256 resolver calls `GetValidationKeysAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult()`. Blocking on an
async call from a request thread is normally a thread-pool hazard.

**What is actually true here.** `SigningKeyService` memory-caches the validation set, and `GetResult()` on
an already-completed task returns without parking a thread. The block is therefore real only on a cache
miss: at TTL expiry, and at cold start — including the first request after a deployment, which is the one
that triggers `CreateAndActivateAsync` and pays for key generation.

**Resolution.** `SigningKeyCacheWarmer`, a `BackgroundService`, refreshes the set every 20s — inside the
30s TTL — so the entry is replaced before it can expire and the resolver's call is always a hit. This is
deliberately *not* a rewrite of the resolver: there is no async seam to rewrite it into. A failed warm is
logged and retried on the next tick rather than thrown, because the resolver can still load the keys
itself and a transient database blip must not take the warmer down permanently.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Auth/SigningKeyCacheWarmer.cs`.

## D-255 · Rate limits are counted in Redis, not per process (2026-08-02)

**Context.** Every limiter used the in-memory `FixedWindow`/`SlidingWindow` primitives, whose counters live
in process memory. Behind N replicas that silently multiplies every configured limit by N. The per-IP OTP
shield is the case that matters: its entire purpose is bounding how fast one host can enumerate phone
numbers, and horizontal scaling quietly relaxed it in proportion to capacity.

**Resolution.** `RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter` counts in Redis. The increment and its expiry run in one Lua
script so they are atomic — a bare `INCR` followed by `EXPIRE` leaks a permanent key if the process dies
between them, and that key then rejects its partition forever.

**Sliding to fixed, deliberately.** A distributed sliding window costs a sorted-set write plus a range trim
per request; a fixed window is one atomic `INCR`. The cost is that a caller can spend two windows' permits
either side of a boundary. That is acceptable for a throughput shield, and irrelevant for OTP, whose
authoritative limits are durable in Postgres (D-005) rather than at the edge.

**Partition keys are now namespaced.** In-process, each policy owned a separate limiter, so the `otp` and
`resume` policies could both partition on a bare IP without colliding. Sharing one Redis keyspace removes
that isolation, so the keys carry an `otp:` / `resume:` prefix. This was a latent correctness bug
introduced by the move, not a pre-existing one — worth stating because it is invisible in the diff of
either policy read on its own.

**Fails open.** An unreachable Redis allows the request and logs a warning. Rejecting would convert a cache
blip into a total outage, and the controls that actually protect credentials are the durable Postgres ones,
not these.

**`heavy` stays local, on purpose.** It is a concurrency limiter, not a window: it caps in-flight work on
*this* instance, which is what protects this instance's thread pool. A shared concurrency counter must also
release its permit when a request ends, so any instance crashing mid-request would leak permits forever —
strictly worse than a local cap that dies with the process that owned it.

**Dev and the test host keep the in-memory path** when `REDIS_CONNECTION` is unset, so local behaviour is
unchanged.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/RateLimiting/RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/RateLimiting/RateLimitPartitions.cs`.

## D-256 · Containers run unprivileged (2026-08-02)

**Context.** All three images ran as root. A remote-code-execution bug in any of them started with uid 0.

**Resolution.** The API uses `USER $APP_UID`, the non-root user the `aspnet` base image already ships, so
there is no `useradd`. The two Next.js images use the `node` user (uid 1000) that the node image ships.

**The writable-path detail is the whole risk of this change.** Dropping privilege breaks anything that
wrote to a root-owned path, and it breaks it at *runtime*, not at build. Two such paths exist.
`LocalDiskStorage` calls `Directory.CreateDirectory` on `LOCALDISK_ROOT` in its constructor, so the
container would fail to start; that directory is created and chowned in the image. `next start` writes into
`.next/cache` for ISR and image optimisation, so the Next.js payloads are copied with `--chown=node:node`.
The published application files stay root-owned and therefore read-only to the process, which is the
desired posture — the app has no reason to rewrite its own binaries.

**Touches** `infra/Dockerfile.api`, `web/Dockerfile`, `admin/Dockerfile`.

## D-257 · The currency symbol belongs to the amount (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `Order.Currency`, `LedgerEntry.Currency` and `Event.SettlementCurrency` have been persisted
per V3 §9.1 since Phase 9 — an event settles in its own currency. No client rendered any of it.
`mobile/lib/core/utils/money.dart` hardcoded `symbol: '₹'`; `web/lib/formatters.ts` took a `currency`
parameter that no call site ever passed; `admin` carried three separate copies of a paise formatter, two
currency-aware and one hardcoded to ₹. A non-INR event therefore rendered as rupees everywhere — not a
formatting blemish but a materially wrong number shown to whoever is being paid.

**Rule.** A money value is never formatted without the currency it is denominated in. Where a payload does
not yet carry one the formatter defaults to INR, so nothing changes until the field arrives.

**Unmapped codes fall back to the code itself** (`AUD 1,200`) rather than to a symbol. A plainly-labelled
amount in an unfamiliar format is recoverable; a confidently wrong symbol is not.

**`Money.fromPaise` became `fromMinor`** rather than gaining an alias: the old name asserts INR in the
signature, which is the bug. Paise are INR's minor unit, cents are USD's, and the parameter is whichever
the amount actually uses.

**Touches** `mobile/lib/core/utils/money.dart`, `mobile/test/core/money_test.dart`, and the four event
widgets that called `fromPaise`.

## D-258 · A stale "not implemented" note is worse than no note (2026-08-02)

**Context.** `org_wallet_page.dart` carried `// Withdrawal button — SECURITY STOP: not implemented yet`
above a permanently disabled button. The claim was false. `WalletWithdrawPage` exists, is routed at
`/org/:orgId/wallet/withdraw` (`app_router.dart:303`), and posts to the real
`POST /v1/orgs/{orgId}/wallet/withdraw`. The flow was already reachable by deep link.

So the note bought no protection at all — it only made a working feature look broken, and it did so in
the vocabulary of a security control, which is the vocabulary least likely to be re-examined.

**Resolution.** The button routes to the page that already existed. The substantive caution is real and
is honoured where it belongs: a withdrawal records a durable `requested` intent and **nothing executes
it** — `Withdrawal.Status` declares `requested | processing | paid | rejected` and no code assigns the
last three. The destination screen says exactly that through `_PayoutNotice` rather than implying money
is moving.

**Rule.** A stop comment states what is unsafe and why, and is deleted the moment that stops being true.
"Not implemented yet" is a fact with an expiry date, and facts with expiry dates do not belong in
comments that read as security controls.

**Not done here, deliberately:** analytics charts on `event_analytics_page`/`org_analytics_page` still
say "coming soon". Rendering them needs a charting dependency, and adding one is a decision, not a
detail. iOS passkeys likewise remain unimplemented: `PasskeyPlugin.kt` exists for Android with no iOS
counterpart, so it is native Swift work, and the Dart side already degrades correctly by returning
`false` from `isAvailable()` on `MissingPluginException`.

**Touches** `mobile/lib/features/organizer/presentation/pages/org_wallet_page.dart`.

## D-259 · The API contract is generated, committed, and gated (2026-08-02)

**Context.** 435 endpoint mappings carried 15 `.Produces<T>()` between them. Responses are largely
hand-written anonymous objects, which Swashbuckle cannot infer a schema from, and Swagger was mapped
only in Development with no spec artifact checked in anywhere. Three clients — web, admin, Flutter —
therefore hand-maintained their own models against an API that published nothing, with no mechanism
that could ever notice them diverging.

**This is not hypothetical; it had already happened, twice, in the money surface.** `/v1/orgs/{orgId}/wallet`
returns `WalletView` straight from `Results.Ok`, and this API configures no JSON naming policy, so the
wire is camelCase. Both `web/lib/api.ts` and `admin/lib/api.ts` declared snake_case Zod schemas for it.
Zod's `.parse()` throws, so `getOrgWallet` and `getOrgWalletAsAdmin` failed on **every** call and neither
finance page could render. Mobile's `WalletDto` annotated camelCase and was fine — which is why the
server was left alone: harmonising it "for consistency" would have broken the one client that worked.
No backend test asserted these keys, so nothing caught it for as long as it existed.

**Resolution.** `scripts/generate-openapi.sh` captures the live spec into `docs/api/openapi.json`, and CI
regenerates it and fails the build on any diff. The spec is normalised through `jq -S` so key ordering
churn is not reported as drift.

**Coverage is partial and that is stated plainly.** Response types are declared on the wallet endpoints —
the surface this bug lived in and the one where a wrong number is most expensive. The remaining ~66
anonymous-object mappers still produce schema-less responses; annotating them is mechanical follow-on
work, endpoint group by endpoint group. The gate is worth landing before that work is finished: it locks
in whatever is described today and makes every subsequent annotation a visible, reviewed diff rather
than an invisible one.

**Touches** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `scripts/generate-openapi.sh`, `docs/api/openapi.json`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/WalletEndpoints.cs`, `web/lib/api.ts`, `admin/lib/api.ts`.

### D-259 addendum · What the gate does NOT catch, and the convention split (2026-08-02)

Two limitations found by *testing* the gate rather than reading it. Both are stated here because a
contract artifact that is trusted beyond its actual guarantees is worse than none.

**1. The spec describes shape, not constraints.** `POST /v1/orgs` rejects `{"type":"Individual"}` with
`validation_failed`, but the generated spec calls `type` a plain nullable string. The constraint lives in
`OrgValidators` as `IsEnumName(typeof(OrganizationType))`, and Swashbuckle cannot see FluentValidation.
So the drift gate catches a renamed, removed or retyped field; it does **not** catch a tightened or
loosened validation rule. Closing this needs either a new dependency
(`MicroElements.Swashbuckle.FluentValidation`) or a hand-written `ISchemaFilter` that reflects over the
validators — a decision in its own right, not a detail, and deliberately not taken here.

**2. The API has two JSON conventions, and the split is now measured.**

| Style | Endpoint files | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| snake_case | 63 | hand-written anonymous-object mappers |
| snake_case | 2 | `[JsonPropertyName]` on a named record |
| **camelCase** | **10** | `Results.Ok(result.Value)` — an Application record straight out, no naming policy |

snake_case is plainly the intended platform convention at 65 of 75 files. The 10 camelCase files are not
a second convention chosen on purpose; they are the absence of one — the default serializer showing
through wherever an endpoint forwards a record instead of mapping it. That is the entire mechanism behind
the wallet bug: web and admin authors reasonably assumed the 65-file majority convention.

**Update — it WAS unified, on request.** The paragraph below records why it was initially deferred; the
concern was real and is what shaped the eventual approach, so it is kept rather than deleted. What
changed the calculus: every consumer turned out to be in-repo, so server and clients could move in one
atomic step, and the mechanism below avoids the breaking-request problem entirely. See "How it was
actually done" at the end of this entry.

**Why it was initially deferred.** Every one of the ten surfaces has live consumers —
`chat` (19 mobile files), `competition` (16), `invitation` (11), `wallet` (8), `approval` (8),
`analytics` (7), `announcement` (5), `series` (5), plus web/admin schemas. Mobile has already *adapted*
to the leak: `WalletDto` annotates camelCase explicitly. So "fixing" the server would break the one
client that currently works, for each of the ten. It is a coordinated, cross-surface, breaking migration
touching `Kurx.Application` records — it needs its own decision, a client migration order, and agreement
across both workstreams.

**The mitigation that IS in place.** The committed spec publishes the true shape of each endpoint
individually, so no author has to infer a convention from neighbours ever again, and the CI gate fails
the build the moment any of those shapes moves. That converts the failure mode from "silent runtime
breakage discovered by a user" into "red build" — which is the actual objective — without a breaking
change.

### How it was actually done (2026-08-03)

**Supersedes the camelCase observations in D-064, D-208 and D-210/D-212.** Each of those recorded the same
symptom from a different endpoint — `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/wallet`, `AttendeeRow`, the `GamificationEndpoints`
family — and D-208 called it "the one endpoint in this API that returns camelCase", which was true when
written and then stopped being true three more times. Those entries stand as history; the wire format they
describe no longer holds. Anything asserting a camelCase response for a type in
`Kurx.Application.Abstractions` should be read as superseded by this entry.

**Mechanism: a write-only converter, not a naming policy.** `PropertyNamingPolicy` was never available —
it governs deserialization too, so it would have demanded snake_case request bodies from every client and
from every already-deployed mobile build. `SnakeCaseResponseConverter` is a `JsonConverterFactory` scoped
to the `Kurx.Application.Abstractions` namespace that overrides **Write** and delegates **Read**
untouched. Requests bind exactly as before; only responses moved. Nesting is handled by serializing once
with default naming and re-emitting the document with renamed keys, so a View containing Views converts
at any depth in one pass.

Scoping by namespace rather than by a `*View` suffix was deliberate: responses are 100 `*View` plus ~40
others (`*Summary`, `*Entry`, `*Row`, `StepUpStatus`…), and a suffix rule would have silently missed the
stragglers — the exact failure mode this work exists to end. `*Input` types share the namespace and are
unaffected precisely because Read is delegated.

**The endpoint count was an undercount.** The "10 files" figure came from grepping
`Results.Ok(result.Value)`. It missed other spellings — `/v1/auth/devices` returns
`Results.Ok(await svc.ListAsync(...))` and leaked camelCase too. Converting by namespace rather than by
call site is what makes the fix complete regardless of how an endpoint spells its return.

**`SnakeCaseResponseSchemaFilter` keeps the spec honest.** Swashbuckle reads the naming policy, not
converters, so without it the published contract would have advertised camelCase for types the API now
emits as snake_case — a wrong contract, which is worse than none. The filter shares
`ToSnakeCaseName` with the converter so the two cannot drift.

**Client migration, and the trap in it.** Web and admin were mechanical (Zod schemas plus call sites;
typecheck found every straggler, including three over-eager renames of `AdminLiveEvent`, which is a
*client-side* type that `use-admin-event-hub` maps the hub payload into and which correctly stays
camelCase).

Mobile held the real hazard. `chat_mappers.dart` parses the wire **and** the offline outbox with the same
functions, and `messageToJson`/`attachmentToJson` have been persisting camelCase onto devices since the
feature shipped. A hard switch would have made every queued message and pending attachment already on a
user's phone unreadable — silent data loss on upgrade, in the one place the app promises not to lose
anything. Both chat and the trusted-device DTOs therefore read through a tolerant lookup that tries
snake_case first and camelCase second. No migration step, no data loss; the fallback can be dropped once
no supported build still holds a pre-migration cache.

**Verification.** Live: `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/wallet` returns `available_paise` and the committed spec
matches field-for-field. Across the spec, response schemas are 116 snake_case properties with 28
remaining camelCase — all of them `*Input` request DTOs, which is correct. Mobile: 266 tests pass, after
updating `org_dto_test.dart`, whose case was literally named "GET /v1/orgs/{id}/wallet is camelCase,
unlike the rest of the API". That test had pinned the bug; it now pins the corrected shape.

## D-261 · An OTP attempt is claimed, not counted (2026-08-03)

**Context.** `OtpService.VerifyAsync` read `VerifyAttempts`, compared it to `MaxVerifyAttempts`, then
incremented in memory and saved. Sequential tests pass against that shape because each request sees the
previous one's write. Parallel requests do not: they all read the same value and all write value+1, so
the counter advanced roughly once per *batch* rather than once per guess.

That matters more here than in most read-modify-write bugs. The cap is 5 over a **6-digit** keyspace, and
it is the only thing between an attacker and 10^6 tries — a limit that only counts a fraction of attempts
does not bound anything. `Consumed` was assigned the same way, so two callers presenting one correct code
could both be told they succeeded: one OTP, two sessions.

**Resolution.** Both are conditional `ExecuteUpdateAsync` claims, the shape
`ChallengeService.VerifyMatchNumberAsync` already uses for its own match-number cap — the codebase had the
right pattern and this path simply had not adopted it. The row is loaded `AsNoTracking` so no tracked copy
can write back over the claims. The attempt is now counted durably *before* the hash comparison, so a
wrong guess costs an attempt whether or not anything later throws.

**Behaviour change, stated plainly: concurrent redemption of one OTP now yields exactly one session.**
`AuthTests.Concurrent_registration_for_a_new_phone_merges_into_one_account` asserted that BOTH parallel
verifications return 200. That was never a reliable property — it passed one CI run and failed the very
next on identical test code, because it depended on how the two racers interleaved. The API was already
inconsistent with itself about this: the phone-change path one test above asserts *exactly one* success
for the same situation.

The property worth keeping is the one the test is named for — a contested phone resolves to **one**
account, never two — and that is now verified directly by re-authenticating and comparing `user_id`,
rather than inferred from both racers winning. The loser gets 401 because the code is genuinely spent.

**The cost is a real one and worth naming:** a client that fires two verifications at once (a double-tap)
now sees one of them fail. That is the correct trade for single-use credentials, and the honest fix for
the UX is client-side single-flighting — which mobile already does for refresh (`_inFlightRefresh`) and
web/admin do in `middleware.ts`. Making verification *idempotent* — returning the winner's session to the
loser — would be strictly nicer and is the natural follow-up; it is deliberately not bundled here, because
it needs a way to hand a second caller tokens it never minted.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Auth/OtpService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/OtpVerifyConcurrencyTests.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Tests/AuthTests.cs`,
`.claude/memory/security-rules.md`.

## D-262 · The Posts module: an explicit feed graph, server-side visibility, and one moderation queue (2026-08-03)

**Context.** The master product flow specifies a 📝 Posts module — feed, create, text/images/video/
documents/polls, event posts, mentions, hashtags, like/comment/reply/share/save/report, my posts —
and none of it existed: no entity, no endpoint, no service, no table. The web client was built first
against a frozen contract, so the shape of the responses was fixed before the backend was written and
the open questions were all behavioural. Four of them decide what this module is.

**Resolution — feed composition.** `/v1/feed` is an explicit graph, not "everything public". It
returns, newest first by the `(CreatedAt, Id)` keyset: the caller's own posts, posts by **accepted
allies** (`AllyConnection`), posts attached to events of **orgs the caller follows**
(`OrganizationFollower`), and posts attached to **events the caller holds a non-void ticket for**.
A public post by a stranger is *not* in the feed — it is reachable through that author's profile and
through hashtag pages, but it does not arrive uninvited.

This is the most consequential call here, so the reasoning is worth stating. A feed of every public
post is a firehose, and the instant it exists the product is no longer ticketing with a feed attached
— it is a ranking problem, because a chronological firehose is unusable at any real scale and the only
fix is a relevance model nobody has scoped. An explicit graph is bounded, explicable to the user
("you follow them / you're going to this"), and can be widened later without breaking a client.
Widening is a one-way door that stays open; narrowing after launch is the one that does not.

Orgs do not author posts. A followed org reaches the feed through posts attached to its events, which
is the only authorship relation an org actually has in this model.

**Resolution — visibility.** Four tiers: `public`, `connections` (accepted allies), `event_participants`
(a live ticket check against `Post.EventId`), `only_me`. Enforcement is one predicate,
`PostService.VisibleTo`, composed by *every* read path — feed, single post, profile, hashtag, event,
saved, comments. A second implementation would be a second chance to disagree with the first, and the
way that disagreement surfaces is a private post in a stranger's feed.

Three consequences worth naming:

- **A post the caller may not see returns 404, not 403** (D-018). A 403 would confirm the post exists,
  which is the exact fact being withheld. The single exception is `post_hidden`, which only ever
  reaches the post's own author, so platform moderation is not silent to the person it happened to.
- **The participation check is live per request** (D-015), never a token claim. Voiding a ticket
  revokes access on the next request, not at the reader's next login.
- **The trending-hashtag roll-up counts only posts the caller can see.** Counting over everything
  would make the tag list a side channel: a tag that trends but shows no posts tells a reader that
  private posts exist and roughly how many.
- **An unknown username answers with an empty page, not 404** — the profile route is public, so a
  distinct 404 would be a free username-enumeration oracle.

**Resolution — share nesting.** Sharing a share re-targets the **original**; it never nests. The
depth a client has to render is therefore bounded by the data, not by client discipline, and one
level is all the response can ever contain (`BuildViewsAsync` recurses exactly once, with
`includeShared: false`). `cannot_share_a_share` is what is left over: the target is a share whose
original has since been deleted, hidden, or become invisible to this sharer, so there is nothing to
re-target to. `ShareCount` is incremented on the original in SQL.

**Resolution — notifications.** Four kinds — `post_like`, `post_comment`, `post_reply`,
`post_mention` — through the existing `INotificationService.NotifyAsync`, so the in-app row, the
unread-count refresh, the SignalR push and the FCM fan-out are all inherited rather than
reimplemented. Nobody is ever notified about their own action, a reply on your own post produces one
notice rather than two, and an edit notifies only the mentions the edit *added* (otherwise the edit
button is a broadcast tool). Every send is wrapped: a failed notice must never undo a committed
write.

**Counters mutate in SQL, never read-modify-write (D-240).** `LikeCount`, `CommentCount`,
`ShareCount`, `VoteCount` and `TotalVotes` are contested by definition — a popular post is one many
people are liking in the same instant — so each is a conditional `ExecuteUpdateAsync` whose new value
Postgres computes under the row lock, and every decrement carries a `> 0` guard in the `WHERE` so a
counter cannot be driven negative. `PostConcurrencyTests` fires the real parallel requests: twenty
simultaneous likes, twenty simultaneous votes, fifteen comments, fifteen reshares. Each of those
passes against a read-modify-write implementation when run sequentially, which is exactly why they
are written as races.

**One vote per person needed a fourth poll table.** A ballot is N rows in `post_poll_votes`, and "at
most one ballot per voter" is not expressible as a constraint over N rows: two concurrent votes from
one account naming *different* options both pass an application-level "have you voted?" check, and
the unique index on `(PollId, UserId, OptionId)` only forbids the same option twice. `PostPollBallot`
holds the unique `(PollId, UserId)` and is inserted first, so the loser fails on the index instead of
stuffing the ballot box. It is one small table against a subtle integrity hole in the one feature
where ballot integrity is the whole point.

Relatedly, **`PostPoll.TotalVotes` counts votes CAST, not voters** — it is exactly the sum of the
option counts. For a single-choice poll the two definitions are identical; for a multi-select they
are not, and counting rows is the definition that stays consistent with the option counts under
concurrency without a second distinct-voter claim.

**What was reused rather than rebuilt.** Reporting extends the existing polymorphic `Report` subject
vocabulary with `post` and `post_comment` — one moderation queue is the entire point of a polymorphic
subject, and a posts-specific report table would have split it. Media follows `ChatAttachment`'s
two-step upload exactly (presign → PUT → confirm, with every authoritative check on confirm because
that is the first moment the server can look at the bytes), including the orphan sweep that a
nullable `PostId` makes necessary. `PostMediaPolicy` is a separate allow-list from
`AttachmentPolicy` rather than an extension of it: posts carry video and chat does not, and extending
chat's list would have changed what every event chat room accepts as a side effect of shipping a feed.

**Kind is derived, not trusted.** The client sends `kind`, and the server ignores it: the kind is read
off what is actually attached (share → poll → video → images → document → event → text). A
discriminator that can disagree with the payload it describes is a bug waiting for a client release.

**Hashtags and mentions are extracted server-side and only server-side.** A client-supplied tag list
