would let a caller attach their post to any trend; a client-supplied mention list would let them
notify anyone. The grammar is character-for-character the one `web/components/posts/post-body.tsx`
tokenizes with — if the two drifted, the client would render a link over text the server never
indexed. Unresolvable handles are dropped silently: a mention is a link plus a notification, and
neither means anything without an account behind it.

**A comment page is a page of ROOTS, not of rows.** The first cut paginated comments flat, newest-first,
which is simpler and subtly wrong: newest-first puts a reply *before* the parent it belongs to, so a
reply to an older comment arrives on page 1 while its parent is still on page 2. The client groups by
`ParentCommentId`, so such a reply is neither a root nor a child and renders **nowhere at all** until the
reader happens to page far enough. A page is therefore `limit` roots, each arriving with all of its
replies (oldest-first, capped at `limit × 10` so one viral thread cannot return an unbounded page). The
response stays flat and the contract is unchanged; only which rows constitute a page moved.

**Counters move in both directions.** Deleting a reshare decrements the original's `ShareCount`, and
deleting a root comment cascades to its replies and drops `CommentCount` by all of them at once. Both
were one-way in the first cut — an increment on create with a matching decrement nowhere — so a post
shared and un-shared a hundred times would have read as a hundred live shares forever. The cascade also
matches what `comment-thread.tsx` already assumed in its optimistic update, which is how it was found.

**Media ceilings are 25 MB for every kind, video included — a platform limit, not a product choice.**
The only storage provider implemented today presigns back at this API, so an upload is an ordinary
Kestrel request bounded by `MaxRequestBodySize` (~28.6 MB); chat's 25 MB was picked against the same
wall. A larger video ceiling would presign happily and then die part-way through the bytes on an opaque
413 rather than being refused at presign with an `invalid_media` the client can explain. Raise it when
real object storage lands and the client PUTs straight to the bucket.

**Deliberately not built.** Video duration and dimensions are never populated: no media probe is wired,
and a fabricated number is worse than the null the contract already allows.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Posts.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IPostService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Posts/*`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Jobs/PostMediaCleanupJob.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Moderation/ReportService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/PostEndpoints.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Validation/PostValidators.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/PostTests.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Tests/PostConcurrencyTests.cs`,
`docs/api/README.md`, `docs/roadmap/README.md`.

## D-265 · Event creation: grouped field inputs, and the fields the wizard could not previously write (2026-08-03)

**Context.** The product flow specifies an 18-step Create Event wizard. Roughly half of it could not
be built, not because the clients were unfinished but because the columns did not exist: an event had
no tagline, no short description, no logo or thumbnail, no rules text, no FAQ, no organiser terms, no
code of conduct, no refund or cancellation policy, no consent, no event-level registration window, no
check-in window, no result date, no certificate-release date, no building/floor/room, no meeting
platform or password, no age or gender eligibility, no event-wide team cap, no platform fee, no tax,
no coupons and no prize pool. Web shipped a 5-step wizard and Flutter a single 236-line form because
those were the only fields `CreateEventBody` accepted.

**Why grouped records rather than more parameters.** `CreateEventInput` and `UpdateEventInput` were
already 25-parameter positional records. Adding twenty-five more positions would have produced call
sites where a transposed argument is invisible at the type level — two adjacent `string?` parameters
swapped compile perfectly and corrupt data silently. The new fields are therefore six optional
trailing groups (`Content`, `Legal`, `Schedule`, `Location`, `Eligibility`, `Commerce`), each a small
named record. Every group is optional and trailing, so every request body that predates this binds
exactly as before — no client migration, no versioned endpoint.

**Null means untouched; empty string means clear.** A wizard PATCHes one step at a time, so a body
naming only `content.tagline` must not null the `content.rules` written by a different step. The
applier therefore treats a null field as "leave alone" and an empty string as an explicit clear. This
is the one behaviour most likely to be got wrong by a later edit, so it is pinned by a test
(`Patching_one_field_in_a_group_leaves_its_neighbours_alone`).

**One applier, two callers.** `ApplyFieldGroups` is shared by create and `ApplyUpdateAsync` — the
same core the D-191 Super Admin emergency edit already reuses. The alternative was the same twenty-odd
assignments written twice, which drift the first time one side gains a validation the other does not.

**Decisions recorded here rather than left implicit:**

1. **`EventVisibility` gains `InviteOnly`, and `Event.IsHidden` is left alone.** The flow names four
   author choices (Public / Private / Invite-Only / Hidden). `IsHidden` already existed as an *admin
   moderation* flag (D-186). Overloading it would mean an organiser choosing "Hidden" is
   indistinguishable from an organiser whose event was hidden by staff, which makes "why can't anyone
   see my event" unanswerable from the data. Author-hidden maps onto the existing `Unlisted`;
   `InviteOnly` is genuinely new because it is the only state where discovery is off *and* joining
   requires an invitation.

2. **Age and gender are stored, and they are separate from `AudienceRule`.** `AudienceRule` (§4.4) is
   an org-membership predicate — unit subtree, role, cohort year, attributes. Demographic gates are a
   different axis and both may apply to one event. They are deliberately plain columns on `Event` and
   not folded into the rule's JSON, because a discrimination-sensitive field that a reviewer cannot
   find by reading the schema is a field nobody audits. `GenderRestriction.Any` is the default and
   means no gate at all — a restriction only ever exists because an organiser set one.

3. **Consent is evidenced, not asserted.** `Event.RequiresConsent` alone would only record that an
   organiser wanted consent. `registration_consents` stores the SHA-256 of the exact text shown plus
   the timestamp and IP. The *hash*, not the text, because an organiser can edit `ConsentText`
   afterwards and a consent row that silently starts pointing at different wording is worse than no
   row: comparing the stored hash to the current text is what reveals that the terms moved under a
   registrant's feet. Requiring consent with no consent text is rejected (`consent_text_required`) —
   otherwise every registrant "accepts" an empty string.

4. **Event-level registration windows bound the per-ticket ones, never widen them.** Sale windows
   already existed on `TicketType`. They can express "VIP goes on sale Monday" but not "registration
   for this event closes Friday", which is what organisers actually announce. The event window is the
   outer bound; a ticket's own window narrows it further.

5. **`MeetingPassword` is a secret.** It is never logged and only ever returned to a confirmed
   registrant. A meeting password on a public listing is not a password.

6. **Coupon `RedeemedCount` is claimed in SQL, never read-modify-write** (D-240/D-261). A coupon that
   over-redeems under concurrent checkout is a money bug, not a display bug. Codes are unique per
   event rather than globally: two organisers both wanting `WELCOME10` is normal, and a global unique
   index would stop the second one existing.

7. **`TicketKind` is orthogonal to price.** `PricePaise == 0` already implied "free", but it could not
   distinguish a donation (payer-chosen above a floor) from an invite-only ticket (not selectable at
   checkout at all). Existing rows backfill to Free or Paid by price, so nothing changes for them.

**Deliberately not built in this pass.** Preview (`GET …/preview`) and the extension of the publish
checklist to the new required-for-publish fields are named as follow-ups, not silent gaps. Prize pool
is descriptive only — nothing pays out from it.

**Files.** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Events.cs`, `EventManagement.cs`, `EventCommerce.cs` (new),
`backend/Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IEventService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/EventService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Migrations/20260803153618_AddEventCreationFields.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/EventEndpoints.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Tests/EventCreationFieldsTests.cs`.

## D-263 · Account settings: preferences that bind, deletion that retains, and no TOTP (2026-08-03)

**Context.** `/settings` shipped with theme, security links, sign-out and legal text. Everything a user
would actually go to settings *for* — change your email, change your phone, control what you get
notified about, block someone, pick a language, delete your account — had no backend at all. Six of
those are mechanical. Two are not, and this entry exists for those two plus one deliberate omission.

**Resolution — TOTP is not built, and that is the decision, not a gap.**

The platform already ships three authentication factors beyond the password: **passkeys** (WebAuthn,
AM3), **trusted devices** with a device-signed step-up ceremony (AM2/AM6), and **recovery codes**
(AM7). TOTP would be a fourth, and it is the weakest of the four: it is a *shared secret*, so it is
phishable in real time and replayable inside its window, while the WebAuthn credential already
deployed is origin-bound and neither. Shipping it would mean adding the least secure factor on the
platform, plus an enrollment surface, plus an "I lost my authenticator" recovery path that recovery
codes already solve — and then defending, forever, why the security page offers a weaker option
alongside a stronger one.

The real gap the request was pointing at is not a missing factor. It is that the existing three are
**invisible**: nothing in `/settings` tells a user they have passkeys available, which devices are
trusted, or how many recovery codes remain. That is what this work ships instead. If TOTP is
revisited, the argument has to be a user need that passkeys demonstrably cannot serve — not parity
with other products.

**Resolution — notification preferences bind at the single dispatch point.**

`notification_preferences` is one row per (user, category) carrying four channel booleans, unique on
the pair. Twelve categories, four channels; **absence of a row means all channels on except WhatsApp**,
so a user who has never opened the screen keeps today's behaviour exactly and no backfill is needed.

The enforcement is the part that matters. A preferences table that no dispatcher reads is decoration,
and this repo has shipped that shape before (D-018). Every notification on the platform goes through
the one `INotificationService.NotifyAsync` — 23 call sites, one method — so the check lives *there*,
inside the implementation, and every existing and future caller inherits it without knowing. Callers
pass a free-form `kind` (`post_like`, `ally.requested`, `chat_mention`, …); `NotificationCategories`
maps kind to category, and an unrecognised kind falls back to `system` rather than to "send anyway",
because a category we forgot to map is a preference the user was never offered.

**`security` cannot be switched off, and that is enforced server-side.** A password reset, a new-device
sign-in, a phone change: these are the messages that tell a user they are being attacked, so consent to
silence them is not consent we accept. The UI renders the row disabled; the server ignores the UI and
refuses the write. Anyone who can send a PATCH is exactly the attacker this protects against.

**Resolution — deletion is scheduled, reversible for 30 days, and anonymises rather than erases.**

India's DPDP Act gives a right to erasure, and it does not override the obligations that require
records to be kept. Those two facts decide the boundary, and getting it wrong in either direction is
worse than not shipping: erase too much and the platform cannot answer a tax query or honour a
certificate; erase too little and the right is not real.

*Cleared on the user row* — name, phone (all four columns, D-089), email, username, avatar and cover
keys, headline, bio, skills, links, education. The row survives with a stable id so foreign keys hold.

*Soft-deleted* — posts and comments the user authored. They are that person's speech; keeping them
attached to a tombstone account serves nobody.

*Retained, deliberately* — orders, order items, payments, refunds, wallet ledger entries, tickets,
certificates and audit logs. These carry statutory retention (financial records, and a certificate is
a claim a third party may need to verify years later), and an audit log that can be edited by the
subject of the audit is not an audit log. They keep pointing at the anonymised id, which is now an
opaque handle rather than a person.

The 30-day grace is a scheduled column, not a job that fires at request time, so cancelling is a
column write and nothing has to be undone. A user in grace can still sign in — otherwise "cancel"
would be unreachable by the person it is for.

**Email change is new; phone change already existed and was hardened in place.** Building this
surfaced a complete user-initiated phone change already shipped at `POST /v1/me/phone/verify`
(`AuthService.VerifyPhoneChangeAsync`): it consumes the OTP, dual-writes all four phone columns
(D-089), revokes every session (D-038) and re-issues tokens. The plan called for a second
`/v1/me/phone/change/*` ceremony; that was written and then **deleted**, because a parallel
half-implementation of an auth path is exactly the failure D-018 exists to stop — and the clients
already call the existing route. What it was missing was the step-up gate and a notice to the number
being replaced, and those were added to it.

Email change is genuinely new, and delegates to `RegistrationService`, which already owns email OTP.
Both are step-up gated. Phone is the primary auth identifier (ADR-A6), so a completed change is treated
as a recovery event. **The old address is notified**; for email that notice is sent on *start*, before
the change completes, because on an account already compromised it is the only signal the real owner
ever gets.

**Blocks do something.** A block that only hides a name is a lie told to the person who asked for
protection. `UserBlock` is enforced on the live read paths in both directions: Posts feed and single
reads, comments, ally requests, and (D-264) DM room creation and delivery.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Users.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Users/*`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Notifications/NotificationService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/*`,
`web/app/(app)/settings/**`, `mobile/lib/features/settings/**`.

## D-264 · Direct messages: one room per pair, requests as spam control (2026-08-03)

**Context.** `ChatRoom.EventId` is non-nullable and unique with `Kind`, so chat is structurally
event-bound — 1:1 messaging is not a feature that was left out, it is a shape the schema forbids.
Event chat itself is complete and heavily tested (attachments D-110, presence D-114, read pointers and
outbox idempotency D-104), and none of it may regress.

**Resolution — a DM is a `ChatRoom`, not a second messaging system.** `EventId` becomes nullable,
`ChatRoomKind` gains `Direct`, and the existing per-event uniqueness index is scoped to
`"EventId" IS NOT NULL` so it keeps meaning exactly what it meant. Everything downstream — messages,
attachments, presence, read pointers, the hub, the mobile offline outbox — works on a DM room without
modification, because a DM room *is* a room. A parallel `DirectMessage` table would have duplicated
every one of those, which is this repo's documented failure mode (D-018).

**One room per pair, enforced by the database.** The room carries the participant pair canonicalised as
`DirectLowUserId` < `DirectHighUserId` with a unique index over it, the same shape `AllyConnection`
already uses. Two people tapping "Message" at the same instant both see no room and both insert; the
index picks a winner and the loser returns the winner's room. An application-level "does a room exist?"
check cannot do this, and the failure it produces — two rooms for one conversation, each holding half
the messages — is silent and unrecoverable once both have traffic.

**Requests are the spam control, and they are not optional.** A DM from someone you have not accepted
as an ally lands `Pending`: the room exists, the message is stored, and **nobody is notified**. It
appears in the recipient's Requests tab and nowhere else until they accept. Allies skip straight to
`Accepted`. Without this, an open DM endpoint is an abuse surface from the hour it ships, and
retrofitting the gate later means retrofitting it against users who already learned there was none.

**Blocks (D-263) are enforced here in both directions**: blocked either way, no room is created and no
message is delivered. Checked live per request rather than cached, for the same reason resource roles
are (D-015) — a block has to take effect on the next message, not the next login.

**`ChatMember.ArchivedAt` is a per-user folder and is deliberately not `ChatRoomStatus.Archived`.**
The room status is lifecycle — derived from the event's own state, one-way, and shared by every member
(D-122/D-124). Archiving is a personal filing decision, per member, reversible, and says nothing about
the room. Merging them would mean one user archiving a conversation locks it for the other.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Chat.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Chat/*`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/DmEndpoints.cs`, `web/app/(app)/chats/**`,
`mobile/lib/features/social/**`.

## D-266 — Event architecture V3: behavioural archetypes, the product axis, M1 foundation

**Status** M1 (foundation) shipped; M2–M10 planned. Full architecture: `docs/architecture/EVENT_CREATION_V2.md`
(§D8 taxonomy, §D9 invitations, §D11 audit, §D12 capability matrix, §D13 freeze + plan) — all four canonical.

**Three independent axes, not one enum.** An event is described by *what it is* (Type → Archetype),
*who may register* (registration policy) and *who can find it* (visibility). Collapsing any pair produces
the contradictions the taxonomy audit removed: a restricted hackathon is a Public product with a
restrictive policy, never a "Private Hackathon".

**`EventArchetype` supersedes `EventKind`.** The 104-type taxonomy answers "what kind of event is this"
for a human choosing from a list; the 14 archetypes answer "how does the platform behave". Two types share
an archetype only when modules, workflow, organiser experience and post-event behaviour are identical —
so Science *Fair* (judged) and Science *Exhibition* (showcase) stay apart despite the names, and Hackathon
and Olympiad merge despite theirs. `EventKind` is archived rather than dropped: existing events reference
it, and its capability defaults came through the name-matched `KindAlias` chain D-188 itself flags as
fragile — that chain is what the archetype layer replaces in M2.

**`Event.ArchetypeSlug` and `Event.Product` are snapshots, not lookups.** Stamped at creation from the
chosen Type, for the same reason `created_from_template_version` is: a later taxonomy edit must never
silently change how a live event behaves. On a type change the archetype re-derives but **`Product` does
not** — re-deriving it would let an edit flip a Public event to Private, which is forbidden outright.
Product only ever moves Private→Public, through the explicit conversion built in M3.

**`EventRegistrationPolicy` is not `RegistrationGate`.** The gate enum is the composable *ticket-type*
mechanism (`RegistrationPolicy.GatesJson`); the new enum is the event author's single declared intent, from
which gates are derived in M3. They were nearly given the same name — `RegistrationPolicy` is already a
table — which would have conflated an event-level intent with a per-ticket mechanism.

**`EventVisibility.Public` is renamed `Listed`; `Private` is deliberately kept.** D13 planned to retire
`Private` into `InviteOnly` in the same step. That is not additive: both values exist in the column today,
so merging them is irreversible — `Down()` cannot tell which rows were which. `Private` is also what 15
public-exposure guards still test, and those guards belong on `Event.Product` once it carries meaning.
Both moves therefore land together in M3. The `Public→Listed` half is a pure rename with an exactly
reversible backfill and shipped now.

**Nullable enums need explicit conversion.** `KurxDbContext`'s global enum→text loop tests
`prop.ClrType.IsEnum`, which is false for `EventProduct?` (its ClrType is `Nullable<T>`), so
`event_categories.ProductClass` first landed as `integer` while the two non-nullable copies of the same
enum landed as `text`. Configured explicitly rather than by fixing the loop: the two pre-existing nullable
enums (`ApproverRole`, `DmRequestState`) are integer columns with live data, and converting them is a
migration on tables unrelated to this work.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/EventArchetypes.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Events.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/ArchetypeSeeder.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/EventService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`,
`web/components/host/create-event-wizard.tsx`,
`mobile/lib/features/organizer/presentation/pages/create_event_page.dart`.

## D-267 · User-first architecture: users own events; organization-centric navigation removed everywhere (2026-08-04)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented across backend, web and Flutter. ⚠️ Partly SUPERSEDED by
[D-305](#d-305--event-creation-is-a-gated-flow-entered-from-profile-not-a-form-entered-from-workspace-2026-08-08)
(2026-08-08)** — which moves the Create Event entry point from **Workspace to Profile** and puts a
verification/eligibility gate (including the Public/Private decision) *in front of* the creation form.
**What stands: users own events, an organization is never required to create one, and there is still no
organizer dashboard.** What changed is only where the door is and what happens on entering it. Read this
entry for the ownership model; read D-305 for how creation is reached today.

Completes D-074/D-075/D-076 by
removing the org-first *navigation* those decisions left standing, and carries out the mobile migration
D-075 reserved as "D-077" — a number the concurrent auth workstream took first (see the banding note at
D-101), so the Flutter migration never got an entry of its own until now.

**The model.** Kurx is a **user-first event platform**. **Users own events.** Organizations are optional
metadata used only for **representation, verification, permissions, payouts and collaboration**. The
primary relation is always `User → Event`, never `Organization → Event`.

**What was removed.** The whole `Workspace → Organizations → Organization → Events → Create Event`
workflow, and `Profile → My Organizations` with it. No compatibility layer, no redirect shims for the
retired addresses:

- **Flutter:** routes `/orgs`, `/org/create`, `/org/:orgId`, `/org/:orgId/events` and their pages
  (`my_orgs_page`, `create_org_page`, `org_detail_page`, `my_events_page`). `/org/:orgId/events/create`
  → `/events/create`; the 18 `/org/:orgId/events/:eventId/…` management routes → `/events/:eventId/manage/…`;
  `/org/:orgId/{wallet,kyc,members,verification,analytics}` → `/representing/:orgId/…`.
- **Web:** `/host/organizations` and `/host/organizations/new` (both already redirect shims), the
  organizer dashboard at `/host` (now a redirect to `/workspace`), `lib/current-org.ts`, the `kurx_org`
  cookie and `setCurrentOrgAction`, `OrgSwitcher`, `WorkspaceNav`, `HostDashboard`, `EventsTable`,
  `RepresentOrgPicker`, `createPersonalOrgAction`, the dead `createEventAction`, and `/host/events`
  (the per-org list, superseded by Workspace). `/host/revenue` and `/host/team` moved to
  `/host/representing/[orgId]/{finance,team}` — org named in the path, where an organization is genuinely
  the subject.
- **API:** `POST /v1/orgs/{orgId}/events`.

**The boundary, stated precisely (owner directive, 2026-08-04).** Removed with the navigation: *My
Organizations*, *Organization Dashboard*, *Organization Home*, Organization → Events navigation,
organization-first routing, and **organization hub pages that existed only to navigate**. The only
organization screens that remain are those tied to representation and verification:

| Kept | Where |
|---|---|
| Search the verified organization registry (during event creation / representation request) | web `/host/representing` |
| Request organization verification | web `/host/representing/new`, mobile Representing step |
| Representation details on the user's profile | web `/settings/representing`, mobile `/representing` |
| Organization verification standing | mobile `/representing/:orgId/verification`, web `/host/verification` |
| Admin verification screens | `admin/` console — unchanged |

Consequently a second pass deleted **organization analytics** (`OrgAnalyticsPage`, `/representing/:orgId/analytics`,
`orgAnalyticsProvider`, the `orgAnalytics` client call) — an organization dashboard by any reading, and
fully covered by per-event analytics — and the **organization member roster** (mobile `OrgMembersPage`,
web `/host/representing/[orgId]/team` with `add-member-form`, `org-invite-form`, `team-actions.ts` and six
now-unused `api.ts` wrappers): an organization roster is org administration, and event collaboration
already lives per event at `…/manage/team`. Mobile's Representing page was rebuilt as representation
*details* rather than a tile grid, and web's dropped its Team/Finance buttons for the same reason.

**Payouts are the one deliberate exception, and are reachable only through an event.** Settlement is
legally organization-bound, so `OrgWalletPage` / KYC / withdraw survive — but nothing browses to them
through an organization: mobile reaches them from the **event's** payment-readiness check ("the account
this event settles to"), and web from the representation detail as *Payout account*. Flagged here rather
than deleted because removing them would take the only payout surface with it; say the word and they go.

**Three backend primitives make it possible** (no schema change; `Event.OrgId` stays a non-null FK, as
D-055/D-075 decided):

1. **`GET /v1/me/events`** — every event the caller hosts across every org they hold a seat in, one flat
   list. Authorization *is* the membership join, so no org id is accepted or needed. Rows carry
   `org_id`/`org_name`/`org_is_personal` as metadata for rendering "representing X" — never as a grouping
   key. This is the root fix: both Workspace surfaces had to enumerate organizations and fan out per org
   *because no such endpoint existed*, which is what made organizations look like the container.
2. **`POST /v1/events`** — `representingOrgId` is a **body field**, chosen inside the creation flow.
   Null means **Personal**: `OrgService.GetOrCreatePersonalOrgAsync` resolves, or on first use creates,
   the caller's own `IsPersonal` org (D-055). The user never sees, names or creates it.
3. **`GET /v1/events/{eventId:guid}`** — authenticated read by event id, authorized against the event's
   *own* org. This is how a client resolves an event's `org_id` instead of tracking a "current organization".

**Why `/v1/orgs/{orgId}/events/{eventId}/…` survives.** Those ~60 management sub-resources (tickets,
speakers, sessions, media, audience, …) are reached only *after* an event is open, and the client now
derives `orgId` from that event rather than from an organization the user selected. Renaming them would be
a very large diff across two clients and hundreds of tests for zero navigational change — the org-first
problem was the *navigation*, not the URL shape of a sub-resource. The per-org event **list** also stays,
for the admin console's view of one organization. Both are stated as retained, with reason, rather than
silently left behind.

**One real bug fixed on the way.** Flutter's `EventManageDto` required `cover_url`, `total_capacity`,
`view_count`, `created_at` and `org_id` — names no row projection has ever emitted — and the data source
read `res.data as List` against an endpoint that answers `{ items, total }`. Every organizer event-list
parse threw; the screen had never rendered a real event (the symptom `docs/DECISIONS.md` D-064 recorded as
"the org header's Events count shows —"). The DTO is now pinned against `ToMyEventRowJson`/`ToEventJson`.

**Trust boundary unchanged.** `POST /v1/events` still routes through `EventService.CreateAsync`, so a
`representingOrgId` the caller has no role on returns `forbidden`; the publish gate
(`pending_org_verification`) and the D-018 404-not-403 rule are untouched. `requireEventOrg` (web) and
`requireRepresentedOrg` (web) both surface a non-member as **not-found**, never forbidden.

**Verification:** backend `dotnet build` 0 errors; full suite in the SDK container against real Postgres;
web `tsc --noEmit` clean and `vitest` 145/145; Flutter `analyze` clean and `flutter test` 281/281.
`mobile/test/features/organizer/create_org_page_test.dart` was deleted with the page it covered.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/{EventEndpoints,OrgEndpoints}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{IEventService,IOrgService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/{Events/EventService,Orgs/OrgService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/{CreateEventRequest,EventFirstTests}.cs` (+42 test files repointed onto the new
create helper), `web/lib/{api,capabilities,event-org,represented-org,event-actions,org-actions,team-actions,membership-actions}.ts`,
`web/app/(app)/{workspace,host}/**`, `web/components/host/create-event-wizard.tsx`,
`mobile/lib/core/router/app_router.dart`, `mobile/lib/features/organizer/**`,
`mobile/lib/features/workspace/presentation/pages/workspace_hub_page.dart`,
`mobile/lib/features/profile/presentation/pages/profile_page.dart`, `docs/**`.

## D-268 · The User owns the Event; representation is an attribute, and there is no "personal organization" (2026-08-04)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.** Corrects the domain model D-267 left half-migrated: D-267 removed
organization-first *navigation*, but the implementation still expressed **Organization owns Event**.

**The model.** Kurx has **Users**, **Events** and **Representations**. It does **not** have organization
accounts, organizer accounts, or personal organizations.

```
User → Event                    Representing: Personal | Verified Organization
```

Representation affects **branding, verification, trust, permissions and payout destination**. It is
never ownership. The owner is always the User.

### 1. Ownership is now enforced from the user, not from a membership

Every event-scoped authorization in `EventService` resolved to `RoleAsync(userId, ev.OrgId)` — the right
to manage an event derived *entirely* from membership of the organization it represents.
`Event.CreatedBy` existed but authorized nothing; it was read only to send notifications. That is the
Organization-owns-Event model, in code.

`CanManageEventAsync(userId, ev, isAdmin)` = **admin OR `ev.CreatedBy == userId` OR org-manage-role**,
applied to transition, update, clone, delete, analytics, workspace and payment-readiness; `CanViewAsync`
gains the same owner grant; `EventPermissionService` gains it as grant **(0)**, ahead of the org and
participant grants. `ListMineAsync` became `CreatedBy == userId OR membership` — it was a membership
join, which is why a person's own events could only be found through an organization.

**This was also the only reason a self-represented host needed a synthetic organization to be a member
of.** Ownership now stands alone.

### 2. "Personal organization" is deleted as a concept

`IOrgService.GetOrCreatePersonalOrgAsync` — introduced by D-267 and the worst offender — promoted a
persistence detail into a public abstraction that taught every reader the model was
`User → Personal Organization → Event`. It is gone. The FK-satisfying row is resolved by a **private**
`EventService.ResolveSelfRepresentationAsync`, documented as persistence, never as domain.

Nothing public mentions it: no API field, DTO, service name, route, label or document. `GET /v1/orgs`
(the "my orgs" list) is now **`GET /v1/me/representations`**, named for its actual responsibility —
"which organizations may I represent?" — and it **excludes the self-representation row server-side**, so
no client filters on an `is_personal` flag because no such flag is sent. `OrgSummary.IsPersonal` and
`is_personal` on the workspace-capability contract are removed.

### 3. The API speaks representation

Event rows carried `org_id` / `org_name` / `org_is_personal`. They now carry:

```jsonc
"representation": { "kind": "personal" | "organization",
                    "organization_id": null, "organization_name": null, "verified": false }
```

`kind: "personal"` carries **no organization identity at all** — the client is not told a row exists,
because in the domain none does. The workspace-capability contract's `organization` block became
`representation` with the same shape plus `represented_as` / `authority`. `CreateAsync` takes
`Guid? representingOrgId` (null = Personal) and its authorization is explicitly *representation
authority*: representing an institution needs a manage-capable seat, representing yourself needs nothing.

### 4. Wallet, verification and KYC — where they belong

- **Personal identity verification** (`user_identity_verifications`, M3) belongs to the **User**. Unchanged.
- **Organization verification** belongs to the **Representation**. Unchanged, and correct.
- **Payout destination** belongs to the **Representation** — settlement is legally to the institution
  you represent. The org-keyed wallet is therefore right, and is reached only through an event (mobile:
  the event's payment-readiness check) or the representation detail (web), never an organization hub.
- **Not moved**, because moving would not produce a cleaner model — it would duplicate the settlement
  account across two owners.

### 5. Technical debt that could not be removed safely

**`Event.OrgId` stores the *representation*, not the owner, and its name says otherwise.** Renaming it to
`RepresentingOrgId` (or making it nullable so Personal carries no row at all) is the honest end state and
is **not** done here: `.OrgId` is dereferenced at **300+ sites across ~30 services** — tickets, orders,
refunds, the ledger, chat, certificates, analytics, search indexing, posts — several on the money path.
D-055 and D-075 each weighed nullability and rejected it for the same ripple. Where the name leaks
incorrect meaning:

| Leak | Where | Correct reading |
|---|---|---|
| `Event.OrgId` | domain entity, 300+ sites | the represented organization |
| `events.OrgId` non-null | DB schema | Personal must point at a self-representation row |
| `/v1/orgs/{orgId}/events/{eventId}/…` | ~60 management sub-resources | event management; orgId is derived from the event |
| `orgEventRowSchema`, `OrgEventRow` | DTOs | an organizer's event row |
| `/representing/:orgId` | mobile + web routes | the id *is* the organization's — accurate for verification/payout, which are genuinely about the organization |

**Ten services still authorize event sub-resources on organization membership alone** — tickets, media,
schedule, speakers, sponsors, attendees, certificates, announcements, invitations, assignments — each
with its own copy of `CanManage`/`RoleAsync` (7 of them byte-identical, and notably omitting
`Representative`). Until they adopt the owner grant, the self-representation row must keep its
`Membership`, which is why that seat still exists. **The fix is to consolidate the rule into one shared
event authority and delete nine copies**; it is a permission change across the attendee/money path and
wants its own security review, so it is not bundled here.

**Verification:** backend build clean; full suite in the SDK container against real Postgres; web
`tsc --noEmit` clean + `vitest` 145/145; Flutter `analyze` clean + `flutter test` 281/281. New coverage:
an owner manages and edits their own event with **no** membership anywhere, a stranger gets 404;
Personal events report `kind: "personal"` with null organization id/name and never appear in
`/v1/me/representations`.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/{EventEndpoints,OrgEndpoints}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{IEventService,IOrgService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/{EventService,EventPermissionService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Orgs/OrgService.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Tests/EventFirstTests.cs`,
`web/lib/{api,capabilities,event-org,represented-org,session}.ts`, `web/app/(app)/**`,
`web/components/host/create-event-wizard.tsx`, `mobile/lib/features/organizer/**`,
`mobile/lib/features/workspace/**`, `docs/**`.

## D-266 M2 — the capability engine is the single source of truth for event behaviour

**Status** shipped. Full reference: `docs/architecture/CAPABILITY_ENGINE.md`.

**The engine performs no authorization.** It answers "what does this event support?" and never "who may do
this?". It takes an archetype, a product, a mode and the persisted matrix; no user id, role or permission
ever reaches it. Authority is D-269's concern and the two are independent by construction.

**"Universal Required" is removed.** The old `CapDef.Universal` flag meant "always on for every event",
which sat above the archetype matrix and contradicted it — D12 marks Feedback unsupported for A14 while the
flag made it mandatory everywhere. Universal now supplies only a **default**: it may enable a capability the
archetype marks Optional and may never enable one it marks Unsupported. Unsupported wins, Required wins,
defaults never override the matrix.

**Absence in the matrix means Unsupported, not "off".** This inverts the retired Kind table, where an
omitted cell meant "available but off" and nothing was ever forbidden. The inversion is the point: "a
Workshop may never enable Leaderboard" is only expressible if the model can say no. Every one of the
14 x 30 cells is stored, negatives included.

**Not every feature is an event capability.** The catalog was 57 slugs; 27 of them were Registration,
Ticketing, Invitation, Scheduling, Eligibility, Finance or Infrastructure concerns wearing a capability
flag, each with a duplicate source of truth in its own subsystem (age vs D-265 `MinAge`/`MaxAge`, walk-in vs
`InventorySegment.WalkIn`, series vs `EventSeries`, and ten more). Reclassifying them removed 13 dual-truth
sites and left exactly D12's 30. A slug belongs in the engine only if two archetypes could reasonably
differ on it.

**The organiser workspace is composed, not generated.** Deriving tabs from the capability catalog meant a
subsystem had to pretend to be an event capability to show a page — proved when `registration` left the
engine and the Registrations tab vanished with it. Each layer now contributes `WorkspaceSurface`s through
`IWorkspaceContributor`. Ordering is deterministic **by design**: every surface declares a unique `Order`,
and a collision fails startup naming both contributors rather than falling back to alphabetical, which
would let position depend on what something happens to be called.

**Backfill keys on the archetype axis.** `BackfillEventCapabilitiesAsync` filtered on `KindSlug != null`,
so every event created after the switch — which carries an archetype and often no Kind — was silently
skipped and left with no capability rows at all. A migration helper that quietly does nothing is worse than
one that fails.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/{CapabilityCatalog,CapabilityResolver,CapabilityService,ArchetypeCapabilitySeeder,CapabilityRegistrySeeder,WorkspaceContributors}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{ICapabilityService,IWorkspaceContributor}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Capabilities.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/CapabilityEndpoints.cs`,
migration `AddArchetypeCapabilityDefaults`.

## D-269 · One event authorization service; eleven copies deleted (2026-08-04)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.** A consolidation, not a permission redesign — but it exposed two
permission defects that the duplication had been hiding, and both are fixed here.

### The defect

Eleven services each carried their own `CanManage`/`RoleAsync` pair or an inline membership query. Seven
were byte-identical; the rest had drifted. Nothing compared them, so the drift was invisible — and two
consequences had shipped:

1. **`Representative` — the platform's primary organizer role since D-075 — could create and publish an
   event but not add a ticket type to it.** Nine sub-resources hardcoded `Owner or Manager` and never
   learned about the role D-075 introduced. `EventService` and `AudienceService` did include it, which is
   exactly why nobody noticed: the event itself worked.
2. **After D-268 an event's creator held no authority over its sub-resources.** Masked only because the
   self-representation row happens to carry an `Owner` membership.

### The architecture

`IEventAuthority` is the single source of truth. It resolves a caller to exactly one ordered level, and
every permission is a threshold on it:

```
None(0) < Participant(1) < Staff(2) < Manager(3) < Admin(4)
```

| Level | Reached by |
|---|---|
| `Participant` | an **active** participation on the event (speaker/judge/mentor/volunteer) |
| `Staff` | a `Staff` seat in the organization the event represents |
| `Manager` | the event's **creator** (D-268, needs no membership) · a `Representative` · an `Owner`/`Manager` seat |
| `Admin` | the `KurxAdmin` platform claim |

`Finance` maps to `None`: money authority over an organization is not operational authority over its
events. Unchanged from every prior service.

`EventPermission` → minimum level lives in one table, `EventAuthority.Requirements`:
`View`→Participant · `ViewAttendees`→Staff · `ViewAnalytics`/`ManageContent`/`ManageLifecycle`/`Delete`→Manager.
**Adding a future event capability means adding an enum value and one row — never authorization logic.**

`ResolveOrgAsync` covers the assets an *organization* owns rather than an event — its speaker roster,
sponsor roster, venue book, series and representation authority. Those are library entries shared across
many events, so "may I edit this org's speakers" cannot be answered from an event. It lives on the same
interface so there is still exactly one role → authority mapping; a second service would recreate the
divergence one layer up. `OrgAuthority.IsMember` is separate from `Level` because several org-asset reads
accept **any** seat including `Finance`, and collapsing them would silently narrow those reads.

### Intentional behaviour changes (both widenings, both architecture-supported)

| Change | Why it is correct, not a redesign |
|---|---|
| `Representative` gains manage on tickets, media, schedule, speakers, sponsors, certificates, announcements, invitations, assignments | D-075 defines it as "a verified, manage-capable role that is not Owner". It already manages the event; being unable to manage the event's tickets was an oversight, not a policy. No authority crosses an organization boundary. |
| The event's **creator** gains manage on the same nine | D-268: the User owns the Event. Already true for the event itself; the sub-resources were the gap. |

Everything else is preserved exactly, including the three surfaces that have **no admin bypass**
(attendees, announcements, invitations — their endpoints never passed one, so those calls pass
`isAdmin: false` explicitly and platform staff continue to use the admin console), `Staff`-only access to
the attendee roster, `Finance` holding nothing, D-191's exclusion of admins from content edit, and every
404-vs-403 boundary.

### Deliberately not consolidated

- **`ApprovalService.RoleAsync`** — an approval step names an **exact** `OrgRole` to match ("this step is
  approved by Finance"). That is a different question from "how much authority does this caller hold";
  collapsing it would make Finance, which sits at `None` on the ladder, unable to approve the step it was
  named for.
- **`OrgService` / `OrgInvitationService` / `OrgVerificationService`** — organization *administration*
  (add/remove member, change role, submit verification) with Owner-only rules such as "the last Owner
  cannot be demoted". That is org RBAC, a different policy domain from event authority, and D-269 is
  scoped to events. Their `RoleAsync` copies remain; consolidating them wants its own decision.

### Kept independent of the capability engine

**`IEventAuthority` decides WHO may act. `ICapabilityService` (D-266 M2) decides WHAT an event supports.**
The two never consult each other. M2 carries no authorization at all — no `CanManage`, no `RoleAsync`, no
membership read, no `isAdmin` parameter — and its endpoints authorize by calling the event read first.
That separation is deliberate on both sides and must survive: a capability is not a permission.

**Verification:** solution builds clean; full suite **1206 passed / 2 failed / 1 skipped of 1209** — both failures are M2 capability-registry tests owned by another session; every authorization test passes. `EventAuthorizationTests` adds 9 cases over real HTTP —
creator-with-no-membership, representative, org manager, staff (roster yes / content no), finance (nothing),
stranger (404 on hidden resources), anonymous (401), platform reviewer (reach yes / content edit no), and a
confused-deputy check that a caller cannot reach someone else's event by naming an organization they do
manage. Full suite run recorded in the session report.

**Touches** `Application/Abstractions/IEventAuthority.cs` (new), `Infrastructure/Events/EventAuthorityService.cs`
(new), `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, and the authorization paths of `EventService`,
`EventPermissionService`, `TicketTypeService`, `MediaService`, `ScheduleService`, `SpeakerService`,
`SponsorService`, `AttendeeService`, `CertificateService`, `AnnouncementService`, `InvitationService`,
`EventAssignmentService`, `AudienceService`, `SeriesService`, `VenueService`, `TemplateService`,
`ApprovalService`; `Tests/EventAuthorizationTests.cs` (new).

## D-271 · Repository terminology audit + contract regeneration — the migration is closed (2026-08-04)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.** The final pass over D-267…D-270. No new architecture; this closes
the vocabulary and the generated artifacts.

**One vocabulary, written down.** [`docs/architecture/TERMINOLOGY.md`](architecture/TERMINOLOGY.md) is now
canonical: a legacy→current table, a *"looks legacy but is correct"* section (so nobody "fixes" `OrgRole`,
`/v1/kinds`, or the lowercase word *organizer*), the authority ladder, and a named naming-debt register.
`.claude/CLAUDE.md` gives it precedence — **a word anywhere that contradicts it is drift, not a variant.**

**Six stale claims fixed in code, not docs.** The worst: `Event.OrgId` and `Event.CreatedBy` — the two
most-misread fields in the domain — carried **no documentation at all**, and `Event.OrgUnitId` said the
unit *"OWNS this event"*. Also corrected: the class/interface summaries on `EventService`/`IEventService`
and the `ManagerGrants` comment in `EventPermissionService`, all of which still described per-service
`Owner/Manager` authorization after D-269 replaced it.

**`docs/api/openapi.json` regenerated** — it had been stale since 2026-08-03 and was *actively wrong*:
it advertised `POST /v1/orgs/{orgId}/events`, which returns 404, and listed the retired
`GET /v1/kinds/{slug}/capabilities`. Being machine-readable, it misled code generators, not just readers.
The diff is exactly the expected delta and nothing else:

```
+ /v1/me/events                                    (D-267)
+ /v1/me/representations                           (D-268)
+ /v1/events/{eventId}                             (D-267)
+ /v1/archetypes/{slug}/capabilities               (D-266 M2)
+ /v1/orgs/{orgId}/events/{eventId}/policy-requirements   (concurrent workstream)
- /v1/kinds/{slug}/capabilities                    (D-266 M2)
  POST /v1/orgs/{orgId}/events                     removed from the retained path (D-267)
```

**Generated without disturbing the shared environment.** `scripts/generate-openapi.sh` rebuilds and
restarts the compose backend, which another session was actively using. Instead the contract was produced
from a throwaway API container on a spare port against a throwaway database — `kurx-backend` stayed up
and healthy throughout. Worth reusing: contract generation should never require taking the dev API down.

**Verification:** backend build clean and the **full suite green — 1232 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped of 1233** (the M2 capability failures that had been outstanding cleared when that workstream completed); web `tsc` + **145/145** vitest; Flutter `analyze` clean + **281/281**; admin `tsc` clean. Repository health:
**0** private `CanManage` copies, **17** services on the single authority, **0** docs asserting
organization-owns-event as current, **0** orphaned components, **0** dead routes.

## D-272 · EventAuthority governs the audience too, not only management (2026-08-04)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.** Closes the gap the D-271 follow-up audit found. No new
authorization model — the existing ladder was extended downward to the rung it already implied.

**What was wrong.** D-269 consolidated event *management* onto `IEventAuthority` and stopped there.
Three checks kept an inline `db.Memberships.Any(m => m.OrgId == ev.OrgId && ...)`:

| Site | Question it asks |
|---|---|
| `PostService.Writes.cs` | may this author attach a post to this event? |
| `PostService.GetByEventAsync` | may this viewer read this event's feed? |
| `ChatService.RemoveStaffMemberAsync` / `AddOrgMembersAsHostsAsync` | who holds chat `Host` by standing? |

All three shared one defect and it is the same one D-268 fixed everywhere else: **they never granted the
event's creator anything.** They worked only because a personally represented event fabricates a
self-representation `Membership` for its creator — delete that row and an owner silently lost their own
event's feed and chat. All three also accepted a `Finance` seat, which holds no authority over events at
any other surface. This was a *coverage* gap, not a design flaw: `IEventAuthority` was already right, three
call sites had simply never adopted it.

**Audience is a permission family, not a management permission.** Gating a ticket holder's post on
`ManageContent` would have been a lockout, so two values were added rather than one reused:

| Permission | Minimum level | Grants |
|---|---|---|
| `Participate` | `Participant` | read the event feed, attach a post, belong to the chat room |
| `ModerateAudience` | `Staff` | chat `Host` — pin, moderate, mention-all |

**A ticket is standing.** `EventAuthorityLevel.Participant` previously meant only an accepted programme
participation (speaker/judge/mentor/volunteer). It now also means *holds a live ticket*. Both are the same
relationship — "part of this event, with no authority over it" — so they resolve to one rung instead of two
parallel concepts every audience surface would check twice. Resolved last and short-circuited, so a manager
acting on their own event never runs either query.

**Two encodings, one mapping.** `PostService.VisibleTo` is an EF predicate over many events at once; it
cannot resolve one caller per row, so the audience floor is *also* expressed as SQL. The role list is the
one thing that could drift, so it is not written twice: `EventAuthority.AudienceRoles` and `ModeratorRoles`
are **derived from `EventAuthority.LevelFor` at load** via `RolesAtLeast`. `LevelFor` moved from
`EventAuthorityService` to the `EventAuthority` table so both sides reach the same switch.

**Intentional behaviour changes**, each verified by test:

- The event's **creator** now holds audience standing with no membership row at all — the point of the change.
- **`Finance`** loses the event feed, post attachment and chat `Host`. It never had event authority anywhere
  else; the audience surfaces were the last place a bare membership was sufficient.
- **Programme participants** (speakers, judges) gain the event feed and post attachment. They previously
  needed a ticket to their own event.
- **Ticket holders** now resolve to `Participant` rather than `None`. The only pre-existing consumer of that
  distinction is `AttendeeService`, where a ticket holder's roster request changes `404 not_found` →
  `403 forbidden`. Deliberate: 404-not-403 (D-018) withholds the event's *existence*, and someone holding a
  ticket to it already knows. `EventPermission.View` has no call sites, so nothing else moved.
- `AddOrgMembersAsHostsAsync(eventId, orgId)` → **`AddEventHostsAsync(eventId)`**. It takes no orgId: the
  event's representation is not the caller's to supply, and the owner's Host seat comes from owning the
  event, not from a seat.

**Still deliberately outside `IEventAuthority`** — all re-verified, none drifted: `ApprovalService`
(exact-`OrgRole` step matching; `Finance` sits at `None` on the ladder yet must approve a Finance-assigned
step), `OrgService` / `OrgInvitationService` / `OrgVerificationService` (organization administration —
`Owner`-exact rules and a last-owner cardinality guard the ladder cannot express), and the financial bar in
`AnalyticsService` / `RefundService` / `WalletService` (`Owner`-or-`Finance`, the inverse of the event ladder
by design).

**One gap reported, not changed.** `GateEntryService.ScanAsync` authorizes ticket scanning as *any org
member (including `Finance`) or an accepted `EventAssignment`* — the identical creator omission and the
identical synthetic-membership dependency, on a check-in path. It is operational authorization rather than
an audience surface, and removing `Finance` from gate scanning is a security-relevant behaviour change, so
it is left for its own decision rather than folded in here.

**Verification:** backend build clean, 0 warnings. Full suite **1268 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped of 1269**
— the authoritative D-272 run, with all 10 `EventAudienceAuthorizationTests` cases green. Web `tsc` clean +
**145/145** vitest; Flutter `analyze` clean + **281/281**; admin `tsc` clean. No API route, verb or error
code changed, so `openapi.json` needed no regeneration.

A final uncontended re-run, once the 2 `AudiencePredicateSqlTests` cases were added, reported
**1268 passed / 2 failed / 1 skipped of 1271**. The arithmetic is the evidence: total rose by exactly the
2 new tests, the passed count held at 1268, and the 2 failures are `KindRegistryTests`
(*"Expected 145 aliases, Actual 94"*) — tests the concurrent taxonomy workstream broke in its own
uncommitted `TaxonomyAliasMap.cs` / `EventTaxonomySeeder.cs` between the two runs. **Zero failures in any
class D-272 touches.** An earlier run under a second contending test container had shown 11 failures; the
9 extra were contention flakes and did not reproduce when run alone.

**The query-side mirror verified against real PostgreSQL.** `EventAuthority.AudienceRoles.Contains(m.Role)`
translates to a native `IN` list — `m."Role" IN ('Owner', 'Manager', 'Staff', 'Representative')` — with no
client-side evaluation and `Finance` absent. `EXPLAIN` resolves every arm through an index
(`IX_memberships_UserId`, `ix_event_participants_unique`, `IX_tickets_UserId_State`, `ix_posts_event_active`)
and hoists the three `EXISTS` into **hashed subplans**, so they are evaluated once per query rather than per
row. `AudiencePredicateSqlTests` pins both the SQL shape and the derivation of the role arrays from
`LevelFor`.

Repository sweep: **0** remaining event-context `db.Memberships` authorization checks outside
`IEventAuthority` and the org-administration services above.

## D-273a · `Event.OrgId` → `Event.RepresentingOrgId` — terminology only (2026-08-04)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.** A domain-language migration, not a feature. Behaviour is unchanged
everywhere; payments, settlement and nullability are explicitly out of scope (see D-273b below).

**Why.** D-268 moved ownership to the user (`Event.CreatedBy`), leaving `Event.OrgId` storing a
*representation* under a name that still reads like ownership. The architecture was right and the word was
wrong — the exact drift `docs/architecture/TERMINOLOGY.md` exists to forbid.

**Name chosen: `RepresentingOrgId`.** Preferred over `RepresentationId` (which implies an FK to a
`representations` table that does not exist — this is an FK to `organizations`) and over
`RepresentedOrganizationId` (accurate but long, and the codebase already says `Org` everywhere else:
`OrgRole`, `ResolveOrgAsync`, `OrgAuthority`). `RepresentingOrgId` reads correctly in situ —
`ev.RepresentingOrgId` is "the org this event is representing" — and matches `RepresentationView`, the
wire shape D-268 already shipped.

**The column was deliberately NOT renamed.** `HasColumnName("OrgId")` pins it, and the two indexes
(`IX_events_OrgId`, `IX_events_OrgId_Status_EndsAt`) and FK (`FK_events_organizations_OrgId`) keep their
physical names via `HasDatabaseName`/`HasConstraintName`. **Zero migrations, zero schema change.** The
reason is the same discipline the API uses: a column rename couples the app deploy to the schema, so the
app could no longer be rolled back without also rolling back the database. The physical name is now an
internal storage detail that appears nowhere on the wire. Renaming it is cheap in Postgres
(`ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN` is catalog-only) and can be done later in its own step.

**The rename was compiler-driven, not text-driven.** Deleting the property and letting the build fail
produced the exact set of Event-scoped references; each was rewritten at the line/column the compiler
reported. `Membership.OrgId`, `LedgerEntry.OrgId`, `OrganizationWallet.OrgId`, `EventAssignment.OrgId`,
`Venue.OrgId` and every other same-named field on a different entity were never visited, because they
never produced a diagnostic. **146 positional rewrites across 52 files, 4 build iterations, 0 mismatches.**
A find-and-replace on `OrgId` would have corrupted all of them.

**API — expand and contract (phase 1 of 2).** Event payloads now emit **both**:

| Field | Status |
|---|---|
| `representing_org_id` | **Current.** New clients read this. |
| `org_id` | **Deprecated.** Same value, kept for clients deployed before the rename. |

Applies to `EventDetail`, `EventSummary`, `AdminEventView` and `PendingEventView`. The contract phase —
deleting `org_id` — is a separate change once no client reads it.

**Clients.** Web and Flutter model `representing_org_id` as required and keep `org_id` optional, so they
parse against a server on either side of the rollout; web resolves it once in `requireEventOrg` and Flutter
once in `EventManageScope`, so the 16 web management pages and every organizer provider needed no
individual change. Admin models it as **required with no alias**, because the console ships with the API it
reads and never faces a pre-rename server.

**Not done, and deliberately: nullability.** `RepresentingOrgId` stays non-null. `LedgerEntry.OrgId`,
`OrganizationWallet.OrgId` and `PayoutSchedule.OrgId` are all non-nullable, `OrderService` hard-throws
*"No wallet row for org … refusing to capture payment"*, and paid events gate on
`GetOrgCapabilitiesAsync(…, ev.RepresentingOrgId)`. A null representation therefore means a captured payment
with nowhere to settle. That is a payee-abstraction redesign, not a rename — **D-273b**, and it must not be
smuggled into a terminology change.

**Verification:** backend build clean, **0 warnings**. Full suite **1270 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped of
1271** — the first fully green run on this branch (the taxonomy failures outstanding during D-272 cleared
when that workstream landed). Web `tsc` clean + **145/145** vitest; Flutter `analyze` clean + **281/281**
after `build_runner` regeneration; admin `tsc` clean.

No migration was generated — confirmed by the suite itself: every test class clones a freshly migrated
template, so a pending model change would have surfaced as a schema mismatch on the first read.

**Contract:** no route, verb or status changed; event payloads gained `representing_org_id` and retain
`org_id`. Purely additive, so no client is broken by deploying the server first.

## D-266 M4 — the event review lifecycle

**Status** shipped. Reference: `docs/architecture/REVIEW_LIFECYCLE.md`.

**`InReview` conflated two states and had to be split.** The pre-M4 model had one review status, which meant
"submitted, waiting for a reviewer" and "a reviewer is working on it" were indistinguishable. A claim flow
needs them apart: without the distinction two reviewers can act on the same event, and releasing a claim has
no state to return to. `PendingReview` and `UnderReview` replace it, with `ChangesRequested`, `Approved` and
`Rejected` completing the lifecycle.

**A Public product cannot self-publish.** The path is `Draft → PendingReview → UnderReview → Approved →
Published`, and `publish_approved` is reachable only from `Approved`. Private products are never reviewed,
so `publish` direct from `Draft` survives for them.

**`submit_review` is now an alias, and this is an API behaviour change.** The legacy action name is kept —
clients still post it — but it lands on `PendingReview` rather than the retired `InReview`. A client that
asserts on the returned status string sees a different value than before. The action was retained rather
than removed because deleting it would break existing callers for no gain.

**Legacy `reject` and M4 `reject_review` are deliberately different actions.** `reject` means *send it back
to the organiser* and targets `Draft`; `reject_review` is a formal rejection carrying an
`EventReviewReason` and targets `Rejected`. Collapsing them would lose the distinction between "needs work"
and "refused", which is the difference between a queue item and an outcome.

**Reviewer decisions are recorded in `VerificationReview`, not a new table.** It already carried subject,
decision, reviewer, reason code and notes, and `VerificationSubjectType.Event` already existed. Only the
three real verdicts write rows — claim and release are queue mechanics, and recording them would bury the
decisions in workflow noise, turning "what did the reviewer decide" into a filtered query.

**The decision and the status change share one save.** A status without its recorded decision, or the
reverse, is an audit gap in exactly the surface an approval trail exists to cover.

**Edits are locked while an event is with a reviewer**, via `EventStatusWorkflow.IsEditLocked` —
`PendingReview` and `UnderReview` return **409 `event_under_review`** on PATCH. `ChangesRequested` stays
editable, because editing is the entire point of that state. An edit landing between a reviewer reading an
event and approving it means they approved something other than what they read.

**Reviewer authorization is `IEventAuthority`'s, not the review engine's.** The workflow declares which
actions are reviewer-scoped (`ReviewerActions`); who may invoke them is resolved by D-269. An organiser who
can manage an event still cannot approve their own submission.

**The publish gate now consumes `PolicyResolver.PublishBlockers`.** It previously did not: `TransitionGateAsync`
had its own validation while `/policy-requirements` reported blockers from the policy engine, so the list a
reviewer read could differ from the rule that actually refused the publish. Two validations for one question
always drift. A test asserts the two agree.

**`legacy_in_review` stays on the `review-counts` contract, reporting 0.** Removing a field is a client
break; leaving it at zero is not. It goes when clients have dropped it.

**Retiring the enum member was not the end of the change — every client held the string too.** The status
is serialized as the lowercased member name, so `"inreview"` was hard-coded across web, admin and Flutter:
status filters, badge maps, action tables and a lifecycle stepper. None of it failed loudly. The web and
Flutter "Pending approval" views simply went empty, and the admin events tab was worse — the backend's
status filter *silently ignores a value it cannot parse*, so a filter that matched nothing became a filter
that matched **everything**. A retired enum member is a repo-wide string sweep, not a backend edit.

**The clients offer only transitions `EventStatusWorkflow.Actions` declares.** Fixing the sweep surfaced
host UIs offering reviewer-only `publish`/`reject`, and a Flutter `cancel` on `ChangesRequested`/`Approved`/
`Rejected` that the cancel table does not accept. Both would have been guaranteed server refusals.

**The `pending_events` dashboard tile counts both review states.** D-058 requires a tile to agree with the
queue it links to, and this one links to `/events/pending`, which lists `PendingReview + UnderReview`. The
M4 split left the tile on `PendingReview` alone, so every claimed event dropped out of the number — and out
of the sidebar badge — while still sitting in the queue. An integration test now asserts the two agree
across a claim, which is the case that regressed.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/{EventStatusWorkflow,EventService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/{EventEndpoints,AdminEventEndpoints,AdminDashboardEndpoints}.cs`,
`admin/app/(console)/events/review/**`, `admin/components/admin/review-actions.tsx`,
`admin/lib/event-tabs.ts`, `admin/components/admin/events-workspace/{events-table,event-workspace-sheet}.tsx`,
`web/app/(app)/workspace/page.tsx`, `web/components/host/event-status-actions.tsx`,
`mobile/lib/features/{workspace/presentation/pages/workspace_hub_page,organizer/presentation/pages/event_status_page}.dart`,
migration `MigrateInReviewToPendingReview`.

## D-274 · Developer Mode is deleted; the only way in is the real authentication flow (2026-08-05)

**Context.** Kurx had shipped three generations of "safe" authentication shortcut. `DEV_OTP_CODE` was a
runtime-gated fixed OTP. `ADMIN_DEV_ALLOW_ALL` handed any authenticated user a fake SuperAdmin in the
console. D-125 replaced both with the Developer Workspace: a `/v1/dev/*` module behind three independent
guards — the `DEV_AUTH` compile constant, `!IsProduction()` on route registration, and a per-handler
`IsProduction() → 404` — that minted *real* sessions for deterministically seeded accounts. Each
generation was defensible on its own terms, and each one existed because the generation before it had
been judged unsafe. That is the pattern being ended here, not one implementation of it.

**Decision.** Developer Mode is removed from the platform in full: no dev endpoints, no dev services,
no seed service, no dev login UI on any client, no compile flag, no environment variable, no
long-press shortcut, no compatibility shim. `IAuthService.IssueDevSessionAsync` — an issuance path with
no credential check, safe only for as long as its compile gate held — is gone from the interface and the
implementation. Every client now reaches a session exactly one way: OTP, password, passkey, or trusted
device, through the same endpoints a real user hits.

**Why not keep it behind the compile gate.** The gate worked; that was never the question. The costs it
could not remove: `#if DEV_AUTH` made Debug and Release compile *different products*, so the test suite
silently changed size with the configuration flag (D-192 lost 8 tests to exactly this and it read as a
clean run); CI had to carry a second build of the whole solution to test the module; the OpenAPI contract
gate had a load-bearing step ordering to stop `/v1/dev/*` leaking into the published spec; and the
platform's single most sensitive invariant — that authority is only ever earned — had a documented,
maintained exception sitting next to it. A guard that must be re-argued at every review is a liability
even when it holds.

**What replaces the two things Dev Mode was genuinely needed for.**

1. **Reaching the admin console on a fresh database.** Nothing in production could grant the first
   `SuperAdmin`; `/v1/dev/auth/login?preset=super-admin` was the only path, so deleting the module without
   a replacement would have locked the console permanently. `SuperAdminBootstrap` (called from the
   Program.cs startup scope, after migrations) grants `SuperAdmin` from `SUPERADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_PHONE`.
   It is deliberately the narrowest thing that works: it runs only while zero live `SuperAdmin` rows
   exist, it **never creates a user** — the person must already have registered through the real OTP flow —
   and it writes an audit row (`platform_role.bootstrap_granted`, actor `system`). Unset is a no-op, which
   is the steady state. Every subsequent grant goes through `POST /v1/admin/staff/grant`. The phone is
   not logged: it is PII and the audit row already names the user id.
2. **A developer completing authentication locally.** No new mechanism was needed — the capability already
   existed and was simply undocumented. The dev provider set is console-backed, so `OtpService.DeliverAsync`
   writes the real, CSPRNG-minted code to the API log (`[sms→console] … Your Kurx code is NNNNNN`; the
   channel follows `OtpChannelPolicy`, so an email-addressed purpose lands in `[email→console]`).
   A developer signs in through the ordinary screens and reads the code from `docker compose logs backend`.
   That is delivery, not a bypass: the code is issued, peppered, rate-limited, attempt-capped and consumed
   by the same production path a real user's is.

**Explicitly rejected:** a seeded developer account set, a fixed OTP for known-dev numbers, a "magic link"
in non-production, and keeping `/v1/dev/auth/preview` (which minted no token) as a standalone capability
probe. Each reintroduces an identity or a code path that exists only for developers, which is the thing
being removed. The capability preview's real value — "what would this configuration be allowed to do" — is
answered by `ITrustService` against a real account, which any test or dev session can already query.

**Consequences.**
- **Deleted:** `backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/Dev/**`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Dev/**`,
  `backend/Kurx.Tests/DevAuthTests.cs`, `web/{app/dev-login,app/api/dev-preview,components/dev,
  components/dev-banner.tsx,lib/dev-actions.ts,lib/dev-session-config.ts}`,
  `admin/{app/dev-login,components/dev-banner.tsx,lib/dev-actions.ts}`,
  `mobile/lib/features/dev/presentation/{pages/dev_login_page.dart,widgets/dev_banner_wrap.dart}`,
  `mobile/test/features/dev/`, `docs/dev-workspace/`.
- **Removed from config/CI:** the `DEV_AUTH`/`EnableDevAuth` `PropertyGroup` in
  `backend/Directory.Build.props`, the `NEXT_PUBLIC_DEV_LOGIN` build arg in `web/Dockerfile`, and CI's
  second `-p:EnableDevAuth=true` test job (with the contract-gate ordering note it forced).
- **The component galleries go too — both of them.** Flutter's
  `mobile/lib/features/dev/presentation/pages/component_gallery_page.dart` (`/dev/gallery`), its test, its
  route and the "Developer → Design System" entry in the *user-facing* Settings page; and web's
  `web/app/gallery/page.tsx` (`/gallery`). Neither had any authentication involvement, so an earlier pass
  kept the Flutter one — but the decision here is that a developer-only surface does not ship, not merely
  that its auth parts don't. Both were reachable in a production build: the Flutter one from a shipped
  Settings screen, and the web one as an ordinary unlisted Next.js route with **no gating whatsoever** —
  publicly routable to anyone who typed `/gallery`. `mobile/lib/features/dev/` no longer exists. A
  design-system catalogue, if wanted again, belongs in a harness that does not ship.
- Historical entries (D-125, D-192, D-196, D-197, D-199) are left intact as the record of what was built
  and audited; D-125 carries a superseded banner pointing here.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Api/Program.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IAuthService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/{Auth/AuthService.cs,Auth/SuperAdminBootstrap.cs,DependencyInjection.cs}`,
`backend/Kurx.Tests/SuperAdminBootstrapTests.cs`, `backend/Directory.Build.props`,
`web/{app/layout.tsx,app/(app)/profile/page.tsx,components/auth/otp-panel.tsx,Dockerfile}`,
`admin/{app/layout.tsx,middleware.ts,lib/roles.ts,STATUS.md}`,
`mobile/lib/{app.dart,core/router/app_router.dart,features/auth/presentation/pages/{phone_entry_page,password_login_page}.dart,features/settings/presentation/pages/settings_page.dart}`,
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `docker-compose.yml`, `docs/auth/AUTHENTICATION_TESTING.md`,
`.claude/memory/{security-rules,testing-standards,mobile-conventions}.md`.
