## D-266 M5 — institutional authorization: the represented institution's consent, per event

**Status** shipped. Extends [D-266](#d-266--event-architecture-v3-behavioural-archetypes-the-product-axis-m1-foundation);
no new architecture decision was required, so this is an M-section rather than a new `D-NNN`.

**"Authorization" here is not `IEventAuthority`, and the collision is the first thing to get straight.**
D-269's authority service answers *may this caller act on this event* — a live permission, resolved per
request, never stored. `EventAuthorization` answers *has the institution this event names consented to being
represented by it* — reviewed evidence that outlives the request. Neither substitutes for the other: full
manage authority over an event still does not let anyone publish it in a college's name without the
college's letter. Both definition sites say which one they mean, and the integration suite is
`EventAuthorizationDocumentTests` so a failing run is never ambiguous about which concept broke
(`EventAuthorizationTests` was already taken by D-269).

**It belongs to the event, not to the organization.** A head of department authorises one event, not every
future event anyone files under the institution. Hanging the row off the organization would silently turn a
single signed letter into a standing licence, and there would be no moment at which it expired. This is also
why it does not replace `Organization.VerificationStatus` (D-044): org verification says the institution is
real, authorization says it agreed to *this*. An event under a verified college still needs its own.

**The blocker originates in `PolicyResolver`, not in the service that owns the data.** The chain is
`PolicyResolver` → `EventPolicyService` → `PublishBlockers` / `ReviewerChecklist` → `TransitionGateAsync`.
`EventPolicyService` reads the three stored facts (does it represent an institution, is there an approved
authorization, does the archetype demand representation) and hands them to the resolver as
`RepresentationFacts`; the resolver decides. That keeps the resolver pure while leaving exactly one place
where the rule is written, so the checklist a reviewer reads cannot drift from the rule that refuses the
publish — the same failure M4 fixed for the rest of the policy engine.

**M4's publish gate only consumed the policy engine on one of its legs, and that was a real defect.**
`TransitionGateAsync` called `PolicyBlockerAsync` in `case EventStatus.Scheduled` and in neither
`EventStatus.Published` branch, so every rule the policy engine owned was reported by
`/policy-requirements` and then ignored by the publish that actually mattered. M4's own decision text claims
the gate consumes `PublishBlockers`; its test only exercised `schedule`, which is why the gap survived. Both
Published legs now consume it. **This is a behaviour change for the legacy `publish` action** — an event
carrying any policy violation could previously go straight to Published from Draft and now cannot.

**`representation_required` is the other half of D12 §6, and it is a different rule from authorization.**
Whether an event must name an institution *at all* is archetype-driven (A7 Recruitment · A12 Festival ·
A13 Ceremonial — a campus recruitment drive run by nobody in particular is not one); whether the institution
it names consented is evidence-driven. An event can satisfy the first and fail the second. The flag lives on
`EventArchetype.RequiresRepresentation` rather than in a branch, per D12's standing rule that no validation
is hardcoded. Without it that column of the frozen matrix would have stayed a label with no behaviour —
exactly the failure D2 catalogued for `AudienceLevelId`.

**Resubmission clears the prior verdict.** Evidence replaced after a reviewer read it has not been reviewed.
Leaving an `Approved` stamp attached would let an organiser swap the letter after approval and publish on a
decision about a different document.

**Decisions are recorded on the row and in the audit spine, deliberately not in `VerificationReview`.**
That store backs `GetReviewHistoryAsync`, which filters `SubjectType = Event`; an authorization verdict
written there would appear in the event's own review history as though a reviewer had ruled on the event.
Two decisions about two different subjects must not share one timeline. The row carries the current verdict
(`Status`/`ReviewerId`/`ReasonCode`/`Notes`) and `IAuditWriter` (D-102) carries the append-only trail.

**Documents are storage keys in, presigned URLs out.** Keys never leave the server: a key is an internal
address, and a client handed one is invited to construct paths, which eventually means constructing someone
else's. Uploads reuse `IStorage.PresignPutAsync` and the `events/{eventId}/authorization/{guid}` prefix
scopes a leaked key to one event.

**The edit lock extends to the evidence.** `PendingReview`/`UnderReview` return **409 `event_under_review`**
on a resubmission, for the same reason a PATCH does: evidence that moves while a reviewer is reading it
means they decide on something other than what they read.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/{EventAuthorization,EventArchetypes}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Domain/Enums/Enums.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IEventAuthorizationService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/{EventAuthorizationService,PolicyResolver,EventPolicyService,ArchetypeSeeder,EventService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/{EventEndpoints,AdminEventEndpoints}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Validation/{EventValidators,AdminEventValidators}.cs`,
migration `AddEventAuthorization`.

## D-280 · A one-time code is an accepted second factor; it was previously refused (2026-08-05)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.** This **reverses** the rule recorded at
`LoginApprovalService.cs:100` — *"OTP is deliberately NOT a login factor (architecture §4.14)"* — and it is
recorded here rather than quietly edited, because the original refusal was correct reasoning about a real
attack and deserves to survive as the record of what was traded away.

**What was wrong.** Password login had exactly two outcomes: a trusted-browser cookie (→ session) or a
trusted-device approval (→ challenge). An account with a correct password and **no enrolled device could not
log in at all** — `PasswordLoginAsync` returned `no_second_factor` and stopped. On mobile that is the common
case, not an edge case: a user who reinstalls the app, changes handset, or has just registered has no trusted
device, and the product told them to enrol one using an app they could not sign in to.

**The trade, stated plainly.** With a code as a valid second factor, **a phished password plus a SIM swap is a
complete account takeover**, and SIM-swap is a mature attack in this market specifically. That is precisely
why §4.14 refused it. Accepting it buys reachability and costs the property that a stolen password alone is
survivable.

**What keeps the cost bounded** — all three already exist and are reused; none are new mechanisms:

- **Ranking.** Device approval and passkey outrank a code wherever both are available, so the strong path
  stays the default and the code is a fallback, not a peer (D-283).
- **The risk engine** (`IRiskEngine`, ADR-AM22) already gates login. An elevated-risk sign-in may still demand
  device approval and refuse the code — a code being *available* is not the same as it being *sufficient*.
- **Step-up** (`IStepUpService`, AM6) already gates the operations that matter. A session established with a
  code cannot mint recovery codes, and the sensitive surfaces keep their existing step-up requirement, so the
  blast radius of the weaker factor stops at "signed in".

**Alternatives rejected.** *Keep refusing* — leaves the dead end, which is what prompted this. *Codes on
mobile only* — the same account is reachable from the web, and an attacker uses the weakest path, so a
per-surface security rule is theatre. *Require enrolment before first login* — an unsigned-in user cannot
enrol.

**Touches** `SecondFactorService` (new), `LoginApprovalService`, `DeviceLoginEndpoints`.

## D-281 · SMS is the OTP delivery channel; WhatsApp is demoted to transactional messaging (2026-08-05)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.**

**What was wrong.** Every production OTP call site passed `OtpChannel.WhatsApp` — login
(`AuthService.cs:64,177`), password reset (`PasswordResetService.cs:19,30`) and account recovery
(`RecoveryCodeService.cs:60,70`). `OtpChannel.Sms` was selected by **no caller**, so `SnsSmsProvider` —
complete, India-DLT aware, singleton-registered, correctly disposed — was unreachable code. Meanwhile the only
`IWhatsAppSender` in the build is `ConsoleWhatsAppSender`, and `WHATSAPP_PROVIDER=cloudapi` throws at startup
by design.

The net effect was not "SMS is dormant". **No OTP could reach any user on any channel** — the login rail
terminated in a `LogInformation` call.

**Decision.** Channel selection moves out of the call sites into `OtpChannelPolicy`. Phone-bearing purposes
resolve to `Sms`; `EmailLogin` and `EmailVerification` resolve to `Email`. WhatsApp remains fully supported as
a channel and keeps its provider seam, its inbound webhook and its message log — it is simply never selected
for authentication.

**Why not keep WhatsApp for OTP.** A WhatsApp account is portable across devices and recoverable through an
account-takeover chain Kurx does not control, so it is a weaker credential path than SMS. It is also a single
vendor with no alternative, which made it a single point of total login failure.

**Also fixed here.** `OtpService.IssueAsync` returned `Ok` whether or not delivery succeeded, because the send
happened after `SaveChangesAsync` and its result was discarded — a user whose send failed saw success and
waited for a code that was never sent. It now reports the failure, which is the prerequisite for any fallback.

**Unchanged:** OTP generation, the peppered hash, `PepperVersion`, the TTL, the atomic attempt claim, the
atomic consumption claim, every durable Postgres rate limit (D-005), and the security-event audit trail. Only
the channel changed.

**Touches** `OtpChannelPolicy` (new), `OtpService`, `AuthService`, `PasswordResetService`,
`RecoveryCodeService`.

## D-282 · Email OTP login is a distinct purpose from email verification (2026-08-05)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.**

**Context.** The platform had no email login path at all: `POST /v1/auth/otp/request` takes
`OtpRequestBody(string Phone)`, and the only email OTP was `OtpPurpose.EmailVerification` on the
`/v1/auth/email/verify/*` group — which is `RequireAuthorization()`, so it needs the session it is supposed to
help create.

**Decision.** A new `OtpPurpose.EmailLogin`, distinct from `EmailVerification`. The two answer different
questions: verification asks *"do you control this address?"* and runs while authenticated, at registration or
on change; login asks *"are you the account holder?"* and runs after a password, before a session exists.

**Why the separate purpose is load-bearing.** `IOtpService.VerifyAsync` matches on `(destination, purpose)`, so
sharing a purpose would let a code minted to verify an address be replayed to authenticate a login. This is the
same cross-ceremony replay defect D-098 found and fixed for challenges; the purpose-binding mechanism exists
because this class of bug is easy to introduce and invisible once shipped.

**Gates.** Email OTP is offered only when `User.EmailVerifiedAt is not null`, the account is neither banned nor
suspended (D-060), and it is not locked. **A login code is never sent to an unverified address** — an
unverified address may belong to someone else, so delivering a login factor to it would be an
account-takeover primitive rather than a convenience.

**No duplicated OTP logic.** Generation, the peppered hash, the TTL, the atomic attempt claim, the atomic
consumption claim and every rate limit belong to `IOtpService` and are reused verbatim. This decision adds one
enum value and a channel selection; if an implementation ever copies logic out of `OtpService`, that is the
signal it was done wrong.

**Touches** `Enums.cs`, `OtpChannelPolicy`, `SecondFactorService`.

## D-283 · The backend decides which second factors exist; clients render, never decide (2026-08-05)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.**

**What was wrong.** Each client hardcoded its own method set — web offered password + passkey + phone OTP,
admin offered password + OTP with no passkey, mobile offered password + OTP with no passkey. Three products
with three different security surfaces, drifting independently, and no way to add or reorder a method without
three client releases.

**Decision.** After the password is validated, the backend returns the account's **available** second factors,
ranked, with server-supplied labels and masked hints, plus a bound single-use continuation token. Clients
render exactly what arrives, in the order given. A client may not filter, reorder, hide or add to the list; a
genuine client-side constraint (no WebAuthn support, say) is reported as a *capability* on the request and the
backend omits the method. The decision stays in one place.

**Ranking is surface-aware, and that is deliberate.** Web ranks trusted-device approval first — it is the
match-number ceremony this platform already built, and the approving phone is a genuinely separate physical
device. Mobile ranks SMS and email OTP first, because on a handset the "trusted device" would usually be the
same device that is signing in, which is not a second factor at all. Ordering is policy data, so changing it is
configuration rather than a release.

**Anti-enumeration.** The list is reachable **only after a verified password**, so it discloses nothing an
attacker did not already have. This is strictly stronger than exposing methods pre-authentication, which was
considered and rejected: that would confirm account existence and then name the weakest enrolled factor. The
existing decoy guarantees on `/passkeys/login/options` and `/recovery/start` are untouched. (`/login/start`
carried one too, until D-285 removed the route.)
Unavailable methods are **absent** from the response rather than present-and-disabled, so a client cannot leak
the distinction through its UI either.

**The continuation token** inherits the discipline `AuthChallenge`'s `poll_hash` already uses: stored as a
hash, bound to the user and to the login attempt, single-use, short-lived, and never sufficient to mint a
session on its own.

**Touches** `SecondFactorService` (new), `LoginApprovalService`, `DeviceLoginEndpoints`, web
`otp-panel.tsx`, admin `login/page.tsx`, Flutter `password_login_page.dart`.

## D-284 · AWS SES implements the email seam (2026-08-05)

**Status: ACCEPTED and implemented.**

**Context.** `AWSSDK.SimpleEmailV2` had been referenced in `Kurx.Infrastructure.csproj` since the provider
inventory was written and was called by **zero** lines; `EMAIL_PROVIDER=ses` threw at startup. Every email the
platform "sends" — tickets, certificates, invitations, announcements, and now login codes — reached a
`LogInformation` call.

**Decision.** `SesEmailSender` behind the existing `IEmailSender` seam, selected by `EMAIL_PROVIDER=ses`, with
`console` remaining the dev default. The provider message id SES returns is propagated to the caller rather
than discarded, so a send can be correlated to a delivery event later.

**Deliberately unchanged:** the `AddProvider` fail-fast contract. An unimplemented or misspelled provider value
still throws at startup rather than falling back to the console sender — a deployment that comes up *healthy*
while delivering nothing is far worse than one that refuses to boot.

**Not in this decision:** bounce and complaint handling, the suppression list, and the DKIM/SPF/DMARC records.
Those gate SES production access and are deployment work, tracked separately. Until they exist SES stays in
sandbox and delivers only to verified addresses.

**Touches** `SesEmailSender` (new), `DependencyInjection`, `.env.example`.

## D-266 M5 addendum · representative details are mandatory, and the account link grants nothing

**Status** shipped. Refines [D-266 M5](#d-266-m5--institutional-authorization-the-represented-institutions-consent-per-event);
no new architecture decision was required.

**Problem.** M5 shipped with the signatory's phone optional and their role as free text on
`HeadDesignation`. Both failed the only job the record has. A reviewer's sole check *independent of the
letter* is contacting the person who supposedly signed it — an optional phone made that impossible for any
filing that omitted it. And free-text roles made "who authorises institutional events on Kurx" unanswerable:
`HOD`, `H.O.D.` and `Head of Dept` are three strings and one fact.

**Decision.**

1. **`OfficialPhone` is required, in E.164.** A signatory who cannot be reached is not a verifiable one.
   Enforced twice on purpose — the API validator refuses the shape, and `EventAuthorizationService` refuses
   it again, because a stored number the platform cannot dial is a signatory nobody can verify regardless of
   which caller wrote it.
2. **`RepresentativeRole` is required and closed** (`RepresentativeRoles.All`, 17 values). Validated
   server-side: an unvalidated vocabulary is free text that merely looks analysable, and a reviewer reading
   "Supreme Overlord" in a role field cannot tell whether the platform vouched for that word. `Other` is the
   escape hatch — a closed list that cannot express a real title pushes people into picking a wrong one,
   which is worse for a reviewer than an open field — and it must carry `RepresentativeRoleOther`.
3. **`RepresentativeUserId` is a LINK, never a grant.** Naming a Kurx account lets a reviewer see the
   signatory is a known person rather than a name typed into a form. It confers **no** authority over the
   event and changes nothing about that account: authority remains `IEventAuthority`'s alone
   ([D-269](#d-269--one-authorization-service-for-events)). The id must resolve, since an unresolvable one
   tells a reviewer nothing while looking like corroboration.
4. **Changing the signatory resets the approval**, on the same rule a document change already followed: a
   verdict describes the details a reviewer actually read, not whatever replaced them afterwards.
5. **An omitted document means "keep the one on file", never "delete it".** A client *cannot* resend a
   document key — reads hand back presigned URLs and never keys, deliberately — so treating omission as
   removal meant correcting a typo in the signatory's phone silently destroyed the letter the record exists
   to hold, along with any supporting documents a reviewer had already read. Making the representative
   details mandatory and editable is what turned this from a latent trap into a reachable one. A **first**
   filing still requires the letter: it is the substance of the claim.
6. **A free-mail official address warns, never refuses.** Plenty of real colleges run on Gmail, so refusing
   would reject genuine institutions; but an address anyone can register corroborates nothing about who
   signed, which leaves the letterhead carrying the whole claim. The reviewer console flags it as a prompt
   to look harder. It lives there rather than in the validator because **a validator can only refuse**, and
   this is advice.

**Rejected — a `representatives` table.** The details describe *one* filing and are re-stated whenever it is
re-filed; a table would imply a roster the institution never agreed to, and re-raise exactly the standing
licence M5 exists to prevent. **Rejected — trusting the linked account as evidence.** An account is not a
letter; treating a link as corroboration would let anyone name any user and inherit their credibility.

**Migration.** `AddRepresentativeDetails`: three `AddColumn`, one `AlterColumn` making `OfficialPhone`
non-null with `defaultValue: ""` — which is the backfill for any pre-existing row. Verified by fresh
install, rollback and roll-forward against a real database.

**Touches** `EventAuthorization`, `KurxDbContext`, `EventAuthorizationService`, `IEventAuthorizationService`,
`EventEndpoints`, `EventValidators`, `web/components/host/authorization-form.tsx`,
`admin/components/admin/authorization-panel.tsx`, `docs/api/README.md`.

## D-266 M5 addendum 2 · the role vocabulary is published, not copied per client

**Status** shipped. Refines the addendum above.

**Problem.** The convention for a closed vocabulary here has been to hardcode it client-side and validate
server-side — `admin/components/admin/review-actions.tsx` holds the review reasons that way, and the M5
roles were added to `web` the same way. Two copies was defensible. **Mobile would have made it three**, and
the failure mode is silent and one-sided: a client offers a role, the organiser picks it, the API refuses
it, and nothing on screen explains which of the two is wrong. The list is small enough to look harmless and
exactly the kind of thing that drifts when someone edits one copy.

**Decision.** `GET /v1/events/authorization/roles` returns `RepresentativeRoles.All` — the same array
`EventAuthorizationService` validates against, so this **publishes an existing source of truth rather than
creating one**. Authenticated (it is not an anonymous surface) and unscoped by event: the vocabulary is a
property of the platform, not of one event. No route ambiguity with `/{eventId:guid}/authorization` — a
literal segment cannot match the guid constraint. Annotated with `.Produces<IReadOnlyList<string>>()` so it
lands in `swagger.json`, per the "annotated at birth" precedent set by `PostEndpoints` (D-262) rather than
adding to the platform-wide response-schema gap.

**A test asserts the two cannot drift**: it fetches the published list and submits an authorization for
*every* role in it, requiring each to be accepted. A value added to the array without the validator
agreeing — or vice versa — fails the suite rather than a user's filing.

**Not done here:** the review-reason vocabulary in the admin console is still a client-side copy. It is a
single client today, so it does not yet have the problem this fixes; the same endpoint shape is available
when it gains a second.

**Touches** `EventEndpoints`, `web/lib/api.ts`,
`web/app/(app)/host/events/[id]/readiness/page.tsx`, `web/components/host/authorization-form.tsx`,
`Kurx.Tests/EventAuthorizationDocumentTests.cs`, `docs/api/README.md`.

## D-266 M6 — invitations: one policy, two delivery methods

**Status** shipped. Implements D9. Extends [D-266](#d-266--event-architecture-v3-behavioural-archetypes-the-product-axis-m1-foundation);
no new architecture decision was required.

**`Invite Only` is ONE registration policy. Username invitations and invite links are methods inside it.**
A policy answers *who may register*; a method answers *how were they told*. Modelling the methods as separate
policies would mean an event could be "invite-only by link" but not "invite-only", and every downstream
question — can this person register, how many seats are left — would have to ask which flavour first.

**A per-invitee token is not a shareable link, so it did not become one.** `EventInvitation.InviteToken`
names ONE person. A link with seats, expiry, single-use and a passcode is a different object with its own
accounting: overloading the per-invitee token would have made "how many seats are left" unanswerable and let
a forwarded token be redeemed by whoever received it. `EventInviteLink` is therefore a separate entity, not
a widened column.

**`UsedCount` is claimed in SQL, and every refusal condition rides in the same WHERE.** A conditional
`ExecuteUpdateAsync` carrying cap, expiry, revocation and single-use means the database decides who gets the
last seat: N concurrent redeemers issue N updates and exactly (MaxSeats − UsedCount) report a row changed.
Read-modify-write would let every concurrent caller read the same value and all succeed — the coupon
over-redemption bug (D-240/D-261) in a new table. Proven at 2, 10 and 100 simultaneous claimants.

**Redeeming twice consumes no second seat (D9 rule 7), and the guard is a unique index rather than a
read-then-write** — which two concurrent redemptions would both pass. When the index catches a racing
duplicate the seat this call claimed is handed back, so a double-tap never leaves the count overstated.

**A wrong passcode is refused before the claim.** Otherwise a guessing attacker drains a link's seats
without ever getting in. Passcodes are hashed with the platform hasher and verified server-side; possession
of the link is never sufficient when one is set.

**The invitation gate lives in `AudienceService.EvaluateAsync`, ABOVE the no-rule early return.** That
method is the platform's only eligibility engine — order creation, both group-join tails, ticket transfer,
gate admission and discovery all route through it — so the rule is written once instead of once per caller.
Placement matters as much as location: an `Invite Only` event almost never also carries an `AudienceRule`,
so checking after the `rule is null` return would have left every invite-only event wide open, making the
policy a label with no behaviour. That is exactly the failure D-266 exists to remove.

**"Invited" has one definition, and `IInvitationService` owns it.** `AudienceService` asks
`HasAccessAsync` rather than querying the invitation tables itself; otherwise the engine and the invitation
surfaces would each carry their own idea of who is in, and they would diverge the first time a method
changed.

**An invitation grants permission to register — never a ticket, never a discount.** Accepting creates no
order and issues no ticket; the order still runs and payment still applies. There is no "invited ⇒ free"
path in D9, and a test asserts that accepting leaves both tables empty.

**`GET /v1/users/search` is an authenticated alias over the existing `SearchUsersAsync`.** A second user
index would be a second answer to "who is on Kurx", and it would be the one that forgot profile visibility.
The consequence is deliberate: a user who has not made their username discoverable cannot be invited by
username, and is invited by email or phone instead.

**`not_invited` is 404, not 403.** Confirming that an invitation exists to someone who was not invited
discloses the guest list one probe at a time (D-018).

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/Invitations.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IInvitationService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/InvitationService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Audience/AudienceService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/InvitationEndpoints.cs`, migration `AddInviteLinks`.

## D-266 M7 — the reviewer's checklist gates approval, and it is derived rather than stored

**Status** shipped. Extends [D-266](#d-266--event-architecture-v3-behavioural-archetypes-the-product-axis-m1-foundation).

**The checklist ITEMS are a live projection of `PolicyResolver.ReviewerChecklist`; only the ticks are
persisted.** Storing the item list would freeze it at the moment the event entered review — a rule added
afterwards, or an event edited into needing one, would be invisible to the person approving it, and they
would tick a complete-looking list while the publish still refused. That is precisely the drift M3 exists
to prevent, so the checklist reads the same array the publish blockers come from, every time.

**`approve_review` returns `checklist_incomplete` until every item is ticked.** This is the milestone's
exit criterion. `unknown_checklist_item` refuses a tick against a key not currently on the event's
checklist: such a tick would count towards completeness without the reviewer having read a real
requirement, which bypasses the gate rather than satisfying it.

**Ticks are per reviewer, not per event.** Releasing and reclaiming a queue item must not let one reviewer
inherit another's sign-off — the entire point of a checklist is that the person approving did the reading.
Two reviewers looking at the same event each keep their own working state.

**Unticking re-blocks, and clears the timestamp.** "Complete" is a statement about the current state, not a
latch; and a `CheckedAt` surviving an untick would read as a confirmation nobody currently stands behind.

**`blocking` distinguishes a rule that refuses the publish from one that merely needs confirming.** Both
must be ticked to approve, but only the first also stops the publish on its own, and a reviewer deciding
what to chase needs to know which is which.

**The pending payload is enriched, and `MeetingPassword` is excluded by construction.** `PendingEventView`
gained status, product, archetype, `is_paid`, `authorization_status` and city so a reviewer can triage the
queue without a call per row. It has **no `MeetingPassword` field at all** — excluded from the type rather
than filtered at each call site, because the next call site is the one that forgets (D-266 §5).

**Copy for requirement codes lives in the console and decides nothing.** The admin label map is
presentation only: the item list is whatever the backend returns, so a rule added server-side appears
immediately — as its raw code until copy is written — rather than being silently dropped by a console that
did not know about it.

**The authorization panel is not `IEventAuthority`.** It answers whether the represented institution
consented; approving there is not approving the event. The two decisions sit next to each other in the
console and are deliberately separate actions with separate audit trails.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/EventReviewChecklist.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IEventPolicyService.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/{EventReviewChecklistService,EventService}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/AdminEventEndpoints.cs`,
`admin/{lib/api.ts,lib/admin-actions.ts,components/admin/{review-checklist,authorization-panel}.tsx,app/(console)/events/review/page.tsx}`,
migration `AddEventReviewChecklist`.

## D-266 M7 addendum · financial review, and M8 · the client renders, never decides

**Status** shipped. Extends [D-266](#d-266--event-architecture-v3-behavioural-archetypes-the-product-axis-m1-foundation).

### Financial review (M7, D12 §6 A11)

**Keyed on the archetype, not on "is it paid".** A fundraiser solicits money *for a cause*, and that is the
risk FinanceOps exists to check; a ticketed concert (A8) takes far more money and carries none of it. So
`EventArchetype.RequiresFinancialReview` is true for `fundraising` alone, and the blocker is
`financial_review_required`. An earlier draft's "Public + paid ⇒ financial review" would have gated most of
the platform on a review that answers a question those events do not raise.

**`POST /v1/admin/events/{id}/financial-review` is FinanceOps, not VerificationReviewer.** Clearing a money
path is a different competence from reviewing an event's content, and the platform already separates those
roles — so the route sits outside the reviewer-gated group deliberately.

**Recorded as columns on the event, not a table.** One decision, no documents, and "is this event
financially cleared?" is a property of the event. The institutional authorization earned its own entity
because it carries evidence; this does not. `notes` is required to fail: a refusal the organiser cannot act
on is a dead end, not a review outcome.

**`FinancialReviewStatus` is nullable, so it needed an explicit `HasConversion<string>()`.** The global
enum→text loop tests `prop.ClrType.IsEnum`, which is false for a nullable enum — the same trap
`EventCategory.ProductClass` documents. Caught by reading the generated migration, where the column had
landed as `integer` while every other status on the platform is text.

### M8 — the client renders capabilities, it never decides them

**A hardcoded event rule in `web/` is a Phase 1 failure (D-266 §9), and there was one.** The create wizard
offered a `Private` visibility that had been dead since migration `RetireLegacyPrivateVisibility`: the
server's `Enum.TryParse` rejected it, so an organiser who chose it silently got the default. It is now
`InviteOnly`, matching the enum.

**`ModulePicker` contains no event knowledge.** It does not know what a Hackathon is or that a Blood Drive
cannot sell tickets — it renders whatever `GET .../events/{id}/capabilities` returns, grouped by the
backend's own `group_slug`. **`locked` is rendered as unavailable and never as an unchecked toggle**: the
backend would refuse the toggle, and `off` (available, unchosen) means something different. Conflating them
is precisely what the retired Kind model could not avoid.

**Registration policies come from `allowed_policies`, visibility values from the enum the server accepts.**
The client offers exactly what the policy engine permits, so it cannot present a choice the server refuses.

**The organiser can now act on the gate M5 introduced.** `AuthorizationForm` files the letter through a
presigned PUT — **bytes never pass through the API**, only the returned storage key — and surfaces the
reviewer's reason code and notes on rejection or changes-requested. Without it, M5's publish blocker would
have been unactionable from the web: the workspace would say "you need an authorization" and offer nowhere
to provide one.

**A refused transition is no longer silent.** `EventStatusActions` discarded its result entirely: a host
clicked Publish, got a 409, and saw nothing at all. It now shows the reason, with organiser-facing copy for
`event_authorization_required` and `representation_required` plus the pre-existing gates
(`pending_org_verification`, `representation_vacant`, `missing_description`, …) that had been equally
silent. Unmapped codes fall through verbatim rather than becoming a generic message, so an unexpected
refusal stays diagnosable.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/{Entities/{Events,EventArchetypes}.cs,Enums/Enums.cs}`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/{PolicyResolver,EventPolicyService,EventService,ArchetypeSeeder}.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/AdminEventEndpoints.cs`,
`web/{lib/api.ts,lib/event-actions.ts,components/host/{create-event-wizard,module-picker,authorization-form,event-status-actions}.tsx}`,
migration `AddFinancialReview`.

## D-266 M4 addendum · a transition is claimed in SQL, not assumed from a read

**Status** shipped. Refines [D-266 M4](#d-266-m4--the-event-review-lifecycle); no new architecture decision
was required — this reuses a mechanism the codebase already had.

**Problem.** `TransitionAsync` read the event, ran every gate against that snapshot, then wrote
`ev.Status = target`. Nothing tied the write to the status it had read. Two reviewers deciding in the same
moment both passed the gates and both wrote: the status became whoever committed last, while **both**
verdicts were appended to `verification_reviews` (which carries no unique index — only
`(SubjectType, SubjectId, CreatedAt)` and `ReviewerId`). The review history could therefore state that one
event was approved *and* rejected. Duplicate `event.status_change` audit entries followed the same way.

**Decision — compare-and-swap, not a lock and not a new mechanism.** The status write became a conditional
`ExecuteUpdateAsync` predicated on `Status == previousStatus`; 0 rows updated returns
**`transition_conflict`**. A losing request decided about a state that no longer exists, so it must not
record a verdict.

**Rejected — `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` / row locks.** [D-231](#d-231) already established this on a different
endpoint and the result is on record: the suite went from ~7 minutes to **5h42m**, because Postgres applies
no default lock timeout and a lock held across an `await` blocks every later writer indefinitely — turning a
lost update into a hang. **Rejected — EF `RowVersion` / `xmin`.** Both would introduce a *second* concurrency
mechanism: the codebase already resolves exactly this shape with a status predicate in `ChatService` (room
status), `OrderService` and `RefundService` (both name the result `claimed`), `ChallengeService` and
`LoginApprovalService`. Consistency is worth more here than novelty, and a conditional UPDATE holds its
row-level lock inside the statement rather than across an await.

**Claim ownership — one reviewer at a time.** The CAS alone makes two simultaneous claims resolve to one
winner, but it cannot say who won: `claim_review` moved `PendingReview → UnderReview` while recording **no
reviewer identity**, so two reviewers could still work one event in sequence, each against their own
per-reviewer checklist, neither able to see the other. `Event.ReviewClaimedBy`/`ReviewClaimedAt` close that.

- **Set and cleared in the same statement as the status**, so an item is never `UnderReview` unowned, nor
  owned while sitting in the queue.
- **`release_review` and the three decisions require the holder** (`claimed_by_another_reviewer`). Deciding
  on someone else's claim is precisely how a second reviewer signs off against ticks they never made.
- **An admin may override.** A reviewer who goes offline holding an item must not strand it — a release
  valve, not a general exemption.
- **A decision releases the hold.** The verdict lives in `verification_reviews`; a decided event is no
  longer anybody's work in progress.
- **The queue exposes the holder** (`review_claimed_by`/`_by_name`/`_at`) so an item reads as taken rather
  than inviting a second reviewer to start it. The name is null for accounts that never onboarded — the id
  is the load-bearing fact.

**Rejected — several reviewers holding one item.** Defensible for a high-volume queue, but the checklist is
per-reviewer by design (D-266 M7), so concurrent holders produce two partial sign-offs and no way to say
which one approved. Confirmed as a product decision, not inferred.

**Blast radius.** One method: `Event.Status` has exactly two writers in the codebase — creation and this
line. Admin suspend/hide use separate `IsSuspended`/`IsHidden` flags, so there is no force-status path. No
migration, no DTO change, no API shape change; one new error code, translated in web and mobile.

**Touches** `EventService.{TransitionAsync,ListInReviewAsync}`, `Events.cs`, `KurxDbContext`,
`IEventService.PendingEventView`, `AdminEventEndpoints`, `web/lib/event-actions.ts`,
`mobile/lib/features/organizer/presentation/pages/event_status_page.dart`, `docs/api/README.md`,
`Kurx.Tests/{ReviewLifecycleIntegrationTests,KurxApiFactory}.cs`, migration `AddReviewClaimOwnership`.

## D-266 M8 addendum · wizard autosave, and the fixes an audit found

**Status** shipped.

**A draft snapshot is opaque, per-user client state.** `EventDraftSnapshot` stores the wizard's
in-progress form as jsonb; the server never parses it and no projection, policy or publish path
ever reads it. Giving it columns would create a second, weaker definition of an event that drifts from the
real one every time a field is added — so it deliberately has none. A test asserts a draft cannot modify
its event, because if it could an organiser would be able to change a live event by typing in a form they
never submitted.

**Per (event, user), not per event.** Two managers mid-edit are each mid-thought: merging their forms
produces something neither typed, and last-write-wins silently discards someone's work.

**Validation is size and "is it JSON", nothing more.** The payload deliberately contains half-filled steps
that would fail real validation — refusing them would refuse exactly the state autosave exists to preserve.

### Defects this audit found and fixed

**The `AddFinancialReview` migration created nothing.** It contained four `AlterColumn` statements against
five columns that no migration ever added, so **fresh install, upgrade and rollback were all broken** —
303 test failures, 176 of them `42703: column "FinancialReviewStatus" of relation "events" does not exist`.
Root cause: a `dotnet ef migrations remove` whose failure output (`Could not execute because the specified
command or file was not found` — the tool was not on PATH in that container) was not checked, followed by
deleting the migration files by hand. The snapshot kept the columns, so the regeneration diffed model
against snapshot and found only a CLR type change. **The lesson is the process, not the file: never delete
a migration by hand, and always assert the exit code of the command that unwinds the snapshot.**

**M6 was reported complete while being unreachable from the product.** Backend, migration and tests for
invite links were all green, and there was no organiser UI at all — the entire D9 Method B feature could
not be used. `InviteLinks` (create with seats/expiry/passcode/single-use, copy, revoke, live seat counts)
now sits on the invitations page. The earlier audit missed it by checking whether the *components written*
were mounted rather than whether the *feature* was reachable.

**M8's components were written but imported by nothing.** `ModulePicker` and `AuthorizationForm` existed
and typechecked while being dead code. Both are now mounted on a real route,
`/host/events/[id]/readiness`, alongside the live publish-blocker list.

**Touches** `backend/Kurx.Domain/Entities/EventDraftSnapshot.cs`,
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/{Persistence/KurxDbContext.cs,Events/EventService.cs}`,
`backend/Kurx.Api/Endpoints/EventEndpoints.cs`, `backend/Kurx.Api/Validation/EventValidators.cs`,
`web/{app/(app)/host/events/[id]/{readiness/page.tsx,invitations/page.tsx,layout.tsx},components/host/invite-links.tsx}`,
`admin/components/admin/financial-review-panel.tsx`,
migrations `AddFinancialReview` (regenerated), `AddEventDraftSnapshots`.

**Correction — jsonb preserves content, not bytes.** The first draft of this section, and the test that
backed it, claimed the payload round-trips *verbatim*. It does not: `jsonb` reparses on write, so
`{"v":2}` returns as `{"v": 2}`, key order is not preserved and duplicate keys collapse. The regression
caught it. The column is right and the claim was wrong — a form restore parses the JSON anyway, and jsonb
buys a database-level guarantee that what was stored is valid. What changed is the contract: **content is
preserved intact, including fields the server knows nothing about; the exact bytes are not.**

> ### ✅ D-NUMBER COLLISION RESOLVED — D-285, D-286, D-287
>
> Two workstreams allocated these three numbers concurrently. The **UI/UX set keeps them**: it
> landed on `main` first and 42 commits, `docs/ui-ux/*` and `UI_REDESIGN_PROGRESS.*` already cite
> those numbers, so renumbering it would invalidate far more references than renumbering the other.
> The auth/phone set was moved to **D-289 / D-290 / D-291**, and every reference to it in
> `docs/auth/*`, `docs/api/README.md`, `.claude/memory/*` and `web/lib/auth-api.ts` was updated with
> it. D-288 (phone conformance corpus) never collided and keeps its number.
>
> Nothing was dropped in the merge; both sets are ACCEPTED and appear below in full.

## D-285 · UI/UX redesign program — scope, verification strategy and terminology (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED.**

A complete UI/UX redesign of all three clients was commissioned as a 58-phase, weighted roadmap
(`UI_REDESIGN_PROGRESS.md` is its live ledger; `docs/ui-ux/` holds the inventories, the frozen-surface
list and the regression criteria). Four calls were ambiguous enough to block work and are settled here.
The palette question they depend on is separate and is recorded as D-286.

**1. Scope is the whole product, not the event core.** The redesign covers all **206 screens**: 88 web
routes, 27 admin routes, 91 Flutter pages. That deliberately includes the surfaces that are not
ticketing — Posts, Chat, the Professional Identity system (allies / journey / heatmap / metrics),
Certificates, Gamification, Competitions, Groups and Workspace — which together are roughly a quarter
of the program by weight. **Why:** they are reachable from primary navigation on both web and mobile;
leaving them on the old visual system would make the redesign visibly half-finished at exactly the
places a returning user spends time.

**2. Visual baselines are captured manually; no screenshot harness enters the dependency graph.**
D-109 deliberately excluded Playwright, Cypress and Storybook from this repository, and
`web/vitest.config.mts` still says so. Adding one for redesign convenience would contradict an accepted
decision. Captures are taken with session-level browser tooling and filed as PNGs under
`docs/ui-ux/baselines/`; nothing is added to any `package.json`. **Why:** the value wanted here is a
before/after reference for human comparison, which does not require the repo to own a test runner.
A screenshot is never accepted as evidence that something *works* — the functional gates in
`docs/ui-ux/regression-criteria.md` §2.2 are independent and always apply.

**3. The token layer gains the scales it never had.** Web and admin currently define **nine colour
tokens and nothing else** — no spacing, sizing, radius, border, shadow, opacity, z-index, duration,
easing or breakpoint tokens, all of which are ad-hoc Tailwind at each call site. Flutter is further
ahead and already ships `KSpace` / `KRadius` / `KMotion` / `kCardShadow`. Phase 4 adds the missing
scales to `packages/ui`, **named to mirror the Flutter ones** so the two systems are translatable by
inspection rather than by memory. **Why:** cross-surface consistency cannot be verified against
tokens that do not exist.

**Colour tokens are also currently duplicated four ways and that is a live defect**, fixed first in
Phase 4.0: `packages/ui/src/styles/tokens.css` and `packages/ui/tailwind-preset.cjs` are the intended
source of truth and `admin/tailwind.config.js` correctly consumes the preset, but
`web/tailwind.config.ts` inlines a verbatim copy of the preset, `web/app/globals.css` inlines a
verbatim copy of the tokens, and `web/lib/design-tokens.ts` is a third hardcoded hex copy. Any future
token edit would have silently applied to admin and not to web.

**4. "Organizer" stays retired.** The commissioned roadmap named a phase "Organizer Experience".
D-271 and `docs/architecture/TERMINOLOGY.md` retired that word: a **User owns an Event**, and an
organization on an event is the one it is **represented by**. The phase is called **Host / Workspace
Experience** and the Phase 43 copy audit checks visible strings *against* TERMINOLOGY.md rather than
inventing vocabulary.

**Baseline recorded at `c66ae16` (2026-08-06), and it is the number Phase 48 must meet or beat:**
backend **1433 total — 1432 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed**; web typecheck/lint clean, **145 tests
passing across 8 files**, build clean at **65 static pages**; admin typecheck/lint clean, build clean
at **29 static pages**, **no test suite exists**; mobile `flutter analyze` **No issues found**,
**275 tests passing**.

Two corrections to documentation this measurement produced. `.claude/CLAUDE.md` §9 records the backend
baseline as **1297** (1296 pass, 1 skip); that was measured on an isolated worktree at `HEAD`+D-274 on
2026-08-05, and `c66ae16` carries additional merged work, so **1433 is the correct figure for this
branch**. And `docs/REMAINING_WORK.md` describes 62 pre-existing Flutter style infos; analyze is now
**clean** — they were cleared by D-212, and that file is a superseded snapshot.

**Verification:** all four suites run locally and green at the values above. `dotnet` needs
`/nowarn:NU1900` in this sandbox — `api.nuget.org` is unreachable, so the package *vulnerability audit*
fails and `-warnaserror` promotes it to an error. That is an environment artifact, not a code defect;
CI has network and needs no flag.

**Files:** `UI_REDESIGN_PROGRESS.md`, `UI_REDESIGN_PROGRESS.json`,
`docs/ui-ux/{inventory-web,inventory-admin,inventory-mobile,do-not-change,regression-criteria}.md`.
No application code changed.

## D-286 · One visual register across web, admin and mobile — the warm direction, corrected to pass WCAG (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Supersedes [D-065](#).**

D-065 chose two visual registers on purpose: the Stitch warm palette for mobile, GitHub-dark/coral
retained for web and admin — *"three surfaces, two visual registers"* — on the reasoning that mobile
is attendee-first (concerts, festivals) while the darker palette suited the other surfaces. The UI/UX
redesign program (D-285) requires the opposite outcome: its Phase 41 and Phase 50 gates are that the
three surfaces read as **one intentionally designed product**. Those cannot both hold.

**Chose:** one register for all three surfaces, built from mobile's warm direction. Web and admin
adopt the ember/teal/warm-paper palette, Plus Jakarta Sans, and the shared radius/shadow/motion
scales. Admin is differentiated by **density, never by palette** — three densities (comfortable /
compact / dense) come out of one token set, which is how it gets the information density its
redesign phase demands without a second design system.

**Why the warm direction rather than the incumbent:** D-065's reasoning was directionally right but
under-argued. The domain model — certificates, competitions, team formation, speakers, sponsors,
institutional verification, KYC, membership claims, professional journey, allies, attendance
provenance — describes **college fests, hackathons and conferences in India**, not nightlife. The
product's centre of gravity is credentialled participation: the reason to come back is that Kurx
holds the record of what you showed up for. GitHub-dark/coral reads as a developer tool and says
nothing about that. Warm-paper does.

**The palette was measured before it was adopted, and neither candidate passed.** Every
foreground/background pair in both existing palettes was checked against WCAG 2.1:

- **`#FFFFFF` on ember `#F0762B` = 2.86:1 — fails AA.** This is `filledButtonTheme` in
  `app_theme.dart`, i.e. **every primary CTA in the mobile app**, Register and Book included. A
  conversion-path control has been below the text-contrast floor since D-065 shipped.
- **Ember text on cream = 2.80:1 — fails.** That is `textButtonTheme`, every text button on light.
- Mobile light `muted` 4.20:1 and mobile dark `teal` 4.37:1 both sit just under 4.5.
- Web light `accent` `#CF4225` = 4.42:1, marginally under.
- **Borders fail 3:1 on all four palettes** (1.30–1.55:1), which matters for WCAG 1.4.11 wherever a
  border is what identifies a control — `field.tsx` draws inputs with `border-border`.

So this decision is emphatically **not** "adopt mobile's palette"; that would have shipped a
known-failing primary button to three surfaces instead of one.

**The correction keeps the brand vivid.** Darkening ember until white text passes needs `#C5540E`, a
muddy brick that discards the warmth the direction rests on. Measurement gave a better answer:
**`#1A1A1A` ink on `#F0762B` ember is 6.08:1** — comfortably AA, AAA at large sizes — so the primary
button keeps its full vivid ember and takes a **warm-ink label instead of a white one**. That fixes
the S1 failure and is also the more distinctive choice: white-on-saturated is the SaaS default, while
ink-on-ember reads like a wristband or a printed ticket.

**Two structural token changes fall out of the measurement**, both implemented in Phase 4.1:

1. **`border` splits into decorative and interactive.** WCAG 1.4.11 governs boundaries that
   *identify a control*; an input edge must reach 3:1 while a card's decorative edge need not. One
   token cannot serve both, which is precisely why all four palettes fail today.
2. **`warning` becomes a real token.** None exists — which is why the audit found `bg-amber-500`
   hand-written into two components.

**Semantic rule introduced:** **ember acts, teal attests.** Ember marks the live and the actionable
(register, publish, primary CTA); teal marks the verified and the attested (provenance badges,
verified sections, certificates, confirmed allies). The product already treats provenance as
first-class (`provenance-badge.tsx`, `verified-sections.tsx`, the trust engines); giving it its own
hue makes a structural truth visible. Teal is therefore **not** generic success chrome — `success`
stays a separate token.

**Consequences:** `mobile/lib/core/theme/design_tokens.dart` keeps its structure and adjusts four
values plus `onAccent`; `packages/ui/src/styles/tokens.css` and `tailwind-preset.cjs` are rewritten
onto the shared palette; `web/tailwind.config.ts`, `web/app/globals.css` and
`web/lib/design-tokens.ts` stop carrying their duplicate copies (D-285). No route, contract or
business rule is touched. D-065 remains in this log as the record of why the split existed; it is
superseded, not deleted.

**Also corrected here:** the doc comments in `design_tokens.dart` and `app_shell.dart` cite "(D-056)"
and "(D-057)" for the mobile palette and bottom nav. Those numbers belong to *Staff & role management*
and the *admin event-approval queue*. The mobile decisions are **D-065** and **D-066**; the citations
are fixed in Phase 32.

**Full direction:** `docs/ui-ux/visual-identity.md`.

**Verification:** every ratio quoted above is reproducible with the contrast script recorded in that
document's §3. No code changed in this phase — Phase 4 implements it.

## D-287 · Anek is the Kurx typeface; Plus Jakarta Sans has no Devanagari (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED. Refines [D-286](#) §Typography.**

D-286 named **Plus Jakarta Sans** as the platform-wide face, on the reasoning that mobile already
loads it via `google_fonts` and it suits the warm contemporary direction. A cross-check against the
`ui-ux-pro-max` typography database while implementing Phase 4 showed that reasoning had a hole:
**Plus Jakarta Sans ships no Devanagari coverage.**

`web/messages/hi.json` exists — Hindi is a shipped locale. Every Hindi string therefore renders in
whatever unrelated face the OS falls back to, producing a visible typeface change mid-page, in the
one market this product targets. That is not a defect the redesign should carry forward, and it
would have been invisible until someone switched locale.

**Chose: Anek** (Ek Type, an Indian foundry). A superfamily with matched cuts across Latin,
Devanagari and eight further Indian scripts, variable on weight and width. The web stack is
`"Anek Latin", "Anek Devanagari", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif`; browsers select per glyph,
so a mixed-script string renders correctly with no runtime branching and no locale-conditional CSS.
Flutter switches to `GoogleFonts.anekLatin` / `anekDevanagari` in Phase 32. It also serves the
"contemporary Indian" brand personality D-286 asserted rather more literally than Plus Jakarta Sans
did.

**Rejected:** the database's own suggested pairing, **Bebas Neue / Source Sans 3**. Bebas Neue is an
all-caps condensed display face with no Devanagari and poor legibility at the caption sizes this
product leans on (88% of its text is caption-sized today — audit S2-3). A display/text pairing was
considered and dropped: one variable superfamily across nine steps carries the hierarchy with weight
and size, and avoids shipping two font payloads to a mobile-first Indian audience.

**Deferred, and tracked:** self-hosting the binaries. `next/font` fetches at build time and this
environment has no network, so the family is declared in the token and the stack degrades to the
previous `ui-sans-serif, system-ui` rendering until the files are vendored. Nothing regresses in the
meantime, and adopting the font later is a token-only change with no code edit.

**Also recorded:** the same cross-check corroborated the D-286 palette *direction* independently
(it recommends warm orange `#EA580C` on cream `#FFF7ED` for this product type) but its concrete
values were **not** adopted, because they fail its own accessibility checklist — `#FFFFFF` on
`#EA580C` is 3.56:1, its primary-as-text is 3.35:1, and its border is 1.10:1 against the 3:1 rule.
Its `MASTER.md` was deliberately not persisted into the repository: that would have created a second,
contradicting source of truth for the palette, which `.claude/CLAUDE.md` §6 forbids. `packages/ui`
remains the only source. Full record: `docs/ui-ux/visual-identity.md` §11A.

**Files:** `packages/ui/tailwind-preset.cjs`, `docs/ui-ux/visual-identity.md`,
`docs/ui-ux/token-map.md`.

## D-289 · Remove the passwordless `/v1/auth/login/start` and `/v1/auth/trusted-browsers/revoke-all` (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Both routes were live, both had zero callers in web, admin and Flutter.

**`POST /v1/auth/login/start`.** The identifier-first entry to device-approval login, from before password
became factor 1 (D-182). It was anonymous, took a bare identifier, and called `PushToDevicesAsync` — so
anyone who knew a phone number could raise approval prompts on that person's devices. That is an MFA-fatigue
primitive, and it was serving no shipped UI: both clients carried a comment saying the route was
deliberately unsurfaced. The rate limit and risk gate bounded it but did not justify keeping it.

*What replaces it:* nothing — `/login/password` already mints the same challenge, returns the same
`challenge_id` / `poll_token` / `match_number`, and is what every client actually calls. The device-approval
ceremony, the SignalR `LoginHub` binding and the poll-token rules are unchanged.

*Anti-enumeration is not weakened.* `/login/start` needed a **decoy** — a fabricated challenge for an
unknown identifier — precisely because it answered before authentication. `/login/password` needs no decoy:
an unknown identifier, an account with no password and a wrong password all return one generic
`invalid_credentials` (covered by `PasswordLoginTests`). A device-less account that *passes* the password is
deliberately told `second_factor` (D-280); disclosing an account to a caller who has already proved factor 1
is not enumeration. The decoy test was therefore deleted rather than ported — the behaviour it pinned no
longer exists. The risk-engine test was ported: a denied login must still mint **no challenge**, which is
now asserted by challenge count rather than by decoy shape.

*Test impact:* ~16 call sites across `TrustedDeviceAuthTests` and `ChallengeHardeningTests` used the route
as the cheapest way to mint a login challenge. They now go through a `StartApprovalLoginAsync` helper that
does the real password-first ceremony, and each fixture's `LoginAsync` sets a password at sign-up.
`SetInitialAsync` writes a credential without cascading, so enrolled devices survive it.

**`POST /v1/auth/trusted-browsers/revoke-all`.** No caller and no UI. Per-browser revoke remains, and bulk
revocation still exists where it is actually used — `RevokeAllForCascadeAsync`, on password change / reset /
recovery, which is covered by the cascade tests. The unused `ITrustedBrowserService.RevokeAllAsync` went
with the route rather than being left as scaffolding (D-018).

**Files:** `Api/Endpoints/DeviceLoginEndpoints.cs`, `Api/Endpoints/TrustedBrowserEndpoints.cs`,
`Api/Hubs/LoginHub.cs`, `Application/Abstractions/ILoginApprovalService.cs`,
`Application/Abstractions/ITrustedBrowserService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Auth/LoginApprovalService.cs`,
`Infrastructure/Auth/TrustedBrowserService.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/{TrustedDeviceAuthTests,ChallengeHardeningTests,TrustedBrowserTests}.cs`,
`docs/api/README.md`, `docs/auth/*`, `web/lib/auth-api.ts`,
`mobile/lib/features/auth/data/datasources/trusted_device_remote_data_source.dart`.

## D-290 · Phone identity is canonical E.164 end to end; the legacy column is never re-normalized (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Closes the India-only assumptions D-089 phase 1 left behind, and the class of defects
that the fix itself exposed.

**1. `NormalizePhone` honours the '+'.** It was `digits.Length == 10 ? "91" + digits : digits` — a length
rule applied *after* stripping the '+', so it could not tell a national number from a complete
international one. Every number whose full E.164 form is exactly ten digits was refiled under India:
`+65 9123 4567` became `+91 6591234567`, and the one-time code went to an unrelated real phone. It now
parses with libphonenumber: a leading '+' is the caller stating their country and always wins; input with
no '+' is still read in `LegacyInputRegion` (`IN`) so pre-E.164 clients keep working, but it must
*validate* there rather than be assumed, and an unplaceable number is returned as its digits rather than
assigned a country. **No length heuristic remains anywhere.**

**2. The rule that fix created: never re-normalize a stored bare-digit phone.** `users.Phone` holds
`NormalizePhone` output — the country code without the '+'. Feeding it back through `NormalizePhone`
re-reads it in the legacy region, and many foreign national numbers are *also* well-formed Indian mobiles,
so a Singapore number stored as `6591234567` returns as `916591234567`. **Anywhere a stored phone is
compared against a freshly normalized one, or re-normalized at all, read `u.PhoneE164 ?? u.Phone`.** Two
live defects came from exactly this:

- **Ticket-transfer claim** (`TicketTransferEndpoints`) fed the legacy column back through the normalizer,
  so an international owner could never claim their own transfer.
- **Blacklist enforcement** (`FraudService.IsUserClearAsync`) did the same, so a ban set on an
  international number matched no row and **failed open** — the account it was set against could sign in.

**3. Cross-country collision in the transfer claim.** `ClaimAsync` compared the *last ten digits*, a
tolerance for the inconsistent formats that predated canonical storage. `+1 987 654 3210` and
`+91 98765 43210` share their final ten digits, so the American number could claim a ticket addressed to
the Indian one. Both sides now come from the same normalizer, so the comparison is exact `string.Equals`.

**4. Canonical form at the messaging boundary.** `WhatsAppLogService` canonicalizes the destination once,
via `PhoneCanonicalizer.ToE164OrUnchanged`, instead of each caller doing it. Restoring the '+' onto digits
that already carry a country code states nothing new, so it can never re-home a number the way a default
region would; anything that still fails to validate passes through untouched, to fail visibly at the
provider rather than silently as somebody else's number. **Consequence worth naming:** that changed what is
stored in `WhatsAppMessages.ToPhone`, and `AnnouncementService` deduplicated resends by comparing that
column against bare digits — which would have re-sent an announcement to everyone already delivered. Both
sides of that comparison now canonicalize.

**5. Phones are masked in logs.** `SnsSmsProvider` and `WhatsAppLogService` logged complete numbers on
failure. One `PhoneCanonicalizer.Mask` (last four digits, length-agnostic so it is correct for every
numbering plan) is now shared by them and `OtpService`.

**6. Every client phone input goes through the shared country picker.** A bare text box submits digits with
no country, which the backend then reads in the legacy region — so an overseas number was silently filed as
an Indian one. Converted: web staff-assignment and guest-invitation forms, the admin staff-grant and
blacklist forms, and the Flutter phone-change, staff-assignment and invitation screens. The Flutter phone
change was the most serious: it is the sign-in identity, so it texted the confirmation code to a stranger
and moved the account onto their number. `packages/ui` `toE164Identifier` also now checks *validity*, not
just parseability, matching the backend and the Flutter twin.

**Display follows storage.** Projections that hand a phone to a client read the canonical column first —
attendee CSV export (organizers paste it into dialers), admin user list and moderation view, group-member
roster, referral list, `/v1/auth/me`. The Flutter profile screen printed a hardcoded `+91 ` in front of an
already-canonical value, rendering `+91 +919876543210` for everyone.

**Deliberately unchanged.** `LegacyInputRegion`/`PHONE_BACKFILL_LEGACY_REGION` (`IN`) and the pickers'
default country: the region only applies to input with no '+', it is validated rather than assumed, and it
fails *closed* — a wrong guess yields no account match and a login error, never a misrouted code. Event
`ContactPhone` stays free text (display only, never an identity key). The organizer authorization form
stays a plain field because its validator is strict E.164 and rejects bare digits outright.

**Files:** `Infrastructure/Auth/{AuthService,PhoneCanonicalizer,OtpService}.cs`,
`Infrastructure/Trust/FraudService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Ticketing/TicketTransferService.cs`,
`Infrastructure/Messaging/WhatsAppLogService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Events/{AttendeeService,AnnouncementService}.cs`,
`Infrastructure/Orders/OrderService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Admin/UserAdminService.cs`,
`Infrastructure/Gamification/GamificationService.cs`, `Infrastructure/Providers/SmsProviders.cs`,
`Api/Endpoints/{TicketTransferEndpoints,AuthEndpoints}.cs`, `packages/ui/src/phone-utils.ts`,
`web/components/host/{assignments-section,add-invitation-form}.tsx`,
`admin/components/{staff/staff-manager,admin/blacklist-manager}.tsx`,
`mobile/lib/features/{settings/.../account_page,organizer/.../assignments_page,organizer/.../invitations_page,profile/.../profile_page,orders/.../ticket_detail_page,auth/.../recovery_page}.dart`,
`Kurx.Tests/InternationalPhoneTests.cs`.

## D-291 · "Remember this browser" was silently dropped on the one-time-code path (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** A defect in D-280's own delivery, found by auditing endpoints against their callers.

`/v1/auth/login/second-factor/verify` issues the httpOnly `kurx_tb` cookie when the password step recorded
a remember request. Neither browser client stored it: web posted without `withCredentials` (the axios
instance sets no global default, and `loginPassword` passes it explicitly), and the admin server action
never called `storeTrustedBrowserCookie`, though its sibling password and poll actions both do. The backend
minted the cookie and both clients threw it away, so anyone finishing sign-in with an SMS or email code was
re-challenged on every login, with **no error** to explain it — the feature looked broken rather than
failing. Fixed on both surfaces.

Also from that audit: `SecondFactorPanel` rendered a heading and no buttons when the backend offered no
code-capable method — a login dead end with no diagnostics. Not currently reachable (every account has a
phone, so `sms_otp` is always offered), but it is now an explained state rather than a blank screen.

**Files:** `web/lib/auth-api.ts`, `admin/lib/auth-actions.ts`, `web/components/auth/second-factor-panel.tsx`.

## D-288 · Phone parity is held by a shared behaviour corpus, not by pinning versions (2026-08-06)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Closes the last operational risk from the D-290 audit.

**Why there is nothing to pin.** The three surfaces use three *independent* libphonenumber ports:
`libphonenumber-csharp` **9.0.19** (backend), `libphonenumber-js` **1.13.9** (web + admin, one hoisted copy)
and `phone_numbers_parser` **9.0.24** (Flutter). Their version numbers are unrelated to each other and to
Google's upstream releases, and none of them publishes the upstream metadata revision it was built from. So
"make all three the same version" is not a thing that can be expressed, and a CI check comparing version
strings would be theatre.

**What is comparable is behaviour.** `docs/api/phone-conformance.json` is a single corpus of inputs with
their expected E.164, region and validity. Each platform has a test that reads *that file* and asserts it:
`InternationalPhoneTests.The_shared_conformance_corpus_parses_identically_here`,
`web/test/phone-conformance.test.ts`, `mobile/test/common/phone_conformance_test.dart`. CI already runs all
three suites, so drift fails the build. The corpus covers the ten required numbering plans, formatting
noise, an unassigned country code, a too-short number, and — the case that actually distinguishes the
libraries — a number that **parses and resolves to a region but is not valid** (`+6512345678` → SG).

**Direction of failure is why this matters.** Submit is gated on client-side validity, so a client whose
metadata is *older* than the server's does not produce a server error — it disables the button. The failure
lands on a person who cannot register and is invisible in logs. This corpus turns that into a red build.

**The rule when it goes red:** the platform that disagrees is the outlier. Bump its metadata. **Never edit
the fixture to match the outlier** — that is how you encode a bug as an expectation. Adding a country means
adding it to the corpus first.

**Also fixed:** the web `vitest` suite was never wired into CI (`web` ran typecheck / lint / build only), so
it had been green-by-absence. It now runs, which is what makes the web half of this gate real.

**Not changed:** `packages/ui` floors `libphonenumber-js` at `^1.11.0` while web and admin floor at
`^1.13.9`. npm hoists a single 1.13.9 for all three, so there is no live split, and the corpus now catches a
real one if it ever happens. Raising the floor without regenerating the lockfile would be half a change.

**Files:** `docs/api/phone-conformance.json`, `Kurx.Tests/InternationalPhoneTests.cs`,
`web/test/phone-conformance.test.ts`, `mobile/test/common/phone_conformance_test.dart`,
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

## D-292 · Messages Phase 1: the request gate, the inbox, and the two rooms nobody reached (2026-08-07)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Correctness pass over the D-264 Messages surface, before any parity work is built on
top of it. Six defects, all found by tracing the flow end to end rather than by a failing test — which is
itself the finding: every one of them fails *silently*.

**1. Replying to a request now accepts it.** `ChatRoom.DmRequestState` gated delivery but nothing ever moved
it out of `Pending` except the explicit Accept button. `SendMessageAsync` only refused `Declined`, so the
recipient could reply — and `ChatNotificationJob` returns early for any direct room that is not `Accepted`.
The result: **the recipient answered, the sender was never notified, and the conversation died silently**
with both parties believing they had sent it. The room also never left the Requests tab, because `ListAsync`
shows `Accepted` only. Replying is now the accept, claimed with a conditional update so a burst of replies
accepts once. Only the recipient can accept this way; the initiator sending again is still an unanswered
message, which is what keeps the gate a gate.

**2. `ChatRoomView` carries the request state.** It previously did not, so a client opening a request could
not tell it apart from an ordinary conversation and rendered a composer. `Capabilities()` also ignored it, so
a **declined** room advertised `CanPost: true` while every send returned `dm_declined` — the user typed, sent,
and got an error with nothing on screen explaining why. `CanPost` now accounts for it, and `dm_request_state`
/ `dm_initiated_by` are on the wire so the client can render Accept/Decline instead.

**3. The event chat list was sorted backwards.** `GetMyChatsAsync` ordered by the member's own `LastReadAt`,
so **opening a quiet room floated it to the top while a room with a new unread message sank** — the opposite
of what the unread badge beside it was saying. `LastActivity` was also `Event.UpdatedAt`, so editing an
event's description reordered Messages. Both now derive from the last message.

**4. Archiving works on any room.** `ChatMember.ArchivedAt` shipped with D-264 and `GetMyChatsAsync` never
read it, so an event chat could be archived and still sat in the list. `SetArchivedAsync` moved from
`IDmService` to `IChatService` — it writes `ChatMember`, which that service owns, and was DM-only by accident
of where it was first needed. `IDmService` delegates, so `/v1/dm/{roomId}/archive` and its clients are
untouched; `/v1/chat/rooms/{roomId}/archive` is the room-addressed pair.

**5. `@all` exists now.** `ChatCapabilities.CanMentionAll` has been on the wire since D-104 **with nothing
behind it** — `ResolveMentionsAsync` matched `@handle` against `Users.Username`, so a host typing `@all`
notified nobody and the flag was a promise the server did not keep. Host-only, matching the flag. Mentions
bypass the online filter, so this pushes to every member deliberately; it is otherwise unbounded, and a
per-room cooldown belongs there if an organiser uses it as a megaphone.

**6. Delegate-assigned seats join the event chat.** `SeatBlockService.AssignAsync` binds a real person to a
ticket and was **the one way to hold a ticket without ever reaching the room** — a college books fifty seats,
assigns them, and all fifty students are absent from the conversation about the event they are attending.
Now enqueues `event.chat_join` through the outbox in the same transaction, exactly as `OrderService` does
(§17.1); reassign and unassign enqueue `event.chat_leave_if_no_tickets`, whose handler re-checks tickets so
it never evicts someone holding one of their own.

**7. The web chat client was parsing a contract that no longer existed.** `web/lib/chat-api.ts` declared
camelCase (`roomId`, `eventTitle`, `presenceEnabled`) against an API that answers snake_case:
`SnakeCaseResponseConverter` (D-259 addendum) covers every record in `Kurx.Application.Abstractions`,
which includes `MyChatView` and `ChatRoomView`, and nothing updated this file — its header comment still
asserted the pre-converter behaviour. So `z.string()` met `undefined` and **every parse threw**. `/chats`
does `.catch(() => [])`, so **the Events tab rendered "No event chats" for everyone** instead of failing
visibly, and every room page `notFound()`. Confirmed against `docs/api/openapi.json`, which publishes
`room_id` / `event_title` / `presence_enabled`; the sibling `account-api.ts` had it right, which is what
gave it away. This is D-245 repeating, in a different module. Keys are normalised on the way in rather than
the schemas rewritten, because the camelCase names are that module's public surface across fifteen files.

**8. Navigation is keyed on ChatRoom identity, not on an event.** `GET /v1/chat/rooms/{roomId}` now exists.
`GetRoomByIdAsync` had shipped with D-264 and never been given an HTTP door — the only way in was
`POST /v1/dm/{userId}` — so web keyed `/chats/[eventId]` on the event, resolved it against the event-chat
list, and answered `notFound()` for anything else. The Messages inbox links a DM to `/chats/{room_id}`,
which by construction matched nothing: **every direct-message row was a dead link.** A direct room has no
event, so eventId cannot be the navigation key; `ChatRoom.Id` is the one identifier both kinds share.

The route is now `/chats/[roomId]` and resolves across both sources (event chats and DMs, including
archived), titling an event room by its event and a direct room by the other person. `/chats/{eventId}`
still works — it redirects to the room, because notification deep links and bookmarks carry the old shape
and a dead link is a worse answer than a moved one. `useChatRoom` takes the room id directly, which also
removes a startup delay: the hub subscription and its event filter previously had to wait for the room
fetch to resolve before they knew which room they were for.

**9. Accept / Decline is answerable inside the conversation.** The composer deliberately stays below it:
replying accepts (see 1), so the banner exists to make **Decline** reachable — it is available nowhere else
once the reader has opened the room — and to say plainly what state the conversation is in. Shown only to
the recipient; the initiator's own pending request gets the ordinary composer. `cannotPostReason` gained the
declined case, which previously fell through to the catch-all "You cannot post in this chat".

**10. Flutter was broken at the same seam, and for the same reason.** Mobile DM was never missing — the
four tabs, all five DM endpoints, request accept/decline and per-row archive have shipped since D-264. But
`_DmRow`, `_RequestRow` and the public profile all pushed `/chats/{roomId}` into a route declared
`/chats/:eventId`, which loaded through `GET /v1/events/{id}/chat`. **Every direct conversation opened onto
a 404**, exactly as on web. The route is now `/chats/:roomId`.

The change is small because the controller was already right: it stored `_roomId = room.roomId` and keyed
messages, the hub, presence, sending and the read pointer on that. Only the *lookup* was event-addressed.
`ChatRoomController.routeId` is resolved once by `_fetchRoom()` — room endpoint first, event endpoint on a
**404 only**, since 403 means the room exists and is not the caller's — and `_roomId` short-circuits it
afterwards, so a refresh or presence resync never pays for the fallback twice. That is the mobile shape of
the web redirect: one navigation model, and every deep link minted under the old scheme still resolves.

Also fixed, both genuine deep-link defects rather than collateral: `push_bootstrap` read only `eventId`, so
a **direct-message push was dropped before it could navigate** — `PushMessage` had parsed `roomId` all
along and nothing used it. And the in-app route builder tested `data['type'] == 'chat'` against a payload
whose key is `notificationType`; that branch had never once been true, and the eventId fallback behind it
carried an event id into a room-keyed route.

**Admin has no chat surface** — its only occurrence of the word is a comment about web's socket pattern —
so the "one navigation model" rule spans web and Flutter, and there is nothing in admin to align.

**Recorded, not endorsed:** `GET /v1/chat/rooms/{roomId}` answers **403** for a non-member and **404** for a
missing room, so the two are distinguishable — the opposite of the 404-not-403 rule D-018 applies to hidden
resources. That is pre-existing `GetRoomByIdAsync` behaviour shared with `POST /v1/dm/{userId}`, not
something this route introduced, and room ids are unguessable GUIDs so the practical leak is nil. Pinned by
a test so that a future fix moves **both** callers rather than one.

**Recorded, not built: `AnnouncementService` owns announcements.** The Event Rooms design contemplates an
`Announcements` room (the `ChatRoomKind` value is reserved). `EventAnnouncement` + `AnnouncementService`
already own that concept, with scheduling, audience selection, multi-channel fan-out (push/email/WhatsApp)
and per-channel delivery counts that a chat room has none of. An Announcements room must therefore be a
**read-only projection of announcements into the chat surface**, never a second writer. Two announcement
systems is the outcome this note exists to prevent.

**Not changed:** whether a sender may flood a pending request. `Pending` already suppresses notifications, so
it fills a tab rather than a phone — a cap can wait for evidence of abuse.

**Files.** Backend: `Kurx.Application/Abstractions/{IChatService,IDmService}.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Chat/{ChatService,DmService}.cs`, `Kurx.Infrastructure/Jobs/ChatNotificationJob.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Events/SeatBlockService.cs`, `Kurx.Api/Endpoints/ChatEndpoints.cs`,
`docs/api/openapi.json`. Web: `lib/{chat-api,chat-actions,chat-merge,use-chat-room}.ts`,
`components/chat/{chat-room-view,room-list}.tsx`, `app/(app)/chats/[roomId]/page.tsx`,
`app/(app)/host/events/[id]/chat/page.tsx`. Flutter: `core/router/app_router.dart`,
`core/push/push_bootstrap.dart`, `features/notifications/.../notifications_providers.dart`,
`features/social/{domain/entities/chat_room.dart,domain/repositories/chat_repository.dart,
