data/datasources/chat_remote_data_source.dart,data/repositories/chat_repository_impl.dart,
data/models/chat_mappers.dart,presentation/providers/chat_providers.dart,
presentation/pages/{chat_room_page,my_chats_page}.dart,presentation/widgets/*}`.

**Verified:** backend `dotnet build -warnaserror` clean and **1453 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped** (floor
1433); web `tsc --noEmit` clean and **298 vitest tests** passing; Flutter `analyze` clean and **326 tests**
passing. Regression cover added for every fix above: 7 for the flow defects, 3 for the room route, 2 for the
Flutter id resolution.

## D-293 · Phase 2A: editing a message, and hiding one from yourself (2026-08-07)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Completes the message lifecycle — send, edit, delete-for-everyone, delete-for-me —
before any further messenger feature is built on top of it. Scope was fenced to exactly these two.

**Edit is speech, so it is gated like speech.** `EditMessageAsync` requires the same right as sending: a
locked or archived room, a ban, a mute and a hosts-only policy all refuse an edit exactly as they refuse a
send, resolved through the one `Capabilities()` the send path already uses rather than a second rule that
could drift. It is bounded by the same 15-minute window as delete, so a conversation everyone has already
read cannot be quietly rewritten afterwards.

**There is deliberately no host override on edit.** A host may *remove* an offending message; a host may
never put different words in someone's mouth under their name. Those are different powers and moderation
needs only the first. The test that pins this asserts both halves — the host is refused the edit and still
allowed the delete — because the rule is only meaningful if the moderation path stays open.

**A no-op edit is refused (`no_change`, 409).** Stamping `EditedAt` for a request that changed nothing
would mark a message "edited" while leaving it identical on screen — a visible change for an invisible
one. The body is trimmed before the comparison, so a stray space cannot do it either. Same refusal the
Posts editor makes, and `EditedAt` mirrors `Post.EditedAt` so the two surfaces read alike.

**An edit never moves a message.** Ordering is `(CreatedAt, Id)` and `EditedAt` is not part of it. Had the
sort key moved, a correction typed an hour later would jump to the bottom of everyone's history and read as
a new message. A test asserts the page order is byte-identical either side of an edit. The broadcast carries
the whole updated view rather than a body patch, so a client that missed an earlier event reconciles onto a
complete row; both clients treat `MessageEdited` exactly as they already treat `MessageDeleted`.

**Delete-for-me is a view decision, and nothing else.** `chat_message_hides` records one (message, member)
pair. The message is untouched — other members still see it, the sender still sees theirs, moderation still
reads the body and the audit spine is unaffected. That is the whole distinction from `IsDeleted`, which is
delete-for-everyone and does redact. It is a table rather than a column because the fact is per member and a
message has no bounded member count; the unique pair is also what makes hiding idempotent, so two taps
converge instead of erroring. It is **never broadcast**: nobody else's view changed, and announcing it would
leak a private filing decision to the room.

**Hiding had to be complete or it would leak.** Every per-member read now goes through one `VisibleTo`
predicate — history, unread counts, the event-chat list preview, the DM list preview, and pinned messages.
Pins matter especially: a pin is room-level, but "hide this for me" has to mean everywhere, or the message
the reader removed reappears at the top of the room. The filter is applied to the *base* query in
`GetMessagesAsync`, not to a fetched page — filtering after `Take` would silently return short pages and
break "load more". Read receipts are unaffected by construction: the pointer is per member and hiding does
not move it.

**Admin is untouched, again.** It has no chat surface, so "update Web, Flutter and Admin in real time" spans
the two clients that have one. Stated rather than quietly skipped.

**Not built, deliberately:** reactions, search, delivered receipts, voice/video, encryption, and the
reliability hardening from the audit. All fenced out of this phase.

**API:** `PATCH /v1/chat/messages/{messageId}` → `ChatMessageView`; `DELETE /v1/chat/messages/{messageId}/for-me`.
`ChatMessageView` gains `edited_at`. New error codes: `no_change` (409), `message_deleted` (410),
`edit_window_expired` (403).

**Database:** `chat_messages.EditedAt` (nullable, additive — null means never edited, so no backfill);
new `chat_message_hides` with unique `(MessageId, UserId)`, an index on `UserId`, and cascade FKs from both
parents. Migration `20260807151052_AddChatMessageEditAndHide`, reversible.

## D-294 · Phase 2B: throttling the hubs, and the eviction that only half existed (2026-08-07)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Three reliability defects from the zero-trust audit, all live. Scope fenced to
exactly these; no feature work.

**1. Hub methods were completely unthrottled.** `UseRateLimiter` is HTTP middleware — it sees the SignalR
`/negotiate` request and nothing after it. Once a socket was up, every hub method could be invoked in a
loop by any client, and the global 300/min per user bought nothing. `ChatHub.Typing` was the worst of it:
three database queries plus a broadcast to every member of the room, per call, uncapped. `LoginHub.Watch`
is **anonymous** and does a database read per call.

`HubRateLimitFilter` is a per-connection fixed window, applied to every method on every hub.

**In-process, deliberately, and this is the opposite of the HTTP limiter's answer.** A connection lives on
exactly one instance for its whole life and cannot move, so that instance's count for that connection is
complete — there is nothing for a shared store to reconcile. The HTTP limiter is Redis-backed precisely
because consecutive requests from one user land anywhere. Using Redis here would add a round trip per
typing event, costing more than the work it protects. Buckets are keyed by connection id and dropped in
`OnDisconnectedAsync`, so the dictionary is bounded by live connections.

The limits are an abuse floor, not a quota — set far above what a correct client sends, so tripping one
means a bug or an attack. A trip throws `rate_limited` and leaves the connection open: dropping it would
turn a burst into a reconnect storm.

**2. A Redis outage stopped chat instead of degrading it.** `ChatHub.CheckRateLimitAsync` let
`RedisException` escape, so it propagated out of `SendMessage` and the send failed outright — "the rate
limiter is unavailable" became "you cannot send a message". It now fails **open**.

Failing open is only defensible because of (1): with the per-connection filter underneath, an outage
degrades the per-room limit to a per-connection one rather than removing throttling altogether. Without
that filter this would be a hole, and the two changes should not be separated.

**3. Eviction existed for a ban and for nothing else — my own audit finding was half wrong.** The audit
said group membership is checked only at join. `EvictFromChatAsync` has in fact evicted banned members
since D-106, and `BanMemberAsync` is its only caller. What no path did was evict on **removal**:
`RemoveMemberIfNoTicketsAsync` — the path a **refund** takes — deleted the `ChatMember` row and left the
socket in the SignalR group, so a refunded attendee kept receiving every message in the event chat until
they happened to disconnect. Deleting the row stops the next *request*; it does nothing to a live socket.

It now evicts, and only when a row actually went, so a re-run of an idempotent job evicts nobody twice.
`EvictFromChatAsync` gained an `eventName` so the wire stops calling a refund a ban.

**Still open, and named rather than quietly skipped:** `SalesHub` and `ScanHub` have the same staleness —
revoke someone's org membership and their socket keeps receiving live sales and scan events until it
closes. Not fixed here because those groups have no connection registry to evict from; `IPresenceService`
tracks chat rooms only, and building a second registry is a larger change than this slice. Chat had the
machinery already, which is why chat is fixed and these are not.

**Files:** `Kurx.Api/Hubs/HubRateLimitFilter.cs` (new), `Kurx.Api/Hubs/ChatHub.cs`, `Kurx.Api/Program.cs`,
`Kurx.Api/Realtime/SignalRBroadcaster.cs`, `Kurx.Application/Abstractions/IRealtimeBroadcaster.cs`,
`Kurx.Infrastructure/Chat/ChatService.cs`, `Kurx.Tests/HubSecurityTests.cs`.

## D-295 · Messaging Phase 2: reactions, search, receipts, forwarding, filing and media (2026-08-07)
**Status: PARTIAL — backend only.** Records what shipped and, just as importantly, what did not, so the
gap is not rediscovered later as a surprise.

**Reactions.** One toggle endpoint, not an add/remove pair: the client taps an emoji and the server
decides whether that means on or off, so two devices can never disagree about which call to make. The
toggle is **delete-first** — if a row went, the tap was a removal. Deciding from a prior read instead
would let two taps both observe "absent", both insert, and the unique triple reject one with an error
when the honest answer is that the reaction is simply on. Summaries are aggregated per emoji and loaded
once per page, because per-message loading would put history reads back at O(page) round trips — the
exact cost D-113 removed from the room lists.

**Search scopes by membership inside the query.** Filtering afterwards would still have let the result
COUNT leak whether a phrase appears in a room the caller cannot see. `websearch_to_tsquery` rather than
`to_tsquery` because it accepts what a person actually types — quoted phrases, `OR`, a leading minus, a
bare apostrophe — and never throws on malformed input. Backed by a GIN index on the *same* expression
the query uses; without that Postgres recomputes the tsvector for every row in `chat_messages` on every
search. Expression indexes cannot be declared through the EF model, so it is raw SQL in the migration.

**Delivered is a pointer, not a table.** `ChatMember.LastDeliveredMessageId` mirrors the read pointer
exactly, including forward-only monotonicity so an out-of-order acknowledgement from a second device
cannot walk the receipt backwards. A row per (message, member) would store O(members × messages) for
information a single pointer already carries.

**Forwarding does not carry attachments.** Re-pointing them would let a forward smuggle a file into a
room its uploader never had access to. The caller must be able to SEE the source, not merely name its
id, or forwarding becomes a read primitive for any room whose message ids leak. Destination rights are
re-derived by `SendMessageAsync` — a forward is an original in the room it lands in, and is gated as one.

**Pin and per-user mute are personal filing**, like archiving. `NotificationsMutedUntil` is deliberately
a **second column** rather than a reuse of `MutedUntil`: that one is a HOST silencing a member and stops
them posting; this one is a member silencing a room for themselves and stops nothing but their own
notifications. Opposite direction, opposite subject — one column would have made "mute" mean two
incompatible things.

**Link previews are sender-supplied and never fetched.** Server-side unfurling means the API issues
outbound requests to arbitrary user-controlled URLs: SSRF against internal metadata endpoints, private
ranges and redirect chains. The trade is that a malicious client can send a card that misdescribes its
target, and that is contained by deriving `Host` server-side from the stored URL and rendering it: the
preview may lie about the page, it can never lie about where the tap goes. Only absolute http(s) URLs
are stored, and a bad card is dropped rather than refusing the message — the words are still fine.

**Voice and video are allowed at the format level only.** ⚠️ They land on the same pipeline as every
other attachment, which today runs `FILE_SCANNER=none` — a NoOp scanner providing **no protection**.
Media is the highest-risk category to accept from arbitrary attendees, so a real `IFileScanner` is a
deployment prerequisite before this is exposed on open events. The magic-byte checks added here are a
format gate and must not be mistaken for a malware gate.

**Event Room types are CANCELLED, not deferred.** An earlier draft of this entry listed Announcements ·
Organizers · Volunteers · Speakers as the largest remaining item, and added `Volunteers`/`Speakers` to
`ChatRoomKind` for it. Both enum values were reverted and the whole idea dropped: **one event has one
room, and every participant — attendee, host, staff — is in it.** Splitting a small event's conversation
across four rooms fragments the only conversation it has; the moderation tools (mute, ban, remove, pin,
hosts-only post policy) already give hosts the control the separate rooms were meant to provide.
`Announcements`/`QA`/`Staff`/`Organizers` stay reserved-but-unused exactly as they have been since D-104.

**Two things named "pin", and two named "mute".** Worth stating because sharing a column for either pair
would have made the word mean two incompatible things:

| | Subject | Effect | Visible to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ChatMember.PinnedAt` | a reader files a CONVERSATION | sorts first in their own list | only them |
| `ChatMessage.IsPinned` | a host pins a MESSAGE | strip at the top of the room | everyone |
| `ChatMember.NotificationsMutedUntil` | a reader silences a ROOM | no notifications | only them |
| `ChatMember.MutedUntil` | a host silences a MEMBER | cannot post | the member |

**Clients and tests: built.** Web and Flutter both carry all ten features; `ChatMessagingFeatureTests`
covers them against real Postgres. Two rules turned out to be missing when the tests were written, and
both were fixed rather than asserted around:
- **A reaction was any string up to 16 characters**, so a member could put arbitrary short text under
  every message, echoed to the whole room — speech that skipped the message pipeline entirely and so
  could not be reported, moderated or deleted for everyone. Now: at least one non-ASCII rune and no
  ASCII letter, which admits skin tones, ZWJ sequences and keycaps while rejecting anything readable.
- **The search minimum disagreed between server (2) and clients (3)**, so both clients silently refused
  a two-character search the server would have answered. Aligned on the server's number, in one named
  constant per client.

**`GetMyChatsAsync` and every per-member message read are now `AsNoTracking`.** Not only a cost fix: pin,
mute and archive are written with conditional `ExecuteUpdateAsync`, which bypasses the change tracker, so
a tracked read taken earlier in the same scope kept serving the pre-write value. A test that muted and
re-listed in one scope read back "still muted" — harmless per-request today, and a real defect the moment
two operations share a scope.

## D-296 · A pinned message expires (2026-08-08)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Pinning a message had no end. A pin is an announcement — "read this now" — and an
announcement nobody cleared is stale within days, so the top of every busy room silted up with last
month's notice until readers learned to ignore the pinned strip entirely. That is the failure mode: not
a wrong pin, but a strip that stops being read.

**One nullable column, `ChatMessage.PinnedUntil`.** Windows are 1 hour to 30 days, defaulting to 7 when a
caller sends none. The clients offer 24 hours / 7 days / 30 days, matching what every messenger offers,
and the API takes `durationHours` rather than an absolute instant so a pin never depends on the client's
clock being right.

**Expiry is evaluated at READ time. Nothing sweeps.** A row whose instant has passed simply stops
matching the pinned filter. So an expired pin needs no job to run, cannot be missed by one that failed,
and un-expires correctly if a duration is ever corrected. Three places had to agree, and all three are
the same predicate:
- the room's pinned strip excludes it,
- `ChatMessageView.IsPinned` is computed as `IsPinned && (PinnedUntil is null or in the future)`, so a
  client that never heard of expiry still stops drawing the badge,
- and the three-pin cap counts only live pins — otherwise a room fills with lapsed pins nobody can see,
  blocking the one everyone needs.

**Out-of-range durations are refused, not clamped.** Silently pinning for 30 days when the host asked for
a year is a worse answer than saying no: they would believe the pin outlives the event. `400
invalid_pin_duration`.

**Null still means no expiry, and only pre-D-296 rows carry it.** Every pin written now gets a window;
the nullable column exists so the migration needed no backfill and no row had to be guessed at.

**Two client gaps this closed on the way.** Neither client could show a pin at all: web parsed
`pinnedMessages` and rendered nothing, and Flutter typed it `List<dynamic>` — parsed correctly,
impossible to render. Both now draw a pinned strip, and Flutter gained the message-pin call it never had.
A pin whose only trace is a small icon on the original bubble surfaces nothing, which is the entire point
of pinning.

## D-297 · The discovery home: four rails that existed but rendered nowhere, and post search (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** A node-by-node audit of the Home/Discover flow against backend, web and Flutter.
Six breaks, all on web except the last, and the shape they share is worth more than any one of them:
**every gap was a client that had stopped short of a working backend.** Nothing here required a new
capability; five of the six were wiring.

**1. Trending, Upcoming and Latest were dead code on web.** `getTrendingEvents`, `getUpcomingEvents`
and `getLatestEvents` have been sitting in `web/lib/api.ts` with **zero call sites** — fully written,
schema-validated, and rendered by nothing. Flutter has shown all four rails since D-019. `/discover`
now renders Featured · Trending · Upcoming · Latest · For you, in that order.

**2. Featured rendered only on the signed-out marketing page.** It was on `(public)/page.tsx` at
`limit=3` and absent from the signed-in discovery surface entirely, so signing in *removed* the one
curated rail a visitor had. It is now on both.

**3. The rails are skipped, not hidden, once a filter is active.** Someone who has typed a query has
said what they want; four rails of things they did not ask for push the answer below the fold. Under
`hasFilters` the five calls are never made — the alternative renders them and then hides them, which
costs five API round-trips per page of every paginated search.

**4. Category browse had no route on web.** `/categories/:id` exists on Flutter and existed on web
nowhere: category was reachable only as a dropdown value inside the filter form. The new route is
deliberately thin — it resolves the category, shows the first page, and hands everything else to
`/discover?categoryId=`, which already owns pagination and the other five facets. A second filter UI
there would be a copy that drifts. Category chips on `/discover` link **out** to it rather than
setting the facet, because a category is a place you go and a kind is a filter you toggle.

**5. Post search did not exist at all — on any surface, at any layer.** `/v1/posts` carried feed,
by-id, by-user, by-event, by-hashtag and trending-tags, and no way to find a post by what it says.
`GET /v1/posts/search` closes it.

It reuses `VisibleTo` — the single visibility predicate every other post read path composes — rather
than filtering after the fact. This is the whole risk of adding search to a module with four
visibility tiers: **search is exactly the route where a leak is invisible in review**, because it is
the one query nobody writes a "can this person see it" test for. Composing the predicate first makes
that structurally impossible instead of remembered.

**Full-text, not ILIKE, because `ChatService.SearchMessagesAsync` (D-295) solved the identical problem
one day earlier.** The first implementation here was `ILIKE '%term%'` with hand-rolled wildcard
escaping. It worked, and it was wrong twice over: a sequential scan over every post body per query,
and a *second* search idiom in a repository that had just standardised on `websearch_to_tsquery`. The
sibling's shape is three lines and strictly better — it takes what a person actually types (quoted
phrases, `OR`, a leading minus), never throws on input `to_tsquery` would reject, and needs no
escaping because there are no LIKE wildcards to escape. Migration `AddPostBodyFtsIndex` adds the GIN
index on the same expression; without it Postgres recomputes the vector for every row on every search,
which is the defect D-295's own migration comment calls out.

An empty term returns an empty page **without touching the database** — the alternative hands anyone
who submits a blank box an unbounded keyset scan of everything they may see.

**6. Home's search offered one of the three things it named.** Events had `/discover`, people had
`/allies`, posts had nothing — and neither client told you the other two existed. Both surfaces now
carry the same three scope chips. They are **links to the surfaces that already own each search**, not
a fourth combined results page: a unified page would be a third implementation of listings that people
and posts each already render correctly, and it would drift from both.

**Not built, deliberately:** post-search ranking (results are chronological, matching the feed's own
D-262 call), search across post *comments*, and the backend's `language` / `lat` / `lng` / `radiusKm`
event filters, which remain uncalled by any client — named as deferred in D-190 and still deferred.

## D-298 · Real malware scanning, voice notes and video capture (2026-08-08)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Closes the three items D-295 named as built-at-the-format-level-only.

### Malware scanning is real
`FILE_SCANNER=clamav` speaks clamd's INSTREAM protocol directly over TCP. `none` stays the default so
a dev machine needs no daemon, and it still provides **no protection** — the startup summary says so
on every boot.

**Why clamd and not a cloud scanning API.** Attachments are attendee-supplied files; shipping every one
to a third party is a data-egress decision nobody asked for, and it puts an external service on the
upload path. clamd runs beside the API, needs no API key, and its signature database updates without a
deploy.

**Why the raw protocol and not a client library.** INSTREAM is a command, length-prefixed chunks, a zero
terminator and one reply. A dependency to write that would be more code to audit than the code it
replaces, and this sits directly on the security path.

**It fails closed, and that is the load-bearing property.** Refused connection, timeout, truncated
reply, unrecognised answer, a file over clamd's `StreamMaxLength` — all return `ScanFailed`, never
`Clean`. The upload path already rejects on anything but `Clean`, so a scanner that is down **blocks
uploads** rather than silently waving malware through. Plan for clamd's availability; do not work
around it. If a future change ever makes a failure path return `Clean`, the protection is gone and
nothing else in the system will notice.

Verified against a real daemon, not only a fake: `docker compose --profile scanning up -d clamav`, then
the EICAR test file reports Infected and an ordinary file reports Clean. Those two tests skip
themselves when clamd is unreachable, so CI stays green and the evidence stays repeatable.

The registration switch is asserted too — on the `ServiceCollection` rather than a built provider,
since what matters is which implementation the config string *selects*. An unknown value (`clamvav`)
throws at startup rather than falling back: a typo must never silently downgrade a production
deployment to no scanning, because a quiet fallback is indistinguishable from working.

The compose service is behind a `scanning` profile because the image pulls a ~250 MB signature database
and takes a minute or two to answer. Its healthcheck is `clamdcheck.sh`, not a port probe: clamd binds
the socket *before* loading signatures, so a TCP check reports ready while every scan would fail.

### Voice notes
Web records with the browser's own `MediaRecorder`; Flutter uses `record`, encoding Opus in Ogg —
roughly a tenth the size of equivalent AAC for speech, and natively encoded on both platforms. Capped
at five minutes: the server enforces a size limit, and discovering that after speaking for ten minutes
is worse than being stopped at five.

**The microphone is released on every exit path** — send, discard, unmount, error. A live capture track
keeps the OS recording indicator lit, and a UI that leaves it lit after the user believes they stopped
is the kind of thing people rightly never forgive. Tested on web, where it is assertable.

### Video capture
Flutter uses `image_picker` (the only one of the two pickers that can open the camera; `file_picker`
picks existing files). Web uses `<input capture="environment">` — the native platform feature: on a
phone browser it opens the camera, on desktop the attribute is ignored and it is a video file picker.
A custom `MediaRecorder` camera UI would add a preview surface, a device chooser and a permissions flow
to win only the desktop case, where people attach an existing file anyway.

### Two bugs this surfaced
- **iOS video capture could never have worked.** An iPhone camera produces QuickTime `.mov`, and the
  allow-list had `video/mp4` only — the platform where video capture matters most would have been
  refused as an unsupported type. `video/quicktime` is now accepted; it is the same ISO-BMFF container,
  so the existing `ftyp` magic-byte check covers it unchanged.
- **Flutter's `guessContentType` had no media entries at all**, so a captured video went up as
  `application/octet-stream` and was refused. The server accepts a *closed* set of types, which makes a
  missing entry a failed upload rather than a cosmetic wrong guess.

### Not done
**E2E encryption for DMs**, deliberately left out. It removes things that only work because the server
can read a message — server-side search over DMs, push preview text, and a moderator's ability to read
a reported message — so it is a product decision with irreversible consequences, not a feature to slip
into a batch.

## D-299 · Two gates that had drifted: the category filter that matched everything, and the online event that could never publish (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Both found by exercising the D-297 discovery flow against real events rather than
re-reading the code — neither is visible in a diff, and neither had a failing test, because **both fail
open**. That is the through-line: a guard that silently permits looks exactly like a guard that works.

**1. `?categoryId=` matched every event, on every surface.**

V3 Phase 16 moved discovery from an EF query onto the `event_search_documents` index. The old predicate
was `e.CategoryId == catId || e.TypeId == catId` — it still sits at `EventService.cs:105`, on a path
nothing calls. The index carried no category column, so the filter was not *broken* in the new query; it
was **absent**. Passing `categoryId` narrowed nothing.

The blast radius was every category affordance the platform has: the Category dropdown on web `/discover`,
the same dropdown on Flutter's filter bar, and the `/categories/:id` browse page D-297 had just added. All
three rendered the full catalogue under a heading naming one category, with an active-filter chip
confidently reading "Category: Professional & Business". Verified before the fix: two different category
ids returned byte-identical lists of all three seeded events; after, 1 and 2 — an exact partition.

§12.3 of V3 already states the rule this broke — *anything filtered is a real column*. It was applied to
City, EventMode, IsPaid, StartsAt, KindSlug and Language, and the one filter that predated the index is
the one that did not get a column. `CategoryId` **and** `TypeId` are both carried, because the filter has
always accepted either level: the browse rail passes a category id, the wizard's taxonomy passes a type
id, and both must select the same events. Migration `AddSearchDocumentCategory` **backfills from the
authoritative rows in SQL** rather than waiting for reindex — otherwise every existing document keeps the
all-zero default and the filter returns *nothing*, which is the same bug wearing the opposite sign. Two
single-column indexes, not a composite: the predicate is an `OR` across the pair and Postgres BitmapOrs
them; a composite could not serve the `TypeId` arm at all.

**2. An online-only event could never be published.**

`ValidatePublishReadiness` demanded a venue unconditionally. An Online event has no venue by definition,
so `publish` refused it with `missing_venue` — and `publish` is the door both wizards and the entire
review lifecycle use. The V3 §14.2 `Scheduled` gate seventy-seven lines below already had the correct
rule (`OnlineUrl` for Online, venue otherwise). Two gates for one concept; the newer one learned about
online events and the older one never did. This is the D-018 pattern again, and the reason the fix is a
copied predicate rather than an extracted helper: **two call sites do not need a helper, they need to
agree**, and a helper would have hidden that they had not.

The Online arm is deliberately kept even though `ValidateMode` refuses an Online event with no URL on
both create and update, making the state unreachable through the API. A publish gate that leans on an
invariant enforced somewhere else is precisely how the venue half got wrong. Its test seeds the row
directly, which is the only way it could arise — a migration, a backfill, an admin tool.

**The refusals were also invisible.** Web's transition-error map carried `missing_venue_or_url` — the
*granular* gate's code — and not `missing_venue`, the one `publish` actually emits, so a host who hit the
far more common refusal saw the raw string `missing_venue`. Flutter's map had neither. Both now carry
`missing_description`, `missing_venue` and `missing_online_url`. Fixing a gate nobody could read the
output of would have moved the failure rather than removed it.

**Not changed:** `EventService.cs:105`'s dead predicate stays where it is — deleting it belongs with the
rest of that legacy search path, not smuggled into this fix. The `city` field is flat in event summaries
and nested at `venue.city` in event detail; that inconsistency is real, harmless, and out of scope here.

## D-299 · Production-readiness audit fixes (2026-08-08)
> ⚠️ **Number collision.** Two unrelated decisions were both filed as D-299 on 2026-08-08 by concurrent
> sessions — the other is the discovery-gates entry above. Deliberately **not** renumbered: **both** are
> cited from code, and the citations reach `Program.cs` (health-probe split), `EventService.cs` (the publish
> readiness predicate), `Search.cs`, `OrderService.cs`, `ParticipantService.cs`, `OutboxDispatchJob.cs` and a
> migration. Renumbering either would mean rewriting comments across files two sessions are editing, to fix
> a heading — strictly more risk than the ambiguity it removes. Cite this one as
> **"D-299 (production-readiness audit)"**; the code references to `chat_staff_removed`, the group-number
> lock and the `/health/live` split all mean this entry.

**Status: ACCEPTED.** A zero-trust audit of the repository against a Google-PRR-style checklist. What it
found is worth stating before the fixes, because the shape repeats: **every defect below is a correct
mechanism that one call site did not use.** None of them is a missing feature, and none showed up as a
failing test.

### C-1 · Revoked staff kept chat Host powers when the chat call failed
`ParticipantService` persisted the state change, then called `IChatService` **inline, after
`SaveChangesAsync`, outside any transaction and outside the outbox**. That call reaches the SignalR
broadcaster, which reads Redis-backed presence — so a Redis blip threw *after* the revocation had already
committed, and nothing retried. A removed organiser stayed a chat **Host**: able to ban attendees, delete
anyone's messages and read everything. Silent, permanent, no reconciliation.

The order and refund paths had this right since §17.1 — `event.chat_join` and
`event.chat_leave_if_no_tickets` are outbox rows staged on the money transaction. The participant paths
were written later and reached for the service directly.

**Fix.** Two new outbox types, `event.chat_join_host` and `event.chat_staff_removed`, staged on the same
unit of work as the participant state change, delivered by `OutboxDispatchJob` with its existing retry.
Both handlers are idempotent. The "no other active participation" test moved *before* `SaveChanges` and
gained `x.Id != p.Id`, since the row being removed is still Active in the database at that point.

**The general lesson, recorded so it is not relearned:** a side effect that must happen *because* a
transaction committed belongs in the outbox. If two call sites do the same thing two ways, the inline one
is the bug — even while it appears to work.

### H-1 · Concurrent group registrations returned 500
`GroupNumber` was `COUNT(*) + 1`, and `groups (EventId, GroupNumber)` is UNIQUE. Two buyers creating a
group on the same event in the same window computed the same number; the loser's INSERT threw an
unhandled unique violation. A 500 on a purchase.

**Fix.** A transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on the event — the idiom `BuyerLimitReachedAsync`
already uses — plus `MAX + 1` rather than `COUNT + 1`, so a deleted group cannot make the counter walk
backwards into a number already issued. Contended only by two people creating a group on the *same* event
at the same instant, so it serialises nothing that matters.

### H-2 / H-3 · Two broadcast events that no client listened to
`ReactionChanged` and `MemberRemoved` were emitted by the server and handled by **neither** web nor
Flutter. Consequences: reactions were not live at all (another member's emoji appeared only after a manual
refresh), and an evicted member — the case a **refund** takes — kept looking at a live room that had merely
gone quiet, with sends failing and nothing explaining why. `MemberBanned`, its sibling, has been handled
on both clients since D-106.

**Fix.** Both added to the room-level event set on each client, resolved by re-reading server state like
every other room-level event.

**Why this class of bug is invisible:** a broadcast with no listener fails no test, logs no error and
looks correct from the server side. The only way to find it is to enumerate what the server emits and
diff it against what the clients handle. Worth doing whenever a realtime event is added.

### H-6 · `/health` would have amplified a database blip into a restart storm
One endpoint carried the Postgres and Redis checks, and the container healthcheck pointed at it. A brief
dependency outage would mark every instance unhealthy, restart the fleet, and hit the recovering database
with a wave of cold starts.

**Fix.** `/health/live` (process only, no dependency checks) for liveness and the container healthcheck;
`/health/ready` (tagged dependency checks) for readiness; `/health` unchanged for humans. **Liveness must
never test a dependency** — restarting an instance cannot fix a database outage, it can only make one
worse. Readiness pulls the instance out of rotation and puts it back, which is the reversible, correct
response.

### Reported, deliberately NOT fixed here
- **H-4 · Speakers and judges receive chat Host.** Every accepted participant in the Organiser,
  Operations, **Content** (speakers) or **Evaluation** (judges) class is added as a chat Host, so a
  speaker can ban an attendee. Whether that is correct is a product decision about what those roles mean,
  not a bug to silently redefine. Flagged; awaiting a call.
- **H-5 · No retry or circuit breaker on provider calls.** Real today only in principle: every provider
  except the file scanner is still a mock or console adapter, and the ClamAV client carries its own
  timeout and fails closed. Building a resilience pipeline for mock providers would be speculative. This
  is a **prerequisite for wiring the first real provider**, recorded as such rather than pre-built.
- **M-2 · `TicketType.Sold` is a read-modify-write mirror.** Lost updates are possible, but the inventory
  pool is authoritative and every read path prefers it; only `AnalyticsService` falls back to the scalar,
  and only when a pool row is missing. Left as documented debt rather than touched on the money path.

### Audit coverage — stated so the gaps are not mistaken for clean bills
Deep: purchase/group concurrency · event-room membership lifecycle · messaging realtime wiring (all 11
broadcast events diffed against both clients) · resilience primitives · health and observability.
Sampled: authorization, API contract consistency, schema and indexes.
**Not covered:** client-side audit of web/admin/Flutter, dead-code enumeration, query-plan performance
work, and the KYC / trusted-device / login-approval concurrency paths.

## D-300 · Chat roles are independent of event roles (2026-08-08)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** Being a Speaker, Judge, Mentor, Volunteer, Staff, Sponsor or VIP does **not** confer
chat moderation authority. An event responsibility and a chat authority are different things, and the
code had been conflating them everywhere.

**Automatic Host is now exactly four things:** the event **creator**, and an **Owner**, **Manager** or
**Representative** seat in the organization the event represents. Everything else is a Member.

**Representative is included though D-300's text named only Owner and Manager.** It is D-075's primary
organizer role and sits at `EventAuthorityLevel.Manager` in the one authority ladder; excluding it would
mean an event's actual organizer could not moderate its own chat. Recorded as a judgement call, not an
omission.

### Every automatic Host assignment, before and after

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Room seeding — event creator | Host | **Host** (unchanged) |
| Room seeding — org seats | Host for `ModeratorRoles` (Owner, Manager, Representative, **Staff**) | Host for `ChatHostRoles` (Owner, Manager, Representative); **Staff joins as Member** |
| Event publish — accepted assignments | Host for **every** assignment role (Volunteer, Videographer, Media Team, Support Team, …) | **Member** |
| `EventAssignment` acceptance | Host, any role | **Member** |
| Participant acceptance | Host for Organiser, Operations, **Content** (speakers), **Evaluation** (judges) | **Member** |

Four of the five paths were minting unintended Hosts. The room seeding one is the subtle one: it borrowed
`ModeratorRoles`, whose bar is `Staff`, so holding an operational seat silently granted the power to ban
attendees. `ChatHostRoles` is a **separate array** rather than a reuse, precisely so that changing one
cannot move the other again.

`AddAcceptedStaffAsHostsAsync` was **renamed** to `AddAcceptedStaffAsMembersAsync` rather than quietly
changed: the old name asserted the behaviour that was wrong, and a caller reading it would have believed
it.

## D-301 · Explicit chat moderators (2026-08-08)
**Status: ACCEPTED.** D-300 removed automatic Hosts; this adds the thing that replaces them. A Host may
**explicitly promote** any Member to Chat Moderator. Promotion is manual, always — no event role grants it.

### The ladder
`ChatMemberRole` becomes `{ Member, Moderator, Host }`. Ordinal order **is** rank order, and the enum is
persisted as `text`, so inserting `Moderator` in the middle needed no migration and no backfill: stored
rows say `"Member"` and `"Host"`, never `0` and `1`.

Three predicates carry the whole model, and every moderation guard routes through them:

```csharp
CanModerate(role)          => role >= Moderator
OutRanks(actor, target)    => actor > target        // strictly greater
AuthorizeModerationAsync   => resolves both rows and applies the above
```

**`>` and not `>=` is the entire protection model.** Equal rank must fail, which is what stops a Moderator
demoting, removing, muting or deleting the messages of another Moderator. A Host outranks everyone, so
nothing special-cases them. Written once because the interesting question is not "may this person
moderate" but "may this person moderate **this** person" — and a per-call-site answer to that is exactly
how a Moderator ends up able to ban a Host.

### Authorization matrix

| Action | Host | Moderator | Member |
|---|---|---|---|
| Send, edit own, delete own, react, forward, search | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Delete a **Member's** message | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Delete a **Moderator's** message | ✅ | ❌ `cannot_moderate_peer` | ❌ |
| Delete a **Host's** message | ✅ | ❌ `cannot_moderate_peer` | ❌ |
| Mute / ban / remove a **Member** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Mute / ban a **peer or Host** | ✅ (Host outranks) | ❌ `cannot_moderate_peer` | ❌ |
| Pin / unpin | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Lock room, post policy, room settings | ✅ | ❌ `forbidden` | ❌ |
| Promote / demote a Moderator | ✅ | ❌ `forbidden` | ❌ |
| Change a **Host's** role | ❌ `cannot_change_host` | ❌ | ❌ |

Pinning takes no rank comparison: it acts on a **message**, not on the person who wrote it, so there is no
peer to protect. Deletion does, and resolves the **sender's current** role — a Moderator promoted after
posting is protected from that moment, the same rule every other action follows.

**Promotion is deliberately not on the ladder.** It is Host-only by an explicit `IsHostAsync`, because a
Moderator who could promote could mint a peer, and one who could demote could strip one — either way the
"cannot act on an equal" rule becomes bypassable in two steps.

**A Host's role cannot be changed through this route at all.** Demoting a Host would be a transfer of room
ownership wearing a moderation button.

### Concurrency, audit, and refresh without reconnect
The role change is a **conditional `ExecuteUpdateAsync`** claiming the row on its expected current role, so
two Hosts acting at the same instant produce one change and one `conflict` — the loser is told, never
silently overwritten. Re-issuing the current role is a no-op that still succeeds, so a retry writes no
second audit row and sends no second notification.

Every change writes `chat.role_change` with actor, target, room, and both roles. Message deletion's audit
now records `by_role` rather than `by_host`: "deleted by a Moderator" and "deleted by a Host" are different
facts to whoever reads the trail.

Capability refresh needs **no new client event**. The change broadcasts `RoomUpdated`, which both clients
already treat as "re-read authoritative room state" — so new capabilities take effect at once, on every
connected client, with no reconnect.

### Two capability flags that are deliberately not implied by `CanModerate`
`CanManageRoom` (lock, post policy) and `CanManageModerators` (promote/demote) are Host-only and separate.
A client rendering lock-room off `CanModerate` alone would offer a Moderator a control the server refuses —
and the clients gate on these, never on role strings. `MyRole` is also on the wire so a badge renders
without re-deriving it from flags.

## D-302 · A storage key is not a URL: the attendee event journey, end to end (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** **Numbered 302, not 300.** The implementation was written against "D-300" while a
concurrent chat workstream was independently landing [D-300](#) (chat roles) and [D-301](#) in this same
file. The code comments were renumbered to 302 rather than the log renumbered, because the log entries were
already published and referenced; the 18 chat-role `D-300` references were left untouched. Two workstreams
sharing one checkout collide on D-numbers — this is the third time — and the resolution is always to move
the *unpublished* side.

### The bug class

`IStorage.PresignGetAsync` returns `{base}/v1/storage/{key}?exp=…&sig=…`. **A bare key is not fetchable.**
Every event projection returned bare keys — `banner_key`, `logo_key`, `thumbnail_key`, `promo_video_key`,
and the whole `EventMedia` gallery — and every client fed them straight to `<img src>` / `Image.network`.
So the platform stored event imagery, returned it on every response, and rendered **none of it, anywhere,
on any surface**. Nothing failed: the cards simply looked like a design that had no pictures.

The shape repeats through this entry: **data that is produced, transported, and silently dropped one step
before it is seen.** Nothing here is a missing feature, and none of it had a failing test.

### What changed

**Presigned companions, never replacements.** `EventMediaView.Url`, `EventContentView.{Logo,Thumbnail,
PromoVideo}Url`, `EventDetail.BannerUrl` and `EventSummary.BannerUrl` sit *beside* the keys. The key stays
on the wire because organiser-side edit forms round-trip it; the URL is what a client renders.

**One card projection.** `SearchService.SummaryProjection` is now the single `Event → EventSummary`
expression, shared by all seven discovery rails **and** `SocialService.ListSavedAsync`, which previously
hand-built its own summary and therefore silently lacked every field the other one gained. One serializer
(`EventEndpoints.ToSummaryJson`) renders it. A saved event and a searched event are the same card, so they
must not be two shapes.

**Facts a card needs.** `event_mode`, `category_name`, `price_from_paise`, `currency`, `is_featured`. Mode
and price were **already filters** — discovery let a person narrow by a value the card then refused to show.
`price_from_paise` is the cheapest live ticket; **`null` means no ticket type exists, which is not free**,
and every client is required to distinguish the two.

**Representation, named.** `EventDetail.Representing` carries `{org_id, name, slug, logo_key, is_verified}`.
The API previously returned only a bare `representing_org_id`, so no surface could name the institution
behind an event — the one fact an attendee uses to decide whether to trust it. A self-represented event
resolves to `null` (an `IsPersonal` row is persistence, not an institution — [D-268](#)), and clients render
the creator alone. `is_verified` is the only trust signal carried; a client must never infer verification
from the presence of a name.

**Booking became real.** Web's booking form collected a name and an email, hardcoded two ticket types
unrelated to the event, and opened Razorpay with **no order id and no amount** — falling through to
`/tickets` when the script was absent. It reported success for a registration that never happened. Ticket
types now come from `GET /v1/events/{id}/ticket-types` and booking from `POST /v1/events/{id}/orders`, via
a server action so the token stays httpOnly, with a per-caller idempotency key. **The gateway is only ever
opened against an order the server created** — an amount decided by the browser is not a price. Until the
Razorpay adapter is real ([D-049](#) still drives `MockPaymentGateway`), an unpaid order says so plainly
rather than opening a checkout that cannot settle.

**The ticket QR, on both clients.** This was the last step of the journey and it worked on neither.

* **Web** drew a decorative `lucide` `QrCode` glyph — a picture of a QR code, identical on every order,
  that no gate scanner can read — on the one screen whose entire job is admitting someone.
* **Flutter** used `Image.network` against `GET /v1/tickets/{code}/qr.png`, which is
  `RequireAuthorization()`. `Image.network` uses its own HTTP client and sends no `Authorization` header,
  so **every request 401'd** and the screen showed its "QR unavailable" fallback permanently.

Both now fetch through the authenticated path. Flutter goes through **Dio**, not a hand-attached header,
so `AuthInterceptor` refreshes an expired token and retries instead of leaving the QR blank until restart.
Web proxies through a same-origin route handler that attaches the Bearer token server-side, which keeps the
token httpOnly — a QR needs a server round trip anyway, so there is nothing to gain by widening it. The
proxy adds **no ownership check of its own**: the API already enforces buyer-or-staff, and duplicating an
authorization rule is how two copies drift apart. Both plates are painted white regardless of theme,
because a QR is read by a camera and dark mode inverting the modules is how a scannable code stops scanning.

### The fix that made any of it render: presigned URLs were 403ing

Presigning the keys was necessary and **not sufficient**. Two defects stood between a correct
`banner_url` and a visible image, and both were found by fetching a URL the code had just produced —
something no test had ever done.

**1. `Uri.EscapeDataString` over the whole key.** `LocalDiskStorage` built
`/v1/storage/{Uri.EscapeDataString(key)}`, which encodes the `/` separators in every real key
(`events/…`, `avatars/…`, `chat/…`) as `%2F`. ASP.NET Core does **not** decode `%2F` back into a path
separator for a catch-all route — that is a path-traversal defence — so the receiver bound
`key = "events%2Fdemo%2Fbanner.jpg"` while the HMAC had been computed over `events/demo/banner.jpg`.
Verification therefore failed and **every presigned URL for a multi-segment key answered 403**, which is
every key the product issues. Replaced with `EncodeKeyPath`, which escapes **per segment** so separators
stay literal and segment contents stay escaped.

Nothing caught it because the provider signs *and* verifies its own URLs, so it is perfectly
self-consistent in isolation: a unit test over `LocalDiskStorage` passed before and after.
`StoragePresignTests` closes that gap by fetching a URL the provider produced and asserting it is not
403 — plus a tamper case, so "make it fetchable" can never be satisfied by dropping the signature check.

**2. `KURX_API_BASE` was never set in compose.** It defaults to `http://localhost:5080`, a port nothing
in `docker-compose.yml` publishes, so every presigned URL pointed at a refused connection even once the
signature was right. Set to the published host port (5001), for the same reason
`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` is: the **browser** is what follows these URLs.

Both were proven against the running API — the pre-fix URL returned `000`/`403`, the corrected shape
returned `200` with bytes identical to the uploaded PNG.

**`application/octet-stream` on the download is deliberate and was left alone.** It stops a stored object
choosing how a browser interprets it, and there is no `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on that response,
so `<img>` still sniffs the image correctly. Worth knowing as a coupling: adding a global `nosniff` header
would break every image in the product.

### Deliberately not fixed here

**Avatars have the identical bug and are out of scope.** `avatar_key` is emitted raw by ~12 endpoints and
`cover_key` by one; `packages/ui/src/avatar.tsx` and `mobile/.../kurx_avatar.dart` pass it straight to an
image source. Nothing in the backend presigns an avatar. That is one fix in two shared components plus the
projections, and it belongs to the Profile & Professional Identity workstream rather than to a change that
would touch profile architecture on its way past.

`representing.logo_key` is likewise raw, but **no client renders it** — the event detail shows the
organization's name and verification badge, not its mark. It needs presigning only if a logo is ever shown.

## D-303 · The contract gate had complete logic and empty inputs; `required` is now derived (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** **Numbered 303.** D-302 records the third D-number collision on this shared checkout;
this entry is the fourth workstream to renumber around one, and the highest published number at the time of
writing was 302.

### The finding that reframed the work

The brief was "the contract validator only validates unknown fields — review why." The obvious reading is
that the other checks were never written. They were: `contract-check.mjs` has always implemented
`missing_required`, `optionality` and `nullable` alongside `unknown_field`. What it lacked was *input*.

Measured on the committed spec before this change: **`required` appeared on 36 of 266 schemas — 53 entries
across 1,301 properties.** Two of the four checks therefore compared against an empty set on almost every
model, found nothing, and reported a clean pass. **A gate reporting zero findings is indistinguishable from
a gate that checks nothing**, and this one had been in the second state, silently, since it was written.

The cause was one line that never compiled. `SchemaGeneratorOptions.NonNullableReferenceTypesAsRequired`
does not exist in **Swashbuckle 6.6.2**, the pinned version — it arrived in 6.7.0. Setting it was a build
error, so the working tree carried a change that had never run.

### The decision

**`RequiredFromNonNullableSchemaFilter` re-implements the switch rather than bumping the package.** Eleven
lines, reading the `Nullable` flag `SupportNonNullableReferenceTypes()` has already computed, so the filter
and Swashbuckle can never disagree — which a parallel `NullabilityInfoContext` walk could. A package bump
would have regenerated the entire spec for a reason unrelated to the contract, on a checkout two sessions
were building against.

Result: **`required` on 245 of 290 schemas, 808 entries.** The two dormant checks now report 31 findings on
models that were already mapped and previously reported none.

A nullable-but-always-present key (`languages`, sent as `null` rather than omitted) is deliberately left out
of `required` — understating in the safe direction, because overstating makes the validator demand a key
some response genuinely omits.

### Typing the profile surface, and the two shapes that are not mechanical

`PublicProfileView` and `IdentityStatusView` had already been typed; the twelve **sub-resources** had not,
and were still projecting through hand-written `ToXxxJson` mappers. Nine were faithful 1:1 projections and
returning the record reproduces them byte for byte. **Two were not, and both would have broken silently:**

- **`PublicCertificateCard.CreatedAt` is emitted as `issued_at`.** The mapper renamed it. Both clients bind
  the renamed key. Pinned with `[JsonPropertyName]`, and now asserted in `CertificateTests` — including that
  `created_at` is *absent*, because the failure mode is a key appearing under the wrong name, not a crash.
- **The Journey nests five fields under `evidence` and adds a constant `source`.** That is `JourneyNodeView`
  now. `JourneyNode` stays flat because `ResumeEngine` reads it that way; reshaping it would push an
  API-surface concern into a type the PDF composer also consumes.

The lesson generalises: **"extract the record and return it" is only safe where the mapper was a projection.
Where it was a translation, the translation is the contract.**

### What the expanded map immediately caught

Coverage went from 4 mapped models to 20 (6 → 36 client comparisons), and found a **live bug of the
D-245/D-292 family — the fourth instance**:

`PublicProfileView.LinksJson` serializes as `links_json`. Web declared `links` and Flutter declared `links`.
Neither key is ever sent, so `_parseLinks` and its web equivalent received `null` on **every profile**, and
social links rendered for nobody. Silent by construction. Fixed on both clients.

Alongside it: web declared `skills: z.array(z.string())` non-nullable while `User.Skills` is `string[]?`
passed straight through, so a person who never set skills produced an explicit `null` and
`publicProfileSchema.parse()` threw. `getPublicProfile` wraps that in `.catch(() => null)`, so the profile
rendered as **"not found"** rather than erroring — again silent. Flutter was unaffected: `@Default([])`
generates `?? const []`, which absorbs the null.

### The gate now proves itself

`scripts/contract-check.test.mjs` asserts each category fires — unknown, renamed, re-nested, nullable,
optionality, missing-required, the `snake_to_camel` adapter, an unimplemented transform, and a negative
control. It also carries **vacuity guards**: that the zod and Dart parsers extract real fields from the real
sources, and that the spec still carries `required` on a majority of schemas. Before the fix that last guard
failed, naming the exact condition; the regression back to a silently-inert gate is now a failing test rather
than a clean pass.

---

## D-304 · Organization authority propagates to already-published Event Rooms, through the outbox (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Completes the lifecycle D-299 and D-300 left half-covered. D-299 made *revocation*
durable; D-300 fixed *who* becomes a Host. Neither made an organization authority change reach a room that
already exists.

### The gap

`IChatService.AddEventHostsAsync` has exactly one caller — the `Published` transition in
`EventService.TransitionAsync`. Membership rows are written in three other places
(`OrgService`, `OrgInvitationService`, `MembershipVerificationService`) and **none of them touches chat**.

So authority granted before publish works, and authority granted after publish does nothing at all. A user
made Owner, Manager or Representative on Monday for an event published on Sunday is not a `ChatMember`,
and `GetRoomByIdAsync` answers `forbidden` — they cannot open the chat of an event they now run. This is the
exact mirror of D-299's C-1 (a revoked staffer *keeping* Host), in the opposite direction, and it went
unnoticed for the same reason: nothing compared the publish-time roster against live authority afterwards.

### The rule (unchanged from D-300, restated because this entry automates it)

Automatic chat **Host** comes from exactly four sources, and no others:

| Source | Authority |
|---|---|
| Event Creator (`events.created_by`) | Host — by D-268, needs no organization seat |
| Organization **Owner** | Host |
| Organization **Manager** | Host |
| Organization **Representative** | Host |

Everyone else — Staff, Speaker, Judge, Mentor, Volunteer, Participant, ticket holder — is a **Member**, and
becomes a Moderator only by an explicit D-301 promotion. `Finance` holds money authority, not operational
authority, and reaches neither list. This entry adds **no** new Host source; it makes the existing four
converge on rooms that already exist.

**Event role ≠ chat role.** Nothing here weakens that separation, and `event.chat_join_host` stays deleted.

### The mechanism

Authority changes reach chat through the **transactional outbox**, never an inline call after commit:

```
membership / authority transaction
  └─ outbox row `org.authority_changed`  (same unit of work)
        └─ OutboxDispatchJob
              └─ IChatService.SyncOrgAuthorityAsync(orgId, userId)
                    └─ per published room: idempotent ChatMember role convergence
                          └─ RoomUpdated → clients refresh capabilities
```

This is D-299's rule applied to its remaining producers: *if a side effect must happen because a transaction
committed, it belongs in the outbox*. An inline `chat.X(...)` after `SaveChanges` reaches the Redis-backed
broadcaster, so a transient there used to leave authority and chat permanently disagreeing with nothing to
retry it. No new mechanism is introduced — the same `OutboxMessage` table, the same dispatcher, the same
random-suffix key idiom as `OrderService`, `SeatBlockService` and `ParticipantService`.

### The payload carries WHO, never the resulting role

```jsonc
{ "orgId": "…", "userId": "…" }     // deliberately no role
```

This single choice is what makes the operation idempotent and concurrency-safe. The handler re-resolves the
user's **live** authority through `IEventAuthority` at dispatch time, so:

- **Repeated delivery** converges — a second dispatch reads the same state and changes nothing.
- **Concurrent changes** converge — whichever dispatch runs last reads the final committed membership, so
  the end state matches the database rather than the order the messages happened to be written in.

A payload carrying `role: "Manager"` would have neither property: two rapid changes could apply out of order
and leave chat asserting a role the organization had already withdrawn.

### The complete lifecycle

| # | Situation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Owner/Manager/Representative granted **after** publication | Added to every published room as **Host** |
| 2 | Authority held **before** publication | Unchanged — publish-time seeding already correct; sync is a no-op |
| 3 | Role changed while the event is published | Re-resolved; converges to Host or Member as the new role dictates |
| 4 | Manager ⇄ Representative | No change — both are Host-level. Sync runs and is a no-op |
| 5 | Owner/Manager/Representative → Staff/Finance | Host → **Member**; evicted only if no other standing (no ticket, no accepted participation) |
| 6 | Membership revoked entirely | Same as 5 — demoted, then removed if no standing remains |
| 7 | Invitation accepted (`OrgInvitationService`) | Enqueues; Host if the invited role is Host-level |
| 8 | Membership verification approved (`MembershipVerificationService`) | Enqueues. Grants `Staff`, so the result is **Member** — verification is not authority |
| 9 | Organization has many published events | One outbox row; the handler fans out across **all** published rooms for that organization |
| 10 | Repeated outbox delivery | Idempotent — see above |
| 11 | Concurrent membership changes | Converge on live state — see above |
| 12 | User already a `ChatMember` | Upgraded in place. `AddMemberAsync` never downgrades and posts no second join message |
| 13 | User is an explicit **Moderator** | Gaining authority raises Moderator → Host |
| 14 | User is already **Host** | No-op. No duplicate row, no second notification |
| 15 | Explicit Moderator whose authority is later withdrawn | Host → **Member**, not back to Moderator — see below |

### Case 15, decided explicitly

An explicit D-301 Moderator grant that was later *shadowed* by org-derived Host authority is **not restored**
when that authority is withdrawn. The row lands on `Member`.

Restoring it would mean storing the pre-Host role — a new column and a migration — to recover a state a Host
re-creates with one click. The failure direction is also the safe one: the user ends with *less* authority
than they might deserve, never more. If this proves annoying in practice, the upgrade path is a nullable
`ChatMember.ExplicitRole` written by `SetModeratorAsync` and consulted on demotion; it needs a `D-NNN` and a
migration, and should not be added speculatively.

### The event creator is never demoted

`RemoveStaffMemberAsync` resolves through `IEventAuthority` and returns early at `Manager` or better, so a
creator with no organization seat at all (D-268) keeps Host through every organization change. Demotion asks
the authority, never the roster the seeding happened to leave behind (D-272).

### Scope

Only **published** rooms are synchronized, and archived rooms are skipped — an archived room's participant
list is frozen (D-122), and `AddMemberAsync` already refuses to modify one. Draft events have no room, and
publish seeds them; that path is untouched.

## D-305 · Event creation is a gated flow entered from Profile, not a form entered from Workspace (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED as the target architecture. Reverses the navigation half of [D-267](#); D-267 itself
is preserved and still authoritative on ownership.** Numbered 305 because 303 and 304 were taken by a
concurrent workstream while this was being written — the fourth D-number collision in this repository.

### What D-267 decided, and what changes

D-267 moved Create Event out of an organization-first dashboard and onto **Workspace**, so that reaching
it required no organization. **That half stands: an organization is still never required, and there is
still no organizer dashboard.** What changes is *where the door is* and *what happens when you walk
through it*.

| | D-267 (previous) | D-305 (new) |
|---|---|---|
| Entry point | Workspace + primary nav | **Profile → Create Event** |
| First thing the user sees | The 11-step form | **A verification / eligibility gate** |
| Public vs Private | A field inside the form (`Visibility`, step 2) | **A gate decision, before the form** |
| Verification | Enforced at **publish** | Enforced at **entry**, reusing existing state |
| Workspace's role | Host home + creation entry | **Activity hub only** — participated + approved created |

### The three surfaces, which must never be conflated

* **👤 Profile** — identity and professional profile. **Owns the Create Event entry point.**
* **📋 User Workspace** (`/workspace`) — the user's event *activity* hub. Exists for **every** user,
  including one who has never created anything, because participation fills it. It lists **Participated
  Events** and **Created / Hosted Events** (approved only). **It is not an organizer dashboard and must
  never become one.**
* **🏗️ Event Host Workspace** — the management surface for **one** approved event, opened *from* a created
  event inside User Workspace. This is what `host/events/{id}` already is.

Participation is wholly independent of creation:
`Discover → Register/Join → 📋 User Workspace ▸ Participated Events`.

### The gate

```
👤 Profile → Create Event
     ↓  ① eligibility check — reuse existing verification state, never re-ask
     ↓  ② choose PUBLIC or PRIVATE
     ↓  ③ eligibility for THAT choice
     ↓  ④ full creation form
   Draft → review/approval → 📋 User Workspace ▸ Created → 🏗️ Event Host Workspace
```

**Never re-ask a passed check.** Phone, government ID, PAN and bank status already live on
`UserIdentity` and are already summarised by `ITrustService`. The gate reads that state and presents
**only what is missing**. It introduces no second verification system.

**The gate is enforced, not offered.** It has to survive a deep link, a restored tab and a typed URL, and
the two clients achieve that differently because the form is a different kind of thing on each. On **web**
the gate *is* the page — `/host/events/new` renders it and the form is a stage inside a component, so
there is no address to jump to. On **Flutter** the form is a route (`/events/create/form`), so it carries
a `redirect` that sends any request without a valid `product` back to `/events/create`. Defaulting a
missing product to Public — the first attempt — was *safe* (a deep link could not manufacture a Private
event) but not *gated*, which is the property this decision actually requires.

### Reconciling the Public/Private gate with the existing domain

The repository already has two distinct concepts, and this decision **merges neither and renames neither**:

* `EventVisibility { Listed, Unlisted, InviteOnly }` — *discoverability*, chosen by the organiser.
* `EventProduct { Public, Private }` — the *product class*, and **today the user never chooses it**:
  `EventService.CreateAsync` sets `ev.Product = taxonomy.Product`, resolved from the chosen **Type**'s
  `EventCategory.ProductClass` (D-266 M1 — "a Wedding can never be Public; a Fundraiser can never be
  Private — the constraint lives here as data, not as code"). It is snapshotted at create, deliberately,
  so a later taxonomy edit cannot change how a live event behaves.

`EventProduct` is the correct domain concept for the new gate — it is already what discovery, series
listing, org profiles, posts and the search index all filter on. The conflict is one of **ordering**: the
gate asks for Public/Private *before* a Type exists, while the domain derives it *from* the Type.

**Resolution: the gate's answer selects the Type list, and the taxonomy still decides.** Choosing Public
offers only Types whose `ProductClass` is Public, and likewise for Private; `Product` continues to be
derived and snapshotted from the Type exactly as it is now. This keeps D-266 M1 intact — one source of
truth, still data-driven — and makes the user's choice a *filter*, not an override. No schema change, no
new field, no third concept.

> **RESOLVED (2026-08-08) — Public and Private carry the SAME verification.** The open question above is
> closed by product decision: the Public/Private choice does **not** change what the caller must have
> verified. It remains a real decision in the flow because it selects the product class (and therefore
> which Types are offered), but it is **not** a trust axis.
>
> The consequence is that the gate has exactly **one** eligibility rule, and it is the one that already
> exists: `TrustService`'s **Free vs Paid** bar. Creating either a Public or a Private event requires
> nothing beyond an authenticated account (`canOrganizeFree = true`); selling tickets requires
> `CanOrganizePaid` wherever it is already enforced. Step ③ of the gate therefore performs **no second
> verification pass** — it records the choice and moves on. No new capability, no new flag, no new axis.

### Penny Drop — the rule that already exists, unchanged

`TrustService.GetUserCapabilitiesAsync` is authoritative:

```
canOrganizeFree = true;                    // any account: free/private events, no KYC
canOrganizePaid = identityVerified && panVerified && bankVerified && fraudClear;
canReceivePayout = canOrganizePaid;
   where bankVerified = BankStatus Approved && PennyDropStatus Passed && BankNameMatch != Mismatch
```

**Penny Drop gates money, not creation.** It is reached only through `bankVerified`, which is reached only
through `CanOrganizePaid` / `CanReceivePayout`. Creating a free event requires nothing. This decision adds
**no** Penny Drop requirement; the gate reuses these flags as they stand. Note that the existing trust axis
is **Free vs Paid**, which is *not* the same axis as Public vs Private.

> ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED by [D-307](#d-307--public-event-creation-requires-the-full-verification-gate-free-or-paid-2026-08-08)
> (2026-08-08).** The paragraph above described the platform as it stood; the **product rule has since
> changed**. Public hosting — *including a free public event* — now requires the full verification set,
> Penny Drop included, evaluated at the gate through a new `CanCreatePublicEvent`. The observation that
> the *then-existing* trust axis was Free-vs-Paid remains historically accurate, and `CanOrganizePaid` is
> deliberately unchanged; what is no longer true is the conclusion that creation requires nothing.

### Consequences

* **Web** — Create Event moves to Profile. The Workspace header button, the Workspace empty-state link,
  the `secondaryNav` entry and the host-analytics link are the four existing doors (verified live) and
  must be reviewed against "one primary door". `/workspace` keeps listing participated + created events.
* **Flutter** — same flow. Its only current door is the Workspace hub card; it must move to Profile.
* **Backend** — no new endpoint, no second Event model, no duplicated validation. The gate composes
  existing reads (`ITrustService`, `IIdentityVerificationService`, `GET /v1/me`); creation still posts to
  `POST /v1/events`.
* **Publish-time gates are not removed.** Org verification and `paid_event_requires_review` continue to
  apply. The entry gate is additive: it stops a user starting work they cannot finish, it does not replace
  the checks that protect publishing.
* **Migration** — events created before this decision are unaffected; nothing about the stored model
  changes. Only the client route into creation and the order of the questions change.

### What this decision does NOT do

It does not delete the 11-step form, reassign any step, merge `EventVisibility` with `EventProduct`, add a
third visibility concept, or make `/workspace` a dashboard. Which creation steps stay in the form versus
move to the Event Host Workspace is a separate pass, deliberately left open here.
