## D-306 · An archived event room must be retrievable, or archiving it is deletion (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Completes the half of D-295's "archive any room" that shipped without its other
half. Found during the Web/Flutter messaging parity audit, one step before the UI for it was written.

### The trap

`POST /v1/chat/rooms/{roomId}/archive` accepts an **event** room and works — it writes
`ChatMember.ArchivedAt` through the same `ChatService.SetArchivedAsync` the DM route delegates to. But
the read side never learned about it:

```csharp
// ChatService.GetMyChatsAsync
.Where(m => m.UserId == userId && m.ArchivedAt == null)     // filtered out…
```

…and `GET /v1/me/chats` takes no `archived` parameter, while `MyChatView` carries `Pinned` and
`NotificationsMuted` but no `Archived`. So an archived event room leaves the only list that can return
it, and **no API this platform exposes can find it again**. Direct messages have the missing half —
`GET /v1/me/dm?archived=true`, backed by `IDmService.ListAsync(userId, archived, ct)`, and
`DmRoomView.Archived` on the wire — event rooms simply never got it.

The consequence is the reason this is a `D-NNN` and not a patch: **a client that offered an Archive
button on an event chat would be offering deletion wearing another word.** Both clients were about to
grow one, on the strength of "the endpoint exists and nothing calls it". The endpoint existing was
never the question; whether the user could get back was.

### The rule

**A filing action must be reversible through the API, or it is not filing.** Archive, mute and pin are
all *personal, reversible* states on `ChatMember` (D-295) — none of them destroys anything, and each
must therefore have a read path that returns what it hid. Anything that hides a row without a way to
enumerate it belongs to deletion's rules, not filing's.

### The change

Event chat adopts the DM shape exactly, rather than inventing a second one:

| | Direct messages (existing) | Event rooms (this entry) |
|---|---|---|
| List | `GET /v1/me/dm?archived=` | `GET /v1/me/chats?archived=` |
| Service | `ListAsync(userId, archived, ct)` | `GetMyChatsAsync(userId, archived, ct)` |
| Wire | `DmRoomView.Archived` | `MyChatView.Archived` |

`archived` defaults to `false` and `Archived` is appended with a default, so every existing caller and
every stored client keeps its current behaviour: the default list is still the un-archived one. This is
additive on both the request and the response, which is what lets it ship without a client release.

### Scope

No new entity, no migration, no new concept — `ChatMember.ArchivedAt` already exists and already means
this. Archive remains **per-member**, so archiving is invisible to everyone else in the room, and it is
emphatically not `ChatRoom.Status == Archived`, which is the room's own lifecycle (D-122) and belongs to
the event's clock rather than to a reader's filing.

## D-307 · Public event creation requires the full verification gate, free or paid (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED as the product rule.** Supersedes the verification half of
[D-305](#d-305--event-creation-is-a-gated-flow-entered-from-profile-not-a-form-entered-from-workspace-2026-08-08);
D-305's flow, surfaces and Public/Private-to-`EventProduct` mapping all stand. Numbered 307 because 306 was
taken by a concurrent workstream mid-write — the fifth D-number collision in this repository.

### What changed, and why

D-305 recorded the platform's *then-existing* rule: `canOrganizeFree = true` for any account, so creating a
free event required nothing, and Penny Drop was reachable only through the paid capability. **That is no
longer the product requirement.**

**Publishing to the public is now itself a trust event.** A free public event still carries the platform's
name, appears in discovery, and can gather a crowd — the harm a bad actor can do with one is not bounded by
whether money moved. The old rule bounded verification by *payment*, which is the wrong axis: it let an
unverified account publish to every user of the platform provided it charged nothing.

**Private is unchanged and deliberately so.** A Private event cannot be Listed, cannot take payment, and is
invisible to every discovery surface (D-305's audit; enforced in `PolicyResolver` and nine services). It
reaches only people who were handed an invitation. There is no public exposure to bound and no money to
settle, so the financial chain — bank, Penny Drop, name match — has nothing to verify and is **not** asked.

### The two new capabilities

Added to `TrustCapabilities`, derived in `TrustService` from the identity state that already exists:

```
canCreatePublicEvent  = identityVerified && panVerified && bankVerified && fraudClear
                        where bankVerified already means
                          BankStatus == Approved
                          && PennyDropStatus == Passed        ← bank OWNERSHIP
                          && BankNameMatch != Mismatch        ← the PAN/account-holder control
canCreatePrivateEvent = true
```

**Penny Drop is not a fifth requirement.** It is one link in the *bank ownership* chain, and it already sits
inside `bankVerified`: "we credited ₹1 and it landed" is what separates a proven account from a typed
account number. Name match is the sibling control that catches a PAN and an account belonging to two
different people. Both are stated here because the gate must *name* them to the user, not because they are
new predicates.

**`CanOrganizePaid` is deliberately untouched.** It has five money-path consumers — `OrderService` (refuses
paid orders), `EventService` (payment readiness, publish gate), `OrgEndpoints` — and it answers a different
question: *may this person take money*, not *may this person publish publicly*. That the two predicates are
currently **identical** is a coincidence of today's requirements, not an identity; giving them one field
would mean a future change to either silently moves the other. Two names, two questions.

`canCreatePrivateEvent` is constant `true` and exists anyway, so both clients render one uniform gate
instead of special-casing a branch — and so that a future non-financial requirement for Private has an
obvious home.

### Consequences

* **The front door gets materially harder.** Any signed-in user could previously create a free public
  meetup; now they must complete government ID or PAN, PAN, and a bank account proved by penny drop. In the
  development database **1 of 23 users** currently qualifies. This is the intended trade and is stated here
  so it is never discovered by surprise.
* **Never re-ask a passed check.** The gate reads `UserIdentity` through `ITrustService` and presents only
  what is missing. It adds no storage, no endpoint and no second verification flow.
* **Verification happens before the form.** Nobody completes eleven steps and then learns they cannot
  create the product they chose.
* **Backend / API:** two additive booleans on `TrustCapabilities`, surfaced through the existing `/v1/me`
  `trust` block. **No migration** — every fact already exists per component on `user_identities`.
* **Web / Flutter:** the gate blocks Public until the capability passes and lists the missing items; Private
  passes and **never mentions Penny Drop**. Both clients enforce it identically, including on direct
  navigation to the form.

### ⚠️ Penny Drop is mocked in this repository

`IKycProvider` binds to `MockKycProvider`, which **approves unconditionally**. So in development the bank
chain passes for anyone who submits an account number, and the gate will appear to work for everyone.

Nothing here is evidence that real penny-drop verification functions. The capability *logic* is tested
independently of the provider; the provider itself is dev-only, and the first real deployment of this rule
will block every account that has not genuinely proved a bank account. Do not read a passing dev flow as a
production-verified one.

## D-308 · Logging out destroys this device's offline data (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Security fix.** Found during the Flutter messaging audit.

### The defect

Logout cleared the tokens and nothing else:

```dart
// SessionController.logout() / AuthRepositoryImpl.logout()
await ref.read(tokenStoreProvider).clear();     // …and that was all
```

The `kurx_cache` Hive box survived, and **its keys carry no user identity** —
`chat_rooms`, `chat_msgs_{roomId}`, `chat_outbox_{roomId}`, `chat_read_{roomId}`, plus the event cache.
They are scoped to a *room*, so the next person to sign in on that device reads exactly the same keys.

Two consequences, both reachable:

**Disclosure.** `ChatRoomController` seeds a room from cache *before* any network call, and both
`latest()` and `myChats()` fall back to the cache when the request fails. So user B sees user A's rooms
and messages — briefly while online, and for as long as they stay offline.

**Misattribution.** Opening a room runs `_flush()`, which reads `chat_outbox_{roomId}` and calls
`_remote.send(...)` on the shared Dio — carrying **whoever is signed in now**. A message user A composed
offline is delivered as user B, under A's `clientMessageId`. The server still authorises the room per
request, so this needs both people to be members of the same room; on a shared or demo device, or in an
event chat, that is an ordinary situation rather than a contrived one.

### The rule

**A cache outlives a request, never a session.** Anything written on a user's behalf and readable without
re-authenticating belongs to that session, and the session ending is the moment it stops being theirs.

Cleared at **logout**, and again at **login**: logout is the correct moment, and login is the backstop for
a process killed between the two — a crash must not be a way to keep the previous user's data.

### What this costs, accepted deliberately

Signing out on your own phone discards offline scrollback and any unsent messages. That is the intended
trade: an unsent message is *addressed from an account*, and there is no honest way to hold it across a
change of account. The alternative — keying every cache by user id — keeps the data on the device and
still leaves it recoverable by anyone who can sign in, which is the same disclosure one indirection later.
Per-user cache keys are the wrong fix for a shared device.

### Scope

Client-only. No backend change: the server already authorises every read and send per request, so this
never permitted access beyond the room's own membership — the leak is what the device rendered from disk
before asking anyone, and what it sent from a queue it should no longer have held.

## D-309 · One chat document. Reverses D-104's seven-file split (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Supersedes the documentation structure of [D-104](#) / [D-105](#)** — those entries'
*architecture* decisions stand; only their filing scheme changes.

### What D-104 did, and why it was reasonable

Chat documentation was "fragmented and, in twelve places, contradicted the code". The fix was seven files,
each the single owner of one surface: `architecture/chat.md`, `database/chat-schema.md`, `api/chat-api.md`,
`realtime/chat-signalr.md`, `security/chat-security.md`, `mobile/chat-offline.md`, `web/chat.md`. One fact,
one home — CLAUDE.md §6 applied literally.

### What actually happened

A single audit on 2026-08-08 opened all eight chat documents and found **every one of them materially
wrong at the same time**:

| Document | What it claimed |
|---|---|
| `architecture/chat.md` | `AddAcceptedStaffAsHostsAsync` — a method that no longer exists; staff seeded as **Hosts** (pre-D-300); `ChatRoomStatus` "has no `Archived`" (D-122 added it); demotion protects any `Staff`+ seat (the bar is Manager) |
| `database/chat-schema.md` | `chat_attachments` "DEFERRED (shape reserved)" — it shipped; `chat_message_reactions` and `chat_message_hides` absent entirely; `Role = Member \| Host`; a correction note that had **inverted** |
| `api/chat-api.md` | Five decisions' worth of endpoints missing; mute/ban/pin documented "Host only" after D-301 made them Moderator-or-Host |
| `realtime/chat-signalr.md` | 9 of the 13 events the server emits |
| `web/chat.md` | Route `/chats/[eventId]` (D-292 re-keyed it); reactions, edit, forward, attachments, presence and search listed as **"out of scope, because the backend does not implement it"** — all shipped |
| `EVENT_CHAT_ARCHITECTURE.md` | Header frozen at "2026-07-19 (D-104 … D-124)" while calling itself canonical and being linked from seven places |

Seven owners did not produce seven maintained documents. It produced **seven independent drift surfaces**,
each individually plausible and collectively describing a system that has not existed for weeks.

### The rule this changes

"One source of truth per fact" (CLAUDE.md §6) is correct and is **not** repealed. What is rejected is the
inference that *more files* enforce it. Splitting by surface multiplies the places a change must land
without adding any force that makes it land there; the D-300 role change had to be written in five files
and was written in none of them.

**A document is maintained in proportion to how often it is opened.** One file is opened by everyone
touching chat, so an error in it is found. Seven are opened one at a time, by whoever already knows which
one they need — which is precisely the reader least likely to notice it is wrong.

One document can still be wrong. It can only be wrong in **one place**, and the next reader notices.

### What was done

All 1,079 lines of per-surface content were **merged into** `docs/EVENT_CHAT_ARCHITECTURE.md` as sections
before anything was removed — schema, REST contract, realtime, security, backend detail, web, Flutter — and
the corrections from the same audit are carried in that merge. The seven files were then deleted, and the
eleven inbound links across `docs/` and `.claude/memory/` repointed at the canonical file. Links inside
`DECISIONS.md` were **left as they are**: this log is append-only history, and its references record what
was true when each entry was written.

### Scope

Documentation only. No code, no contract, no behaviour. `docs/realtime/` and `docs/web/` are now empty.

## D-310 · The workspace composer described a product that does not exist (2026-08-08)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** A correctness-and-honesty pass over the capability engine's workspace layer. It
changes no capability resolution and no authorization; `ICapabilityService` still **describes** and never
enforces, exactly as before. Numbered 310 because 308 and 309 were taken by a concurrent workstream while
this was being written — the sixth D-number collision in this repository.

### What was found

Three claims in the capability engine were not true of the shipped product. None had a failing test,
because none is the kind of thing a test asserts.

**1. The catalog said "~45 capabilities". There are 30.** D-266 M2 cut the catalog from 57 to 30 — "a slug
belongs here only if the answer to *does this archetype fundamentally support this behaviour* can differ
between archetypes" — and updated the inner summary but not the class header sitting three lines above it.
Two contradictory counts in adjacent comments, and the wrong one read first.

**2. `WorkspaceSurface.Route` was computed by every contributor and read by nothing.** It is written in
seven places (`$"/events/{eventId}/registrations"`, `…/tickets`, one per capability tab) and referenced in
**zero**. It never reaches the wire either: `WorkspaceTabView` carries only the tab name and its
capabilities, so the route was assembled and dropped inside the same request.

It could not have been correct in any case. Web routes event management at `/host/events/{id}/{tab}` and
Flutter at `/events/{id}/manage/{tab}`; a single server-side string cannot be right for both. **Client
routing is the client's concern** — the server's job is to say *which surfaces exist*, identified by
`TabId`, and let each client resolve that to its own URL. Removed rather than corrected.

**3. No client has ever called `GET …/{eventId}/workspace`.** The composer runs on every workspace read,
`WorkspaceComposer.ValidateAsync` runs at **boot** and can fail a deploy over contributor ordering — and
both clients hardcode their sixteen management tabs. Eighteen of the thirty capabilities name a workspace
tab (Booths, Judging, Mentors, Submissions, Volunteers, …) that no screen renders on any surface.

### What changed, and what deliberately did not

* The header now says 30, citing D-266 M2.
* `Route` is gone from `WorkspaceSurface` and every construction site.
* The endpoint and the composer are **kept**, with their status stated in code: this is a generated
  workspace nothing consumes yet, not a live contract. Deleting it would throw away a working
  contributor model — the thing that stopped subsystems having to masquerade as event capabilities to
  show a page — for a layer that costs nothing while unused.
* The eighteen tabless-in-practice capabilities are **left alone**. A capability answers "does this
  archetype support this behaviour", which is independent of whether a client has built a screen; erasing
  `WorkspaceTab` would destroy the intent and change seeded data for no present benefit. What was wrong
  was never stating that the screens do not exist.

### Why this matters beyond tidiness

The pattern is the one this repository keeps producing: **a mechanism that is internally consistent and
externally untrue.** The composer validates itself at boot, orders itself deterministically, and resolves
capabilities correctly — while emitting routes for pages nobody built, to an endpoint nobody calls. Every
individual part is right. Nothing checks that the whole describes the shipped product.

## D-311 — Onboarding completion is one rule, and it includes a password and a date of birth

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-09 · **Supersedes the split rule in D-011/D-037**

### The problem

"Is this account onboarded?" had two implementations that had already drifted. `GET /v1/me` tested
`user.Name == "" || user.Username is null`; `GET /v1/auth/registration/status` tested
`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(user.Name) || user.Username is null`. An account whose name was a single
space was therefore onboarded according to one endpoint and unfinished according to the other.

Neither consulted the credential store, so an account with **no password at all** reported itself fully
set up. The mobile ceremony read that flag, and on any failure of the status call defaulted to
`_status?.hasPassword ?? true` — "assume they have one" — and jumped straight to the success screen. A
new user could complete registration having never been shown a password field.

Date of birth existed nowhere: not on `users`, not in the domain, not in any contract — while
age-restricted events already carry `MinAge`/`MaxAge` eligibility with nothing on the account to
evaluate it against.

### The decision

One rule, in `Kurx.Domain.Onboarding`, called by both endpoints:

```
incomplete = name is blank || username is null || date_of_birth is null || no password
```

* **Password is required**, not offered. An account reachable only by SMS code is locked out the moment
  the number is lost, and every surface's sign-in screen is password-first. The client's "Skip for now"
  is removed — it could only ever produce an account the server considered unfinished, which the router
  would bounce straight back into this flow on the next launch.
* **`users.DateOfBirth`** is added as a nullable `date` (migration `AddUserDateOfBirth`). `DateOnly`,
  not `DateTime`: a birth date has no time and no zone, and `timestamptz` would shift the calendar day
  for every user outside UTC. Minimum age 13, validated server-side.
* **`created_at` is now served by `/v1/me`.** The column has been written on insert since the beginning
  and was simply never exposed, so no client could show "member since". No migration — the data was
  always there.
* **Email verification and device enrolment stay non-blocking.** They appear in `remaining` but not in
  `needs_onboarding`, because neither can be completed by a user who mistyped an address or is on a
  handset that cannot enrol — trapping them in the ceremony would be worse than an unverified email.
* Step order is now `complete_profile → create_password → verify_email → enroll_device` on both the
  server's `remaining` list and the client's wizard. Email used to lead, putting the one skippable step
  ahead of the two the account cannot be finished without.

### What was deliberately NOT done

**The OTP entry point still issues a code for a number that already has an account, and the API still
refuses to say whether one exists.** That was reported as a bug; it is the design. `POST
/v1/auth/otp/verify` is a *combined* sign-in-or-register ceremony (D-011/D-037): an unknown number gets
an account, a known one gets a session. Answering "is this number registered?" before the code is
verified would hand any anonymous caller an account-enumeration oracle over phone numbers — the exact
property `/v1/auth/password/reset/start` already goes out of its way to avoid by returning an identical
response either way.

What was actually wrong was the **labelling**, which is fixed instead: "First time? Sign in with a code"
became "Use a one-time code instead", and the phone screen now states the branch up front — "We'll sign
you in, or set up a new account if you don't have one yet." The state machine already distinguished the
two cases correctly via `IsNewUser`; only the words claimed otherwise.

### The new requirements are not retroactive

A password is required in the account-**creation** flow. Applying it backwards would take people who
registered under the old contract — and have been using the app since — and lock them out of it until
they satisfied a rule that did not exist when they signed up. Onboarding is a gate for new accounts, not
a migration tool.

So `IsIncomplete` splits: **identity (name + username) binds every account**, as it has since D-037;
**date of birth and password bind only accounts created at or after
`Onboarding.RequirementsEffectiveFrom`**. That constant is the timestamp of the `AddUserDateOfBirth`
migration (`20260808193940`) — the instant the column began to exist, which makes the boundary a fact
about the schema rather than a date somebody picked. An account older than the column could not possibly
have been asked for a date of birth.

Grandfathered accounts are prompted, never trapped: `complete_profile` and `create_password` still appear
in `remaining`, so Security settings can offer them, while `needs_onboarding` stays false.

### Every client that creates accounts had to change, not just mobile

Web runs the same ceremony off the same `/registration/status`. Leaving it alone would have produced two
concrete failures: its profile step submitted name + username with no date of birth, so the server would
keep returning `complete_profile` and the wizard would **loop on that step forever**; and it had no
password step at all, treating one as an optional follow-up advertised on the success screen — which
would have created web accounts that mobile immediately pushed back into onboarding. Web's wizard now
carries a date-of-birth field and a password step, in the server's `remaining` order.

`completeProfileAction` (`web/lib/registration-actions.ts`) was **deleted** rather than updated: an
unused second copy of `completeOnboardingAction` that did not send `dateOfBirth`. Two copies of one rule
drifting apart is the exact failure this decision exists to fix; leaving a dormant one to be wired up
later would have reintroduced it.

### The profile write surface had no server-side bounds at all

Adding `bio` to onboarding exposed a second instance of the same class as the password mismatch above:
`PATCH /v1/me/profile` was wired `.RequireAuthorization().WithTags("me")` with **no validator**, so
`name`, `headline`, `bio` and every collection were unbounded — while mobile's onboarding form capped
`bio` at 300 characters. A form limit is a UI hint; an authenticated caller could store a field of any
size straight past it.

`UpdateProfileBodyValidator` now bounds all of them, mirroring the organisation profile's limits
(`bio` 2000) so the two halves of the platform's "profile" concept do not disagree. Username format and
uniqueness deliberately stay in the endpoint — they need the database and the reserved-word list.

The rule this keeps producing: **a constraint enforced only where it is convenient to enforce is not a
constraint.** Client-stricter-than-server is a UX choice; client-looser-than-server, or server-absent, is
a defect.

## D-312 — Account creation time is served at two precisions: exact to the owner, month-only in public

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-09

### The existing field

`users.CreatedAt` already existed — `timestamptz`, non-null, defaulted to `DateTime.UtcNow` on the
entity and therefore assigned once at insert. A grep for `.CreatedAt =` across `Kurx.Infrastructure`
and `Kurx.Api` returns **no** assignment to a user's stamp anywhere outside that default, so it is
already immutable in practice: nothing on the login, onboarding, profile-edit, password or
device-registration paths writes it. **No new column, no migration, and no backfill** — the requirement
was never storage, it was exposure. The field simply was not on any response.

### The decision

Two precisions, because the audiences are different:

* **`GET /v1/me` → `created_at`**, the full UTC ISO-8601 instant. It is the owner's own account
  metadata, behind authentication.
* **`GET /v1/public/users/{username}` → `joined_at`**, ISO year-month only (`"2026-08"`).

The public value is truncated **in the projection**, not formatted down in the client. The exact
moment an account was created is a behavioural fact about a person — it pins when they were at a
keyboard, and it correlates accounts registered in the same minute — and nothing a public profile needs
to say ("how long has this person been here") requires it. Truncating server-side means the precision is
never on the wire to leak, whatever a future client does with the field.

`joined_at` joins the D-221 provenance map as `verified`: it is the account row's own stamp, not a claim.

### A year-month is a label, not an instant

Both clients format it without ever constructing a moment from it. The obvious implementation —
`new Date("2026-08")` / `DateTime.parse('2026-08-01')` and then formatting — reads as midnight UTC, so
in any negative-offset timezone it renders the **previous month**, and for January the previous *year*.
Web's `formatJoinedMonth` pins `timeZone: "UTC"`; Flutter's builds the string from the parsed parts. Both
are tested against exactly that slip.

The exact timestamp is the opposite case and *is* converted: the server sends UTC, and each client calls
`.toLocal()` / lets `Intl` apply the runtime zone. No offset is ever computed by hand, and no local
formatted string is ever stored.

On web this forced the settings display into a small client component: the settings page is a server
component, so formatting there would have rendered the **server's** timezone and quietly told a user in
Kolkata their account was created five and a half hours earlier than it was.

### Existing accounts

Nothing is rewritten or fabricated. Every row already carries a trustworthy stamp from its own insert,
including the pre-existing development account (`2026-08-08 19:09:39Z`), and it keeps it.

## D-313 — The API contract describes its own success responses, and an anonymous object is no longer one of them

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-09 · **Extends D-259 (generated + CI-gated contract), D-303 (the gate made real)**

### What was actually wrong

The reported defect was "~382 operations expose anonymous response objects". Measured, that was wrong in
kind. **Zero** operations carried an anonymous *object schema*. What 396 of 518 operations carried was
**no `content` block at all** — Swashbuckle's output for a minimal-API delegate returning `IResult`
without `.Produces<T>()`. The spec did not describe those bodies vaguely; it did not describe them at
all, so a generator reading it produced `void`.

Two further facts the count had hidden:

* **No operation declared `204`** — including the 32 that return `Results.NoContent()`. The spec asserted
  `200` for all of them, which was simply false.
* **The whole API declared exactly 5 error responses**, despite RFC7807 `ProblemDetails` being the one
  error model (CLAUDE.md §2). The contract claimed the platform never fails. Deliberately **left alone**
  here — see "Not done".

### The decision

A success response is part of the contract and must be declared. The rule for how is not "add a DTO
everywhere":

1. **Already returns an `Abstractions` type** → declare it. No new type.
2. **Mapper is a 1:1 snake_case projection of its View** → delete the mapper, return the View. No new type.
3. **Mapper *translates*** → a named record carrying the translation verbatim.
4. **Repeated anonymous shape** → one shared contract, never one per endpoint.
5. **204 / empty 200 / binary** → declared as what they are; no DTO invented.

### The load-bearing constraint

`SnakeCaseResponseConverter` selects response types **by namespace**. A response record declared beside
its endpoint serializes camelCase and breaks every client **with a green build and passing tests**. Every
response DTO therefore lives in `Kurx.Application.Abstractions`, and `ResponseContractTests` asserts the
raw bytes over HTTP rather than deserializing — a case-insensitive read would succeed against either
spelling and prove nothing.

### The trap that governs the whole exercise

Of 48 hand-written `To*Json` mappers, **22 are 1:1 projections and 26 translate**. The dominant
translation is **57 `.ToLowerInvariant()` calls** on status/type/role/kind/state/level fields: the wire
has always carried `"published"` while the View carries `"Published"`. **Returning the Views directly —
the obvious "simplification" — would silently change every status value on the wire**, across events,
orgs, orders, tickets, refunds, sessions, sponsors, waitlists, invitations and memberships. Plus four
renames (`org_id` ← `RepresentingOrgId`, `category` ← `CategoryName`, `ticket_type` ← `TicketTypeName`,
`org_id` ← `Id`). **A mapper is not boilerplate. Diff it key-by-key AND value-by-value before touching it.**

Equally: a mapper that omits a View property is not 1:1 either — returning the View would *add* fields.
Both directions are checked before any mapper is removed.

### Binary downloads

Six endpoints declare `byte[]`, which Swashbuckle renders `format: byte` — base64, in OpenAPI 3.0. They
stream raw bytes. `BinaryResponseSchemaFilter` corrects these to `format: binary`, scoped to **non-JSON
response content types** so a `byte[]` genuinely nested in a JSON body keeps its correct base64
description.

### Result

`518` operations: undeclared **396 → 38**; strong **122 → 439**; `204` **0 → 35**; binary **0 → 6**;
schemas **290 → 365**. **296 operations fixed with 39 new records**, because 80 endpoints collapsed onto
one `OperationAck` and 22 mappers resolved to Views that already existed.

All **26 translating mappers** are converted. The largest, `ToEventJson` (`EventDetail`, served by the
public `GET /v1/events/{slug}` as well as every organiser read), publishes **44 keys against the original
mapper's 44 — none lost, none gained**. Two nested shapes pass their View through unchanged because they
proved 1:1 (`EventVenueView`, `TeamMemberView`, `GroupMemberView`); `EventMediaView` deliberately does
**not**, because it carries a `Url` the projection never emitted and passing it through would add a field
to a public wire.

### Not done, deliberately

* **Error responses are still undeclared.** Documenting ProblemDetails across 518 operations is a large,
  separate diff and is its own phase.
* **The two token shapes stay separate.** `otp/verify` and `refresh` return 6 fields (with
  `is_new_user`); password / passkey / recovery / device-login return the same 5 minus it. Unifying would
  *add* a field to five endpoints — an API change with no demonstrated need.
* **Webhook acks stay empty `200`, not `204`.** Meta and Razorpay only read the status; the change would
  be gratuitous.
* **34 operations remain undeclared** (plus the 4 intentional). Every one is listed in
  [`api/UNDECLARED_TRACKER.md`](api/UNDECLARED_TRACKER.md), generated from the spec and the allow-list so
  it cannot drift: admin 8, auth 7, events 6, me 3, orgs 2, and 8 singletons.

  Two of those need a **product decision, not code** — `POST /v1/auth/login/password` (three shapes by
  outcome: session / device_approval / second_factor) and `POST /v1/auth/login/status` (two). Both are the
  same polymorphism as `/v1/gate/scan` and most likely take the same ruling. Two more are legitimately
  dynamic: the passkey `*/options` routes return raw WebAuthn `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions` passed
  through verbatim from the library, so `options` must stay untyped rather than acquire a fabricated
  schema. `GET /v1/orgs/{orgId}/workspace-capabilities` is the largest single piece of remaining work.

  **Two traps, both of which bit during this pass.** Never annotate an **envelope** with its element type:
  three separate attempts declared `IReadOnlyList<T>` on a `Results.Ok(new { items = …, total })` body.
  And a **conditional** `value is null ? NoContent() : Ok(value)` must declare BOTH outcomes — declaring
  only the 200 describes the misleading half, since a generated client reads it as "a body always
  arrives"; three such endpoints (two on the event-wizard autosave path, where a new draft's very first
  load returns exactly the undeclared case) were caught only by a source-reading test,
  `NoContentDeclarationTests`. `.Produces<T>()` is metadata the compiler never checks, so regenerating the
  spec and diffing is the only thing that catches either class.

### The ratchet

`scripts/openapi-response-check.mjs` + `docs/api/undeclared-allowlist.json`, wired into CI after the
client-contract gate. It fails when an operation not on the list is undeclared (a new endpoint that never
said what it returns) **and** when a list entry has since been declared, so the list cannot quietly become
permission never to finish. Four operations are marked permanently intentional with their reasons: the
two webhook acks, the local-disk storage receiver, and `POST /v1/gate/{eventId}/scan`.

A second gate, `scripts/response-shape-check.mjs`, closes the gap the first cannot see: it proves a
declared type is the type the endpoint's mapper actually returns. A declaration can be present and
**wrong**, which is worse than absent — clients are generated from it and `contract-check.mjs` then
validates them against a lie.

A companion readable inventory, [`api/UNDECLARED_TRACKER.md`](api/UNDECLARED_TRACKER.md), is generated by
`scripts/tracker.mjs` from the spec + allow-list + check script, so the tracked list can never disagree
with what CI enforces.

A ratchet rather than "all must be declared" for the same reason D-246 used one: a gate that fails on day
one gets switched off, which is precisely how the client gate spent months reporting a vacuous pass
(D-303). Both failure directions were **tested by deliberately breaking the list**, not assumed.

## D-314 · The UI/UX redesign is merged; four of its changes are refused (2026-08-09)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Merges `origin/naveen` (the UI/UX redesign program, phases 39–50, 299 files) into
`feat/messages-settings`. Numbered 314 because 311–313 were taken by a concurrent session while this was
being written — the fifth D-number collision in this repository, and the second this session had to route
around.

### Why a merge needed a decision at all

A redesign branch is supposed to be safe to take wholesale. This one was not, and the reason generalises:
**a branch that predates a fix will re-delete it.** `origin/naveen` forked before D-302 and D-305 landed,
so its authors correctly identified two defects, fixed them by *removal*, and those removals now read as
regressions against work that had since fixed the same defects *properly*.

### Taken

- The redesign itself — `packages/ui`, `web/components`, `web/app`, `admin/*`, `mobile/lib`, `docs/ui-ux`.
- **`SelectCard` / `SelectCardGroup`** — real `<input type="radio">` groups replacing grids of `<button>`.
  The wizard's five single-select steps were, to a screen reader, N unrelated buttons with no group name
  and no way to tell which was chosen: selection was carried entirely by `border-accent ring-1`.
- **The `OrgEndpoints` workspace-capability fix.** Representing yourself satisfies the
  verified-representative gate *vacuously* — that gate exists to stop someone acting for an institution
  they have not proven they belong to, and a personal representation has no such claim to prove (D-268).
  Applying it anyway made the matrix answer `tickets: ["view"]` to an event's own creator, so the client
  hid the ticket form and a personally-hosted event could never be sold or registered for. `IEventAuthority`
  was accepting those writes the whole time (D-269 resolves ownership first and on its own), so **the
  matrix was lying, not protecting**. Narrowed to `opsEdit`; publish, wallet, settings and
  `can_host_paid_events` are untouched, pinned by a test.
- **admin's first test suite** — vitest + testing-library, 27 tests. Admin had none.
- **`/tickets` and its `TicketQr`.** Both branches independently built a real QR through a
  token-attaching proxy; theirs carries a test, so ours (`components/events/ticket-qr` +
  `app/api/tickets/[code]/qr`) is deleted. One component, one route.
- Deletion of five genuinely unreachable `/host` routes, verified orphaned on this side too.

### Refused, each for a stated reason

| Refused | Why |
|---|---|
| `docs/DECISIONS.md` | Its D-288…D-291 collide with ours, dated two days earlier. Four numbers, eight decisions. Theirs must renumber above the current maximum. |
| Deletion of `booking-form.tsx` | Removed there as a fake checkout that opened Razorpay with no order id and no amount — **the exact defect D-302 had already fixed properly here**. Ours posts a real order with an idempotency key. |
| `book/[slug]/page.tsx` | Its replacement is a "booking works on mobile" hand-off. That was true before D-302 and is not now. |
| Workspace's "Create event" button | D-305 removed it deliberately: a primary creation button is what made `/workspace` read as an organizer dashboard. |

`visibilityFor`, `canChoosePaid`, `shownCategories` and `hostName` are likewise kept and re-rendered
*through* the new primitives — the D-268/D-305 rules survive the redesign rather than being replaced by it.

### What the incoming tests caught in our own code

The redesign shipped four discipline tests, and every one of them found a real defect on this side:

- `text-fg` is not a token — six chat sites named a colour that does not exist; it is `text`.
- Four decorative images carried `alt=""` with no `aria-hidden`, so intent was inferred from silence.
- Two restored `/host` loading shells still imported the pre-redesign `@/components/ui` shim.
- `profile_header` and `profile_skeleton` animated durations nothing could clamp; the skeleton is an
  unbounded pulse, which is precisely the WCAG 2.2.2 case. It now stops, reusing `ShimmerBox`'s own
  implementation rather than a second one.

**And two of those tests were themselves broken on Windows**: both built a path from `Directory.listSync`
(which yields `\`) and compared it against `/`-keyed allow-lists, so every allowance silently missed and
the palette's own definition file counted as a violation. A discipline test that cannot be satisfied is a
test that gets deleted; separators are now normalised.

Separately, `WorkspaceCompositionTests` still passed the `Route` argument **D-310 removed**, so the test
project did not compile. That was pre-existing on this branch, not from the merge, and
`CAPABILITY_ENGINE.md` still documented the field — both corrected.

### Verification

web typecheck + 478 passed / 1 skipped · admin typecheck + 27 passed · `flutter analyze` clean + 395
passed · backend build 0 warnings / 0 errors · backend suite **1576 passed / 1 failed / 1 skipped of
1578** in the SDK container.

The one failure — `InviteLinkConcurrencyTests` expecting 25 seats and seeing 24 — is **recorded as
unconfirmed, not as a pass**. It claimed one *fewer* than the cap, so the invariant the test is named for
held; it passed in an earlier run when that container was the sole occupant of Postgres, and failed only
when a second full suite and a live `kurx-backend` were writing to the same server. Per §9 it needs an
isolated re-run before it is called either a defect or a flake, and that run has not happened.

## D-315 · A refusal that cannot be read is a refusal that did not happen (2026-08-09)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Fixes the registration password step on both clients. Reported as "it could not
set password" on the phone — which turned out to be the app's own copy, quoted back verbatim.

### What was actually broken

Nothing in the password path. The API was correct throughout: `POST /v1/auth/password/set` accepted a
valid password and refused an invalid one with the right code, verified live against the running stack.
What failed was the last inch — **turning that code into a sentence.**

| surface | mechanism | what a user saw for `password_breached` |
|---|---|---|
| mobile registration | `switch (e.code)` on `weak_password` | "Could not set your password. Try again." |
| web registration | `apiErrorMessage` → `problemMessage` | "Something went wrong. Please try again." |
| web reset / manage | `passwordErrorCopy` | "That password is too common…" ✅ |

`weak_password` **is not a code this backend has ever emitted.** The mobile switch matched on an invented
one, so every real refusal — `password_breached`, `password_contains_identifier`, `password_too_short` —
fell to its default. On web the code reached `problemMessage`, which had no password entries, and
`looksLikeCode()` then suppressed the `detail` that carried the same token. Two different mechanisms,
one outcome: the server explained itself and the client discarded the explanation.

**The trap that made it certain to be hit.** `PasswordPolicy.Breached` is dominated by *exactly
twelve-character* strings — `password1234`, `qwerty123456`, `welcome12345`, `admin1234567` — because it
exists to catch what a "12 characters with a number" instruction produces. So the platform tells a user
to use 12 characters, they comply, they are refused, and they are told nothing. Reproduced live:
`password1234` → `400 password_breached`; `Welcome@12345` → `200`.

### The decision

**Error copy for a stable backend code lives in the one shared table per platform, never in a
hand-rolled switch at the call site.** `PROBLEM_COPY` (`packages/ui`) and `ApiError._messages`
(`mobile/lib/core/network`) are those tables; they already mirror each other and a test already compares
them. The eight `password_*` codes join them. `passwordErrorCopy` keeps only the codes whose wording is
genuinely positional — "your current password is incorrect" means nothing outside a change form — and
delegates the rest, so it can no longer disagree with the signup screens about what `password_breached`
says.

A per-screen switch is how a client ends up matching a code the server does not emit: there is nothing to
compare it against. The new web test reads `PasswordService.cs` and asserts every code it can *return*
has copy, so a future rejection reason fails the build instead of reaching a user as a shrug. It found
its first false positive immediately — `password_changed`/`password_reset` are audit action names, never
client codes — which is why it matches returned values rather than any `password_*` string.

### The second bug, in the same function

`_savePassword` set `_step = _Step.success` outright instead of re-reading the checklist. **On mobile the
email-verification step was built, listed in the checklist, and unreachable in a single sitting** — the
user's other report. Web never had it because web always refreshed. The existing mobile test passed
throughout because it starts already email-verified.

Three copies of the step ladder existed in that file; two ended at `success` and so skipped email. They
now all route through `_firstStep`. **A wizard step reached by a hard-coded assignment is a step nobody
re-derived from server state** — the same class of defect as D-311, where two implementations of
"is this account onboarded?" had already drifted.

### Also found, not fixed here

`PasswordPolicy.DerivedFromIdentifier` tests the stored E.164 string and its digits, never the **national
significant number**. For `+919876501234` the password `9876501234xyz` is accepted, because it lacks the
`91` the stored form carries — and the national form is exactly how an Indian user writes their own
number. Verified live. Recorded rather than fixed: widening the check needs its own pass over the
false-positive rate.

### Verification

`flutter analyze` clean · mobile 413 tests (was 395) · web typecheck clean · 495 passed / 1 skipped (was
478) · admin 27. **Both new mobile tests were confirmed to fail against the unfixed code** before being
kept. The live browser walk of the fixed web flow was blocked by CORS on the scratch port used to run it
(`ALLOWED_ORIGINS` is 3000/3001/8081) — a property of the test setup, not of the fix, and named here so
it is not later mistaken for a defect.

## D-316 · Signing in must never look like signing up (2026-08-09)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Reported as "clicking login goes to the create-account page, and it says phone
number verified". Both observations were accurate, and the second is what made the first alarming.

### The chain

`/login` sends an already-authenticated caller away from the form, which is right — you cannot sign in
when you are signed in. Where it sends them depends on `needs_onboarding`:

```
/login page.tsx:33   if (session) redirect(me.needs_onboarding ? "/register" : "/discover")
```

`Onboarding.IsIncomplete` (D-311) now also requires a password and a date of birth, so an account
created after that cutoff and missing either lands on `/register`. That page was titled
**"Create your Kurx account"** unconditionally, above a checklist already ticking **"Phone verified"**.
An account that demonstrably exists was being told to create itself.

D-311's grandfathering is correct and untouched: accounts predating the `AddUserDateOfBirth` migration
keep the old name+username rule and are never routed here. This affects only accounts created under the
new contract with the new steps outstanding — which, today, is every recently created account.

### The part that was a trap rather than a wording problem

`/register` had **no sign-out and no account switcher**. Combined with the redirect above, that means a
signed-in account with unfinished setup could not reach a login form *by any route* — pressing "Log in"
returned them to the same page, indefinitely, with no way to switch accounts or start over. A dead end
reachable from the primary navigation is worse than a confusing heading, and it is the reason this is a
decision rather than a copy tweak.

### The decision

**A page reached by resuming states that it is a resumption.** `/register` now branches on
`initialStatus`: a fresh visitor still gets "Create your Kurx account"; someone already signed in gets
"Finish setting up your account" and their own phone number back, so the checklist's ticks read as
progress rather than as a contradiction.

**Any surface that can be reached while signed in carries a way out.** The resume path renders
"Not you? Sign out" through the existing `logoutAction` — a new `SignOutLink` only because settings'
`LogoutButton` is a block `Button` in its own form and cannot sit inside a sentence. Same action, same
server side.

Not changed: the redirect itself, `needs_onboarding`, and D-311's rule. The destination was right; what
was missing was telling the user where they had arrived, and letting them leave.

### Verification

web typecheck clean · **499 passed / 1 skipped** (was 495). `web/test/register-resume.test.ts` pins all
four properties — the create copy sits inside the else arm, the escape route exists, it renders only on
the resume path, and `/login`'s redirect is the reason it is needed, so removing that redirect fails the
test rather than quietly orphaning the copy. Asserted at source level: the page is an async Server
Component calling `cookies()`, which does not exist under vitest.

## D-317 · A number that cannot exist is refused before a code is minted; a throwaway address is measured, not blocked (2026-08-10)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Two signup-hardening gaps, implemented as two phases. Neither is an authentication
bypass and neither changes how anyone signs in — this is input validation and fraud measurement.

### Part 1 — the phone fallback was a defect

The premise this started from was that libphonenumber had been deliberately avoided. **It had not.**
`libphonenumber-csharp` is a dependency and `NormalizePhone` calls it on both branches. The comment that
looks like a refusal sits on a different function:

```csharp
// AuthService.ToOtpDestination — "…a key format only — deliberately NOT run through
// libphonenumber, which rejects numbers this login contract has always accepted."
```

That is a **correctness guard, not a policy**: D-290 §2 forbids re-normalizing a stored bare-digit phone,
because many foreign national numbers are also well-formed Indian mobiles and a Singapore number stored as
`6591234567` returns as `916591234567`. It stays exactly as it is.

The actual defect was one word. `NormalizePhone` **validates but does not reject**: on failure it returns
the input's bare digits — right in itself, since inventing a country is what once sent a user's code to a
stranger — and `RequestOtpAsync` then accepted those digits on length alone. `+911111111111` was issued a
code for a destination that cannot exist.

Nothing about it was insecure: the code went nowhere, and no account exists until `VerifyOtpAsync` consumes
one. It was **a dead end presented to the user as a sent message**, and it let one caller mint rows against
unbounded fictional destinations. The fix is to reject at the boundary, reusing the existing `invalid_phone`.

**Why the guard cannot refuse a good number:** both success branches of `NormalizePhone` return
`parsed.E164[1..]`, so restoring the `+` reconstructs exactly the E.164 libphonenumber produced. Only the
branch that never parsed can fail it. Pinned by a test, alongside the bare Indian national number a
pre-E.164 client still sends.

### What the fix exposed, which is the more useful finding

The full suite went to **283 failures**. Not a regression — **27 phone generators across 26 test files were
producing numbers that cannot exist** (`$"9199{seq:D7}"` is an eleven-digit Indian number). They passed only
because of the fallback being removed. Every one now emits exactly ten digits, each class keeping its
distinct prefix so the unique index still separates them.

That is why this defect survived: **a suite whose fixtures are impossible numbers can never catch a bug
about impossible numbers.** No production row was affected — all 8 accounts carry valid E.164 with a
resolved region, verified against libphonenumber directly before any change was made. No migration exists.

### Part 2 — disposable email is a signal, not a gate

`FraudSignalKind.DisposableContact` had existed with **no producer**. It now has one, and deliberately
nothing more.

**A hard block would be wrong here specifically.** Email is not an authentication factor on this platform —
phone OTP is — so a throwaway address buys an attacker far less than it would on an email-first product.
Blocking at registration would fall hardest on students using temporary institutional addresses and on
privacy-conscious attendees, neither of whom is the threat. The capability that carries real risk,
organising paid public events, is already gated on identity + PAN + bank + fraud-clear (D-307). So detection
feeds that existing score and the existing gate decides: no second verdict, no new table, no new endpoint,
no new engine.

- **The list is configuration** (`DISPOSABLE_EMAIL_DOMAINS`), absent by default, so the feature is inert
  until an operator opts in. These lists change continuously and carry false positives; a wrong entry must
  be fixable without a deploy.
- **Score 10 against a threshold of 100.** This phase measures. Raising it to a blocking weight is a
  separate decision to be made against observed volume, not in advance.
- **Emitted after the commit, only on success.** Scoring a submitted address would score people who typed a
  domain and never proved they hold it, including anyone who mistyped.
- **De-duplicated per (user, address).** Re-verifying adds nothing — doing a legitimate thing twice must not
  push someone toward the threshold. A *different* throwaway address is a separate fact, or one recorded
  signal would cover an unlimited cycle of them.
- **Best-effort.** The verification has already committed; a signal write that throws must not turn a
  completed verification into an error the user sees. Recording nothing is a measurement gap, not a security
  one — the gate it feeds fails closed on identity, never on the absence of a signal.
- **Existing verified accounts are never re-scored.** The producer lives on the verification path, so an
  address verified before this existed is never revisited.

### Also changed

`invalid_phone` joins `PROBLEM_COPY` and Flutter's `ApiError._messages`. Without it the new refusal reached
users as "Something went wrong. Please try again." — the same defect D-315 fixed for passwords, and it would
have made "return a clear `invalid_phone`" untrue at the only layer the user sees. `validation_failed`
already covers input that is not phone-shaped at all; the two codes stay distinct because they ask the user
to fix different things.

### Verification

Backend build 0/0. `InternationalPhoneTests` 49/49 (was 47). Auth suite 116/116. `DisposableEmailTests`
20/20. Full regression **1614 passed / 8 failed / 1 skipped of 1623**, from 1339/283 before the fixture
repair. The 8 are a concurrent workstream's: three `EventAudienceAuthorizationTests` and one `PostTests`
answering `NotFound` where an event is expected (`EventEndpoints.cs`, +53/−112, not touched here), a
`NoContentDeclarationTests` that did not exist that morning, and three `InviteLinkConcurrencyTests` already
failing beforehand.

**No route added, removed or renamed. No migration. No stored phone data rewritten. Legacy bare-national
login compatibility intact. No account-enumeration surface introduced** — `invalid_phone` is a format
verdict returned before any account lookup, so it is identical whether or not anyone holds the number.

## D-318 · One dev API port, and an emulator that can reach it (2026-08-10)

**Context.** The repo carried two dev API ports. `backend/Kurx.Api/Properties/launchSettings.json`,
`.env.example` (all three client vars), `infra/docker-compose.yml`, `docs/api/README.md` and the default
in every client — `web/lib/site.ts`, `web/middleware.ts`, `admin/lib/site.ts`, `admin/middleware.ts`,
`mobile/lib/core/network/app_config.dart` — said **5080**. The root `docker-compose.yml` published
**5001** and baked `localhost:5001` into the web and admin bundles at build time.

Consequences, all silent:

- Switching between `dotnet run` and `docker compose up` broke every client until its config was
  hand-edited, because a `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` value is compiled into the bundle and cannot be corrected at
  runtime.
- **Mobile could not reach a compose-run backend at all.** `KURX_API_BASE` defaults to
  `http://localhost:5080` with deliberately no alternate fallback (D-017), so `flutter run` against the
  documented stack hit a refused connection with no diagnostic.
- D-302 had already been bitten by the same split from the other side: `KURX_API_BASE` was unset in
  compose, defaulted to 5080, and every presigned banner, avatar and attachment URL pointed at a port
  nothing published. That was patched by pinning `KURX_API_BASE` to 5001 — treating the symptom, leaving
  the two ports in place.

**Decision. 5080 is the only dev API port.** Compose now publishes `5080:8080`; the `KURX_API_BASE`
default, both Next.js build args and the surrounding comments follow. 5001 was the minority — 5080 was
already canonical in eleven places — so this is the smaller change *and* the one that makes the two run
modes interchangeable. Postgres and Redis keep their compose remaps (5433/6380) on purpose: those exist
to avoid colliding with a native local instance, which is a different problem from this one.

`ci.yml`'s web and admin build args moved to 5080 as well. They are placeholders for `next build` and
reach no live server, but a second number in the repo is exactly how this drift started.

**Decision. `localhost` stays, and `adb reverse` is how a device reaches it.** On a phone or emulator
`localhost` resolves to the device itself, never to the developer's machine — so the default could not
work no matter which port it named, which is the timeout this decision started from.

`adb reverse tcp:5080 tcp:5080` tunnels that port back over USB and fixes it for **both** a physical
device and an emulator, with no flag, no code branch and no rebuild. Verified live against a USB-attached
RMX3840 (Android 16): `adb shell curl http://localhost:5080/health` → **200**.

A platform check rewriting the loopback host to `10.0.2.2` was written first and **reverted**. It is
emulator-only: on a real device it rewrites a working tunnel into an unroutable address, so it would have
converted "works after one adb command" into "silently broken, with a plausible-looking reason in the
source". That is the D-017 stale-fallback bug class wearing a platform check. `AppConfig` therefore has no
platform branch at all.

`AppConfig.webBase` gets no equivalent treatment and could not: it is encoded into share links and QR
codes that other people open on their own devices, where any loopback address resolves to their phone.
Set it explicitly for anything a third party will open.

**Verified.** `docker compose config` resolves `published: "5080"` on `kurx-backend`;
`flutter analyze` clean across the whole package; `kurx-backend` now publishes `0.0.0.0:5080`; and the
phone reached `/health` through the tunnel. **The web and admin bundles still carry `localhost:5001`** —
`NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is baked at build time, so they need an image rebuild to follow. Not done here: the
working tree holds another session's uncommitted `EventService.cs`.

**No production impact.** Every published port here is dev-only; deployed environments set the origin
through env vars and never use these defaults.

## D-319 · An invitation nobody can see is an invitation that was never sent (2026-08-10)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Completes the event staff-assignment round trip. No authorization model changes:
`RespondAsync` already refused every actor except the invitee, and it still does.

### The break

`POST /v1/orgs/{orgId}/events/{eventId}/assignments` created an `EventAssignment` with
`Status = Invited` and did nothing further — no notification, no email, no push. `RespondAsync` is the
only path to `Accepted` and it refuses the organiser who sent the invite, a platform admin, and everyone
else (`EventAssignmentService.cs:88`); the invitee is the sole permitted actor. Yet
`GET /v1/me/assignments`, `/v1/assignments/{id}/accept` and `/decline` — all shipped and tested with
D-064 — had **zero callers on web, admin and mobile**.

So the invitee learned nothing: no notification, no screen, not in the event chat (access is granted on
acceptance, deliberately), and not on their profile (`PublicProfileService.cs:534` filters to
`Accepted`/`Completed`). The row existed, the organiser could see it, and the one person who could act
on it had no way to discover it.

Downstream, §14.2's go-live gate is satisfied by an `Accepted` assignment and nothing else
(`EventService.cs:1624` → `no_staff_assigned`). Mobile shipped a **Go live** button that could therefore
never succeed. `Live` is optional — `complete` runs from `Published` directly — so nothing was stranded,
but one lifecycle state was unreachable and one button was permanently broken.

### What changed

1. **`AssignmentView` carries event context.** It held the *assignee's* identity, which is what the
   organiser's team list needs and exactly backwards for the invitee's own list. Added `EventTitle`,
   `EventSlug`, `EventStartsAt`, `RepresentingOrgName`, batched through one join per list.
   **`RepresentingOrgName` is null for a self-represented event** — D-268 says a personally-hosted event
   carries no organization identity, and the representation row is named after the person, so emitting
   it would surface an internal row on every invite. Clients render nothing, never a fallback label.
2. **The invitee is notified.** `NotificationKinds.StaffInvited = "staff.invited"`, which the `staff.`
   prefix maps onto `NotificationCategory.StaffInvitations` — a category switchable in settings since
   D-263 that **nothing had ever emitted into**. Sent after the save, so a notification failure cannot
   lose the assignment; re-inviting is idempotent.
3. **Web and mobile both get an `/assignments` inbox.** Its own page and nav entry on each,
   deliberately *not* merged into `/invitations`: that page grants permission to *register* and its
   copy works hard not to read as a ticket. A staff assignment is a team role carrying chat access and
   a profile credential. Conflating them would undo the distinction D-266 M6 was careful to draw.

   Mobile's sits beside the org-invitations inbox in Profile and is the **actionable** one of the two —
   `OrgInvitationsPage` has no buttons because org accept/decline are keyed by a token the list
   endpoint does not return, while an assignment is keyed by id. `staff.invited` notifications
   deep-link to `/assignments` through the standard `route` field. `AssignmentDto`'s new fields are
   `@Default`ed rather than required, so a client running ahead of the API degrades to a thinner card
   instead of throwing on every row.
4. **Web lifecycle parity.** Web offered 7 of the 11 transitions mobile has had all along, missing
   `open_registration`, `go_live`, `complete` and `cancel` — an event could be published from web and
   then never opened, taken live or completed. `cancel` is terminal (D-101) so it confirms first.
5. **`not_pending` and `user_not_found` got readable copy** (D-315). Answering an invite twice is
   ordinary — two tabs, a back button — and read as "Something went wrong", i.e. as a bug rather than
   as the already-settled state it is.

### Deferred, deliberately

`docs/api/openapi.json` is **not** regenerated here. It requires `docker compose up --build backend`,
and a concurrent session has a live stack on this checkout plus an in-flight port change (D-318).
Rebuilding would take their dev API down mid-change. CI regenerates the spec and fails on any
difference, so this cannot be silently missed — it must be run before the commit lands.

> **Closed 2026-08-11 by [D-326](#d-326).** The regeneration this deferred ran as part of that entry's
> contract fix and carried this one's four `AssignmentResponse` fields (`event_title`, `event_slug`,
> `event_starts_at`, `representing_org_name`) plus two `required` additions into the committed spec. The
> debt was measured against the live spec *before* that change, so it was closed knowingly rather than
> discovered in a diff.

Mobile's lifecycle screen already offered `go_live`, `open_registration`, `complete` and `cancel` — it
was web that was missing them, and that button could never have succeeded before this change.

## D-320 · A one-time code is how you get an account, not how you skip your password (2026-08-10)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Client-only — the OTP rail is untouched.** `git diff` on
`backend/Kurx.Infrastructure/Auth/` and `AuthEndpoints.cs` is **empty**: `/v1/auth/otp/request`,
`/v1/auth/otp/verify`, `IOtpService`, the peppered HMAC store (D-215) and every test that logs in
through them are exactly as they were.

**The problem is a cost one, and it is caused by the placement of one control.** The sign-in screen
offered a one-tap alternative to typing a password:

| surface | control | destination |
|---|---|---|
| app | `Use a one-time code instead` | `Routes.loginOtp` |
| web | `First time? Sign in with a code` | the in-panel `OtpFallback` |
| admin | `First time? Sign in with a code` | `OtpForm` |

Given a choice between recalling a password and tapping a button that texts you a code, a returning
user takes the button every time. So the shortcut was not an occasional fallback — it was the
**default path**, and each use mints and *delivers* a code. Password-first (D-182) was the design;
this control quietly inverted it, and the platform pays per message for the inversion.

**Decision: remove the manual one-time-code control from all three sign-in screens.** Nothing else.

**What still runs on a code, deliberately:**

- **Signing up.** The OTP ceremony both signs in a known number and creates an account for an unknown
  one (D-011/D-037), and at signup no other factor can exist yet. Web keeps `/register` (which owns
  its own `sendSignupOtpAction`/`verifySignupOtpAction`, so deleting `OtpFallback` cost it nothing);
  the app keeps **"New to Kurx? Create an account"**, which already pointed at the same route the
  removed shortcut did — so the app lost a *label*, not a capability.
- **Factor 2 after a correct password.** `SecondFactorPanel` (D-280/D-283) renders whichever factors
  the account actually holds, ranked by the backend. A code delivered there is a second factor, not a
  password bypass, and `Remember this browser` makes it once per browser rather than once per login.
- **Recovery.** `Forgot password?` → `/reset`, unchanged. OTP alone still never resets a password
  (INV-B): a recovery code or device step-up is required.
- **Admin's lockout guard.** `login/page.tsx` still auto-switches to `OtpForm` on
  `no_second_factor` — a staff account holding nothing else must not be locked out of the console.
  That is a guard the console reaches for, not a shortcut a user can pick, and console volume is a
  handful of people, so it carries no meaningful delivery cost.

**Two stale copy strings were corrected in the same pass**, because both pointed at the removed
control and would otherwise have told users to click something that is not there. Web's
`no_second_factor` message said *"Use a one-time code below"*; it now matches the app's wording word
for word, which is also more accurate post-D-280 — that error is reachable only when the account holds
no factor at all. Admin's said *"Sign in with a code below"* and now says a code is being sent, which
is what its own handler actually does.

**Verified.** web `tsc --noEmit` + `next lint` clean; admin typecheck + lint clean and **32/32** tests
pass; `flutter analyze` clean and **79** auth + guest-browse tests pass — including
`guest_browse_test`'s assertion that the sign-in screen is not a dead end for a new user, which taps
"New to Kurx? Create an account" and still lands on the code screen. Backend untouched, so no suite run
was owed.

**Numbering.** Claimed D-319 first; a concurrent session had appended its own D-319 between the read
and the write — the exact race recorded in the concurrent-workstream notes. Renumbered to D-320 across
five code comments before anything was committed.

## D-321 · A personal name is not an institution — the public profile said otherwise on three cards (2026-08-11)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** Contract change (three fields become nullable) plus a client fix on each surface.
No authorization change, no schema change, no new table.

### The break

D-319 added event context to `AssignmentView` and was careful about one thing: `RepresentingOrgName` is
**null** for a self-represented event, because the row that satisfies `Event.RepresentingOrgId` is a
persistence artifact named after the person (`EventService.cs:1825` — `user.Name.Trim()`, or
`"Personal events"`). D-268 is explicit that an `IsPersonal` row is filtered out of every user-facing
surface, and `EventDetail` (`EventService.cs:1725`), `MyEventRow` (`:1464`), `OrgService.ListMine`
(`:188`) and `EventPolicyService` (`:47`) all do exactly that.

Three sibling projections did not. `PublicProfileService` joins `Organizations` for a display label in
`CompetitionResultsAsync`, `GetAssignmentsAsync` and `SpeakerSessionsAsync`, and all three emitted
`o.Name` raw. So on a **public profile**, a judge/volunteer/speaker card for a self-hosted Public+Listed
event printed the **host's own personal name** in the position that everywhere else on the platform
means "the institution that ran this". Not a permission leak — the data is public either way — but it
asserts an affiliation that does not exist, which is the specific claim the trust system is for.

D-319 did not cause this; it made it visible by doing the right thing one file away.

### What changed

1. **The label is nulled, never the row.** `.Join(Organizations.Where(o => !o.IsPersonal), …)` would
   have been shorter and is **wrong** — an inner join deletes the whole card, so a judge at a
   self-hosted event would vanish from their own profile rather than lose one line of attribution. The
   join carries `IsPersonal` and the projection emits `IsPersonal ? null : OrgName`, matching
   `EventAssignmentService.cs:151` exactly.
2. **`CompetitionResultCard.OrgName`, `AssignmentCard.OrgName`, `SpeakerSessionCard.OrgName` become
   `string?`.** Requiredness is derived from nullability (`RequiredFromNonNullableSchemaFilter`,
   D-303), so this moves all three out of `required` in the published contract. That is the honest
   description: the field is genuinely absent for a whole class of event.
3. **Both clients required it, which is the D-245 failure mode.** Web declared `org_name: z.string()`
   on all three schemas — one null and `.parse()` throws, taking the entire verified block down rather
   than one label. Flutter's `ProfileAssignmentDto` had `required String orgName` and would have thrown
   on deserialization. Both now nullable. Flutter wires only the assignment card; the other two routes
   have no mobile DTO.
4. **Two web render sites joined on the separator, not the value** — `{c.stage_name} · {c.org_name} ·
   {date}` renders `Finals ·  · Mar 2026` when the middle term is null. Both now filter before joining,
   the idiom `profile-sections.tsx` already used. The assignment card never rendered `org_name` at all,
   so it needed only the schema fix.
5. **`scripts/generate-openapi.sh` still defaulted to port 5001.** D-318 made 5080 the one dev API port
   across compose, CI, `.env.example` and every client, but did not touch this script — so the one
   command a deferred contract regeneration depends on would poll a port nothing binds for 180 seconds
   and then fail. CI was never affected (it sets `ASPNETCORE_URLS` to 5080 directly). Fixed here
   because this change is what made someone run it.

### Deferred, deliberately

`docs/api/openapi.json` is **still not regenerated** — now owing both D-319's four added fields and
this entry's three nullability changes. Regeneration runs `docker compose up -d --build backend`, which
takes down the dev API a concurrent session has been running for five hours. CI's drift gate fails on
any difference, so this cannot be missed; it must run before the commit lands, and it closes both
debts in one pass.

> **Closed 2026-08-11 by [D-326](#d-326)**, and in one pass exactly as predicted. The regenerated spec
> carries this entry's three `org_name` removals from `required` (`AssignmentCard`,
> `CompetitionResultCard`, `SpeakerSessionCard`) alongside D-319's four fields and D-326's own
> `product_class`. Total diff: 28 insertions, 3 deletions.

**Verified.** Backend Release build `-warnaserror` clean. Web `tsc --noEmit` clean, **504 passed /
1 skipped**. `flutter analyze` clean, **416 passed**. Two new backend tests pin both directions — a
self-represented event emits `org_name: null` **and still returns the card**, and a genuinely
represented organization is still named (without the second, a projection that dropped the field
entirely would pass the first).

## D-322 · A family occasion in the private branch was classified Public (2026-08-11)

**Status: ACCEPTED.** One taxonomy data correction. No schema change, no contract change, no
authorization change, no client change.

### The break

`event_categories.ProductClass` is not chosen per Type — it is derived from the Type's archetype, and
`ArchetypeSeeder.TypeArchetypes` maps Type **name** → archetype slug. Keying on name is deliberate and
correct (`student-workshop` and `public-workshop` are both `learning` — "a Workshop behaves like a
Workshop whoever runs it"), but it means a name can be read by the wrong neighbour.

`"Graduation Party"` was mapped to `ceremonial`, sitting in the A13 block between `"Freshers Party"`,
`"Farewell Party"` and `"Department Event"` — all genuinely institutional campus occasions. The taxonomy
places it somewhere else entirely: **Private Events ▸ Family Celebrations**, between
`Housewarming Ceremony` and `Retirement Party`, every one of whose twelve siblings is
`private-gathering`.

Verified against the running database, not the seeder source:

```
$ SELECT a."Name", c."Name", t."Name", t."ProductClass", t."ArchetypeSlug" …
Private Events | Family Celebrations | Graduation Party | Public | ceremonial
```

The only `Public` row in the entire Private Events branch, out of 111 Type rows.

Two consequences, and the second is the one that matters:

1. `Event.Product` came out `Public` — so a graduation party got public discoverability and public
   moderation, and the Create-Event gate offered the type only on the **Public** path, meaning it was
   unreachable from the private flow an organiser would actually be in.
2. `ceremonial` carries **`RequiresRepresentation = true`**. A family occasion therefore demanded an
   organization to represent and the full D-307 verification gate. `private-gathering` requires neither.

### What changed

1. **The map entry moves from `ceremonial` to `private-gathering`**, into the A14 block in taxonomy
   order. Fixes fresh databases only — the seeder's backfill deliberately touches nothing whose
   `ArchetypeSlug` is already non-null.
2. **A conditional repair in `ArchetypeSeeder` for databases already seeded.** Guarded on the exact
   drifted triple (`Slug='graduation-party' AND ArchetypeSlug='ceremonial' AND ProductClass='Public'`)
   rather than a blind `UPDATE`, for the same reason the backfill only touches nulls: a deliberate
   re-map must survive a restart. `CategoryService` never assigns `ArchetypeSlug`, so there is no admin
   write surface to race today — the guard is the cheap insurance against one being added, not a live
   concurrency control. Idempotent by construction: after the first run the predicate matches nothing,
   which is what lets `ArchetypeFoundationTests` keep running the seeder twice.
3. **Not a migration**, though a data repair is normally a migration's job. This seeder already exists
   to reconcile populated databases on every boot (the D-266 M5 flag backfill directly above it does the
   same thing), and it is the only writer of both columns. Hand-authoring a migration for a
   no-schema-change repair would mean copying a full model snapshot into a `Designer.cs` while a
   concurrent session has that snapshot modified — cost and risk for no behavioural difference.
4. **A structural test replaces a named one.** `Private_types_are_classified_private_and_public_types_public`
   pins four types by name and passed throughout, because "Graduation Party" was not one of the four.
   `Private_branch_and_private_product_agree_in_both_directions` asserts over the whole tree instead: no
   Type under Private Events classifies non-Private, and no Type outside it classifies Private. The
   navigation branch and the product class are two independent recordings of one decision, so
   disagreement is always a defect — and the failure mode is by definition a type nobody thought to name.

### No event is reclassified

`EventService` **snapshots** `ArchetypeSlug` and `Product` onto the row at create (`:410`, "Snapshot,
not resolved-on-read, so a later taxonomy edit can never change how a live event behaves"). Any
Graduation Party event created before this entry keeps `Public` and keeps behaving exactly as it did;
only events created after it get `Private`. That is the correct outcome — silently re-scoping a live
event's discoverability and moderation is precisely what the snapshot exists to prevent. The dev
database has zero events, so nothing is affected there either way.

### Not changed

The name-keyed map itself. Keying on name is what makes one archetype serve the same type under two
audiences, and re-keying on slug would break that for the seven cross-audience types. The lesson is not
"stop keying on name" — it is that the taxonomy branch is a second, independent recording of the product
decision, and nothing was checking the two against each other. Now something is.

**Verified.** Release build `-warnaserror` clean. `ArchetypeFoundationTests` green in the SDK container
(part of a 51-test run across the archetype, taxonomy, trust and fraud classes — 0 failures).

The `ExecuteUpdateAsync` against a nullable enum with a string converter — the one thing a build could not
prove — was confirmed **twice, independently of the suite**: the dev backend rebuilt on 2026-08-11 and ran
the repair against the live database, taking it from 93/18 to **92 Public / 19 Private**, and
`GET /v1/categories` now serves `graduation-party` as `Private`. The repair executed, translated, and was
idempotent on the reboots after it.
