## D-331 · A card whose identifiers its holder typed is a template for forgery, so the organization issues it (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Phase 1 (data model, rendering, verification) in progress; editor and admin console
follow.** ID cards are issued *by* a verified `Organization` to a verified member. The holder never sets
the identifiers the card asserts.

**What the request assumed, and what the domain actually had.** The brief asked for a college ID card
carrying a student ID, department, course and year, and required that "ordinary users must not modify
protected identifiers such as the officially assigned student ID". Nothing in this domain could assign
one. There is no college registry; `College` is not an entity. The nearest thing is
`User.EducationJson` — free text the user types, parsed best-effort into
`CollegeAffiliation(Institute, Degree, Branch)` by `PublicProfileService.ParseCollege`. There is no
student-ID column anywhere.

So the naive build — read `EducationJson`, let the user fill in the rest — produces a document that
asserts an affiliation on the strength of the holder having typed it. The "protected identifier"
requirement would be satisfied by refusing to let the user edit a value the same user had just invented.
That is not a protection; it is a spelling of one. An ID card exists to let a third party trust a claim
its holder is making about themselves, and a card anyone can mint for any college is a forgery template
with a QR code on it.

**The decision.** An `IdCard` is issued by an `Organization` whose `VerificationStatus` is `Verified`
(the M5 review already used by the paid-organizer gate), to a `User` holding a `Membership` on that org
with `IsVerified = true`. The issuing org sets `StudentId`, `Department`, `Course`, `Year`, `ValidFrom`
and `ValidUntil`. The holder may edit presentation (template, layout, photo crop) and their own
contact/emergency fields, never the asserted identifiers. The two authorities the platform already
trusts — org verification and verified membership — are exactly the two the card leans on, so the card
can claim no more than the platform already knows.

**Rejected: self-declared, marked unverified.** Cheapest, and it is what the event-badge half of the
generator effectively is. As a *college* ID it fails the one job: `ParseCollege` would happily render
"Indian Institute of Technology Bombay" for anyone who typed it. Marking the verification page
"self-declared" does not help, because the failure mode is a printed lanyard being glanced at, not a
page being read.

**Rejected: platform-admin-assigned.** Trustworthy, but a Kurx admin does not know any college's roster,
so it relocates the trust problem rather than solving it, and requires manual data entry per card.

**What verification exposes, and why less than was asked for.** The public page follows D-036's
certificate pattern: anonymous lookup by `VerifyCode`, gated on `IsPublic`, and a revoked card still
returns `200` because confirming a revocation is the endpoint's purpose (contrast D-018's hide-to-404).
It returns holder name, issuing organization, status and validity window — and deliberately **not** the
student ID or department the brief listed:

| field | on the card | on the public page | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| name, college, validity, status | yes | yes | the question a verifier is actually asking is "is this card genuine and current" |
| student ID | yes | **no** | a lanyard photographed across a room would otherwise yield an enumerable institutional identifier, and the page is unauthenticated |
| department, course, year | yes | **no** | adds nothing to authenticity; DPDP data minimisation applies to a page with no access control |
| phone, email, DOB, blood group, address, emergency contact | some | **never** | these exist for the holder and for medical staff reading the physical card, not for anyone who scans it |

**Consequence, stated plainly.** A user with no verified membership of a verified organization cannot
obtain a *college* ID card. That is the decision working, not a gap: the platform has no basis to assert
their affiliation. Event badges are unaffected — they are issued by the event's organizer against a
ticket, which is an authority the platform does hold, and they carry no institutional claim.

**New personal data, and its gating.** The card requires fields the domain does not have: blood group,
address and emergency contact. Blood group is health data and emergency contact is a *third party's*
personal data, both under the DPDP Act this schema is already shaped by (see `Onboarding.MinimumAgeYears`).
They are therefore optional, holder-supplied, never required to issue a card, never exposed by the
verification page, and never populated by inference from any other field. The migration adding them is a
sensitive-schema change and carries the mandatory security review.

---

## D-332 · "Can never be verified" was a comment, not a constraint (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED as a recorded defect. NOT fixed.** `OrgVerificationService` does not check
`Organization.IsPersonal`, so a personal organization can be verified through the ordinary
submit → admin-review flow. D-055's rule that a self-represented event cannot sell paid tickets rests
on that being impossible.

**Where the invariant is stated.** `EventService.GetOrCreatePersonalOrgAsync` documents the personal-org
row and says of it: *"never enters the registry or search (M4 filters on `VerificationStatus == Verified`),
never appears in the caller's representations, and **can never be verified — so a self-represented event
can never sell paid tickets**, which is the pre-existing product rule (D-055)"*. The paid path leans on
it directly: `PaidOrganizerGateAsync` returns `org_not_verified` unless
`GetOrgCapabilitiesAsync(...).IsOrgVerified`, which is nothing more than
`VerificationStatus == Verified`. Nothing anywhere asks whether the org is personal.

**Reproduction, performed on 2026-08-13 against local dev.** As the owner of a personal org:
`POST /v1/orgs/{orgId}/verification/submit` with one document → `pendingreview`; then, as a SuperAdmin,
`POST /v1/admin/orgs/{orgId}/verification/review {"decision":"approve"}` → `verified`. Neither call
consults `IsPersonal`. The local database now contains
`Personal events | IsPersonal = true | VerificationStatus = Verified`, which the codebase asserts cannot
exist. It was produced by the documented flow, not by a direct write.

**Why it matters.** The consequence is precisely the case D-055 exists to prevent, and it is the one
involving money: once the personal org is verified, `PaidOrganizerGateAsync` passes and a
self-represented event sells paid tickets. The personal org is an implementation detail of a non-null
FK — it "carries no name a user chose" — so payouts would settle against a row that represents nobody.
The failure is silent: every gate reports satisfied, because each is individually doing what it was
written to do.

**The shape of the fix, not yet applied.** Refuse at both ends of the flow — `SubmitAsync` and the admin
review — rather than only at approval, so a personal org cannot even occupy the queue. Both refusals want
their own error code and copy, since "this organization cannot be verified" is a different sentence from
"this organization is not verified yet". Two questions have to be answered first, which is why this is
recorded rather than done:

| question | why it is not obvious |
|---|---|
| what happens to an already-verified personal org | silently downgrading one revokes a capability a user may have been relying on; leaving it keeps a row the invariant says is impossible |
| whether the check belongs in verification or in the paid gate | verification is where the invariant is stated, but the paid gate is where the damage happens, and defending only the stated end leaves any future reader of `IsOrgVerified` exposed |

**Related, and deliberately separate.** There is no operation to move an existing event between
organizations: `CreateAsync` takes `representingOrgId` only at creation and `CloneAsync` copies
`src.RepresentingOrgId`. An organiser who picks the wrong representation must recreate the event. That is
a product gap rather than a defect, and wants its own entry.

## D-333 · Create Event gets a second door on Workspace; the gate behind it does not move (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Reverses the navigation half of [D-305](#d-305--event-creation-is-a-gated-flow-entered-from-profile-not-a-form-entered-from-workspace-2026-08-08)
only. D-305's surface rule and its eligibility gate both stand.**

### What changes

`/workspace` regains a **Create event** action in its header, alongside the one D-305 placed on Profile.
Profile keeps its entry point; this is a second door, not a relocation.

### What does not change, and why that is the whole point

D-305 made two separate moves and they are worth separating again here:

1. **Where the door is** — Workspace + primary nav → Profile. *This is the half being reversed.*
2. **What is behind the door** — an 11-step form → a verification / eligibility gate that settles
   Public vs Private *before* any event detail is typed. **This half is untouched.** The new link
   targets `/host/events/new`, the same gate, so verification is still enforced at entry and the
   visibility decision is still made there rather than as a field in step 2.

D-305's rule that **Workspace is an activity hub and must never become an organizer dashboard** remains
binding. A link to a gated flow is not an organizer surface: Workspace still lists participated events
and approved created ones, still exists for users who have never created anything, and gains no
management tooling from this change. The line D-305 drew was against Workspace accumulating *organizer
capability*; a creation entry point on its own does not do that. If Workspace later grows event
management UI, that is the drift D-305 warned about and this entry does not license it.

### Why reverse it at all

Discoverability. Workspace is where a user goes to see the events they run — the "Hosting" and "Drafts"
counters are on that page — and it was the one place a would-be organizer looked and found nothing to
click. Profile is a reasonable home for the action but a poor place to *discover* it, because a user
thinking about running an event is not thinking about their profile.

### Cost accepted

Two entry points to one flow is duplication, and duplication drifts: a future change to how creation is
entered must now be made in two places, and a divergence between them would be invisible. The mitigation
is that both link to the same route rather than reimplementing anything — the gate is the single source
of truth for what creation *is*, and neither call site encodes any of it.

## D-334 · A claim on a lunch is not a discount code, so it is not a Coupon (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Phase 1 (domain + migration + capability) implemented; services, API, redemption and
UI are later phases.**

### The naming, first, because it is the constraint everything else bends around

`Coupon` and `CouponRedemption` already exist (D-265) and mean **a discount code**: a percentage or flat
amount off an order total. The feature being added here — a participant holding a claim on a lunch, a
t-shirt, entry to the after-party — shares none of that mechanically. It has a quantity, it is redeemed
at a counter by staff, it can be partially spent, and it has no relationship to order arithmetic.

Two things called Coupon in one codebase is a defect waiting to be written, so the domain says
**Entitlement**: `EntitlementProduct` (what the organiser defines), `EntitlementGrant` (one holder's
claim), `EntitlementRedemption` (one spend). The organiser-facing UI still reads **"Food & Coupons"**,
because *coupon* is the word organisers use and the collision is a code-level problem, not theirs.

### What is reused rather than rebuilt

The brief asked for inventory, purchase, refunds, QR security and audit. All five already exist:

| Concern | Existing mechanism |
|---|---|
| Purchase | the `Pass` → order path; `PricePaise` here is the list price an order line copies |
| Refunds | `ValueAllocationRecord`, already the sole basis so reporting and refunds cannot diverge |
| Inventory | `InventoryPool` — see the caveat below |
| QR | the 10-char base32 `VerifyCode` convention shared by `Certificate` and `IdCard` |
| Audit | `AuditLog` |
| Optionality | the `Capability` registry |

No parallel commerce path is introduced. Nothing here prices, charges or refunds anything itself.

### Concurrency: the counter moves in SQL, or the guarantee is a wish

`EntitlementGrant.RedeemedQuantity` is a shared counter and is mutated **only** by a conditional update:

```sql
UPDATE entitlement_grants SET "RedeemedQuantity" = "RedeemedQuantity" + @n
WHERE "Id" = @id AND "RedeemedQuantity" + @n <= "Quantity"
```

Rows-affected **is** the outcome: 1 redeemed, 0 refused. This is D-240/D-261 applied to a new counter,
and the reason is the same one `Coupon.RedeemedCount` has it — two staff at two doors reading, deciding
and writing in application code would both read 0, both write 1, and one lunch would be served twice.
That is a food-cost bug, not a display bug.

`EntitlementRedemption.IdempotencyKey` is uniquely indexed, which covers the other half: the conditional
update stops two people spending one unit, and the unique key stops one person spending it twice by
pressing the button again on a flaky connection.

### One grant, whichever way it is delivered

`EntitlementDelivery.Both` is a **rendering** choice. A product set to Both still issues exactly one
`EntitlementGrant`; the printed coupon and the in-app card display the same row, so spending the paper
leaves nothing on the phone. Two rows would be two claims, which is precisely the failure the brief
called out.

### Optionality is data, not a code branch

New capability slug `entitlements` ("Food & Coupons", commerce group), **Optional in all 14 archetypes
and Required in none**, mode-gated to Offline/Hybrid.

Optional in all 14 rather than a chosen few because catering is orthogonal to what an event *is* — a
hackathon, a graduation and a fundraiser can each feed people, and `Unsupported` would be the matrix
asserting "this archetype may never serve a meal", which is not true of any of them. The real constraint
is the mode gate: a coupon redeemed at a counter is meaningless for an online event.

Because the archetype matrix stores every cell including the negatives, a capability absent from it is
`Unsupported` — *unusable*, not merely off. Adding the slug without the 14 Optional entries would have
shipped a feature no organiser could ever enable. The Phase 1 test asserts both halves: Optional
everywhere (an organiser **can**), Required nowhere (it is never turned on **for** them).

### Accepted limitation — inventory authority is not ours to claim yet

`InventoryPool` is currently a **Phase-7 shadow**: the scalar remains the oversell authority and the
§17.1 conditional-decrement contract that would make pools authoritative is Phase 9 and unbuilt. Phase 1
therefore does **not** route entitlement stock through pools; the grant's own quantity is the only
counter with teeth today. Full pool-backed inventory for entitlements depends on that cut-over and must
not be claimed before it lands — a reservation that looks authoritative and is not would oversell
lunches while reporting that it could not.

---

## D-335 · The issuer of an event ID card is the person who runs the event, not an organization (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Implemented.** Supersedes D-331's issuance model. An ID card is proof of
participation in an **event**; the authority that can vouch for that is the event's verified
creator/organizer. Organization verification is no longer required to issue one.

**What changed and why.** D-331 modelled the card as a *college ID*, so it leaned on the only
institution-shaped authority the platform had: a verified `Organization` plus verified membership.
That answered "which institution vouches for this person" — but it is the wrong question for a
document whose subject is an event. It also produced a rule nobody could satisfy without an
institution, and a permission bar that turned out to be far too wide: `CanManageAsync` asked only
whether the caller held *any* verified membership of the card's org, and
`MembershipVerificationService` mints a verified `Staff` seat for every approved member — so any
student could issue, revoke or regenerate a colleague's card. Rebinding to the event closes that as
a side effect, because event authority is per-event and creator-first.

**The rule.** Four conditions, each resolved through an authority that already exists rather than a
new one:

| condition | mechanism |
|---|---|
| the issuer controls the event | `IEventAuthority.ResolveAsync(...).Can(ManageLifecycle)` — creator-first (D-269) |
| the issuer is verified | `TrustCapabilities.CanCreatePublicEvent` |
| the issuer is not the holder | `input.UserId != actorId` |
| the holder belongs to the event | `IEventAuthority.ResolveAsync(holder, ...).Can(Participate)` |

**Why the capability and not the fact.** "Verified" is read from `CanCreatePublicEvent`, not from
`TrustCapabilities.IdentityVerified`. D-323's bypass relaxes capability gates while leaving the
reported facts truthful, so gating on the fact would make the feature untestable anywhere the
proofs are mock-backed while asserting nothing extra in Production, where the capability already
means identity + PAN + bank verified and fraud-clear.

**No migration.** `IdCard.OrgId` stays and stays non-null — every event carries a
`RepresentingOrgId`, so it is populated from the event and kept for display and for the card-number
sequence. It is now **descriptive, not authoritative**: nothing checks its verification status.
Existing cards therefore remain readable and verifiable unchanged, and the change is reversible
without touching data. `EventId` becomes required on the issue input; the column stays nullable so
rows written under D-331 are still valid.

**Error codes.** `org_not_verified`, `holder_not_a_member` and `holder_not_verified` no longer apply
to issuance and are replaced by `not_event_organizer`, `issuer_not_verified`, `cannot_issue_to_self`
and `holder_not_a_participant` — all 403, because in each case the request is well-formed and what
is missing is authority, verification, or the holder's standing in the event.

**Unchanged.** The anonymous verification projection (D-036/D-331) still withholds the student ID,
department and contact data. The holder still cannot edit an asserted identifier. Revoked cards
still resolve.
---

## D-336 · Three producers race one registration row, and the unique index is the only thing holding (2026-08-12)

**Status: ACCEPTED — reported and fixed in the same pass.** One statement added to
`EventRegistrationService.MirrorOrderCoreAsync`, one key helper beside the existing one, one test. No schema
change, no migration, no contract change, no client change.

**Observed.** Full suite against `61797f4`: **1743 total / 1736 passed / 6 failed / 1 skipped**, 14.2 min.
Five failures are the documented environment artifacts (4 `ClamAvUploadPathTests` needing a clamd that was
deliberately left down, 1 `NoContentDeclarationTests` `ArtifactsPath` artifact). The sixth is new to that
list:

```
Failed Kurx.Tests.WalletConcurrencyTests.Concurrent_captures_in_one_org_credit_the_wallet_once_each
  Npgsql.PostgresException : 23505: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "IX_registrations_OrderId"
```

Re-run in isolation: **3/3 passed**. It is load-dependent, which is why the baseline never recorded it.

**Not caused by the commit it surfaced on.** `IX_registrations_OrderId` dates to `f911c05` (V3 Phases
1–15); none of that commit's three migrations touch `registrations`; `WalletConcurrencyTests.cs` was
unchanged; and the sole `OrderService` edit was a read-path `ThenByDescending(o => o.Id)` pagination
tie-breaker, which cannot affect an insert.

**The mechanism.** `EventRegistrationService.MirrorOrderCoreAsync` resolves the row by order and inserts
when absent — a **check-then-act**, the shape this repo has already banned three times (D-240 wallet,
D-242 count-based limits, D-261 OTP attempts):

```csharp
var reg = await db.Registrations.FirstOrDefaultAsync(r => r.OrderId == orderId, ct);
if (reg is null) { reg = new Registration { … }; db.Registrations.Add(reg); }
```

**Three independent producers can run that for one order at the same time:**

| Producer | Entry point |
|---|---|
| Money path, in-transaction | `OrderService:189` (order create), `:266`, `:379` (capture), `:729`; `RefundService:147` |
| Boot-triggered convergence | `DataBackfillJob` → `registrations.BackfillAsync` — and `Program.cs:675` calls `jobs.Trigger("data-backfill")` on **every** boot |
| Self-healing reconciliation | `RegistrationReconciliationJob` → `registration.RepairAsync` |

The advisory lock in the core is keyed `(tree root, person)` and guards the **credential**, not the
registration row, so it does not serialise two producers on one `OrderId`. `BackfillAsync`'s own comment
says it "anti-joins the whole orders table and then projects order-by-order in its own transaction each" —
which is exactly a long-running writer over the same rows a live capture is projecting.

**Why it only shows under load:** the boot-triggered backfill must still be running when a capture lands.
A 23-second isolated class run does not overlap it; a 14-minute suite does.

**The money is not at risk, and that is the trap.** `IX_registrations_OrderId` holds — no second
Registration, no double admission, no double wallet credit. The durable record stays correct while the
*guard* does not, which is the same signature as D-240 and D-241: what fails is the **error shape**. The
losing producer throws an unhandled `DbUpdateException` and the caller gets a 500, where the §17.1
duplicate-callback contract promises an idempotent no-op returning the original. On the real capture path
that means a gateway webhook retry can be answered with a 500 — and a gateway that sees a 500 retries,
which is the loop this contract exists to prevent.

**The fix: the lock this method already uses, on the row it left out.** Twenty-five lines below the racing
read, the same method takes a **transaction-scoped advisory lock** per `(tree root, person)` before
resolving credentials, and its comment states the reason exactly — "two concurrent orders for the same
person both commit — the later reuses the credential the earlier committed instead of colliding on the
unique index and rolling back its money." That is this defect, already solved, one row over. So:

```csharp
var (orderLock1, orderLock2) = OrderLockKey(orderId);
await db.Database.ExecuteSqlInterpolatedAsync($"SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock({orderLock1}, {orderLock2})", ct);
```

acquired immediately before the resolve-or-insert. `pg_advisory_xact_lock` releases at commit, so the loser
waits, then **reads the winner's committed row** and updates it rather than inserting a second.

Three properties that make it safe:

- **It sits inside `MirrorOrderCoreAsync`, so all three producers inherit it.** Patching only the capture
  path would have left the backfill and the reconciliation job still racing each other.
- **It cannot deadlock with the credential locks.** The order lock is always taken first and never after,
  and the per-person locks are already acquired in sorted order, so the global order is order-then-persons
  for every caller.
- **Every producer is in a transaction**, which the lock requires to be meaningful: the money path owns one,
  and `MirrorOrderAsync` opens one for the backfill and repair paths.

`ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING` was the alternative and was **not** chosen: the entity is added to EF's change
tracker and flushed by the *caller's* `SaveChangesAsync`, so intercepting the conflict would mean either
reaching around the tracker for this one row or catching an exception raised at a call site that does not
know what it was projecting. The advisory lock keeps the whole concern inside the method that owns it, and
matches the surrounding code rather than introducing a second idiom for one race.

**The test is a real reproduction, verified in both directions.**
`EventRegistrationTests.Concurrent_projections_of_one_order_insert_exactly_one_registration` deletes the
registration (the exact state `BackfillAsync` selects on) and fires six concurrent `MirrorOrderAsync` calls.
**Reverted the fix and it failed with the 23505; restored the fix and it passes**, alongside the
`WalletConcurrencyTests` class the defect originally surfaced in — 27/27. A concurrency test that has never
been seen red proves nothing, so it was run red on purpose.

---

## D-337 · n8n is deleted; Hangfire owns every background job (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED — verified against a live stack before deletion.** No code change, no schema change, no
API contract change, no client change. Two compose files, one init script, three docs.

**The question.** Are we using n8n, or is background work Hangfire's? And if Hangfire, why is n8n still here?

**What n8n actually was.** A repo-wide grep at deletion found `n8n`/`N8N` in exactly **seven** files, and
**not one of them is application code**: `docker-compose.yml`, `infra/docker-compose.yml`,
`infra/postgres-init/01-n8n-db.sql`, three docs, and a `CHANGELOG.md` history line. Nothing in `backend/`,
`web/`, `admin/` or `mobile/` referenced it. No workflow was ever authored. `docs/EXTERNAL_SERVICES_AND_PROVIDERS.md`
had carried it as "Not Started … no defined purpose in the application per the code … worth either securing
it properly or removing it" since the 2026-07-12 audit — this closes that open question in the direction the
audit already pointed.

It was not free, either. The service published **`:5678` to the host**, held the Postgres credentials, could
execute arbitrary workflows, and shipped a dev-default `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and basic-auth password. And
`infra/postgres-init/01-n8n-db.sql` ran `CREATE DATABASE n8n` on **every fresh Postgres volume** — confirmed
live in this pass: a stack brought up from an empty volume had an `n8n` database sitting beside `kurx` with
nothing that would ever write to it.

**What Hangfire actually is here — measured, not assumed.** A stack was built and booted for this decision:

```
Starting Hangfire Server using job storage:
  'PostgreSQL Server: Host: postgres, DB: kurx, Schema: hangfire'
  Worker count: 4 · queues: 'default' · poll interval 00:00:15
```

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM hangfire.set WHERE key='recurring-jobs';   --  18
SELECT version FROM hangfire.schema;                            --  23
```

**18 recurring jobs**, live: `account-deletion`, `chat-attachment-cleanup`, `data-backfill`,
`database-health-probe`, `event-reminder`, `expire-seat-holds`, `expire-waitlist-offers`,
`inventory-reconciliation`, `leaderboard-refresh`, `ledger-collected-to-available`,
`lock-expired-chat-rooms`, `notification-cleanup`, `outbox-dispatch`, `post-media-cleanup`,
`registration-reconciliation`, `search-index-refresh`, `signing-key-maintenance`, `wallet-reconciliation`.
Plus two enqueue-driven jobs (`ChatNotificationJob`, `PhoneE164BackfillJob`) that carry no schedule.

**Why they are not substitutes, which is the actual reason this is a deletion and not a migration.** Every
one of those jobs reads and writes the application database through EF Core *inside the app's own DI scope,
transaction and advisory locks* — `WalletReconciliationJob` compares the wallet against the ledger,
`DataBackfillJob` takes the same `pg_advisory_xact_lock` D-336 just added, `OutboxDispatchJob` drains a
table written in the same transaction as the domain change. An external workflow runner cannot reach any of
that without an HTTP endpoint per job: strictly more attack surface, strictly less type safety, and a
network hop inside what is currently one transaction. Hangfire also already guarantees **one runner across
every replica** — the exact property `DatabaseHealthProbeJob`'s comment cites for choosing a recurring job
over a hosted service. n8n's real niche is glue *between* SaaS products; Kurx has no such case today, and
"we might want one later" is not a reason to run a credentialed container with a published port now.

**Not claimed:** this says nothing about n8n as a tool. If ops automation is wanted later (Slack alerts on
job failure, runbooks over third-party APIs), re-adding it is a new `D-NNN` — with auth, a real encryption
key and an unpublished port, none of which the deleted service had by default.

**Certificates are the one thing that is *not* Hangfire's, and that is worth recording.**
`CertificateService.GenerateForEventAsync` renders every certificate **synchronously inside the HTTP
request** — a QuestPDF render plus an `IStorage.PutAsync` per eligible ticket, in a loop. Correct today and
deliberately batched at the database layer (DB-3 removed two N+1s from it), but at a 5,000-attendee event
that is 5,000 renders on one request thread. Moving it behind Hangfire is a real candidate and is **not**
done here — it changes an API's response contract from "generated: N" to "accepted", which is its own
decision. Named so it stops being invisible.

**What was removed.** The `n8n` service, the `kurx_n8ndata` volume and the `:5678` mapping from both
`docker-compose.yml` and `infra/docker-compose.yml`; `infra/postgres-init/01-n8n-db.sql` and the now-empty
`postgres-init` directory, together with the `:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` mount that pointed at it; the
`N8N_*` entries in `docs/security/secret-management.md`; §17 and the summary row in
`docs/EXTERNAL_SERVICES_AND_PROVIDERS.md`; and n8n from the running-stack line in
`V3_IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP.md`. `CHANGELOG.md`'s historical mention is left alone — it records what was true
when written.

**Existing dev volumes keep their empty `n8n` database.** Deleting the init script stops it being created
on fresh volumes; it does not retroactively drop it. `DROP DATABASE n8n;` is safe on any dev machine (the
container that would have used it is gone), or `docker compose down -v` clears it with everything else.
Not done automatically: dropping a database is not something a doc-and-compose change should do silently.

**Verified.** `docker compose config` parses clean on both files with no `n8n` key and no `kurx_n8ndata`
volume; the stack (postgres · redis · backend) comes up healthy without the init mount; Hangfire re-announces
its server and all 18 recurring jobs on boot; repo-wide grep for `n8n`/`N8N` returns only `CHANGELOG.md`
history and the unrelated `.claude/worktrees/template-engine` checkout, which is a different branch.

---

## D-338 · The malware scanner covered two upload paths out of eight, and `none` was legal in Production (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED — both defects found by inspection, fixed and covered in the same pass.** One new class,
one DI registration, one startup guard, six call sites, fifteen tests. No schema change, no migration, no
API contract change beyond two new refusal codes on paths that previously could not refuse.

### Defect 1 — `IFileScanner` was wired into 2 of 8 upload paths

D-298 shipped a real ClamAV adapter and D-110 built the presign → PUT → confirm pipeline around it. But
`grep -rln "IFileScanner scanner"` returned **two** files: `ChatService` and `PostService`. Every other
path that presigns a key wrote bytes to storage and persisted the key with **no scan at any point**:

| Path | Presign | Where the key is claimed | Was scanned |
|---|---|---|---|
| Event media | `MediaService.PresignUploadAsync` | `MediaService.AttachAsync` | no |
| Org verification evidence | `MediaService.PresignOrgDocAsync` | `OrgVerificationService.SubmitAsync` | no |
| Membership claim evidence | `MediaService.PresignClaimDocAsync` | `MembershipVerificationService.SubmitAsync` | no |
| Representation request evidence | `MediaService.PresignRepresentationDocAsync` | `OrgService.SubmitRepresentationRequestAsync` | no |
| Institutional authorization evidence | `EventAuthorizationService.PresignDocumentAsync` | `EventAuthorizationService.SubmitAsync` | no |
| Profile avatar / cover | `MediaService.PresignProfileImageAsync` | `PATCH /v1/me/profile` | no |

**The risk is shaped badly.** Four of the six are *verification documents* — government ID, PAN, letters on
institutional letterhead, membership proof. Those are precisely the files a `VerificationReviewer`
downloads and opens inside the admin console. A chat attachment is opened by a peer who chose to open it;
an org-proof PDF is opened by an employee doing their job, on a machine with console access. The one path
with a human obligated to open the file was the one with no scanner.

**No documentation was wrong**, which is why this survived. The "always invoked" line in
`EVENT_CHAT_ARCHITECTURE.md` is scoped to the chat pipeline and is accurate there. Nothing anywhere stated
the coverage *boundary*, so "Kurx has real malware scanning" read as "uploads are scanned".

### Why the gate is not in `PUT /v1/storage/{*key}`

That endpoint looks like the single choke point every upload passes through, and **today it is** — but only
because `LocalDiskStorage.PresignPutAsync` signs a URL back to our own API. An S3 presigned PUT uploads
*directly to S3* and never enters this process. A gate there would cover all eight paths right up until the
S3 adapter ships, then silently cover none — with no test failing, because the tests would still pass on
local disk. **A fix that quietly un-fixes itself on an unrelated change is worse than no fix**, because it
also removes the reason anyone would look again.

The scan therefore sits where the server first **claims** a key — the same place chat and posts already put
it, and the only place that stays true for any `IStorage` implementation.

### The shape: one gate, six call sites

`Kurx.Infrastructure/Providers/UploadScanGate.cs` — scan → audit → delete the object → return an error code,
or `null` when the key may be persisted. Scoped, not singleton: it stages the audit row on the caller's unit
of work, so a rejection commits with the request that caused it (D-102).

Only `Clean` passes. `Infected` → `file_infected`; `ScanFailed` and `Unsupported` → `scan_unavailable`, the
same vocabulary chat already returns. A missing object reaches the same place without a special branch:
`ClamAvFileScanner` reads bytes through `IStorage`, so an absent key throws inside the scanner and returns
`ScanFailed`. A null or blank key passes — "nothing was claimed" is not a scan failure, and gating it would
mean a scanner outage broke every profile edit that only changed a headline.

**Chat and posts were deliberately left alone.** Both already scan, both are covered, and both return
domain-specific codes that are part of a tested client contract. Rewriting two working call sites to share
this helper would risk those contracts to buy symmetry. Two idioms plus one shared gate is the honest state,
and it is recorded here rather than hidden.

Three ordering choices worth keeping:

- **Membership claims** scan *before* the duplicate-claim check, so an infected upload is refused even when
  the claim would have been rejected anyway — the bytes never linger waiting for a sweep that does not exist.
- **Representation requests** scan *before* the placeholder org is created, so a refused submission leaves
  no hidden `PendingReview` institution and no pending Representative membership behind it.
- **Institutional authorization** scans only the keys *this call is claiming*, never the values already on
  the row. `letterhead`/`signature`/`docs` fall back to what is stored when omitted, so re-scanning them
  would re-refuse a submission whose evidence was accepted before the scanner existed, on an edit that
  never touched a document.

### Defect 2 — `FILE_SCANNER=none` booted in Production

Every other dangerous default in `AddKurxInfrastructure` already refuses Production:
`SIGNING_KEY_PROTECTION=none` throws, `IDENTITY_VERIFICATION_BYPASS` throws, a missing `REDIS_CONNECTION`
throws. The scanner did not — it resolved `NoOpFileScanner`, which reports every file `Clean` **without
reading it**, and logged one warning.

A deployment that simply omitted the variable therefore served every upload unscanned and reported healthy.
`.env.example` ships `FILE_SCANNER=none`, so omitting it is the default path rather than an unusual mistake.
Now it throws at startup, with a message naming what it protects.

### Verification

`dotnet build -warnaserror`: 0 warnings, 0 errors. 15 new tests, all passing.

`UploadScanCoverageTests` points a real `ClamAvFileScanner` at a **dead port**, so every scan returns
`ScanFailed` and a correctly-gated path must refuse. That is deliberate and complementary to
`ClamAvUploadPathTests`, which proves the engine detects EICAR against a live daemon: this proves the gate is
*wired at each call site* and **runs anywhere** — no clamd, no signature database, no `--profile scanning`.
A coverage regression is now caught on every developer machine and in CI, not only where a daemon is up.
Each test also asserts the refusal is total: no `VerificationDocument` row, no `MembershipClaim`, no
placeholder `Organization`, no `EventMedia`, and the org never entering `PendingReview`.

`FileScannerProductionGuardTests` covers unset / `none` / `NONE` / `" none "` throwing in Production,
`clamav` being accepted there, `none` still permitted outside it, and an unrecognised value still refused
everywhere.

**Run red on purpose.** The scan was removed from `MediaService.AttachAsync` and
`Event_media_attach_is_refused_when_it_cannot_be_scanned` failed with `Expected: False / Actual: True`;
restored, it passes. A test that has never been seen red proves nothing.

**Four of the eight initial failures were bugs in the tests, not the fix**, and each named a real repo
convention worth carrying: `Staff` is not a `MembershipClaimRole` (`Employee` is); `OfficialPhone` is
E.164-validated server-side; `events.ShortCode` is unique and two slugs sharing a three-letter prefix
collided; and `PATCH /v1/me/profile` binds **camelCase in** — `avatar_key` bound nothing, so the gate saw a
null key and the request succeeded. That last one is the camelCase-in/snake_case-out rule biting exactly as
`docs/api/README.md` warns.

### Not claimed

This does not close the presign TOCTOU that all eight paths share: a presigned URL stays valid for its TTL,
so bytes can in principle be replaced after the scan and before the object is read. That predates this work,
applies equally to chat and posts, and closing it means invalidating a presign on claim — its own decision.
Named so it is not mistaken for covered.

## D-339 · `infra/docker-compose.yml` is deleted; the root compose is the only one (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED — one file deleted, six doc references corrected. No application code, no schema, no
API contract touched.**

`infra/docker-compose.yml` was the original local-infra stack: Postgres + Redis, with the API behind a
`full` profile, documented as "a lighter alternative … if you're running the backend/web natively but
still want containerized infra". The root `docker-compose.yml` grew past it and D-337's predecessor
removed profiles from the root file so one `docker compose up` starts everything. The two had since
drifted into direct conflict:

| | root `docker-compose.yml` | `infra/docker-compose.yml` |
|---|---|---|
| project name | explicit `name: kurx` | none → derived `infra` |
| postgres container | `kurx-postgres` | `kurx-postgres` — **same name** |
| postgres host port | 5433 (deliberately, to dodge a native 5432) | **5432** |
| redis host port | 6380 | 6379 |
| services | postgres, redis, clamav, backend, web, admin | postgres, redis, api |

The identical `container_name` and the overlapping ports meant the two stacks could never run at the
same time — starting the infra one while the root stack was up failed on the name collision, and its
5432 binding reintroduced exactly the native-Postgres shadowing the root file's 5433 mapping exists to
avoid. It also carried its own copy of the postgres volume name, which is how it survived the D-338-era
sweep and had to be fixed a second time in `aeb614e` immediately before this deletion. A second compose
file that cannot run alongside the first, duplicates its services, and needs every infra fix applied
twice is a maintenance trap, not an alternative.

**Chose:** delete it. The root compose covers the containerized case; running Postgres/Redis natively is
still supported and documented (see the native fallback the file's own header pointed at), and needs no
compose file at all.

**Kept:** `infra/Dockerfile.api` and `infra/terraform/`. The Dockerfile is load-bearing — the root
compose's `backend` service, `scripts/push-ecr.sh` and `.github/workflows/cd.yml` all build from it.
`infra/` is now deploy inputs, not a runnable stack.

**Docs corrected in the same commit** (they described a file that no longer exists): `README.md` ×3,
`docs/PROJECT_HANDBOOK.md` ×2, `docs/deployment/README.md` ×1, plus the port-rationale comments in
`docker-compose.yml` and `.claude/memory/deployment.md` that cited it as corroborating evidence for
D-318's single 5080 port. Historical entries above that mention the file are left as written — they
record what was true when decided.

## D-340 · Cloning an event kept 47 of its 110 columns and silently defaulted the rest (2026-08-14)

**Context.** `EventService.CloneAsync` built the copy from a hand-written property list — `new Event { … }`
naming 47 columns. `Event` has 110. Seven are runtime identity that must not travel. The remaining **56
were never mentioned**, so they landed on their C# defaults in the copy. This was not a decision to blank
them; it was a list nobody extended. Every column D-265 added (presentation, legal, location detail,
lifecycle windows, eligibility, commerce) and every column D-266 added (`RegistrationPolicy`, the four
taxonomy attributes) updated the entity and `ApplyUpdateAsync` and left `CloneAsync` alone.

**Measured, not inferred.** Against the running dev API: an event created through `POST /v1/events` with all
six D-265 input groups populated, then cloned through `POST /v1/orgs/{org}/events/{id}/clone`. Diffing the
two rows in Postgres: **36 columns differed, 6 legitimately** (`Id`, `Slug`, `ShortCode`, `Title`,
`CreatedAt`, `UpdatedAt`) — **30 were silent configuration loss.** The three that were dangerous rather
than untidy:

| Column | Source | Clone |
|---|---|---|
| `RequiresConsent` | `true` | **`false`** — the copy stops collecting consent; `registration_consents` gets no rows |
| `GenderRestriction` | `Female` | **`Any`** — with `MinAge`/`MaxAge` null, an 18+ event's copy admits minors |
| `TaxInclusive` | `false` | **`true`** — same rupee prices, opposite tax treatment |

The damage was worse than blankness because the clone kept each dropped field's partner: ticket types copied
verbatim while `RegistrationPolicy` reset to `Open`; every `PricePaise` copied while `TaxPercent` and
`PlatformFeePercent` vanished; `TicketType.SaleStarts/SaleEnds` copied while the event-level window that is
meant to bound them was dropped; `BannerKey` copied while `LogoKey`/`ThumbnailKey`/`PromoVideoKey` were not;
`EventMode` and `OnlineUrl` copied while `MeetingPlatform` and `MeetingPassword` were not.

**Decision.** Invert the default. The clone is now a `ShallowCopy()` of the source and the exceptions are
named explicitly — 27 of them, in four groups: fresh identity (9), runtime state (5), admin moderation
(4, D-186), review outcomes (6, D-266 M4/M7) and lineage (3, V3 §3.4 rule 5). Everything else travels.

A new column is therefore inherited unless someone deliberately excludes it. That is the right failure
mode: a column that should not have been inherited produces a visible wrong value someone reports, while a
column that should have been produces silent config loss nobody notices for months — which is exactly what
happened here.

`CreatedFromTemplateVersion` now travels with `TemplateId`, which was already copied. A clone that claimed a
template with no version snapshot defeated the purpose of the column (V3 §13.1).

**Not changed.** No schema change, no migration, no contract change — the DTO is identical and
`openapi.json` is unaffected; only the values are now correct. `TemplateService.CloneAsync` is a different
method and was not touched. Web, admin and Flutter need no change: they already render these fields.

**Verification.** `EventCloneTests` (3 tests, all green in the SDK container). The load-bearing one
enumerates `Event`'s properties by **reflection** rather than listing them, probes every inheritable column
with a non-default value straight through the DbContext (so columns with no API write path are covered),
clones over real HTTP, and compares property by property — collecting every mismatch so a regression names
all of them at once. Confirmed red-on-purpose: reintroducing three drops made it fail with
`RefundPolicy: source=probe-RefundPolicy clone=null`, `MinAge: source=7 clone=null`,
`TaxInclusive: source=False clone=True`. The reset list is asserted from the same reflection sweep, so
adding a reset in `CloneAsync` without recording it here fails the build.

## D-341 · Coupons are a complete surface with no consumer, and stay that way for now (2026-08-14)

**Context.** D-265 shipped per-event discount codes: `Coupon` and `CouponRedemption` entities, the
`coupons`/`coupon_redemptions` tables, `ICouponService` with create/list/update/delete plus `/quote`, five
routes under `/v1/events/{eventId}/coupons`, and `CouponTests`. `RedeemedCount` is documented on the entity
as a shared counter mutated in SQL only (D-240/D-261).

Nothing consumes any of it. `ICouponService` has exactly one non-test caller: its own endpoint file.
`OrderService` never reads a coupon code — `CreateOrderInput` has no field for one — never writes a
`CouponRedemption`, and never increments `RedeemedCount`. `grep -ri coupon` across `web/`, `admin/`,
`mobile/` and `packages/ui/` returns nothing: no client has a coupon input anywhere. A quote can be
produced; a discount can never be applied.

**Decision.** Leave it. Record it here so it stops reading as a defect in every future audit — it is an
unfinished D-265 surface, not a bug.

Wiring it is a feature, not a fix: a new field on order creation (contract change → `openapi.json` regen →
the CI contract gate), discount arithmetic inside the order total that propagates to the ledger, wallet,
refunds and the gateway amount, a conditional-UPDATE increment for `RedeemedCount` (D-240/D-261), a
`MaxPerUser` check that races, checkout UI on web and Flutter, and a mandatory security review under §7 of
the operating manual because it moves money.

**Finish condition.** Either that work lands under its own `D-NNN`, or the surface is deleted with a
migration dropping both tables. Shipping a CRUD surface with no consumer is what made this ambiguous;
whichever way it resolves, it resolves deliberately.

## D-342 · Nine phone lookups still read the legacy column, and that is deliberate for now (2026-08-14)

**Context.** D-089 is replacing `users."Phone"` (bare digits, carrying `AuthService.NormalizePhone`'s
"10 digits ⇒ India" assumption) with `users."PhoneE164"`. The migration is staged: `Phone` is non-nullable
and still written on every path, `PhoneE164` is backfilled by `PhoneE164BackfillJob`.

`AuthIdentifiers.cs:39` resolves a user by `PhoneE164 == e164 || Phone == digits`. Nine other sites match
the legacy column alone — `EventAssignmentService`, `ParticipantService`, `InvitationService`,
`OrgInvitationService` (three call sites), `OrgService`, `SuperAdminBootstrap`, and `AuthService`'s own
uniqueness check.

**Decision.** Leave them. There is no live symptom: `Phone` is non-null and dual-written, so every one of
those lookups resolves correctly today.

Widening them now costs more than it buys. It changes *who matches* on the authentication and invitation
paths — an invite acceptance could resolve to a different user than it does today — and an `OR` across two
independently indexed columns loses the index, which is the exact shape D-231 had to rewrite as a `UNION`
after it took a query from 37.7 ms to 75× worse. Paying that on an auth path to fix debt with no symptom is
the wrong trade.

**Finish condition.** When `PhoneE164` is fully backfilled and `Phone` becomes droppable, the nine sites and
`AuthIdentifiers` move together to a single lookup helper — one choke point, so the column can be dropped in
one edit rather than ten. Until then this entry is the record that they are known, not overlooked.

## D-343 · Verification splits into two tiers: identity gates Public, the financial chain gates Paid (2026-08-14)

**Status: ACCEPTED. Refines [D-307](#), does not reverse it.**

**The question.** Why does creating a **free** public event demand a penny-dropped bank account?

**What was there.** `TrustService` folded all three proofs into one predicate and handed it to both gates:

```csharp
var proofsSatisfied      = bypass || (identityVerified && panVerified && bankVerified);
var canOrganizePaid      = proofsSatisfied && fraudClear;
var canCreatePublicEvent = proofsSatisfied && fraudClear;   // byte-identical
```

D-307 wrote the second line deliberately and noted the two predicates were "identical today, and that is a
coincidence of current requirements, not an identity". The coincidence was the bug. A free public event had
to prove ownership of a bank account that would never receive a rupee — four submissions to establish a fact
the event cannot use, and a hard block for anyone who has a passport but no bank record on file.

**The split.** Each proof answers a different question, so each gates the thing that asks it:

| Tier | Proof | Answers | Gates |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | govt ID **or** PAN approved | *who is behind this event* | `CanCreatePublicEvent` |
| **Financial** | PAN + bank approved + penny drop passed + holder name not mismatched | *whose account receives the money* | `CanOrganizePaid`, `CanReceivePayout` |

Which yields four cases, three of them reachable:

| Product | Money | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| Private | Free | nothing |
| Public | Free | identity tier only |
| Public | Paid | identity + financial |
| Private | Paid | impossible — a Private event can never sell |

**D-307's reasoning is kept, not discarded.** "A free public event still carries the platform's name and
reaches every user through discovery, and the harm a bad actor can do with one is not bounded by whether
money moved" is exactly why the **identity** tier still gates Public. What D-307 over-applied was the
**financial** half: nothing settles on a free event, so there is no account to own and no ownership to prove.
Bounding *identity* by payment was the wrong axis; bounding *bank ownership* by payment is the only axis
there is.

**PAN is deliberately absent from the public bar.** PAN is a tax identity and Indian tax reporting is keyed
on it — which is why it stays mandatory for taking money. A free event reports no income, so requiring PAN
there asks for a tax document for a non-taxable act, and locks out every passport or Aadhaar holder who has
no PAN. `identityVerified` is already `GovtId Approved || PAN Approved`, so either satisfies it.

**The two fields stay separate.** D-307 kept `CanCreatePublicEvent` and `CanOrganizePaid` as distinct fields
"so a future change to either is forced to be deliberate". This is that change, and the separation is what
made it a five-line edit instead of an archaeology exercise. They are now genuinely different predicates.

**One consequence, considered rather than inherited.** `IdCardService` gates issuance on
`CanCreatePublicEvent` — "a card asserts something about its holder, so the person asserting it has to be
someone the platform has actually checked". That concern is the identity tier exactly; the bank account was
never related to it. The relaxation is correct there too, and the comment still reads true.

**D-323 is unchanged.** `IDENTITY_VERIFICATION_BYPASS` now relaxes both tiers rather than one lump.
`fraudClear` stays outside it and is still ANDed into all three capabilities, and the reported
`identity_verified` / `bank_verified` facts are still never forged.

**The gate UI stops lying while it is here.** The first gate screen ("Before you start") listed *Create a
free event* and *Sell tickets* as bordered cards with circled check icons — the same chrome the real
selectors use one screen later — but they were inert `<li>`/`_CheckRow` elements. The accessibility tree of
that whole card exposed exactly one control, the Continue button; only the visual design misled. People
clicked them expecting to choose free or paid. That screen is deleted. The gate is now two screens, both of
them real questions, and the pair selects the tier:

```
① Who is this event for?      Public | Private
② Are you charging?           Free | Paid   (Paid inert for Private)
   → the requirements for THAT pair, and only those
```

The answer is carried into the wizard as `initialPricing` rather than asked twice. It stays changeable on
the Pricing step, which is safe: that step's Paid card is gated on `canOrganizePaid`, so entering as Free and
switching to Paid cannot escape the financial tier.

**No taxonomy change.** Public/Private keeps filtering the Type catalogue through `ProductClass` exactly as
before (D-266 M1, D-326); Free/Paid selects a verification tier and nothing else. `EventProduct` is still
derived from the chosen Type and is still not a user-editable field.

**Verified.** Backend `TrustTests` 10/10 and the dependent `IdCardTests` / `IdentityVerificationTests` /
`IdentityVerificationBypassTests` 42/42, both against real Postgres. `TrustTests` now pins both directions:
identity-without-bank creates a public event but cannot take money or receive a payout and stays at `L1`, and
a government ID with no PAN at all clears the public bar. Web 528 passed / 1 skipped, Flutter 426 passed,
`flutter analyze` clean, web `tsc` clean.

**One test inverted, and that is the decision rather than a weakened assertion.**
`Identity_without_bank_still_cannot_create_a_public_event` asserted the exact behaviour this entry removes;
it is now `Identity_without_bank_can_create_a_public_event_but_cannot_take_money` and asserts more than it
did — the money capabilities and the trust level as well as the publishing one.

## D-344 · A leak that cannot fire yet, and nine seeders outside the migration lock (2026-08-15)

Two startup/auth defects found by an external read of `Program.cs`, both fixed. Recorded together because
the interesting part of each was **the severity, not the fix** — one was reported as urgent and is dormant,
the other was reported as a missing comment and is a boot crash.

### 1. The ES256 resolver abandoned an `ECDsa` per request — but nothing reaches it

`Program.cs`'s `IssuerSigningKeyResolver` called `ECDsa.Create()` inline and never disposed it.
`ECDsaSecurityKey` does not take ownership of the `ECDsa` it wraps, and nothing else disposed it either, so
every request taking that branch abandoned a native crypto handle to the finalizer queue and re-ran a
base64 decode plus an SPKI import that produce the same answer every time.

That it was a defect is not in doubt: **it was the only un-disposed `ECDsa.Create()` in the repository.**
`JwksEndpoints:42`, `DeviceSignatures:28`, `SigningKeyService:184` and `TokenService:87` all use `using` —
and `TokenService` wraps its instance in an `ECDsaSecurityKey` and *still* disposes it, which is the
clearest possible statement that the wrapper does not own it.

**The reported severity was wrong, and checking is what showed it.** The report said this runs "on every
authenticated request". It runs on every request carrying a `kid` — and **no request carries one**. All six
issuance sites (`AuthService:365`, `LoginApprovalService:394`/`:539`, `PasskeyService:258`,
`PasswordResetService:97`, `RecoveryCodeService:112`) call the synchronous HS256 `CreateAccessToken`;
`CreateAccessTokenAsync` has zero callers. Verified against the running API rather than by reading: the JWT
header of a live token from `/v1/auth/otp/verify` is `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`, no `kid`. This is
D-099's documented "built but OFF" state (`AUTHENTICATION_ARCHITECTURE.md` §4.8), not drift.

Fixed anyway, and that is the decision worth recording: a dormant defect on the hottest path in the
application, which goes live as part of a cut-over whose reviewers will be reading *issuance* code, is
cheaper to fix now than to rediscover under load later.

`ValidationKeyCache` parses each key once. **It is a parse cache and never an authority**: the
`published.FirstOrDefault(k => k.KeyId == kid)` lookup still runs first, so a retired or compromised key
never reaches the cache and cannot be resurrected by it. The cache key includes the SPKI, so re-publishing
different material under an existing `kid` re-parses. `GetOrAdd` wraps a `Lazy` with
`ExecutionAndPublication` — a bare factory can run on several threads and discard the losers, which would
abandon exactly the handle this class exists to stop abandoning.

**Coverage gap this exposed:** `A_compromised_key_is_dropped_immediately_with_no_grace_period` asserts at
the *service* layer and never makes a request, so it would pass even if the resolver served a stale cached
key. `An_es256_token_stops_being_accepted_once_its_signing_key_is_compromised` closes that over HTTP. It
mints its token through `CreateAccessTokenAsync` directly, because no login path will produce an ES256
token — so this is currently the only coverage the `kid` branch has, and it keeps working unchanged when
the cut-over lands.

### 2. Nine seeders ran outside any lock on every replica

The startup block applies migrations and then runs nine reference-data seeders. EF Core 9 takes its own
lock for `MigrateAsync`, but that lock ends with the migration; the seeders sit outside it and every
replica of a rolling deploy runs them simultaneously.

They are read-then-insert. `KindRegistrySeeder` SELECTs existing slugs into a `HashSet`, diffs the catalog,
inserts the difference. Two replicas booting together both observe the same slug missing, both insert, and
the unique index on `event_kinds."Slug"` turns the loser into a `23505` **inside the startup try block** —
so that replica refuses to start. Narrow (it needs a cold database, or a deploy that adds catalog rows) but
a bad failure mode: a boot crash in the middle of a deploy.

**Decision: serialize the block, do not make nine seeders individually conflict-tolerant.** The hazard is
"N replicas run this block concurrently", not any one seeder — so a `pg_advisory_xact_lock` around the
whole block also covers seeders added later, which `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in nine files would not. The
second replica then finds everything present and its already-populated checks correctly do nothing. Same
idiom as `SeatBlockService` and `OrderService`.

**Verified rather than assumed: advisory locks are per-database.** Probed against the real Postgres — a
lock held on the same key in database A was acquirable in database B (`t`) and refused in A (`f`). That is
what makes this safe for the suite: every test class runs on its own `kurx_test_<guid>`, so the ~176
`WebApplicationFactory` boots never contend, while production replicas all share `kurx` and serialize.

The transaction also makes seeding atomic. Previously a failure left rows from the seeders that had already
run; now it rolls back. The startup `catch` refuses to serve traffic either way, so the change is strictly
an improvement: the next replica seeds from a clean state rather than inheriting a half-seeded one.

**Accepted trade-off:** `pg_advisory_xact_lock` blocks rather than failing. A replica wedged mid-seed makes
its siblings wait at boot instead of crashing fast. That is the correct semantic — they cannot serve a
request without this data — but it is a deliberate choice, not an oversight.

### Not fixed, because they were not defects

Two further items from the same report were checked and rejected. **`UseCors()` after
`UseExceptionHandler()` is correct** — it is Microsoft's documented order, and a minimal app reproducing
Kurx's exact pipeline returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on a 500: `CorsMiddleware` registers a
`Response.OnStarting` callback on the way in, and `ExceptionHandlerMiddleware.ClearHttpContext()` clears
headers but not those callbacks, so they re-apply when the ProblemDetails response starts.
**`jobs.Trigger("data-backfill")` on boot is deliberate**, guarded by `DisableConcurrentExecution` as its
own docstring says.
